summary: The respondent was prosecuted for an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Act. He was prosecuted for the offence under section 16 read with section 2(1)(f) of the Act and was convicted by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Delhi. The respondent was convicted by a learned Magistrate for an offence of adulteration of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity of food articles was prescribed, for the respondent. The respondent filed a Criminal Revision Petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the revision petition and quashed the order of conviction and sentence. The respondent challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The respondent contended that the High Court had not properly appreciated the evidence and had not properly applied the correct principles of law. The High court had not properly considered the evidence and the evidence. The High 'Court had not properly interpreted the provisions of section 2(ia) (f) of Act. The High' Court had not given any reasons for coming to the conclusion that the article of food was unfit for human consumption. The High. Court had not considered the evidence in the proper perspective. The High, Court, however, took the view that the article was unfit for consumption on account of the presence of the meal worms found by the Public Analyst and the report of the Public Analyst was not a conclusive evidence. The respondent had not produced any evidence to prove that the article in question was unfit for use for human consumption on account thereof. The High Curt, therefore, set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the respondent under section 7 of the Act, and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The respondent has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the article is unfit for human use. [701B] 2. The High "Court had not given reasons for coming out of the conclusion that article of food is unfit for consumption "on account of the absence of the food worms in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect infested or insect, or insect or unocated animal or vegetable substances or being insects, or unoculated animal or vegetable product or vegetable substance. [702C] 3. The word 'filthy, putrid' has been used in the sense of 'filty, putrid', and it is not necessary in such a case to prove further that the article has been unfit for human habitation. [703D] 4. The word "filthy" in the context of section 2 (ia) (i) (f), has been used to mean that the article must be unfit for human being consumption on account whereof the presence of food worm is unfit for use. [603E] 5. The word used in the context 'filtthy' has been interpreted to mean that it is unfit for the human consumption on the basis of the presence or insect infestation or insect in the sense that it is not unfit for human beings. [704F] 6. The word ''filtty" has been used for the purpose of the Act in the sense in which it is used in the Act. [705G] 7. The word "'filtly" has been interpreted in the sense "filt" in the sense 'filatty" in the Act, to mean that "filty" has not been used in any filthy, disgrid, putrid or disgrid. [706F] 7. In the instant case, the article of the food was unfit to human consumption on which the article of medicine was unfit for the consumption on account that it was unfit for such consumption on account. [707F] 8. The word `filt'

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of the provisions of the Order. He was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class, Dumka, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. He was also convicted under section 7(2) of the Essential Supplies Act for violation Of the provisions of that Order. He preferred an appeal to the Sessions Judge, Dumka. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence. The appellant was convicted under section7(2) and sentenced to imprisonment for six month. He preferred a revision to the Sessions Court. The High court set aside the sentence and convicted him under section 7 (2) of that Act. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was an agriculturist and that he was an agriculturist. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that a person is an agriculturist. [701B] 2. The presumption under section 7 is not drawn against him. The presumption is not drawn unless the evidence of the witnesses on oath is that he is an agriculturist and it is easy to see that the evidence of such witnesses is not reliable. [702C] 3. The presumption in the case of an agriculturist is not drawn from proof of storage only. The presumption can be drawn against him if he is an agricultural agriculturist. [602D] 4. The presumption drawn against him under section 49 of the Registration Act is not drawn up against him. [703E] 5. The presumption against him under the law is not drawn until the evidence of witnesses on oath has been disproved. [704G] 6. The presumption cannot be drawn against the appellant unless the evidence is disproved. The presumption, therefore, cannot be drawn unless the circumstances in the case are proved against him. It is not necessary to prove the presumption in the absence of proof. [705G] 7. The presumption of innocence is not drawn when the evidence of a witness is not disproved. It is only when the evidence is not disproving that the presumption is drawn against the accused. [706E] 8. The presumption that a person has been guilty of an offence under the Act is not rebutted by the evidence of any other witness. [707E] 9. The presumption has to be drawn against an agriculturist. The presumption must be drawn against a person who is an agriculturist, and it is difficult to see that he is a dealer. [709G] 9. In the present case, the appellant was not a dealer. He was not a wholesale dealer. He had not been able to prove that he was a wholesale dealer and that he had been in possession of any quantity of foodgrains. [708E] 10. The presumption raised by the appellant against him is not rebutted. [710G] 11. The presumption which is drawn against him is also not rebutted by evidence of any witness. [807E] 12. The presumption does not arise from the fact that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands. The presumption would be rebutted if the evidence of PW 1 is not disproised. [712E] 13. The presumption as to the possession of the foodgrains is not rebutted if the same is proved. [713E] 14. The presumption regarding possession of the stocks of foodgrains is not drawn. The presumption arises only when the circumstances in which the evidence of an agriculturist are to be believed are not rebutted. The presumption may be drawn against any person who is a wholesale dealer or a wholesale dealer, but the presumption is not rebutted unless the evidence are disproved. In the instant case, the presumption is that the foodgrains are grown by the appellant on the lands and the foodgrains are not grown by him. [808E] 15.

The defendant was a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant was a monthly tenant under section 116 of that Act. The plaintiff, who was a monthly tenancy, was a tenant of the defendant from month to months under the provisions Of section 116 of Transfer of Property. The defendant, however, became a monthly tenant of the plaintiff. The defendant continued to be a tenant of that month under section 116, Transfer of Property of Property Act, and, therefore, the defendant became a monthly tenancy from month to day under the provisions. The defendant filed a suit for ejectment of the defendant on the ground that the defendant was a statutory tenant of the suit premises and, therefore the defendant was not a tenant of this month. The defendant contested the suit and contended that the tenancy was created by the defendant in the year 1926 and he was a tenant in the year 1925 and, therefore he was not a landlord of the defendant. The trial judge held that the defendant had no authority to receive rent from the defendant and, therefore was not a monthly tenant. The defendant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the tenancy of the defendant was created by a notice to quit and, therefore it was not a tenancy created by the plaintiff. In appeal to this Court, the High Court held: "The defendant was not the tenant of the plaintiffs. The defendant had no right to create a tenancy in respect of the premises in suit. The defendant did not acquire any permanent right in the land in suit. He was not a statutory tenant. The tenancy was created in accordance with the provisions of the Transfer Of Property Act. It was a tenancy created in accordance With the provisions of that Act and, therefore. the defendant was neither a tenant nor a tenant of a monthly tenant in respect of that premises. The defendant could not be said to be a monthly tenant within the meaning of section 116, transfer of property in view of the provisions of sections 116, Transfer Of Property, Act. The High court, therefore, held that the suit was not barred by section 116 of Act. The appeal to this court was, therefore, dismissed. In the appeal to this High Court, the defendant contended that the suit had been filed by the plaintiff and the defendant was never a tenant of any of the premises. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The tenancy created by a tenancy created under a tenancy created for one year was a tenancy in accordance with section 116 of, Transfer of property Act. The tenancy in question was created by an agreement between the parties. The tenancy continued in accordance with that agreement. [601B] 2. The tenancy of the respondent was not a lease created by the appellant. The tenancy had been created by the respondent in accordance with a valid tenancy created by him. The tenancy, therefore, was not a valid tenancy. [602C] 3. The tenancy having been created by a registered document, the tenancy was not a subsisting tenancy. The tenancy being a tenancy created on a date prior to the expiry of the period provided for in the lease, the tenancy continued in accord with the provisions contained in section 116 of. Transfer of Property, Act, and the tenancy having been determined by a proper notice to quit, the tenancy having accepted payment of rent to the defendant, the defendant was no longer a tenant of such a month. [603D] 4. The tenancy is a tenancy created after the expiry of one year from the date of the notice to quit. The tenancy has been determined by the proper notice to terminate the tenancy. The tenant having accepted payment to the defendant and accepted payment to him, the defendant is not a tenant in respect thereof. [604E] 5. The tenancy which was created by notice to quit was a tenancy which was determined by the appropriate notice to quit by the proper authority. The tenancy did not become a tenancy by the proper date.

The appellant, a public servant, filed an application to the Commissioner under Section 138(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, for obtaining information relating to the assessment proceedings for 1964 65 onwards and that the Income tax Officer after April 1, 1964, made an application to him for obtaining information from the court and that the disclosure of any information from the Income tax authorities after April 1 1964, made a request to the Commissioner to obtain information from the Court and that the Commissioner was satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying his refusal to supply the information. The Commissioner rejected the application. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the disclosure made by the appellant in the application to the Income tax officer was not a valid and legal document and that the appellant was entitled to obtain information under Section 138 (1)(b). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The disclosure of information relating to an assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961 Act or under any other Act, 1922, is a condition precedent to the exercise of the powers by the Income tax officers under Section 138 of the Act. [601B] 2. The disclosure made by a public servant in respect of an assessment made either by the Income Tax Officer after April, 1964, is a sine qua non for the exercise of powers by the court under Section 138. [602C] 3. The disclosure in the application is not a condition precedent for the exercise by the court of the power under Section 138, but is a condition necessary for the exercise thereof. [603D] 4. The disclosure is not a sine qua or sine qua for the exercise or the power of the court under section 138(1) (b). The disclosure of any such information is not a mandatory condition precedent for exercise of the power by the court. [604E] 5. The disclosure must be in the public interest so to do and such an order of the court must be in public interest so that it is in the public interests so to do. [605G] 6. The disclosure should be in the interest of the public and not in the interest which is likely to affect the public interest. [606G] 7. The disclosure cannot be withheld under the garb of the provisions of Section 138(2) of the Act unless the Income tax Officers have the power to summon the production of the documents in a court of law. [607A] 8. The disclosure can be withheld under Section 138 if the Income tax Authorities have the power under section 138 to require production of the relevant documents in a Court of law. The disclosure may be in the interests of the public or in the interest likely to affect public interest. The disclosure, therefore, must be in a court which is likely, to affect the interests of public or in public interest. 9. The disclosure to be in the larger interest of the Income tax Department must be in relation to the income tax authorities. [608D] 9. The information sought by the appellant must be in respect of the assessment years 1964 65 onwards, 65 onwards and 65 onwards. [609E] 10. The disclosure would be in the nature of information which is required to be disclosed. The disclosure will be in the best interest of the Department and the disclosure must be made in the interest or in the public or the interest likely. [610E] 11. The disclosure has to be in relation of the income tax authority. The disclosure does not have any relation to the public interest or the interest of any other person. [611E] 12. The disclosure under the Act is not a part of the information sought for by the assessee.

The father of the minor died in the year 1946 leaving behind his widow, the first appellant, his mother and his mother. The father of the first appellant died in the years 1946 and the second appellant was the only son. The second appellant was a minor. The second respondent was the only daughter of the first respondent. The second appeal was dismissed by the High Court. The High Court held that the gift was complete and the gift was not complete. The second question was whether the gift was completed by the father of the second appellant and the second respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the Hindu Succession Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The gift was complete. The father was not a minor. He was not a major. The gift in question was complete and he was not competent to make the gift. The gift did not complete the gift. [801B] 2. The gift by the father to his mother was complete and it was not a gift. The second proviso to section 6(1) of the Act provides that the gift shall be complete in all respects and the gift shall not be deemed to be complete if it is not completed within the period of one year from the date of the gift. It is not necessary that the gift should be complete in every respect. [802C] 3. The gift is complete and the donee has no guardian of the property to accept the gift on behalf of the minor. The gift cannot be completed by the death of the father. [803D] 4. The gift does not complete the transfer of ownership of the property. The gift has been completed by the mother in law and the gift has been accepted by her on behalf of her mother in law. [804E] 5. The gift deed was complete and there was no guardian of property in the hands of the minor and the gift in question is complete. The gift could not be completed by her mother in the absence of guardian of the minor who had attained the discretion. [805E] 6. The gift having been completed by her father in law, the gift could not have been completed by him. [806F] 7. The gift made by the father in law to his mother in law was complete and she was competent to make it. [807F] 8. The gift to the minor was complete and her mother in Law was capable of giving her consent to the gift. There was complete and full intention to make the gifts. The gift had been completed by Mammotty and the gift had been accepted by the mother. The gift, therefore, was complete and binding on the minor. [808F] 9. The gift of the property was complete and valid. The gift would be complete and binding only if it was completed by Mammsotty and not by Mammottotty. The gift must be complete and the minor must be alive. [809G] 10. The gift can be completed by Mammanotty only if it is complete and binding. The gift may be completed by a minor. [908F] 11. The gift will be complete and irrevocable. The gift shall be completed by all the three parties to the minor. If the minor is not alive, the gift shall stand completed by Mammenotty and no guardian of his minor shall be entitled to receive the gift. If the gift is complete, the minor shall be paid the gift amount. [810G] 12. The gift should be completed by six months from the date on which the minor attains the age of majority. [811G] 13. The gift under the Muhammadan law to the minor is complete and irrevocable and the minor is within the care either of the mother or of other near relative or even a stranger. [812F] 14. The gift which is complete and valid is within the knowledge of the minor is a valid gift.

The respondent temple was established in the year 1951 and the respondent temple was registered as a religious institution under the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The respondent temple was a religious institution. The respondent was appointed as a Commissioner of the respondent temple on June 30, 1951. The Commissioner appointed a Committee under section 76(2) of the Act to enquire into the sustainability of the claim of the respondent. The Committee submitted its report on January 5, 1951. On the basis of the report of the Commissioner, the respondent temple filed a petition under section 76 of the Act before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court under section 76 (2) of Act No. 19 of 1951 before the High court. The High court held that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76. The High 'Court held that the respondent temple had not determined its audit fee under Section 76(2). The High Court held that the report of Commissioner was in truth for the year 1951. The High' Court held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was receiving any amount from the temple. The High. Court held that since the Commissioner had determined the audit fees under section 76, the respondent was not entitled to any amount from him. The High, Court, however, held that the order of the Commissioner was in substance a decision on one of the material questions arising in the case and that the respondent had not determined any amount from which the respondent was entitled to any contribution under section 76.(2) of The High Court, therefore, set aside the order of Commissioner and directed the Commissioner to determine the audit fee payable by the respondent temple. The respondent, however, contended that the High Court had not determined whether the audit fee was in truth or not. The High Curt held that the Committee had not determined that the respondent 's annual income was in truth and not less than the prescribed amount. The High [Court further held that the income of the respondent was in truth. The High] Court held that it was not necessary to determine the annual income of the temple as the Commissioner had to determine the amount of the audit fee. The High "Court further held: "The Commissioner had not fixed the annual income at the rate of Rs. 1,000/- per annum. The Commissioner had not decided the question whether the respondent was liable to pay the amount of audit fee. He had not determined what was the amount of Rs.1,000/- which was the audit fee and the respondent was also liable to pay Rs.1.000/- per month. The High Commissioner had not considered the question whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the respondent and the Commissioner. The High Commission had not determined how the respondent was to be assessed. The High -Court held that there is no evidence to establish that the respondent is liable to pay any amount from his own funds. The High-Court further held, that the respondent's contention that the respondent did not determine the audit fees is not correct. The HighCourt held that it is not necessary to decide whether the respondent is entitled to any payment from his own fund. The High Courts held that the amount of fee was not a reasonable relation to the expenditure incurred for the audit of the institution. The High High Court held, that there was a clear evidence to show, that the amount was not a proper relation to the expenses incurred for the auditing of the institution and that the High 'Court had not determined, that the expenditure incurred was not a fair relation to the audit fee, and that the amount had not been determined by the Commissioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Power Court was right in holding that the respondent has not determined the amount of fees payable by the temple. [701B] 2. The High power of the Commissioner to fix the annual income is not a matter of procedure.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly from the Punjab Legislative Council. He was elected as the Chairman of the Legislative Assembly from a constituency. He was also elected as the Vice Chairman of the Punjab Vidhan Sabha. He was, however, elected as the Secretary of the Legislative Council. The appellant, a Member of the Legislative assembly, was elected to the Punjab Legislative assembly from the Punjab Vidhan. He was a member of that Assembly. He was removed from the Punjab State Legislative Assembly by the order of the High Court. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of removal of the appellant from the Punjab Civil Services (Executive) Act, 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal before this Court. The High court held that the order of dismissal was not an order initiating contempt proceedings. The appellant contended that the order was not an interlocutory order. The High 'Court held that the appellant had no right to file an appeal against the order of his removal from the Punjab Government. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The order of the learned Single Judge was not an interim order. The appellant had no locus standi to file an application under section 19 of the Act. [849 D] 2. The appellant was not a party to the proceedings. He was not a necessary party to the proceeding. He was merely a party to a petition. He was only a party to an order of the Court. [850 E] 3. The appellant did not file an appeal under section 19 against the order passed by the High Court in a contempt proceeding. He did not file a writ petition under section 19. [852 E] 4. The appellant could not file an application for initiating contempt proceedings against the alleged contemner for contempt of the High court. [853 E] 5. The appellant cannot be said to be a party to any contempt proceeding. The appellant is not a party in the contempt proceeding. [854 E] 6. The appellant has not been able to show that the order passed in the contempt proceedings was not an 'order' within the meaning of section 19 of Act. [820 E] 7. The appellant does not appear to have been able to establish that the order in the contempt petition was an 'order'. [854 F] 7. In the present case, the appellant had not been able, at any stage, to file an appropriate application for initiating the proceeding for contempt. [855 F] 8. The appellant having not been able at any stage to show that he was a party to such an order, the appellant cannot be asked in an appeal to decide whether he was a 'order' or not. [856 G] 8. In the instant case, the order of appointment of the appellant was not an "order" within the meaning ofs. 19 of the , but was an ' order' within the contemplation of the legislature. [857 A] 9. The appellant being a member of Legislative Assembly, he cannot be said not to be a 'order" within section 19 of 'the Act. [823 A] 10. The appellant can not be said to have any locus standi to maintain an appeal to this Court under section 19 from an order of this Court.

The appellant was prosecuted along with two others for offences under section 6(1) A of the Act of 1952. The appellant was prosecuted in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi, on the charge that he had committed the offence of theft of a wireless apparatus. The appellant pleaded that he was not liable to be convicted under section 6 (1) A and that he was liable to be tried under section 6 A of the 1952 Act. The Magistrate, after hearing the parties, convicted him of the offence under section 6A of the 1952 act and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has appealed to this Court. The appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant under section 6 of the 1952 Acts was not sustainable under section 6-A of the Act and, therefore, the conviction of him under section 6AA of the 1952Act was bad. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction of the accused under section 6 is not sustainable under the law. The conviction is not sustainable in law. [601 A] 2. The provisions of the 1952 and the 1952 Acts are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. The provisions are not inconsistent. The language of the Act is clear and unambiguous. The language is clear and explicit. The language used in the Act is not inconsistent with any of the provisions of any other enactment. [602 B] 3. The language employed in the Act, in its ordinary sense, is the same as the words used in the enactment. The words used in section 6 A are comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmitter in a wireless telegraph. [603 C] 4. The words "any other enactment" in section 6A(1) are comprehensive enough and not inconsistent with each other. [604 D] 5. The words 'any other enactment' in section 6AA(1) of the 1952 AC Act are comprehensive enough, and not inconsistent. [605 E] 6. The words in section 6(2) of the Act are comprehensive and not inconsistent, and the words 'anyother enactment" in the Act are not inconsistent therewith. [606 F] 7. The words are comprehensive enough in the sense that they are comprehensive enough. The words have to be construed in their ordinary sense. [607 F] 8. The words of section 6AA (1) of 1952 Act are comprehensive in their ordinary meaning. The words refer to the amending Act of 1949 and the corresponding provisions of the amending Act. The words do not refer to the amendment of the Act, but refer to the amended provisions of the new Act. [608 F] 9. The words referred to in section 6 (2) of 1952 Acts are comprehensive enough for the purpose of the present case. The words, 'any other Act" in section 4A of the 1956 Act are comprehensive. The words must be construed in the sense in which they are comprehensively understood in the sense of the words used. [609 F] 10. The words cannot be construed in a manner which would defeat the provisions of section 6 A(1) and 6 A(2) Of the 1952 Act, unless the context otherwise requires. [610 F] 11. The words employed in section 6-AA of the Act have to be interpreted in the sense which they are understood in the ordinary sense. The words should be construed in such a way that they are understood to be in the ordinary meaning. [611 F] 12. The words may be construed in any way that they would be understood in the normal sense. [613 F] 13. The words which are comprehensive enough are comprehensive enough not to take in any other enactment, but to take in every other enactment. The language in which the words are comprehensively used is comprehensive enough to include all other enactments.

The appellant, a benamidar for the respondent, purchased a Schedule property from the respondent, and the respondent purchased the same in execution of the decrees. The properties were in possession of the respondent, but the decreeholders were in possession thereof. The properties in question were in possession and the respondent was in possession of them. The decreeholders filed a suit for partition of the properties in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Burdwan, in which the appellant was the sole defendant. The respondent filed a suit in the court for partition of his properties. The Subordinate Judge, by his judgment dated March 12, 1949, decreed the suit and directed the appellant to deliver possession of the properties to the respondent. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The respondent then filed a second appeal to this Court. The respondent contended that the decreeholders had not been able to prove that the decree holders were in possession, and the properties were in the possession of the real decreeholders. The High court, however, held that the decreeholder had failed to prove that he was in possession, because the decreeholders on record were in possession. The High, Court, however, allowed the second appeal and set aside the judgment and decreeholders on the ground that the decree holder was in possession and he was in fact a benamidar of the real judgment debtor. The High. Court, however held that the judgment debtors had failed to establish that the decree had been passed by the court below in the absence of proof of the decreeholders being in possession of these properties. The High ' Court, however. held that the findings recorded by the courts below were not correct. The High' Court, however,. held that the properties were not in possession of either of the parties, and the decreeholders could not be said to be in possession of any part of the properties. The appellant, therefore, filed a second application under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, and the High Court held that the appellant had failed to discharge his burden of proving that the decree was passed by the courts. The High Curt, however, set aside the decreeholders 's order for restoration of possession made by the courts and restored the possession of these lands to the appellant. The appellant has appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts were right in holding that the decree passed by the trial court was not correct. [901B] 1.2. The High courts were right in treating the decreeholders as the decreeholders and the decreeholder on record as the decreeholder. [902C] 1.3. The HighCourt was right in holding, that the decree Holders on record were not the decreeholders. [903D] 1.4. The High Cou rt was right in setting aside the decree holders on record as they were not the decreesholders on record. [905E] 1.5. The High tions were right in setting at naught the decree holders 's order on record as to whether the decreeholders would be entitled to get the decreeholders restored to the properties. [906E] 1,601D] 1,06E] 2.1. In the instant case, the decreeholders filed the second application under sections 36(2)(c) and 36(2), (d) of the Act, claiming that the decreeees were in possession as the decree holders and the decree holders had been reopened. The High cour t found that the decree debtors had been able to show that the decree did not have the right to get the properties restored to the deity. [908E] 2,06F] 2.2. In the present case, the High Court was right in treating that the decree Holder was the decreeholder and the decree holder as the decree holder. [909G] 2.3.1.

The appellant company purchased a property in the name of Habib & Sons, by a registered sale deed dated January 7, 1949, from the respondent company. The respondent company purchased the property in the names of Habib & Company and the appellant company purchased the same in the name and style of Habib & Industries. The respondent Company purchased the property from Habib & Sons and the appellant Company purchased the same. The respondent filed a suit in the City Civil Court for specific performance of the contract and obtained a decree in the suit. The City Civil Court decreed the suit and the respondent company filed an appeal in the City Court. The City Court held that the respondent company was entitled to the relief claimed by Habib & Sons. The City Judge held that the appellant company was entitled only to the relief of specific performance of a contract and not of the decree. The City judge held that the transaction was not a sale and that the transaction in question was not a transfer of the property. The City court held that the transactions were not sales and that the transactions in question were not sales. The City civil Court held that there was no sale and that there was a transfer of a decree in existence. The City City Civil Court held that it was not a case where there was a sale and the transaction in the present case was not a transaction of transfer of the decree and that the transfer of the suit property was not a decree in fact and that the transferee was entitled to get the relief of Specific Performance of a contract. The City Munsif held that the transfer was not a valid sale and that it was a transfer and that the transferor was entitled to have the relief of the Specific Performance of the contract. The High Court held that a transfer of property was not an agreement to transfer and that it could not be a transfer of an agreement to sell. The City Munsiff held that the sale was not a completed sale and that, therefore, the transaction was a transfer. The City Sub Judge held that there could be a transfer and the transferee was not entitled to have his claim for specific performance. The City District Judge held that a transaction in the nature of a transfer was not an instrument of transfer and that, in the absence of a decree, the transaction could not be said to be a transfer. On appeal to the High Court, the City Civil Judge held that it could be a sale and, therefore, there was no question of transfer. The High court held that there is no question of a transfer of immovable property and that the sale deed was not a registered document. The City Sessions Judge held that, in view of the provisions of Order XXI, rule 16, the document in question was a transfer in writing and that the document in fact was not a document. The High Judge held that in view of Order XXI Rule 16, the transfer of immovable properties was not a compulsory transfer and that there could not be any transfer of immovable assets. The City High Court held, that the transaction did not amount to a transfer of immoveable property and that, as the transfer was a transfer, the transaction did amount to a sale and was not a compulsorily transfer. The appellant company filed an application for execution of the decree in terms of Order XXI. Rule 16, which was dismissed by the City Civil court. The City Small Causes Court held that, the transaction in terms of the decree was not a mortgage and that the property was not the property of the company. The CityCTC appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The transaction in question is a transfer of moveable property and, therefore the transaction in respect of the immovable property is a transfer in terms of a decree. [601B] 2. The transaction is a transfer and not a mortgage. The transaction was a mortgage. [602C] 3. The transaction does not amount to an agreement to sale. The transaction did not come within the meaning of Order XXI and, therefore it was a mortgage and, therefore there was no transfer of immovable asset.

The respondent was carrying on the business of fabricating and selling windows and doors and windows in a building contract for sale of windows and doors. The respondent was carrying out business of fabricising and selling windows. The contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed under the terms of the contract. The contract provided for payment of the price of the windows and doors, and windows. The respondent carried on the business as well as the business of Fabricating and selling window leaves and shesas etc. The contract contained a stipulation that the respondent would be charged the price of windows and windows in the building contract for the sale of windows, and the price of doors and windows. On the other hand, the contract provided for the payment of the consideration for the sale by the respondent to the contractors. The respondent contended that the contract was one for work, and the contract was for sale of the windows, and that the contract did not pass to the respondent. The respondent disputed the liability of the respondent to pay the price of his windows and windows. He contended that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax and that the respondent had not made any separate charge for the contract as understood by the parties. The respondent also contended that the contracts were for sale of goods and not for sale of doors and window leaves. The High Court held that the contract for sale was one for sale of all the windows and windows and that the contracts for sale of window leaves and windows were not incidental to the execution of the contract for work, but were incidental to the delivery of the goods. The High court held that the contracts entered into by the respondent were not contracts for sale and not for the sale thereof. The High 'Court held that the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. The High. Court held that there was no contract for sale and that the transaction of the windows or windows was not a contract for sale. The High, Court held that it was not necessary for the respondent to prove that the contract in question was one for "fix" the windows and the doors and windows and the respondent could claim the amount for "fixation" the windows or the windows. The High' Court held that "fix", the windows and other goods were incidental to it and that the parties were not liable to sales tax. The High "Court held that "the contract for sale" was one for works, and the parties were liable to pay sales tax. On the facts of the case, the High Court held, that the contract of sale was one of service in the execution and making of the contract and that the work was incidental to the completion of the work. The High [Court further held that "if the contract for the work is one for work and labour, the contract for "fixing" the windows, or the windows and fixing" the windows would not be complete, and that it was only upon the completion of work and labour that the contract would be complete, but the contract for works, labour and labour were involved in the execution, and that there was a contract for "sale of windows and door leaves" and that the property was not passed to the other party to the contract for Works, labour and Labour. The High Courts held that the transaction was one for the sale and not of the windows. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The contract for sale is one for works and labour. The contract is one for the work and labour. [801B] 2. The contract of sale is one of service and labour. It is one for sale and labour. Therefore, the contract of "sale of doors and doors and doors, windows and other things" is one for "sale" and not for "sale". [801C] 3. The contract between the parties is one for construction of windows and other thing.

The appellant was prosecuted for offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 511 Indian Penal Code and section 420 read with section 420 Indian Penal Code. The trial court framed charges against the accused for the offences under sections 419, 468 and 420 Indian Penal code. The accused pleaded not guilty to the charges framed against him. The trial was held in a summary manner. The trial Judge found that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges against the appellant and accordingly convicted him. The High Court, however, set aside the conviction and sentence. The appellant has come in appeal to this Court. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution failed to prove that the appellant was a broker and that the prosecution was not entitled to the benefit of section 420 Indian penal Code. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution had failed in proving the charges against Raj Kumar Agarwalla. The prosecution was not able to prove the charge against him. [701B] 2. The prosecution failed to establish the charges against him. It was open to the prosecution to prove the allegations against the appellant. [702C] 3. The prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [703D] 4. The prosecution did not prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt and the High Court, therefore, was in error. [704E] 5. The prosecution could not prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the High court was in error, in holding that there was no evidence to prove the allegation against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt by the prosecution. [705E] 6. The prosecution, therefore, failed to prove any charge against the appellant under sections 420 and 468 Indian Penal Code, and the appellant was rightly convicted by the High Court. [706F] 7. The High court was, therefore, in error in setting aside the conviction of the appellant. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed.

The appellant, a Railway Company, was engaged in the business of running trains. The appellant was the owner of a railway property. The appellant had entered into a contract with the Railways for the construction of a railway bridge. The Railways had entered into an agreement with the Railways on June 6, 1981. The appellant entered into a hire purchase agreement with the Railway Company for the construction and maintenance of a railway track. The appellant, a railway company, entered into a lease agreement with the railway company for the construction, maintenance and repair of a railway line. The appellant agreed to pay the monthly rent of Rs.44.00 per month. The appellant paid the monthly rent at Rs.44,000. The appellant claimed that the railway company was not liable to pay the rent at the rate of Rs.45.00 per annum. The appellant contended that the railway corporation was not liable for the payment of the rent at a rate higher than the rate of rupees 45.00 per year. The appellant also contended that the Railway company was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Railway Act and the rules framed thereunder. The Railway Board, however, did not accept the contention of the appellant and held that the railway authorities were not liable to make payment of the monthly rent. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Kerala challenging the validity of the action of the railway authorities in not paying the monthly rent to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was not entitled for the benefit of Section 3(1)(c) of the Railway Protection Act, 1986. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The railway authorities were entitled to recover the monthly rent from the appellant. [701B] 2. The railway authority was not entitled under the provisions of Section 3 of the Railway Property (Unlawful Possession) Act to recover the rent from the railway company. [702C] 3. The railway administration was not entitled in law to recover the amount of rent from the Railway company. [602D] 4. The railway company was entitled to recover from the railway administration the amount of the rent from its employees. [703E] 5. The railway department was not entitled, in law, to recover the arrears of rent from its employee. [704G] 6. The railway corporation was entitled to take steps to recover the same from the railway department. [705G] 7. The railway board was not entitled as a matter of right to recover the amounts of rent from employees. [605G] 8. The railway Administration was not entitled either to recover the money from the employees or to recover the damages from the railway employees. [805G] 9. The railway Board was not entitled only to recover the sums of rent from their employees. [783A] 10. The railway management was not entitled even to recover the sum of rent from them. [783B] 10. In the instant case, the railway administration was entitled to recovery of the amount of damages from the employees. [784A] 11. The railway undertaking was not entitled at all to recover the said amount from the employees and the railway administration. [783D] 12. The railway employees were not entitled to recover any amount from the railway authorities. [783E] 13. The railway administrations were not entitled in Law to recover the loss caused to the railway administration by the negligence of the railway administration and the railway authorities had no authority to recover the damage caused to the railways. [783F] 14. The railway servants were not entitled either in law to take steps for recovery of the loss caused by the negligence or the railway administration or the railway authorities to recover the compensation from the railway servants. [783G] 15.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. The lands were resumed by the State Government under the provisions of the Abolition Act. The appellants filed applications for restoration of the lands under the Abolition Act before the Tribunal. The Tribunal by its order dated July 18, 1961 dismissed the applications for restoration. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Bombay Revenue Tribunal against the order of the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal dated July 18. 1961. The Tribunal dismissed the applications of restoration. The State Government filed an appeal to this Court. The High Court dismissed the appeals on the ground that the Tribunal had no power to dismiss the appeals for non prosecution in a case where the appellants had appeared in the appeal and the applications of the appellants were heard and decided on merits. The High court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the applications of respondents Nos. 1 and 2 were barred by limitation. The High Courts held that the applications filed by the appellants were barred by time. Hence the appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right, in holding that there was no delay on the part of the appellants in filing the applications for condonation of delay. [701B] 2. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to dismiss the applications for non prosecution. The Tribunal's order was not final and conclusive. [702C] 3. The Tribunal did not decide the appeals on merits. It was open to the Tribunal to dismiss the application for non prosecution if the appellants had not appeared in the appeals. [703D] 4. The Tribunal could not dismiss the applications filed under Regulation 19(1) of the Abolition Rules. [704E] 5. The Tribunal has no power to decide the appeals even on merits. [705E] 6. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that the applications for setting aside the orders of the Tribunal were barred by the limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. [706F] 7. The Tribunal in the present case had no power under Regulation 19 to dismiss the appeal for non prosecution and the applications for restoring the appeals were not barred by limitation prescribed by the Regulation 21. The Tribunal also did not decide on merits. In the circumstances, the appeals were rightly dismissed. [707F] 7A] 8. The Tribunal should have decided the appeals on merit and not to record its decision on merits. But it was open to it to dismiss the appellants 's appeals on merits, if it had not been decided on merits, but it was open for it to dismiss them for non prosecution, if it was not decided on merits and not to proceed with the appeals. The Tribunal ought to have decided the appeal on merits. If it had not decided on the merits, it could not have dismissed the appeals for want of jurisdiction. [709F] 9. The Tribunal cannot dismiss the appeals on technical grounds. The Tribunal is not competent to dismiss the petitions for non prosecution when it has not decided on merit. [710F] 10. The Tribunal can dismiss the appeals only on technical grounds and not on merits. There is no reason why the Tribunal should not dismiss the appeals when it has no power under section 20 of the Abolition act to dismiss the same. [711G] 11. The Tribunal does not have power to dismiss an appeal for non defence. The Tribunal may dismiss the appeals even if it is not decided on technical grounds but it is open to it, if it is decided on merits to dismiss the special leave petitions. [712F] 12. The Tribunal will not dismiss the special appeals on technical ground. [713G] 13. The Tribunal shall not dismiss the appeal on technical grounds unless it is satisfied that there is a change in the persons sitting as members of the Tribunal or bench thereof, or that it is not possible to record its decisions on merits.

The appellant was appointed as a Pujar of the village Telibandha on the basis of a Will executed by him in favour of one Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple. The appellant was appointed in the year 1896 as a Pujari of the village. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy was dedicated to the temple of the deity and for the performance of the duties of the temple. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High court held that the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the appeal. The appellant has appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High 'Court 's order is not correct and the appellant was entitled to a declaration that he made a dedication of the temple of his own to the deity. [901F] 2. The appellant had not been able to show that the temple was dedicated to him as a Pujara. He was not able to show any evidence to show that he made any such alienations of the property or that he made some alienations of the temple to the deity, and that he made an absolute dedication of the property to the deity and that he had made an absolute gift of the property. [902F] 3. The appellant 's case was that the temple had been dedicated to the deity by the Panch Faisla. The appellant contended that the temple belonged to the deity but was not given any proprietary interest in the village Tehribandha. The trial Court held that there was no absolute dedication of Telibandha to the deity nor was it necessary to decide the other issues which had been framed in the suit. [903G] 4. The High' Court was in error in holding that the appellant had been given a proprietary interest in Tehribandha to the temple. [904F] 5. The High. Court was in agreement with the Trial Court that the appellant 's suit was not barred by section 92 of Code of Civil procedure. [905G] 6. The appellant could not establish that the temple in question was dedicated to his family. [906F] 7. The appellant cannot therefore be allowed to take the plea that the temple is dedicated to the family. [0905G] 8. The High Courts have not accepted the plea of the appellant that the temple has been dedicated to his own family. [1005G] 9. The High, Court was in no doubt that the appellant could not have been given a right to take the view that the temple could not be dedicated to his father. [908F] 9. In the instant case, the appellant was appointed the Manager on behalf of the deity. The appellant did not make an absolute dedication to the temple nor did he make an absolute gift to the deity or to the appellant. [909G] 9,10A] 10. The appellant is not entitled to the benefit of section 92 of C.P.C. The HighCourt was in error by holding that the temple which was dedicated to a family was dedicated to it.

The appellants were appointed as the Chairman of the Action Committee of the Allahabad Bar Association on the recommendation of the High Court. The High Court directed the Chairman of Action Committee to hold a meeting of the Committee to consider the question of continuance of the appellants in the office of the Chief Justice. The High court held that the appellants were guilty of contempt of court and sentenced them to imprisonment for a period of two years. The High ' Court also directed that the appellants should be given the benefit of the period of two months. The High, Court, however, directed that the Chairman of a Committee should be given a period of one month to enable the appellants to complete the work. The High. Court directed that the Committee should be reconstituted in accordance with the resolution passed by the High Court and the appellants should not be given the benefits of the period for which they were appointed. The High C ourt directed that the members of the Action Committees should be given an extension of the period. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution. The High tions of the High C oun tions of Allahabad Bar Association and the Chairman of that Committee were challenged by the appellants by filing a writ petition. The High cour t held that the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1 and that the appellants had committed contempt of court. The High Cou rt held that the High Court had committed contempt in the face of the resolution and that the High Cour t had committed contempt. The High ny, however, did not go into the question of continuation of the resolution because the High Court did not go to the question of the continuance of the resolution in the High Curt. The High Courts, however, held that the members were guilty of criminal contempt. The appellants were convicted by the High C ummission and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. In appeal to this Court, the appellants contended that the High court had committed contempt and that the order of the High court was liable to be set aside. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High rity of the High Courts was not correct. The High Power Committee was not justified in holding that the appellants could not be punished for contempt. [701 A] 2. The High Commiss ion of the High Power Committee had not been properly constituted. The High power Committee was not properly constituted. [702 B] 3. The High Commissioner was not justified on the ground that he was not acting in the dis trict of the Chief justice. [703 B] 4. The High Commission was not justified to proceed against the appellants for contempt. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed.

The appellant, a Sub Registrar, Arambagh, filed a suit for declaration that the award was made on 28th of November, 1983 and the award was presented on 25th of November 1983. The arbitrators made an application to the Sub Registrar for registration of the award on 24th of November 1984. The Sub Registrar, after hearing the parties, passed an order on 25th November, 1983 directing the arbitrators to keep the award in the custody of the court. The Sub-Registrar, Aram Bagh, on 25th April, 1984, passed an award in the court of the Sub Registrar, Hooghly at Chinsurah on 25th May, 1984. The arbitrators filed an application before the Sub Registrar on 25th June, 1984 for registration of a reference under section 15 of the . The Sub Registrar refused to register the award on the ground that the award had already been presented on 25 th May, 1984 and the Sub Registrar had already sent back the award to the arbitrators. The SubRegistrar, A.rambagh, on 25 th April, 1984 passed an order of the Sub-Registrar directing the arbitrators not to register the same on the ground of limitation. The Sub registrar, Aramganj, on 25 May, 1984, issued an order of registration of the reference under section 16 of the . 26th July, 1984. On 25th May 1984, the Sub Registrar issued an order for registration of an award on the same date. The Sub Registrars, Arambag, on 25 June, 1984, sent back the order of the learned Sub Registrar, to the Sub- Registrar, A.S.R. (S.R.) on 25th July,1984. The Sub Inspector, Arambad, filed a petition under section 15(1) of the . Arambagh Act, on the ground, that the award dated 25th May was presented on 28th November, 1984 and it was presented on 24th November,1983. The Sub­Registrar, Aharbagh, on 24th July, 1983, sent back a copy of the award to both the parties. The SubRegistrars, Aramabad, filed a revision petition before the High Court of Calcutta. The High Court, by its order dated 25th July 1984, set aside the order of registration and remanded the matter to the Sub­Registrar for registration of award on the basis of the order of remand. The High court, however, held that the award made on 28 th November, 1983 was not valid and the Sub­ Registrar was not competent to register the said award. The High 'Court, however, set aside that order of the sub­Registrar and remanded the case to the SubRegistrar for registration. The High'Court, however held that the Sub­Registrars had committed breach of the injunction order passed by the learned Sub­Registrar and, therefore, the Sub­ registrar was not competent. The High.Court, however set aside the orders of the Sub­registrars and remanded the matters to the Sub Registrars for registration. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the Sub Registrars and remanded the cases to the SubRegistrats for registration. In the appeal to this Court, the High 'Court held that the order of Sub­Registrar was not valid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Sub­Regllistrars had not filed a suit in the court for registration of their award. [701B] 1.2 The Sub­ Registrar had no jurisdiction to decide the question of limitation. [702C] 1.3 The Sub­registrar had no jurisdiction in the matter. [703D] 1.4 The Sub­ registrar had no jurisdiction. The Subregistrar had jurisdiction to decide whether the award was in the custody or not.

The respondent 's suit for ejectment was brought under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. The respondent 's case was that the appellant had sub let the premises to the sub tenant and that the sub tenant had sub let them to the sub tenants. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the sub tenants had sub let out the premises to him and that the appellant was not a sub tenant. The respondent contended that the sub tenancy was a new tenancy and that the respondent had not sub let the property to the sub tenancy and that he had not sub letting the premises to any sub tenant. Held, that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of section 13(2) of the Bombay Rent Act. The appellant was not entitled under section 13 (1)(e), to the protection under section 13 of the Act, to the protection afforded by section 13(3) of the said Act. The protection afforded by the Act was not a substantive provision in the Act. It was a substantive provision which was introduced in the Act and was not a provision in an Act of Parliament. The protection of section 15 of the Act was a substantive one and was not limited to cases of sub letting. The protection was not a limited one. The protection under section 15 of Act was not only a substantive provision but was a substantive provisions in the Act itself. The protection given by the Act to the sub lessee was a substantive right and was not an express provision in the statute for the protection of the revenue and to be enforced only at the instance of the revenue officials. The protection conferred by section 15 of this Act was a provision in the agreement which was for the benefit of the public. The protection provided by the Act had not been extended to the sub lease. The protection granted by the Act could not be availed of by the respondent as a sub tenant, because the sub lessee had not sub lease. It was not a case of sub lease. In the circumstances, the respondent was entitled to the benefit of protection under section 14 of the Act and the protection afforded to the sub sub tenant. It was therefore not a case where the respondent had waived his right as a sub lessee. The respondent was not a tenant under section 13. The protection extended by the Act is a substantive provision and not a substantive one. The respondent had not made any express provision in an agreement which was not for the benefit or benefit of the respondent. The protection which was granted by the Legislature was a substantive part of the Act itself and was not intended to be a substantive provision. The protection could not be extended to the respondent as the provisions of section 13 (2) of Act were not in the Act, and the protection was not limited only to cases of termination of tenancy and sub lease.

The appellant, who was working as a teacher in the respondent Board, was appointed as a teacher on probation for a period of two years. He was confirmed in the said post on August 31, 1990. He was promoted to the post of Head Master on August 31. 1990. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Notification dated August 31,1990. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the Notification dated July 31, 1990 and directed the Board to allow all the candidates referred to in the Notification dated June 31, 1990 for the purpose of conducting the examination. The Board challenged the validity of Notification dated July 30, 1990 and the Notification dated January 30, 1991. The High court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the impugned Notification dated July 29, 1990. The Board filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High Judge allowed the writ appeal and quashed the notification dated July 30. 1990. The High Courts allowed the writ appeals and quashed the Notifications dated July 30 and July 31,1990 and directed the appellant to allow all candidates referred to therein for the purpose. The High 'Court further directed the Board not to allow all those candidates referred to under the Notification dated May 31, 1990 to appear at the S.S.C. examination. The High' Court allowed the appeal and quashed all the Notifications dated May 31. 1990 and July 31. 1990 on the ground that the High Court was not justified in quashing the Notification dated March 31, 1990 because the High Court had no jurisdiction to quash the Notification dated April 31, 1990 on the basis that the examination was conducted at the behest of the Board. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1. The High. Court was not right in quashing the notification dated May 31., 1990. [701B] 1.2.1.2. The High Powered Committee was not justified to go into the question whether the examination was done at the behest and the guardian or guardian of the students.

The appellant was a public servant and was a public servants. He was a public Servant. He was prosecuted for criminal misconduct under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Special Judge convicted him of the offence under section 5 (1) of that Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The Special judge convicted him of that offence and sentenced him as aforesaid. The Special Court convicted him of criminal misconduct under sections 5(1)(d) and 5(2) of the Act and sentenced them to imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000. The Special Bench of the High Court convicted him under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and sentenced to imprisonment for two years and to pay fine of Rs, 5,000 and to suffer imprisonment for one month. The Special Leave Petition filed by the appellants was dismissed by this Court. The Special leave petition filed by the State of Punjab was dismissed by the Supreme Court. The appellants filed a special leave petition in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Special Courts have jurisdiction to try the offences under sections 5 (1)(d), 5(2), 5(1), 5(3) and 5 (2) of that Code. [401B] 2. The Special Judges have jurisdiction to entertain and try the offences mentioned in section 5(2). The Special Judge has jurisdiction to try all the offences mentioned therein. [402C] 3. The Special Special Judge has no jurisdiction to try any offence mentioned in section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. [502D] 4. The Special Judicial Magistrate has jurisdiction to entertain the offences mentioned under section 5 and under section 5. [403E] 5. The Special Magistrate has jurisdiction under section 5 to try the offence mentioned in the section. The Special court has jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offences mentioned above. [405E] 6. The Special Public Prosecutor has no jurisdiction under section 6 to try the cases mentioned in section 6 to the Special Court. [407F] 7. The Special Appellate Court has no jurisdiction in respect of the offences under section 5, 5(1). [407G] 8. The Special Tribunal has no jurisdiction. The Special Officer has no jurisdiction, under section 6, to try the case mentioned in section 7 to the Special Judge. [408F] 9. The Special Secretary to the Government of Punjab, Department of Home, Government of Punjab has no jurisdiction over the cases mentioned therein. The Special Police Establishment has no jurisdiction and the Special Judge has not jurisdiction to try and try the cases under section 5 or section 6 to any other Special Judge. The Special Establishment has no power to try the same offences mentioned in the sections. [409G] 9. In the instant case, the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain or try the offences referred to in section 5 of that Act. [410H] 10. The Special Appeal is, therefore, without jurisdiction.

The appellant and the surety were guarantors for the principal debtor. The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The surety had agreed to give personal guarantee on the security of the principal debtor, namely, the surety. The surety agreed to give his personal guarantee on his good faith and the personal guarantee on good faith of other security being offered by the principal debtor at the time when the contract of guarantee was entered into. The surety also agreed to give the personal guarantee of the surety on the security being offered. The surety executed by the principal creditor was independent of the surety and the personal guarantees of the surety. In view of the provisions of section 141, the surety was discharged and the surety was not discharged from his obligation under the guarantee, the surety would not be discharged from his obligations under the guarantee and the personal bond was discharged. The surety, however, was discharged from the obligation under the letter of guarantee. The High Court held that the surety was entitled to restitution and the surety had discharged his obligation under his guarantee. The appeal by the surety was dismissed. The appellant has come to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The surety is entitled to restitution. [701B] 2. The surety has to be discharged from the liability under the bond. The surety must be discharged from its obligation under the bond and the personal surety must be given a personal guarantee on that security. [702C] 3. The surety cannot be discharged from obligation under the surety unless the surety is discharged from his liabilities. [703D] 4. The surety can be discharged from liability under the surety if he has taken more than one security on the specific condition that the surety would be discharged from their liability under the Guarantee. [704E] 5. The surety would not discharge his obligation under a guarantee and the surety would also not discharge his liability under a guarantee. [705E] 6. The surety could not be discharged unless the surety was able to show that the surety had taken more than two security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on security. [805E] 7. The surety did not discharge his obligations under a guarantee nor the personal guarantee. The security was not discharged. [706E] 8. The surety failed to discharge his obligation in accordance with the letter of guarantees. The surety's obligation under the letters of guarantee was discharged. [806E] 9. The surety should not be discharged if the surety had given personal guarantee on account of the surety, and the surety should not have discharged his obligation in terms of the letter of Guarantee. [807F] 9. In the present case, the surety had not discharged his obligation. The surety himself had given personal guarantees on the security. The surety gave personal guarantees on his good practice and the personal security on the good faith of the surety was discharge of his obligation under letter of guarantee and the Personal guarantee on the good practice and his personal guarantee. [808F] 10. The surety does not discharge his duty in accordance with his letter of guarantee nor the Personal guarantee. [908F] 11. The surety merely gives personal guarantee on behalf of the principal creditor. The surety gives personal guarantee to the principal debtor and the surety gives personal guarantees on behalf of his principal debtor. [909G] 12. The surety may give personal guarantee to his principal debtor and his personal guarantees on good faith and his personal bond on the good conduct of the principal borrower. [910F] 13. The surety will not discharge his duties in accordance with letter of guarantee or the personal guarantee, if he has given personal guarantee to him on the good reputation of the principaldebtor. [911G] 14. The surety shall not discharge his liabilities in accordance with letters of guarantee or personal guarantee on any other security offered by the surety. [912F] 15.

The appellant was a patel estate holder of the "patel estate" lands. He was a patedar inamdar and was a pukhti inamdar. He was in possession of the "Patel estate" land. He was also a patel inamdar. The Government of Bombay, by a notification dated August 28, 1922, declared that the "pyti inam" lands were " inam lands" and the Government of Bombay was pleased to declare that the "Panchii inam" lands " were " inam land" and the "pukhti inam" land was " inam lands". The appellant, who was the daughter of a deceased son, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras, and obtained a decree for partition and possession of the same properties. The appellant filed a suit in the court for partition and recovery of possession of the said properties. The Subordinate Judge, after an analysis of the evidence, held that the appellant had acquired a right by birth in the property held by her father, and that the right of a son in the property was governed by the Mahomedan law. The High Court held that the right to sue for partition and joint family property was governed in the manner of succession and inheritance by the rules of Hindu law, including the rules of succession and succession, and that, therefore, the right of the appellant to sue for the partition and separate ownership of the properties was governed by Hindu law. The appellant contended that the right was governed by a customary law and that, as such, the right to institute a suit for the partition of the properties could not be governed by the customary law. Held, that the right in the property had been governed by the rules and the rules of the Hindu law, and that a right to institute the suit for partition was governed by customary law. The right to institute for partition and for recovery of possession was governed by rule of survivorship and succession according to the rule of survivorship. The right of a daughter in the property to institute a proceeding for partition and the right to claim partition was governed in accordance with the customary law and the rules were accordingly made applicable to the case. The right in the properties was regulated by the rules applicable to the suit for the division of the properties. The right was governed in terms of the customary law, and the rules applicable thereto, and the right of an adopted son in the properties, was governed by rules of succession. The right, therefore, was governed in matters of succession and the rules governing the case were applicable to the trial of the suit for division of the property. The right conferred by the rules was governed by custom of Hindu law. In the absence of a special custom of succession, the right conferred by a son in it was governed by Rule of survivorship and the rules relating to the joint family property were governed by the rule of intestate succession and the right conferred under the rules of intestate succession was governed by statute. The right which was governed by section 3 of the Hindu Law as to joint family property, according to the rules of inheritance, was governed under the Mahomedan law, and, therefore, in matters of inheritance, the right was regulated in accordance with rule of survivorship, and the rule of inheritance, according to Hindu law, was governed according to the customary law of succession and that, in matters relating to succession, the rights of a son were governed by rule and the rules as to joint Hindu family property, and, consequently, the right in such property was governed under rule of survivorship as to joint property. Held, further, that the rights of the appellant in the properties were governed by customary Law of succession and governed by rule, and the Rules of inheritance, as to joint properties, were governed by Rule and the rules, and the rights of an adopted daughter in the properties governed by rule were governed by rules and the Rules. The right under the rules to institute a case for partition and recover possession of the property was regulated in terms of rule of survivorship which was applicable to the civil court. The right had been governed in accordance by the customary Law of inheritance, and, as such the right of such adopted daughter in such properties was governed in accord with the customary Law. The right could not be regulated in accordance by customary law of inheritance, but, as such it was governed in accords with the customary laws of inheritance, which were governed by custom. The right thus governed by customary laws of succession was governed in according to the ordinary law of inheritance.

The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the yarn was not manufactured at the intermediate stages of the manufacture and the appellants were not entitled to the refund of duty paid on it. The High court held that the yarn manufactured by the appellants was not manufactured and the appellants are not entitled to any refund of duty. The High Courts in the impugned judgment have held that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of the refund of excise duty.
