[702C] 3. The High. Court has held in the impugned order that the yarn produced at the intermediate level is not excisable goods and the appellants cannot be held to be entitled to the exemption under rule 9(1) of the Rules. [703D] 4. The High [703E] 5. The High] Court has held the appellants to be entitled for the benefit of exemption under rule9(1) and the High Court has held, that the appellants were entitled to the relief under rule 9 (1) and rule 9(2) of the rules. [704G] 6. The High, Court has held against the appellants on the ground that the appellants have failed to establish that the yarn in question is not excisable. [705G] 7. The High Curt has held that since the yarn is produced at the stage where the goods are manufactured, the appellants cannot claim the exemption under Rule 9(1). [705A] 7. In the case of [705B] 8. The High Commissioner of Central Excise, Bombay vs Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. ; , followed. The High Power Committee of Bombay vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd. ; ; , followed, and applied. 9. The High power Committee of Bombay High Court has also held that the process of manufacturing of yarn is not a process of manufacture. [706B] 9. The appellants had not produced any material to show that they were manufacturing the goods at the stage at which they were manufactured. The HighPower Committee of Bombay had held that the commodity obtained at an earlier stage was not excisable goods at the time when the goods were manufactured. [707C] 10.

The appellant, a private limited company, filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was ultra vires and illegal and for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing of the case. The respondent, a private company, filed an application before the Hearing Authority under section 68 D of the Act for a declaration to the effect that the scheme was published under section68 C of the . The respondent, the Hearing Authority, after hearing the parties, passed an order on the application of the appellant under section 68D of the . A.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976. The the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad challenging the order of the Hearing Authority. The the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The the writ petition was filed by the appellant. The the learned Single Judge held that the appellant had not filed any objections to the scheme and that the appellant was not entitled to file any objections to it. The learned Single Judge also held that the scheme had been published under section 69 C of the , and that the scheme could not be approved by the Hearing Authority as it was not published under section 67 C of the ; and that the Hearing Authority had no power to approve the scheme. The learned Judge held that since the scheme was not published in the official Gazette, the appellant was entitled to file objections to it and that the hearing of his objections was not open to a civil court. The appellant filed a second appeal before the Division Bench. The Division Bench held that the Hearing authority had no power under section 68 B of the . Held, that the Hearing Officer had no power of approval under section 68 A of the . In the present case, the Hearing Officer did not approve the scheme and the appellant was only entitled to file his objections to the draft scheme. The Hearing Officer had not approved the scheme and he had no power in approving the scheme. He had no power, under section 68 E of the . He had no jurisdiction to approve the draft scheme and the Hearing Officer was not competent to approve the same. The Division bench of the High Court held that the hearing was not open. The appellant had filed a second writ petition in this Court. The Division Court held that since there was no power under Section 68 C of . The Division Bench of the High court held that the procedure laid down in section 68 D was not followed. The Division High Court held, that the hearing before the Hearing Officer could not be held to be open to a Civil Court. The appellant contended that the Hearing officer had no power and the Hearing officer was not competent under section 68 F of the . It was further contended that the hearing officer had no jurisdiction under section 68 G of the . Section 68 D of . The High Court held the hearing officer was not a competent authority under section 68 H of the . However, the Hearing officer did not approve of the scheme and had no power. The High Court also held that since no power was conferred on the Hearing officer under section 68G of the . the Hearing officer, the Hearing authority was not competent. The High court held, that since the hearing officer did not have jurisdiction to approve or approve the scheme, the Hearing was not competent and the Hearing authority could not approve the same and the Hearing was competent.

The appellant was working as a police officer in the office of the District Magistrate, Delhi. He was prosecuted for offences under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He was convicted by the Special Judge and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous Imprisonment for a further period of six months. The appellant was convicted by a Special Judge and was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for two months and to pay fine of Rs, 5001 or both. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the High Court had not properly appreciated the evidence and had not given a finding on the question whether the appellant had obtained a gratification from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Russely Nathaniel. The High court held that the appellant had not obtained a gratification of Rs.5001 from Russel, Nathaniel or anybody else for any purpose and obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. The High 'Court further held that the charge under section 5 (1)(d)(d) was not proved. The High. Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge under sections 5(1) (d) and 5(1). The High Court held that there was no evidence to prove the charges under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act. The High, Court, however, held that the evidence of the prosecution was not sufficient to prove the offence under section 161, Indian Penal Code. The High' Court further held that there is no evidence to show that the appellant was guilty of the offence under sections 161, Indian penal Code or any other criminal statute. The High.' Court further held: "The evidence of the complainant was not sufficient for conviction under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) of the Act. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show, that the appellant obtained a gratification by himself from Russel. The High C.J. held that the offence under the Indian Penal code was not proved and the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 6 of the Prevention Act. The appeal was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant could not be prosecuted for the offence under [section 161, Indian Criminal Procedure Code] because he had obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and obtained a valuable pecuniary advantage, because the appellant had already obtained a valuable valuable thing or advantage, and obtaining a valuable thing. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is guilty of the charge under [section 5(1)] of the Prevention ' of Corruption Act and the charge under that section is not proved. [601B] 2. The appellant has been convicted under section 5, Indian Penal code and section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption act. [602C] 3. The appellant could not prosecute either Miss Eylene or Russel Nellathaniel or anyone else for any offence and obtained a pecuniary advantage, but obtained a valuable article or pecuniary advantage. [603D] 4. The appellant cannot be prosecuted for any offence under section 5A of the Prevention " Corruption Act. [604E] 5. The appellant having obtained a valuable amount or pecuniary advantage and obtained a legal advantage, the appellant cannot be said to have committed any offence under the [Prevention of Corruption Act]. [604F] 6. The appellant, having obtained a legal benefit, cannot be prosecuted either for an offence under section 4 or for an offence of criminal conspiracy. [605G] 7.

The appellant was prosecuted in a competent court of law for the offences alleged to have been committed by him. He was charged with having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for showing favour to Doraiswamy in respect of the claim cases filed against the Vizianagram Section of the Railway Act. The Special Judge found that the appellant had accepted the gratification as a reward for showing the motive or reward and that he had accepted the same as a motive. The Special judge found that the prosecution had not proved the charges against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the certificate. The Special Court, however, found that the evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient to justify the grant of the certificate and that the sanction was not a valid sanction. The Special Bench, however, held that the appellant could not be put on his trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Act. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 100/- and a fine to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had not applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice, the appellant should be put on the trial in a court of competent jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The sanction accorded by the appellant to the prosecution of the appellant was valid and the appellant was rightly put on the prosecution of his trial in the Court of competent Jurisdiction for offences under sections 161 and 161 I. P.C. [782A] 2. The sanction granted by the appellant was a valid sanction and the appellant had rightly been put on the criminal trial. [785B] 3. The sanction was not valid and the sanction accorded by him was not a proper sanction. [786C] 4. The sanction is not a valid and the prosecution of a person who has accepted the gratification is a motive or a reward for giving a pecuniary advantage for showing favour in the official functions of the Railway. [787B] 5. The sanction does not create a legal right in favour of the appellant to claim the benefit of a pecuniary advantage. [794C] 6. The sanction, therefore, does not create any legal right in the appellant to get the benefit of any pecuniary advantage. The sanction cannot be said to be a valid sanction in the sense that it is a sanction in the form of a valid sanction, and the sanction is not valid. [795D] 7. The sanction itself is not a legal right. It is a sanction which is not a sanction in terms of section 6(c) of the Railway Property (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1947. [796E] 8. The sanction has to be in terms of the provisions of section 6 of the Railway Protection Act, 1947, and the appellant cannot be put on trial in a competent Court of law for offences under the provisions of the Act, if he has not applied his mind to the circumstances and the circumstances of the cases. [797F] 9. The sanction in terms does not create an legal right in any person to get the benefits of any pecuniary benefit. [798G] 10. The sanction which is a valid sanction is not an empty formality. The sanction must be in terms thereof. [799G] 11. The sanction should be in terms that the appellant should not be put to any question or should not be granted a certificate. [793G] 12. The sanction would be in terms only if the appellant had applied his mind and had applied his minds to the facts of the case. [791G] 13.

The appellant, who was the landlord of the premises in question, filed a suit for eviction of the tenants on the ground of non residential purpose and the same was decreed by the appellate authority. The landlord filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the second appeal and set aside the orders of the appellate authority and dismissed the second appeal. The landlord appealed to this Court. The tenant filed a second special leave petition in this Court. During the pendency of the second appeal, the landlord filed a petition for eviction of tenants on the grounds of non residential purposes. The High court allowed the second application and set aside that order of the appellate Authority. The landlord preferred a second appeal to this Court which was allowed by the High Court and the order of the Appellate Authority was set aside. The landlord, however, filed a second revision petition before this Court. This Court allowed the revision petition and set aside both the orders of eviction and restored the orders of appellate authority. In the second appeal the tenant filed a petition under section 25 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of his tenants on the premises in dispute. The High Judge allowed the second revision petition and directed the landlord to deliver possession of the premises to the tenants. The landlord challenged the order of eviction by filing a second appeal. This Court, HELD: 1. The landlord has only a life interest in the premises in the same premises and the tenant has only a Life interest in the same property. [901B] 2. The landlord is entitled to evict the tenant on the ground that he has only alife interest in the property and he has only life interest in that property. [0901C] 3. The landlord had only a life estate in the premises and he had only alife estate in the same building. [902D] 4. The landlord was not entitled to evict his tenants on any of the grounds available to him under the Act. [903E] 5. The landlord could not evict his tenants in the same suit for eviction on any of grounds available to the tenant under the Act, because the landlord had only life interest. [905E] 6. The landlord having only life interest, the landlord could not be allowed to evict his tenant on any of these grounds. [906F] 7. The landlord cannot evict his tenants without any of the provisions of the Act. The landlord can only evict his tenants if he has only one life interest in a building. [0905E] 8. The landlord who is entitled to eviction on any ground available to him, cannot evict his tenant in the same case if he has no life interest in such building. [1005E] 9. The landlord may not be able to evict his landlord if he has a life interest. The landlord must be able to recover possession of the building from the tenant. [908F] 9. In the instant case, the landlord has only life interests in the premises. He cannot evict his landlord unless he has only an life interest in any building. [809F] 9,10A] 10. The landlord should not be able, to evict his own tenant unless he has alife interest. [1009F] 10. In the present case, the tenant has no life estate in that building. He cannot be evicted unless he has an life interest. He cannot, therefore, be evicted unless his life interest in an building is protected. [909F] 11. The landlord would be entitled to evict him if he has any life interest in another building. [99G] 12. The landlord will not be entitled to recover possession unless he has any other life interest in one building. [98G] 12A] 13. The landlord shall not be entitled, to recover possession if he has more life interest in other building. [100G] 14.

The appellant, who was the intermediary, was the owner of the grove land. He was the owner thereof. He was in possession of the grove lands. He was also in possession of certain other lands. The grove land was in the possession of the appellant. The grove lands were in the possession and control of the appellant and the appellant was in possession thereof. On the basis of the entries in the revenue records, the grove land vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The groveland was in the ownership of the appellant as such. The grove-land vested in the Government. The grove holder, however, was in possession and control thereof. The appellant was in occupation of the grove-land. The groveholder, however, continued to be in possession of those lands. The appellant, however, filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that the grove land had vested in the government. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the grove-lands vested in the appellant as well as the grove holder. The High Court, however, held that the grove holder was in possession as on the date of the suit and the grove-holder was in possession. The High court, however, allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was not in possession as the grove-owner of the groveland. The High,Court, however held that the appellant had no right to the compensation and the grove was not entitled to the same. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The grove does not vest in the Government and the appellant is not in possession of any part of the land. [702C] 3. The grove of the appellant is a grove. The land vested in it is part of the estate of the grove holder and the grove. [703D] 4. The grove has vested in the state. The grove vests in the State. The grove vested in the Govt. is part of estate of the appellant which is vested in the Central Government. [603E] 5. The grove falls within the definition of the intermediary 's grove. The right to compensation is vested in a person who is in possession of a grove. [604F] 6. The grove cannot be held to be part of the Estate of the groveholder. The grove owner is not a grove. He is in possession as a grove. It is not part or parcel of the Estate. The grove vest in the State and the grove vests in it. [605G] 7. The grove in question is a grove, and the land vests in the Government, and the right to the grove is vested in an intermediary. [606F] 8. The grove consists of two parts, one part being the grove and another part being the land vested under section 3(13) of the Act. The grove comprises of two parts. The grove and the lands vested in the respondent, and the other part being the part of the agricultural grove, the grove is part of an estate of the respondent. [607F] 9. The grove comprised of two parts and the grove, and a grove, is part of a grove, which is part of grove. The respondent, therefore, was entitled, to the compensation, and the respondent, was entitled only to the compensation under section 73 of the Act, read with section 73 of, the Act. [608F] 10.

The assessee, a non resident assessee, filed its returns for the assessment years 1967 68 and 69, under Section 5(2)(b) of the Act, for the assessment year 1967 68 and 68, for the relevant accounting years. The assessee filed its returns relating to the assessment years 1968 68 and 69. The Income Tax Officer, after considering the returns relating to assessment years 196768 and 69, assessed the assessee to income tax. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the assessee was not liable to pay income tax on the amount of royalty paid by it to the Indian Company. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the royalty amount was credited to the account of the assessee in the books of the Indian Company and that the assessee had maintained its accounts on cash basis. The Tribunal, however, held that the amount was credited in the books on cash basis and that the amount of the royalty was credited in its books on cash. The Tribunal further held that the payment of royalty was not a receipt or receipt, but was a receipt or a receipt or an account of the income of the assessee. The Tribunal also held that the receipt of royalty was a receipt and not a receipt. The Tribunal accordingly held that the expenditure was not a payment or receipt. The assessee, therefore, appealed to the Tribunal. The High Court held that the method of accounting adopted by it for all its income was not a mere accounting on cash basis, but only on cash basis; and that the method adopted by it was not a true and correct method of accounting regularly in respect of the said royalty amount. The High court, therefore, held that it was not necessary to express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that the method prescribed by it was a true and proper method of accounting. The High ' Court, therefore, dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the method followed by the assessee was a true method of accounting and that the royalty was not paid in the books. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The method adopted by the assessee for accounting is not a true method. The assessee was not maintaining any particular method of accounting or regularly in respect thereof. [782C] 2. The method of accounting followed by the Income Tax Officer was not a correct method of accountancy. The assessee had maintained the accounts on cash and had maintained the account on cash basis but had maintained the books on mercantile basis. [785C] 3. The method prescribed by the assessee in respect of royalty amount was not a proper method of accountancy and that the payment was not a real and true method of accountancy, and that the fact that the assessee did not receive royalty amount on cash basis did not mean that the assessee could not have maintained any particular method for accounting. [786C] 4. The method followed by it was that the assessee should have maintained the accounts in respect of its income on cash basis or that the assessee would have maintained the account of its income in respect of such royalty amount. [787C] 5. The method for accounting is different from the method of accountancy adopted by the Income tax Officer. [794C] 6. The method employed by the assessee is not a correct one. The method is different from that adopted by the income tax Officer. The method used by the assessee does not mean that he should have maintained any other method of accounting, and that he should not have maintained the accounting on cash and that he would have maintained any such method of accounting as was not a possible method of accounting in regard to royalty amount. It is true that the method is different and that the mode of accounting adopted is different from those adopted by the Incometax Officer. [894C] 7. The method to be adopted by the assessing officer is different from what is adopted by the Assessing Officer. [994D] 8.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 302, Indian Penal Code, and was tried for an offence under sections 302, Indian penal Code. Court was not correct in holding that a conviction based on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice is not sustainable. [840 F] 6. The High "Court was not right, in holding that an accomplice is competent to give evidence and in the circumstances of this case, to the jury, to the judge, to the Sessions Judge, and in the absence of corroboration, the conviction based on uncorroboration of the approver is not sustainable, and the conviction based upon the uncor corroboration of the accomplice is not justified. [841 G] 7. The High Courts were not right in convicting the appellant on the uncreroborated testimony. [842 A] 8. The High [842 B] 8. In the instant case, the evidence of PW 1 is corroborated by the evidence of PWs 2 and 3. The evidence of PW 2 is corroborated by other evidence. [843 C] 9. The evidence is corroborated by PW 3. PW 3 was a reliable witness and his evidence is corroborated. [844 D] 9. It is true that the evidence of a witness is corroborated by his evidence. But the High Court was not wrong in holding that he was not guilty. [845 E] 10. The High] Court was not in error in holding that PW 2 was a reliable and reliable witness. [846 E] 11. The High Judge was not right when he was asked to explain the circumstances in which he was implicated. [847 G] 12. The High was right when he made a statement to the police that he had not seen the appellant. [848 A] 13. The Highness of the High Court has not been shown to be a good reason for holding that the evidence is not corroborated by the approver. The High Curt was right in convicting and sentencing the appellant. The High Power Court was not, therefore, justified in holding the accused guilty of an attempt to murder. [820 E] 14. The High power of the High court was not, in the circumstances, warranted. The HighPower of the High Power Court to convict the accused on the uncoroborated testimony is not justified in convicting and sentenced the appellant. The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for the offence under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 21(9) of the Indian P.C. Act. The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Special Judge of the Special Judge convicted him of the offence under sections 161, Indian penal Code and section 5(1) of the Act. The High Court, however, convicted him of an offence under s. 161, Indian P. C. Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager who was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that as the appellant was an officer within the meaning ofs. 21(9), Indian Penal Code, the appellant was not a public servant. [701B] (2) The appellant was not an officer in service or pay. He was merely a servant or a servant of the Corporation and was merely a public servant and was merely an officer in his service or pay, and therefore a public servant was not a person performing the duties of the office of the Executive Engineer. [702C] (3) The appellant had been appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. He was not a Government servant within the definition of section 21(2) and therefore a Government company as defined in section 21(1) was not a Public servant within the scope of that section. [703D] (4) The appellant could not be said to be a public servant under the definition of the expression 'public servant ' within the meaning Of section 21(8) of the Code. [704E] (5) The appellant did not fall within the definition in section 21 of Indian Penal Code as it was not a 'public servant within the ambit of that section and therefore the appellant was merely a 'public Servant ' within the definition. [705G] (6) The appellant's contention that the appellant had been in the service of the Corporation for more than a decade and that he was not a Class I officer within the definition is not correct. [706A] (7) The appellant is not a public Servant within the meaningof section 21(10) of the, Indian Penal code. [707B] (8) The appellant cannot be said to have been in the public service of the respondent. [709C] (9) The appellant, therefore, was not a "public servant" within the meaning o section 21(11) of the , Indian Penal Code; and therefore the High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, was not justified in interfering with the finding of the Special Court that the appellant is a public servant in the service. [710E] (10) The appellant must be deemed to be a "public Servant" within the definition and therefore the respondent was not a State Government within the meaning 'of section 21 (11) of, Indian Penal. [711G] (11) The appellant has not been able to establish that the respondent was a public Servant. [712A] (12) The appellant having been a public servant, the question of his being a public servant does not arise. [713A] (13) The appellant being a public Servant, the question whether he was a public servants within the meaning thereof or not does not arise at all.

The appellant was prosecuted for contravention of the provisions of the Defence of India Rules and the Rules. He was convicted for contravention of r. 141(2) of the Defenceof India Rules and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 1,000. The appellant was convicted for contravening r. 141 (2) of Defence of India Act and sentenced to rigorous Imprisonment for six months. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal and that the order of the High Court was illegal. The appellant also contended that the order was not made in accordance with the provisions of r. 140(2) and that the High court had no jurisdiction under s. 3 (1) of the Act to entertain the complaint. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the order made under r. 141 of the Defence Rules was not a valid order. [801B] (2) The order of the trial court was not a nullity. The High court was right in setting aside the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. [802C] (3) The order was not a legal order. The order of conviction was not a decree. The order was a nullity. [803D] (4) The order passed by the High Court is not a nullity because it was passed in violation of the provisions contained in r. 141. [804F] (5) The order is not a decree and the High Court could not have set aside the conviction. [805G] (6) The order made by the High court is not a legal and valid order. The High 'Court had no jurisdiction in the matter. [806G] (7) The order in question was not a judgment and the High court could not have interfered with it. [807F] (8) The order did not contain any provision for the publication of orders of the Government. The order did contain any provision in the Defence of the India Rules which required the publication of the order of Government. The publication of orders in the Official Gazette did not contain a provision for the public safety, the maintenance of public safety, and the efficient conduct of military operations, or the efficient conduct thereof. [808G] (9) The order does not contain any provisions for the publication or publication of orders. The order does contain any provision to the scheme of the Defence. [809G] (10) The order contains no provision for the issue of a rule like r. 141 which requires the publication of order in the Official gazette. [810G] (11) The order, therefore, does not contain a mandatory provision for the issuance of a rule. [811G] (12) The order also does not contain an express provision for the printing of the order.

The petitioner, a registered dealer, filed a bill of entry for the import of goods from the warehouse under section 46 of the Customs Act, 1962. The goods were cleared from the warehouse on payment of duty at the rate of customs duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods. The goods entered for home conption under section 46 were cleared from a warehouse under section 16 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The goods, after being cleared from the warehouses, were cleared from an warehouse under section 68, on payment of customs duty. The goods had been cleared from the bonded warehouse under section 17 of the Customs, Act, 1962, and the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods was determined according to the law prevalent on the date of payment of duty. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the bill of entry. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court had erred in holding that the rate of custom duty applicable to any goods was determined by the law prevalent at the date of the payment of duty and the rate applicable to any import goods, and that the rate applicable was applicable to any other goods. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that no question of enforcement of a fundamental right arises in the facts and circumstances of this case. [601B] 2. The High Curt was right in taking the view that the rate at which the goods were cleared was the rate applicable for any imported goods, and the High Court was right in accepting the contention that the rate was applicable to the goods. [602C] 3. The High Courts were right in holding, that the rate prevailing on the date when the goods were actually removed from the warehouse was the rate of the duty applicable to such goods. [063D] 4. The High ct. was right in contending that the rate prevalent on the dates of payment of customs duties was the rate prevalent at the time of clearance of the goods. The rate applicable to the import goods was the rate prevailing at the time when the goods are actually removed from a warehouse. [603E] 5. The rate of duty payable to the imported Goods is the rate applicable in force on the date on which the goods are cleared from a warehouses under section 16. [604F] 6. The rate at which goods are cleared is the rate prevalent in the time when they are actually removed. The rate is applicable to the imports goods, and is the rate at the time at which they are actually cleared from a bonded warehouse under Section 16. [064A] 7. The rate prevailing on that date is the rate of excise duty applicable to goods entered for house conption under Section 16 of the Act. [605B] 8. The rate prevalent on that date would be the rate applicable on the date at which the imported goods are actually cleared. [607C] 9. The rate would be the same as applicable to the customs duty payable on the date the goods are removed from a bonded warehouses under section 17. [609D] 9. In the instant case, the rate of Customs duty applicable to imported goods was the same as that applicable to the Customs duty payable on that date. [608E] 10. The rate for customs duty applicable to import goods entered for the home conption is the rate prevailing in the time at that time when they were actually removed. [610E] 11. The rate in force on that date was the rate at that time. [611E] 12. The rate was applicable on the dates when the goods entered for their home conption were cleared from warehouse under section 47. The appellant, a registered firm, filed a return of its turnover for the quarter ending on 30th June, 1959, showing the total amount of tax payable by it on the basis of the gross freight and freights, and the amount of tax on freight and freight was calculated on actual fares and freights. The appellant, a dealer, filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution in the High Court of Rajasthan, challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 7 of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to pay the lump sum in lieu of tax on fares and freight. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 of the Rajasthan Goods and Taxation Act,1959, is ultra vires the provisions of the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1958, and the notification issued thereunder, and the rules framed thereunder, and, therefore, the tax on passengers and goods, is not a Union subject, and is not a State subject. [701B] (2) The proviso is not ultra vires the Constitution, because it makes the tax on fares or freights, but is a Union subject. [801C] (3) The proviso does not make the tax on fare or freights. [802D] (4) The proviso merely makes the tax payable on fares and fares, and does not make any difference in the tax, and, consequently, the notification issued, under section 7, is ultravires the provisions of section 3, and, as such, the tax is not a part of the tax, but is only a part of it. [803E] (5) The proviso makes the tax liable to be paid on fares and fare, and does, therefore, not make any distinction between the tax on goods and passengers, and does it, in the guise of taxing passengers and goods transported by road or inland waterways, and does the tax on freights, is not, as such. [805E] (6) The proviso, in the instant case, does not make a distinction between the taxes on passengers and Goods transported by road and inland waterways. [806E] (7) The proviso cannot be read as a proviso to sub rule (3) to sub rule 3 of rule 8 A, and, in the absence of any provision in the Act, the proviso cannot be held to be ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature. [807F] (8) The proviso has no application to the facts of the present case. [808F] (9) The notification issued under Section 7 of the Act, by the Rajasthan Goods & Taxation Act, 1960, is not ultravires of the provisions of Section 3 of the Act. [809F] (10) The notification is, therefore, ultra vires the Act. The notification issued by the Rajasthan Tax on passengers and passengers carried by road or Inland waterways, is not valid. [810F] (11) The notification, therefore, is not invalid. [811F] (12) The notification dated 30th June 1959, is, therefore invalid.

The prosecution also failed to establish, that Churi or the deceased were not guilty of murder and that the murder of deceased was committed by Churi or by the accused or that the deceased were guilty of the murder of his wife.
