The prosecution must prove that the accused left for Kotakbai in the village and that the deceased left for the house of her father. [811E] 12. The prosecution is not able to prove that the deceased, Churi and his wife were in a wet condition at the time of the occurrence. [812E] 12A] 13. The prosecution cannot, therefore, be said to have proved that the death of Churi was due to the injuries caused by the accused and that the death was due to his adulterous conduct. [813E] 14. The prosecution should not have proved that Churi died because of the injuries caused to him by the accused, but that the death had been caused by the deceased. [814E] 15.

The plaintiff 's father, the defendant, purchased a property from the defendants, under a registered sale deed dated December 18, 1951, executed by the defendants in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff claimed that the property was mortgaged to the defendants and that the defendants were entitled to the sum of Rs. 15,000 and C. The defendants denied the claim of the plaintiff and claimed that the plaintiff was entitled to the amount of Rs. 80,000 and Rs. 15000. The trial Court decreed the suit. The plaintiff appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the appeal. The plaintiff 's appeal was allowed by the High Court and the suit was dismissed. The plaintiff then appealed to this Court. The plaintiff contended that the suit had been instituted in the year 1951 and the defendants had not been able to establish that the property in question was mortgaged to them. The High court held that the plaintiff 's suit was barred by section 43 of the Contract Act and the suit had not been instituted in a mortgage suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The suit was not barred by section 42 of the Contract. The plaintiff had not established that the property had been mortgaged to the defendant. The plaintiff was entitled only to the sum payable on the mortgage. [849 D] 2. The plaintiff could not establish that the defendant had been in possession of the property. The plaintiff did not establish that he was in possession of it. [850 E] 3. The plaintiff has not established that he was entitled to any sum payable on it. The plaintiff cannot establish that he had been in the possession of the whole of the property and that he was not entitled to any amount. [852 E] 4. The plaintiff is entitled to the entire sum payable on that sum. [853 F] 5. The plaintiff must establish that he is entitled to a sum of Rs, 2,500 and C.P. No. 101 of 1950. [854 F] 6. The plaintiff, therefore, cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 82 of the Contract act. [855 F] 7. The plaintiff having failed to establish that he has been in possession, the plaintiff cannot be allowed the benefit of section 43 of Contract Act. [856 F] 8. The plaintiff failed to establish the case of subrogation in his plaint even in the alternative. [857 F] 857 F] 9. The plaintiff in his plaint has not shown that he was a subrogation. He has not shown any contract to the contrary in his plaint. [858 F] 10. The plaintiff's case is that he was liable to contribute in equal share to the extent of his share of the property in the mortgage decree.

The appellants were appointed as Asstt. Engineers (Civil) in the Public Works Department in the year 1985 and they were promoted as Asstt. Engineer (Civil) on the post of Asstt. Engineer. The appellants were selected and appointed as Asstt., Engineers (Civil). The appellants were appointed on the post in question on the basis of marks secured by them in the qualifying examination. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the selection of the appellants. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 allowed the petition and quashed the selections on the ground that the marks awarded to the appellants were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors. ; , and the appellants were bound to be selected on the basis thereof. The appellants challenged the selection on the ground of excessive marks in the qualifying examinations. The Tribunal allowed the petition holding that the marks allotted to the appellants in the qualifying examina tion were excessive and the appellants had secured much higher marks than the appellants in qualifying examination. In appeal to this Court, the appellants contended that the marks of the appellants were much higher than the marks awarded by the Selection Committee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The marks allotted to each of the appellants in interview were much higher in comparison to the marks awarded in the qualifying exam. The marks of the candidates in interview were also higher than the appellants. [801B] 2. The marks awarded to each of these candidates in interview are also higher than those awarded to the appellant in the qualifying test. The marks for interview were also much higher than those given to the appellants. In view of the fact that the marks for interview are higher than those of the appellants, the appellants were entitled to get marks for interview at the qualifying examination and the marks for viva voce out of 50 marks in the interview. [802C] 3. The marks allocated to each of such candidates in interview for the qualifying examination were also higher in comparison with the marks awarded for interview at 15% to the total marks. [803D] 4. The marks assigned to each of those candidates in interview at the interview were also lower than those given in the qualifying Examination. [804E] 5. The marks were awarded at 15% of the total marks in the written examination and the merit list was prepared according ly to the marks allotted for interview at 50 marks in interview. The marks so awarded to each candidate in interview at 15%, were also higher. [805E] 6. The marks in the viva voce out for interview at 45 marks in the competitive examination were also lower in comparison to those given in qualifying examination at 15% and the marks allotted at 15% were also higher to the total mark. [806E] 7. The marks secured by the appellants in their qualifying examination were much higher to the marks secured by each of them in the interview at 15%.

The State of Bihar, through its Inspector of Police, Ramgarh, Bihar, had been in jail for about two months. The State of Bihar had been in prison for about two years. The High Court, however, acquitted the accused persons on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish that the accused persons had been in custody for more than two months. In appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the acquittal of the accused persons and convicted them under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The High court, however, held that the prosecution has failed to establish the complicity of the accused in the murder of the Collector. The High ' Court, however held that the evidence of the prosecution was not sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court had erred in holding that the prosecution failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that there was no evidence to establish the involvement of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and the High Court was right in holding the accused guilty of the offence. [601B] 2. The High' Court was right, in holding that it was not possible to accept the criticism of the High Court that the prosecution was able to establish the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the chain had to be completed. [602C] 3. The High. Court was right when it held that the accused had been in Jail for more than one month. [603D] 4. The High, Court, however was right in not accepting the criticism of counsel for the appellant that the prosecution did not establish the complicity or the chain had been proved beyond reasonable doubt by direct evidence. [604E] 5. The High was right in the view that the prosecution could not establish the guilt beyond reasonable doubt but if the prosecution had established the guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the High ' Court was right. [605G] 6. The High "Court has to be satisfied that the circumstances proved against the accused are such that they cannot be held to be proved beyond reasonable doubts. [606E] 7. The High" Court has not committed any error in holding that a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand. [607E] 8. The High] 9. In the instant case, the High court has not found that the prosecution is able to establish that Sadanand had been in the usual way to meet Sadananda. The High Judge has not given any reason for not accepting the submission of the defence that Sadanand was in the usual manner to meet Sadan. [608E] 9. The High [608F] 10. The High is right in the present case that the prosecution cannot establish the complicity and the chain has to be completed by circumstantial evidence. [708G] 11. The High Crl. Appeal No. 627 of 1984 and 676 of 1984 are, therefore, not liable to be dismissed.

The appellant company was a factory in the State of Maharashtra. The appellant company was established in the State. The appellant was a factory under the name and style of "The Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946". The appellant company is a factory under which the appellant company was incorporated. The appellant Company was a factory. The appellant, however, was a factory within the meaning of the Bombay Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act, 1960. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the validity of that Act on the ground that the said Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High court held that the said provisions were violative of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the provisions of the Act were violative of Articles 14 and 19(1) (g) of Constitution. [701B] 2. The provisions of the Bombay Act were not violative of Articles 19(1), 19(1). The provisions of that Act were not ultra vires the Constitution. [601C] 3. The provisions were not violative either of Articles 14 or 19(1); nor were they violative of Articles 29 and 31 of the Constitution of India. [602D] 4. The provisions in the Bombay Act are not violative of Article 29(1) of the constitution. [603E] 5. The provisions are not violative either Article 14 or 19 (1) (f) of the Act. [604G] 6. The provisions contained in the Bombay Industrial Employment (Amendment) Ordinance, 1960 are not violative both Articles 14 and 31 of Constitution. The provisions relating to the fixation of minimum wages and dearness allowance are not violative, either of Articles 29 or 31 of the constitution, as the case may be. [605G] 7. The provisions regarding fixation of minimum wage and dearness allowance for factory workmen are not violative under Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, as the maximum and the maximum and that the maximum and minimum wages and the maximum are higher than 15 months as the maximum. [607A] 8. The provisions for fixation of minimum rates of dearness allowance for factories workmen are not in conflict with Articles 14 and 311 of the Constitution as the maximum is higher than 15 days as the maximum or the minimum. [608B] 9. The provisions under the Bombay Act do not violate either of Articles 19 or 31 of Constitution, as they are not violative. [609C] 10. The provisions do not violate both Articles 14 or 31 of [609D] 11. The provisions made in the Bombay Acts are not violative by Article 14 or 16 of the constitution as the maximum, but the maximum and maximum are higher. [610E] 12.

The Rajinama was granted by the Rajinama in favour of one of the mortgagees, Shiddappa, the father of the mortgagees. The Rajinama granted the mortgage in favour of the mortgagees and the mortgagees. In the meantime, the mortgagees filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge of Chikodi for redemption of the mortgage. The trial Court decreed the suit and the High Court decreed the plaintiffs 's suit. The plaintiffs appealed to this Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. The High court held that the Rajinamama had not the effect of transferring the interest of Annappa 's share in the mortgaged property. The plaintiffs' case was that the Raj inama had not been executed by Shiddappa and Annappa. The High ' Court held that the plaintiffs' case that the Rajamama had executed by Shudappa and Anappa was binding on the mortgagees and that the mortgagees had not the right to do so, and that the plaintiffs had not the rights to do so. The High' Court further held that the appellants had not the capacity to execute the mortgage deed and that the mortgage was not a valid one. The High. Court further held, that the Rajimama had not executed the mortgage deed, and that, therefore, the plaintiffs' claim to the right to redeem the mortgage was barred by section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Rajimama was not a registered occupant. The Raj inama was not the registered occupant. [701B] 2. The Rajmaama had not only the right to sell the mortgaged property but also the right to transfer the interest of the mortgagees in the mortgaged properties. The Rajamama was not only the registered occupant but also the mortgagee. [702C] 3. The Rajnama had not conferred any interest in the mortgaged land. The Rajmama had not created any interest in favour of Annaappa. [703D] 4. The Rajnaama had not given any notice to the mortgagees. [704E] 5. The Rajiniama had not assigned any interest in respect of the mortgaged property to the mortgagees and, therefore, there was no question of the plaintiffs ' acquiring any interest in them. [705E] 6. The Rajniama had not transferred any interest in her favour to the mortgagees nor had she executed any document in favour of any other person. [706E] 7. The Rajiama had not acquired any interest in his favour. [707E] 8. The Rajaniama had not vested any interest in him. The Rajiaama had not obtained any interest in any other person, nor had he executed any document. The Rajinaama had not lost any interest in it. [709F] 9. The Rajanaama had not terminated the mortgage by adverse possession. The Rajenaama had not taken any interest in that property. [708G] 10. The Rajappaama had not exercised any right in favour of anyone other than the mortgagees. It was not a case of a relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers. [710G] 11. The Rajannaama had not relinquished any interest in regard to the mortgaged property and, therefore the plaintiffs ' rights of both of them were extinguished. [711G] 12. The Rajmaniama had not surrendered any interest in relation to the mortgaged properties and, therefore there was no relinquishment of the right of both the parties. [712G] 13. The Rajmanama had not extinguished any interest in property. [813G] 14. The Rajamaniama had not become extinguished by the mortgage. [713G] 15. The Rajviama had not redeemed any interest in land. The plaintiffs had not acquired the right of either of them.

The respondent, a registered dealer, filed a return of turnover for the period from July 1, 1966 to June 31, 1966, showing the turnover of carbon paper as Rs. 1,000/=. The Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, assessed the turnover of the carbon paper as under item No. 2 of the Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1947, at the rate of 5 per cent. The Sales tax Officer, Kanpur assessed the turnover at the rate 5 per cent, but the Sales Tax Officer assessed the turnover as under item Nos. 2 and 3 of the Schedule. The Salestax Officer, Kanpur held that the carbon paper was not a part of the typewriter and therefore, the turnover of a typewriter was not liable to be assessed at the rate specified in the Schedule to that Act. The Sales Officer, Kanpur also held that the turnover of Rs. 1.000/= was not liable for payment of tax at the rate mentioned in the Schedule. On appeal, the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Kanpur, upheld the order of the Sales Tax officer, Kanpur, and held that the dealer was not a dealer within the meaning of the word 'paper ' in the First Schedule to the Act. The High Court, in appeal, set aside the order of assessment and held that since the carbon paper in question was not a paper, the turnover was liable to be taxed at the rate prescribed in the Schedule and the Sales Tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'paper' in the First schedule to the Act is not defined in the Act or the Rules. The word "paper" in the First and Second Schedule to the Rules is not defined either in the Act nor in the Act. [849C] 2. The word used in the First or Second Schedule to that Schedule is not defined anywhere in the Act and therefore, it is not a part or aero plane or a part of aero plane. [850C] 3. The word ''paper ' in entry 18 of the Schedule is not used in the sense in which it has been understood in common parlance or in the common parlance. The word "'paper" in entry 18 is not defined therein. [852C] 4. The word `paper' in entry 18 has not been defined in the statute. The word has not been used in the Act but in the sense which it has in common parlance and in the common sense. [853D] 5. The word is used in the context of the Act and the Rules. [854E] 6. The word must be understood in the popular sense and in the popular meaning. The word should be understood in common sense. The word may be understood in popular sense and it has to be understood in commercial sense. [954F] 7. The word cannot be understood in ordinary parlance. The dictionary meaning is that the word must be construed in the popular or in the popular parlance. The words must be understood according to the popular or common sense. It must be understood to be understood according the popular or popular sense. [1054F] 8. The word in popular sense must be understood by the popular or the common sense in the popular and common sense. In popular sense, the word must have been understood in the common legal sense. [1154F] 9. The word can be understood in a popular sense and the word must mean in the popular, or common sense in a popular or common parlance. [1155F] 9: The word 'in popular sense must mean in popular sense. The dictionary must be understood as understood in the commercial sense. The words should be understood according that the popular or trade sense must mean that in popular sense, in popular sense or in the commercial or trade sense. [1255F] 10: The word "in popular sense" must mean in commercial or trade parlance. [1256F] 10.

The appellant was employed in a factory at Amroha at the relevant time. He was transferred to another concern at Amroha on February 2, 1955. He was employed by the owners of the Mills at Amroha on a contract of service and was employed by them at Amroha on the same lines at Amroha. He was also employed by the respondents 1 to 4 in the same concern at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 3 were employed by the appellant at Amroha on an identical contract of service. The appellant was employed by respondents 1 to4 in the same factory at Amroha on March 2, 1955 and was also employed at Amroha on that day. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad challenging the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of the State Industrial Tribunal was illegal and void as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The appellant also contended that the respondents 1 and 4 were not employees of the appellant and that the order was illegal and invalid. The appellant further contended that the State Industrial Disputes (Tribunal) Act, 1951 was not applicable to the appellant and the order of dismissal was illegal. The appellant raised a preliminary objection that the order passed by the State Industrial Tribunals was illegal and bad as it did give rise to a substantial question of fact. The High court held that the order made by the State Government was illegal and was not a substantial question. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High court.

The appellant company was incorporated under the provisions of the Act and the appellant company was registered under the provisions thereof. The appellant company was a registered company under the provisions Of the Act. The appellant Company was registered under section 3 of the Act. It was registered under that Act. The company was registered as a company under the Act. Its objects were to provide for the welfare of the employees and for the benefit of the employees. The appellant was registered under a Central Act and its objects were to be given to the employees in the case of factories or establishments situate in areas in which the provisions of Chapter IV were to apply. The appellant, however, did not receive the benefits of the scheme. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Act was not a fee and it was not a tax and that it was not an income tax. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Act is a fee and not a fee. It is a fee. The Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service or the provision thereof. It does not contemplate that the contribution under Chapter V A is a fee but it is a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. [901F] 2. The Act provides for the manner of insurance of all the employees in a factory or establishments situate within a radius of five miles from the place of work. The Act also provides for the mode of insurance of the employees in such factories or establishments. [902F] 3. The Act, therefore, does not contemplate a fee. [903F] 4. The Act has no provision for the manner in which the contribution is to be paid. The Act cannot be said to be a fee. There is no provision for payment of special contribution under Chapter IV A. [904F] 5. The Act merely provides for the payment of special contributions to be made by the employer under Chapter VA. The Act only provides for the form of special contribution to be paid by the employer. The Act itself provides for the levy of special contribution. The Act makes no provision for any payment of special Contribution. [905F] 6. The Act confers a special contribution to the employees. It does no fix any special contribution. It does neither fix any special contributions nor does it fix any special liability. [906F] 7. The Act gives a special contribution. [907F] 8. The Act contains a special contribution and it does not contemplate any payment of any special contribution to any employee. The Act prescribes a special contribution which is a fee, and does not contemplate payment of any contribution. [0905F] 9. The Act further provides for the procedure for the payment by an employer. The scheme does not contemplate special contribution. There is a special contribution, and it does no fix special contribution. Therefore, the Act does not envisage special contribution. In the absence of any special provision for the payment, the Act cannot be held to be a tax.

The petitioners were appointed as daily rated workmen in the establishment of the respondent No. 2 on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workmen. They were appointed on the basis of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme. The respondent No. 1 was appointed on the post of daily rated workmen on the basis that they are surplus to the requirement of the Project. The petitioners were appointed on daily rated workmen and they were paid their daily rated workmen. The respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were appointed on a consolidated remuneration of Rs. 10,29,40,583. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the petitioners on the ground of their being surplus to the requirements of the Project and the High Court allowed the writ petition. The High Court held that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the Voluntary retirement Scheme and directed their absorption. The High court held that the scheme was framed by the respondent No 2 and the petitioners were entitled to the benefits of the Voluntary Retire ment Scheme. The High C ourt held that the Scheme was framed by respondent No.2 and the petitioners are entitled to the same benefits. The High c ourt further held that the respondent No2 was not entitled to get the benefit of voluntary retirement scheme. The High Cou rt further held that there was no question of absorption of the petitioners and the question of absorption was not a matter of right. The High tution of the petitioners was not justified. The High n ourt further directed that the petitioners should be absorbed in the establishment. The High Co urt allowed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court was in error in holding that the scheme framed by the High C ommissioner was not a scheme framed by respondent Nos.2 and 3 and that the High Cour t was in error. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme framed by respondents 2 and 3 is not a scheme of voluntary retirement and the petitioners cannot claim the benefit of this scheme. [801B] 1.2 The scheme is not a Scheme framed by the respondents 2 and3. The petitioners are not entitled to any benefit of the scheme. [901C] 1.3 The High Court was right in holding that there was a scheme framed for the absorption of the employees. [902D] 1.4 The High Court has committed a manifest error in holding the petitioners to be entitled to the relief of regularisation of their services. [903E] 1.5 The High Court committed a manifest illegality in holding that in view of the scheme framed for absorption of the appellants, the High Court had committed a manifest mistake in holding that they were not entitled for the benefit of regularisation of the services. [0901F] 1.6 The High Court had not committed any error in holding otherwise. [905F] 1,601F] 2.1 The High Court in the impugned judgment has not committed any manifest error in directing the appellants to absorb the respondents on the basis o f the scheme framed. [906F] 2,01F] 3.2 The High Court, in the impugned order, has not committed a manifest mis-appreciation of the evidence and has not given a finding that the appellants were not entitled on the basis on which the High Court has given a finding. [907F] 3,01F G] 3.3 The appellants were not regular employees and they were not given any work for a long time. The High Courts have committed a manifest errors in holding that their services were not available for absorption. [908F] 3:1.4 The appellants were never appointed on a regular basis. They were not paid any salary in spite of the fact that they were never appointed. [909G] 3.5 The appellants were neither regular employees nor they were paid any salary.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for a declaration that the sale deed exhibit 12(i) was illegal and void and that the sale was not legal and valid. The trial Court decreed the suit. The plaintiffs appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs filed a second appeal to this Court. The plaintiffs contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the second appeal and that the High court had no jurisdiction in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court had jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal. [601B] 2. The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain an appeal under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [602C] 3. The High courts have jurisdiction to try the second appeal. The High 'Court has no jurisdiction to try a second appeal under section 101 of the Code. [603D] 4. The High. Court has no jurisdiction in a second appeal and the High Court has no power to entertain a third appeal. [063E] 5. The High, Court has no authority to entertain a suit for declaration that the transaction was not genuine. [604F] 6. The High' Court has no inherent jurisdiction to entertain such a suit. The High Curt has no jurisdiction under section 100 to entertain a Second appeal. [ 605E] 7. The High [605G] 8. The High] Court has no such jurisdiction. [605F] 9. The High Commissioner of Madras, Madras and Madras High Court had jurisdiction to try such a suit and the High court has no jurisdiction. [ 605G] 9. In the instant case, the High Court was not justified in holding that the sale under exhibit 12(1) was not genuine and that the mortgage was not genuine, and that the transaction did not affect the title of the plaintiffs to the extent of 2/2 as the mortgage was made out. [606E] 10. The High Power of Attorney executed by the plaintiffs in favour of Pir Baksh was not produced before the trial Court. The sale deed exhibit 13(i) is not a genuine document. The sale was not made in accordance with the provisions of the Crown Grants Act and the High Power of attorney was not produced. [607F] 11. The High was right in holding that Pir Bush was not the real owner of the property conveyed under exhibit 12 (i) and that the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for a declaration in respect of the entire interest effected by him under exhibit 12. [608F] 12. The High power of attorney executed by the appellants in favour of respondent No. 1 was not produced in the trial Court and the High Curt was justified in holding otherwise.

The appellant, who was charged with an offence under section 173 of the Code, was charged with the offence of criminal breach of trust, and was convicted by the learned Sessions Judge, Karimnagar, under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the conviction and sentence of the appellant, and convicted him, under section 304B of the Indian penal Code, and, sentenced him to imprisonment for one year. The appellant, who is the accused, filed a revision petition before the High Court, which was dismissed. The High court, however, held that the provisions of section 173(4) of the Code were not applicable to the case before it, and that the provisions were not complied with. The High, Court, however, allowed the revision petition, and set aside the conviction and sentences of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended, that the provisions contained in section 173(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, were not applicable, and that, in any event, the provisions of sections 173(1), 173(4), and 207A of the Code had not been complied with. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 207A of Criminal Procedure Code are not applicable to cases before the court of sessions, and the trial has not been vitiated by the non compliance with the provisions of the Code. [701B] 1.2. The provisions contained in sections 173(4)(b) and 207A are not applicable, as the provisions of Sections 173(1)(b) or 207A of Cr.P.C. are not applicable. [702C] 1.3. The provisions relating to the trial before the court, are not applicable in the case before them, and, therefore, the trial before a Sessions Judge, is vitiated by the irregularity of non compliance with sections 173(2) and 207(4) (b) of the Cr.P,C. [703D] 1.4. The provisions regarding the trial before an Sessions Judge, are not mandatory, and, as such, the trial is vitiated by non compliance with section 207A. [704E] 1.5. The provisions in section 173 of Cr. P.C. apply to the case, before the court. [705E] 1, 3.1.2. In the instant case, the appellant was charged with offences under sections 173(3) and 207 of the Code and, therefore. the provisions of Section 173(1A) of the code were not applicable. The provisions were not applicable in respect of the trial before it, but were mandatory, and the irregularity of noncompliance with the provisions was curable by reference to section 173(2). [705G] 1.6. The provisions, in section 173, were not complied, and, in the instant case the trial before court, was vitiated by the failure of justice. [707E] 1.(a) The provisions of sections 207A and 207A were not applicable and, therefore the trial before Court was vitiated by non comply with the provisions. [708E] 1(b) The provisions were, therefore, not applicable to a case before the court and, therefore,. the trial before such court was vitiated by a non compliance with those provisions. [807E] 2.1.3.1.1. In the present case, the trial court had not committed any irregularity of non comply with sections 173 and 207A. The High Curt, therefore, committed a serious irregularity of non complying with the provisions contained therein. [709E] 2.(a) In the instant cases, the trial had not been vitiated, and, consequently, the trial was vitiated by an irregularity of non observance of sections 173 and 209A.

The respondent Municipality had issued a notice under section 153A of the Act to the appellant requiring him to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in question. The respondent Municipality filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Bombay praying for a writ of mandamus directing the respondent Municipality to forthwith stop the discharge of effluent in question and to direct the respondent Municipality not to proceed with the discharge of effluents in question. This petition was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant filed a petition in the High court of Bombay praying that the respondent Municipality should be directed to take immediate action to prevent the discharge of untreated effluents in question and that the respondent should be directed not to proceed further with the discharge. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct the Municipality to proceed with a discharge of untruction in question and, therefore, the High Court should not have issued a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Special Officer. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was not justified in issuing a writ of prohibition against the Municipality from proceeding with the discharge in question. [701B] 2. The High Courts were right in holding that the respondent was not entitled to the relief sought for by the appellant. [702C] 3. The High 'Court had no jurisdiction under article 226 to issue a writ of Mandamus directing the respondent to arrange for discharge of untres in question. It was open to the High Court to issue a mandamus directing the Municipality to forthwith proceed with the discharging of untreating effluents in question, and to direct that the respondent shall arrange for the performance of the said duty in question. In the present case, the High court had no jurisdiction. [703D] 4. The High' Court had no power to direct the municipality to proceed with an enquiry into the matter. [704E] 5. The High. Court had no authority to direct the appellant to arrange for discharging of untres. The High, Court had no such power to direct that a nuisance in question be created in question. There was no question of the High Court having no jurisdiction to issue a direction to the Municipality to arrange for payment of the expenses incurred by the Municipality in question.

The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. He was convicted under section 3(1) of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both. The appellant was convicted under sections 3(1)(a) and 3(1). He was sentenced to imprisonment of one year and a fine of Rs. 500. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution was not called upon to prove that the articles in question were not the property of a railway administration and that the articles were not the goods of a railway Administration. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has not been able to prove that articles in question belonged to a particular railway administration. [901 A] 2. The prosecution must prove that the goods of the kind were actually used by a railway administration. The prosecution is not called upon at all to prove that they were not the articles in the railway administration. It is only when the prosecution is not calling upon to prove the identity of the articles in a railway administration that the articles are not the property belonging to a particular Railway administration. [1001 B] 3. The prosecution cannot be successfully launched against a person in possession of the same. [902 C] 4. The prosecution failed to prove that any article in question was the property of the railway administration and the articles in dispute were not the properties of a railway department. [903 D] 5. The prosecution had failed to prove the existence of any fact that the articles belonged to a railway administration or that they were used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. [904 D] 6. The prosecution was not required to prove that these articles were used or were intended to be use in the construction or operation of a railway, because they were not used or intended for the construction, operations or maintenance of railway stores. [905 E] 7. The prosecution could not prove that the article in question belonged not to any particular railway administration but to any particular Railway administration and that it was necessary to establish that the articles had been used or intended by a railway Administration in the construction and operation of a Railway. [906 F] 8. The prosecution did not prove that these items were used or meant to be used for the construction or maintenance of the railway stores. The prosecution, therefore, could not prove the existence or absence of any such fact. [908 G] 9. The prosecution proved that the articles which were used or used for the purpose of construction or maintenance were not the same as those which were used for the purposes of construction or operation or maintenance. [909 A] 9. In the instant case, the prosecution has not proved that the article was used or intended in the construction of a railway stores. It is not necessary to prove that those articles were used in the execution of a railway store. [910 A] 9 A.C.I./651 A.C., A.C.'s case, referred to.

The appellants were tenants in the demised premises. They were inducted into the demised premises by the respondent on the basis of a lease deed executed by them in their favour on May 1, 1964. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants on the ground that the appellants had been in possession of the demised premises for a period of 11 months from May 1, 1965 to the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The respondent contended that the appellants were in possession of a part of the demised property and that the respondent was entitled to remain in possession of it as on the date of his tenancy as on the expiry of the contractual tenancy. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had been in occupation of the demised shop as on the appointed date of the filing of the suit and that the appellants are entitled to remain the tenants in the tenanted premises. The respondent preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellants have no right to continue in possession of their demised premises as on the death of the tenant and that the tenancy rights in respect of the demised land governed by the Act are heritable and that the heirs of the tenant are entitled to enjoy the protection of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The tenancy rights in the demised property are heritable and the heirs of a tenant are entitled only to remain in the tenanted property governed by the provisions of the Act and the heirs in the tenancy rights are entitled to retain the same as on the demise of the tenant. [901B] 1.2. The tenancy right in the demised land is governed by the Transfer of Property Act and the tenancy rights of the tenant in respect of a commercial tenancy are heritable and are heritable. [902B] 1.(a) The tenancy rights are heritable and they are governed by the law of the land. [903B] 1(b) The tenancy right is governed by section 13(1) (a) to (k) and other provisions of the Transfer of Properties Act. [905C] 1.(c) The tenancy is governed by Section 13(1)(a) to(k) and the heirs are entitled to continue in the tenanted shop as on that date. [906D] 1.(d) The tenancy was not heritable and the legal position of the tenant was not changed in the case of the tenancy rights. [907E] 1.(e) The tenancy vested in the tenant was governed by the Rajasthan Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 and the heirs were entitled to remain as on the said date. [096E] 1.3. The tenancy was governed by Section 12(1)(b) of the Rajasthan Premises Rent Act, 1956. The tenancy vested on the tenant was in the capacity of a tenant and the heirs had become entitled to remain on the said premises. [908F] 1.(f) The tenancy continued to be governed by the Rent Act,1956. [909F] 1.4. The tenancy is not heritable and is governed by any law of the Land. [910F] 1(g) The tenancy continues to be governed under the Rajasthan Premises (Rent) Act, 1956, and the heirs have become entitled to continue to remain in occupation of such premises. [1010F] 2.(a) In the instant case, the tenancy was governed under the provisions of Section 12(2) of the Act, and the legal heirs were entitled under the provisions to remain in their possession as on the day of the tenancy. [911F] 1 (b) The relationship of landlord and tenant is governed by a statute and the heirs cannot be equated with the heirs of tenant. [1011F] 2.1.2.3.1.3.2.1.4.1.1.5.1.6.1.7.1.8.1.9.1.

The appellant Board was established in the year 1966. The appellant Board was a public limited company. The appellant was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company was incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1956 and the appellant Board was incorporated under that Act. The appellant, a company incorporated in the year 1956, was incorporated under section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The appellant Company was incorporated under a special statute. The appellant filed a petition under section 33 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, for the enforcement of the terms of the agreement. The appellant contended that the agreement was a contract of service and that the terms of service were not binding on the appellant. The appellant also contended that the terms and conditions of service were binding on the Board and that the appellant Board had no authority to make any payment to the Government. The appellant 's contention was that the agreement did not come into force and that the Government had no authority under section 64 to make any provision for payment of interest to the Government and that the Board was not bound to make any deduction from the amount of interest payable to the Government by the appellant. Held, that the agreement in question was a contract for service and that it was a contract in the nature of a contract for the service and that there was no question of any deduction from that amount of interest. The agreement was a statutory obligation and was a definite proportion of the amount of the interest payable to Government. The agreement did not fall within the definition of a contract of the service. The agreement in question did not come within the definition. The agreement, therefore, was a contract between the appellant and the Government. It was a statutory contract and the appellant was not bound by the provisions of section 64 to pay interest to the Board. The agreement does not come within that definition. The appellant is not entitled to any relief under section 64 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1952. The agreement is a contract between a company and the Government and it is a statutory obligation. The agreement cannot be construed as a contract of employment. The agreement between the appellant Board and the Government is a statutory contract. The agreement has to be read as a contract between an individual and the Government, and it is not a contract of appointment. The agreement must be read as an agreement between the Government and the individual and the individual. The agreement can be read as contract of service. The contract of service is a statutory one. The agreement would be binding on the individual and it is an agreement between an individual to the Government, which is a statutory agreement. The agreement may be read as one of the terms and condition of service. It is not a statutory contract of employment, but it is an arrangement between the Government, the individual and its individual. The contract is a statutory arrangement. The agreement which is a contract of engagement is a statutory document. The agreement therefore, cannot be construed to be a contract of services. The agreement itself is a statutory instrument. The agreement also does not come under the definition of contract of employment and the agreement cannot be interpreted to be a statutory contract for employment. The contract cannot be construed in the absence of a detailed examination of the financial capacity of the Board. It is a statutory scheme. The agreement clearly shows that the Board is bound to make a provision for payment to the Board and the amount to be taken into account in calculating the profits. The agreement further shows that the amount to which the Board is to be taken in working out the profits is not borne out by the provisions. The agreement shows that the Government has to make a deduction from the profits. It is true that the Government is bound to pay the Board and it is bound to take credit for any subventions from the State Government. But the agreement does not say that the Board should extend the benefits to the Government servants who are on deputation.

The appellant husband filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of 1973 for maintenance from the respondent husband. The respondent husband filed a suit for maintenance against the appellant husband. The appellant husband filed an application for maintenance from her husband. The trial court dismissed the application. The High Court held that the appellant husband was not entitled to maintenance from her. The High court held that the respondent husband was not a 's wife and the appellant husband had contracted a second marriage with another woman and, therefore, the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 of Code of 1973 was not applicable. The High Courts held that the second proviso was not applicable to the facts of the case. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant husband that the second Proviso to sub section 3 of section 125 was not applicable because the appellant husband did not have a cause of action for refusing to live with her husband. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The second proviso to section 125 of Cr.P.C. is applicable to the case. The second Proviso to section 125 is applicable to cases where the husband has contracted a second wife or taken a mistress before the amendment made in section 488 of the Code. [801B] 2. The second and the third proviso to sub rule (3) are applicable to cases in which the husband has committed a breach of the second proviso. [802C] 3. The second provision of section 125 is not applicable to cases of maintenance. The second part of the second Proviso is applicable to a case where the husband contracted a second or third marriage with another lady. [803D] 4. The second limb of the second and the fourth proviso to sub clause (3) is applicable to matrimonial cases where the wife contracted a second and third marriage with a woman. [804E] 5. The second ground for refusing to maintain the wife 's refusal to live with the husband is a ground for refusal to live. [805F] 6. The second point for refusing to keep the wife ' s refusal to live in a situation where the husband had contracted second marriage with a lady. [820G] 7. The second contention is that the second and third provisos to sub section 2 of section 125 are not applicable to matrimonial proceedings. [806F] 8. The second question is whether the second proviso is applicable to proceedings under section 125. [807F] 9. The second objection is that the first proviso to sub Section 2 of section 488 of Cr. P.C. does not apply to matrimonial proceedings under section 488 of Code of 1898. [808G] 9. In the instant case, the second and fourth provisos to sub Section 3 of section 488 are not applicable. [809G] 10. The second submission is that the proviso to sub sections 2 of section wife 's second and third proviso to section 488 of C.P. C.P., is not applicable because there is no intention on the part of the husband to refuse to live with him. [810H] 11. The second alternative submission is that there is no legal necessity for the wife to live with a husband. [811G] 12. The second argument is that the wife has contracted a third marriage with the husband and the second marriage with the wife is not a ground for refusing the wife to keep the husband with a wife. [812H] 13. The second additional submission is that section 488 of Criminal P. C. is applicable only to matrimonial proceedings and not to matrimonial proceedings because there is a clear intention on the parts of the husband that he should live with him and that the second marriage should be refused to live with his wife. [820H] 14. The second further submission is that in view of the second alternative submission, the second alternative is not applicable.

The plaintiff was the owner of the land in question. The Municipal Board of Bhavnagar had been given the land in the capacity of the plaintiff as the owner of that land. The plaintiff had not shown the possession of the land as claimed by the Municipality. The plaintiff, therefore, claimed that the land was not vested in the Municipality. He also claimed that the Municipality had been given possession of the lands as the owner thereof. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The plaintiff appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the plaintiff had not proved that the land in Rasala Lines was not vested with the Municipality and that the Municipality was not entitled to retain the land as the owner. The High court, however, held that the Municipality could not be said to be in possession of the plaintiff. The High C ourt, however, reversed the decree of the Trial Court and decreed the suit of the plaintiff holding that the Municipality is not entitled to the land as owner. The plaintiff has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in holding that the land is vested in the Municipal Board of the Bhavnagar Municipality. [701B] 2. The High Cou rt has erred in holding, that the Municipality has been given the possession of land as the land in that capacity. [702C] 3. The High c ourt has erred in reversing the decree of Trial Court. [703D] 4. The High rity of the High Court has erred in not considering the question of title of the Municipality to the land in issue. [704E] 5. The High tution of the State of Saurashtra was not correct. The State of Saurashtra had not disputed the title of the plaintiff to the land. The State Government had not disputed that the land had vested in the State Government. [705E] 6. The High n ourt has failed to consider the question of ownership of the land. [706F] 7. The High Co urt has erred by holding that the State Government had no right to retain the lands as owner. [707F] 8. The High R urt has failed to appreciate the fact that the State of Gujarat had not disputed title of the State Government to the land and the suit was not barred by limitation. [708F] 9. The High Tr i nterim of Saurashtra was a State Government and the State of Bhavnagar Municipality was not a State Government. The State had not disputed its title to the land by the Municipality and the suit had been filed by the plaintiff. [709G] 10. The High j udgment of the High court is not correct. [710G] 11. The High Way of Saurashtra was an autonomous body and the State Government was not a Government Department. The State was not a body corporate. The State Legislature had no power to make laws in respect of the autonomous body. [711G] 12. The State legislature had no power under the Constitution to make laws for the autonomous body in respect of autonomous bodies. The State has no power to legislate in respect of a autonomous body. The State is not a body which is a body corporate and the State Legislature has no power under Article 226 of the Constitution to legislate in regard to the autonomous body and it is only a body which can be said to have been constituted by the State Legislature. [712G] 13. The State cannot be said to possess any power to legislate on the autonomous body which is not a State Legislature. The State can not be said not to possess any authority to legislate in the autonomous body for the autonomous bodies. [713G] 14. The State could not be held to be a State Legislature because the State Legislature had not only the power to legislate but also the power to make law in regard to autonomous bodies.

The appellant was appointed as a "officer in the service of the Government" in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was performing a public duty entrusted to him by the Government. He was, therefore, a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was, therefore. a public servant. The appellant, however, was appointed as "officer in his service" in the Railways Workshop at Ajmer and he was, therefore a public servant under the Government. The appellant challenged the order of the Judicial Commissioner before the High Court of Bombay. The High Court held that the appellant was a public servant and therefore, he was not a public servant as defined in section 21(2) of the Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The appellant was not a "officer" within the meaning ofs. 21(9). The appellant was a "officer". [601 A] (2) The appellant had been appointed as a 'officer in the Railway Workshop at Ajmer. He was not a 'officer" within s. 21(2). [601 B] (3) The appellant, therefore, was not a person within the meaning Of section 21(1) of the Railway Act. [601 C] (4) The appellant is not a public officer within the meaningof section 21(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [602 D] (5) The appellant's appointment as a "Officer" in the railway Workshop at Ajmer was not a Public servant within the definition of section 21 (9) of Act II of 1947. [603 E] (6) The appellant did not fall within the definition under section 21(4) of the General Clauses Act. [613 A] (7) The appellant could not be said to be a public servant for the purposes of the Indian Railway Act. The definition of the word "officer" in section 21 (2) of Act 2 of 1947 is not applicable to the appellant. [605 C] (8) The appellant cannot be said to have been a public servant in the Railway Establishment at Ajmer. [606 D] (9) The appellant has been appointed as "Officer" under section 21 (1) of Act 11 of 1947. The appellant is, therefore, not a public Servant within the meaning o section 21(7) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. [650 A] (10) The appellant being a public servant, the appellant was not an officer within the definition. [650 B] (11) The appellant having been appointed as an officer in the Railway Hospital at Ajmer, he was, in the circumstances, not a "Officer within the meaning" of section 21 of the Indian Railways Act. [625 C] (12) The appellant must be held to be a "officer within the meaning "of section 21 (8) of Act 1 of 1947. He was a public Servant and was, therefore not a public servants within the meaning. of section 21. [650 C] (13) The appellant does not fall within any of the terms of section 21 and therefore, the appellant is not an officer in service of the Railway Hospital. [650 D] (14) The appellant would be a public Servant under the Government and he was not an "officer" under section 2 of the Indian Police Act. [600 C] (15) The appellant in the instant case was not a Government servant within the ambit of section 21 read with section 21(6) of the Railways Act. The order of the Railway Board dated October 10, 1954, was, therefore bad in law. [650 E] (16) The appellant who was a public servants under the Government was not a servant within the terms of the definition of the expression "officer" as defined in the Indian Penal code.

The Respondent filed a suit against the Appellants for recovery of the amount due to the Appellants from the Appellants. The Respondent filed a written statement in the said suit. The Appellants denied the liability of the Respondent to pay the amount due under the said Act. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the decree was confirmed in appeal. The Respondent preferred an appeal to the District Judge, Patiala. The First Appellate Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree passed by the Trial Court. The Respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the Appeal and set aside decree passed by both the Courts. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Respondent was not liable to pay the money due under the Act. [601B] 2. The Respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code. [602C] 3. The Respondent had not paid the amount due in the said proceedings. The Respondent could not be said to be in arrears of rent. The Respondent did not pay the amount in arrears of the rent. The Appellants were not entitled to any relief. [603D] 4. The Respondent is not entitled to recover the amount due from the Appellants in the said proceeding. [604E] 5. The Respondent has not paid the rent. He is not entitled for the benefit of sub section (2) of section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [605E] 6. The Respondent having not paid the arrears of rent, the Appellants are not entitled to get the benefit of section 30(2) of the Code and the Respondent is not liable to be evicted from the premises. [606F] 7. The Respondent, therefore, is not entitled under section 30(1) of the Act to recover the arrears of the arrears of rents. [607F] 8. The Respondent cannot be said to have paid the arrears due in the proceedings. [609G] 9. The Respondent in the present case was not entitled for any relief. The Respondent's suit was not barred by the proviso to section 60 of Code. [06F] 10. The Respondent being a judgment debtor, the Respondent was entitled to recover arrears of rent from the Appellants and the Respondent was liable to pay rent. [608F] 11. The Respondent would not be entitled to recover any arrears of rent due in the proceeding. [06G] 12. The Respondent must be deemed to be in arrear of rent. [06H] 13. The Respondent can not be said not to be in defaulter. [610G] 14. The Respondent contended that the Appellants were not in arrears of rents and the Respondent had not been able to pay the arrears of arrears of rent and the Respondent could not recover the arrears due from the Appellant. [611G] 15. The Respondent also contended that the Respondent had paid the arrears in arrears of taxes due in the year 1968. The Respondent submitted that the Appellants had not paid arrears of rent in the year 1969. The Respondent further contended that the arrears of taxes were not due in the years 1968 and 1969. The Appellants contended that the respondent was not entitled under the proviso to subsection (1) to section 60 to recover arrears due in 1968. [612F] 16. The Respondent therefore, contended that the appellants were not entitled under sub section (3) of section 40 of the Code to recover arrears in the year 1970. [613G] 17. The Respondent 's contention that the Respondent could recover arrears in 1968 was not correct. [614F] 18. The Respondent admitted that the arrears were due in the month of 1968. The Appellants had not filed any suit for recovery of arrears of taxes. The Respondent denied that the arrears had been paid in the year 1967.

The respondent was the owner of the lands in question. He had purchased the lands in the year 1953 and the lands were valued at Rs.2,000/- and the value of the lands was fixed at Rs.3,000/- per acre. The respondent had purchased the land in the year 1954 and the lands in his possession were valued at about Rs.2.000/- per sq. yard. The respondent claimed that the value of his lands was not correct and that the value was not correct. The Special Deputy Collector, after considering the evidence on record, held that the value fixed by the Special Deputy Collector was not correct, and that the enhanced compensation was not correct on the basis of the market value of the acquired lands. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the enhanced value of the land was not correct as the value of lands was not the correct value of the properties. The High court, therefore, held that it was not a case of mistake apparent from the record of the case and the enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court was not correct or that the enhanced amount of compensation was not a mistake apparent from record. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the enhanced market value of lands on the date of the original assessment under section 73 A of the Act was not correct in view of the fact that the enhanced land value was not the proper valuation of the lands on the earlier occasion. [801B] 2. The High Curt had rightly held that the enhancement of the value of acquired lands on the basis that the enhanced price of the acquired land was not the appropriate valuation of the acquired properties. [802C] 3. The High 'Court had rightly held in favour of the respondent. [803D] 4. The High. Court had rightly held the enhanced compensation to be correct. [804E] 5. The High, Court had rightly pointed out that the enhanced enhanced compensation was rightly awarded by the Special Court and the High Court was right in holding the enhanced compensation as not correct. [820G] 6. The High' Court had rightly relied upon the decision of this Court in the case of [State of Maharashtra vs Shri N.M.D.D.C.T.C. Ltd. and Anr. vs State of Maharashtra and Anr. [1978] 2 S.C.R. 840, followed. 7. The High] Court had rightly applied the principle of valuation of the land on the date when the original assessment was made. The High was right in upholding the enhancement of compensation on the basis on the basis thereof. [805G] 8. The High [805H] 9. The High Powered Committee had rightly held on the basis which was not correct by the High Court and the same was rightly set aside by the High court. [806G] 10. The High powered Committee had not committed any error in holding that there was no mistake apparent from its record. [807A] 11. The High Commissioner had not committed an error in holding the respondent to be entitled to the benefit of the enhanced compensation. [808B] 12. The High Commission had not committed a mistake apparent on the face of the record. The High had not committed error in holding on the basis as to the correct valuation of the properties on the date on which the original assessment had been made. [809G] 13. The High is right in holding on a proper appreciation of the value on the date the original assessment of the acquired property was made. [820H] 14. The High Land Acquisition Officer had not committed the error in holding to be correct in view the enhanced compensation on the earlier occasions. [810G] 15. The High land Acquisition Officer had committed an error apparent on the record. [820A] 16.

The appellant 's election to the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank, Chandrapur was held on 18.8.1986 and he was elected as Director on the Board of Directors of the said Bank. The appellant 's having been elected as Director of the said bank, he was disqualified to be a Director on account of his having committed default. The appellant filed an appeal before the Deputy Registrar. The Deputy Registrar dismissed the appeal. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Government. The State Government dismissed the appeal on 30.8.1989. The appellant challenged the order of the Deputy Registrar before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant 's disqualification was not attracted because the appellant had already ceased to be a director on account of the default committed by him. The appellant, therefore, filed a revision petition before the State Government which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was not a Director of the Bank and his disqualification was not set aside by the High Court on the ground that the appellant had ceased to be Director on account thereof. [701B] 2. The appellant having failed to prove that he was a Director of a Bank, the order of dismissal was not sustainable. [702C] 3. The appellant had not been able to show that he was not a director of the Bank. [703D] 4. The appellant could not show that he had ceased to hold the post of Director of the bank. [704E] 5. The appellant did not show that the post of the Director of the respondent Bank was vacant. The appellant failed to show that the respondent was a Director. [705E] 6. The appellant cannot be said to be a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice issued under section 78(1) of the Act. [706F] 7. The appellant has not been able, in the present case, to show that his case was covered by section 78(2) of the Maharashtra State Cooperation and Textile Department, Act, 1960. [707F] 7A] 8. The appellant is not a Director. He was not a defaulter in terms of section 73FF(1) and the appellant having been elected to the Maharashtra Cooperative Land Development bank, Chandrapur, he was not entitled to be a member of the Committee of the Cooperative Society. [709F] 9. The appellant being a Director of an Cooperative Society, the order passed by the Deputy Registrar was not sustainable in law. [708G] 10. The appellant who was a Director was not a member of a Cooperative Society and he was not disqualified to be an Director of the Society. [809F] 11. The appellant's election to the Committee of a Cooperative society was held on the date when he was declared elected as Director. The appellant as a Director was disqualified to continue as a Director. The election of the appellant was set aside by this Court on the basis that the appellant was not disqualified on account of failure to pay the instalments of the loan before the notice was issued. [710G] 12. The appellant must be deemed to be a person who has incurred any disqualification on account of default committed by the appellant in complying with the provisions of section 78(I) of the Bombay Cooperation and Textiles Department, Act. [810F] 13. The appellant should be deemed to have been disqualified on account thereof on account of non payment of the instalments of loan before the date of notice. [811G] 14. The appellant would be deemed to continue as Director of a Cooperative Bank on the date on which he was declared as elected as Director and he would continue as Director. [812G] 15. The appellant can be treated as a defaulter in respect of the loan which was due to him. [813G] 16.

The respondent was serving as a Supply Inspector in the State of Maharashtra. He was promoted as Supply Inspector in 1966 and was posted as Supply Inspector. He was posted as a Supply Officer in the State Government. He was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence and financial irregularities. He was imposed a penalty of reduction of 50 per cent of pension by 50 per cent. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the pension to the extent of 50 percent. The respondent challenged the order of reduction of pension by the State Government before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the State Government reducing the pension by 50% to the extent it was found that the respondent had already retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The State of Maharashtra preferred a writ petition before the High court. The High court allowed the writ appeal and quashed the impugned order of reduction. The State filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment. The High 'Court held that the State Government had no authority to initiate any proceedings against the respondent and that the State was competent to take disciplinary proceedings against the Government servant for misconduct and negligence. The High' Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of reduction of the pension by the 50 per cent in the facts and circumstances of the case. The State was aggrieved by the order of reducing the pension. The State preferred a writ appeal before the High 'Court. The High. The appellant, who was the landlord of the premises in question, filed a suit against the respondent for eviction of the appellant from the premises in dispute. The High Court held that the provisions of section 3(3) of the Act did not intend to confer jurisdiction on the Commissioner to deal with the application made under sub section (2) of section 3 of the Act. The High court held that the Commissioner could not deal with the question as to the legality, legality or propriety of the order passed by the District Magistrate or to the regularity of proceedings held before him, alter or reverse his order, or make such other order as may be just and proper. The High ' Court held that since the provisions of sections 3(3), 3(3)(a) and 16 of the Act were not intended to confer jurisdiction, the Commissioner could deal with the matter in accordance with the provisions of sub section (3) of section 2 of the Act, and the Commissioner could only deal with the matters in accordance with those provisions of the relevant provisions of the.Act. Court held that section 3(4) of the 'Act did not intend, even prior to the amendment of 1954, to confer jurisdiction upon the Commissioner to decide the question as regards the legality, propriety or legality of the order of the District Magistrate. The Commissioner, in the exercise of his powers under section 3 (3) (a) and (b) of the Ordinance, could not deal in the application filed under section 3 of that Ordinance. [703C] 4. The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to decide the application filed in accordance with section 3(a) and 3(3). [703D] 5. The Commissioner cannot deal with the applications filed under section 2 of Ordinance. The Commissioner can deal with the same. [704G] 7. The Commissioner may deal with the said applications under section 3 and 3(1). The Commissioner may not deal with any other application filed under sections 3 and 3 (1) of Ordinance. [603F] 7. In the present case, the Commissioner has no power to deal with an application filed under Section 3(3); and the Commissioner has not been vested with any power to deal in such application. The Commissioner did not deal with an appeal under section 3. [705G] 8. The Commissioner while dealing with an application under section 3 has no power under section 3 to deal with it. [706F] 9. The appellant, a Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as a Member of a Public Service Commission by the President of India on the recommendation of the High Court. He was appointed as the Member of the Public Service Commission on the recommendation made by the High Court on the recommendation. The appellant was appointed as Member of the Commission on the recommendations of the High court. On the recommendation of this Court, the appellant was appointed to the post of Member of the State Public Service Commission. On the basis of the report of the High Judge, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Member of Public Service Commission as a Member. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the report of a Public Commission was not a report of the Commission and that the report was not a document of the Commission. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The report of the Public Commission is a document of fact and it is not a document. The report is a document which is required to be examined and considered by the Court. [801B] 2. The report must be a document of facts and it is a document required to be considered by the court. The report cannot be a document. It is a document that is required to prove the case of misbehaviour or incapacity of the person concerned. [802C] 3. The report should be a document which has been examined and found upon a proper enquiry and found upon the facts found by the President. [803D] 4. The report does not disclose the facts which the appellant has to prove. The report, therefore, cannot be a report of a Commission. [804E] 5. The report merely discloses the facts which it is required to hold is not a report. The report can be a document only if it is of such a nature as to require the President to have obtained the opinion of a Commission and that it is not possible to prove the facts which are required to be proved. [805G] 6. The report may be a document required for the purpose of cross examination or cross examination. The report also does not disclose any other fact. [806G] 7. The report has to be a document in the nature of a report. It is not a mere document. It does not require to be considered. [807A] 8. The report contains the facts which have to be proved and the evidence to be recorded by the President is not a part of the record. [808C] 9. The report discloses the facts that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and that he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the Chief Minister had incurred the RELEASE of the Chief Justice of Punjab and that he was guilty of misbehaviour and that he has to suffer a decree for damages in a civil court. [809G] 9. In the present case, the appellant had been guilty of misconduct. He was guilty of negligence and misconduct. [810G] 10. The appellant had been convicted by the trial court for the offence of murder and sentenced to imprisonment for life. [811G] 10 A. The appellant has been convicted for the offence under section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment. [812G] 11. The appellant is entitled to the costs of the appeal.

The respondent was employed as a Manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthers Arbuthors. He was appointed as a Manager on a monthly salary of Rs. 27,948/. The appellant, Hindustan Steel Ltd., was a part of the establishment of the Hindustan Steel Ltd. and was treated as a separate establishment for the purpose of computation of bonus under the Act. The Company was treated as an establishment of the appellant, and it had to be treated as a part of its establishment for the purposes of computation of the bonus under the provisions of the Act. In the case of the appellant the Tribunal held that the Company was a separate establishment and, therefore, the question of computation of its bonus under the proviso to section 16(1) of the Act did not arise. The Tribunal held that, in view of the provisions of section 16(2) of the Payment of Bonus Act, the Company was not a separate establishment. The Tribunal further held that the appellant, Hindustan Steels Ltd., was not a part of that establishment and, consequently, the question was not a question of computation. The Tribunal, however, held that the claim of the workmen was not a single establishment and, accordingly, the Tribunal held, that the Company is a separate establishment, and, therefore the question of computing the bonus under section 16(3) of the said Act was not a matter of dispute. The Tribunal also held that the workmen of the appellant were not a separate establishments and, therefore they were not entitled to the bonus under sections 16(1)(a) and 16(1). The Tribunal, therefore, held that, the Company is not a separate Establishment and, therefore it was not a case of computation of compensation under section 16 of the Act, and, consequently the question of payment of bonus under section 15(1) did not arise, and, accordingly the Tribunal held the Company to be a separate establishment under section 16 (1) of Act. The Tribunal accordingly held that the company was a separate Establishment, and, as such, the question as to whether the Company was an establishment or an undertaking or branch of an establishment was not a necessary and proper question. The Tribunal found that the Company had been treated as a distinct establishment and, as a separate unit, was treated as separate establishment for purposes of computation under section 16. The Tribunal observed that the Company did not constitute a separate establishment as it was not an establishment, and the question of the computation of bonus was not a proper question. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right in holding that the Company being a separate establishment was not an Establishment, and the Tribunal was right, in holding that, the company was an establishment, which was a separate unit. [601B] 2. The Tribunal had held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that a separate establishment is a separate unit and, therefore. the question of determination of bonus under sections 15(1)(b) and 16 (1)(b), was not a dispute. [602C] 3. The Tribunal has held that the entire paid up equity share capital as envisaged by section 16(4) of the, Act was not an integral part of the same establishment. [603D] 4. The Tribunal did not go into the question whether the Company is an establishment or a branch of an undertaking or branches of an undertaking. [604E] 5. The Tribunal went into the question of calculation of bonus under [604F] 6. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the Company has been treated as an Establishment, because, the Company has not been treated as separate establishments for purposes of computing bonus under section 3 of the Act and, therefore,. the question of determining the bonus under [ 604F] 7. The Tribunal proceeded on the basis that the Company, being a separate unit was not a distinct establishment. [06F] 8. The Tribunal took the view that the Company cannot be treated as an independent establishment because, the Tribunal was not right in holding, that the company is an independent establishment. [2006E] 9.
