The High, Court, however, held that the fact that the practice carried on by a person was not a profession within that meaning of the Act, 1934, was not a relevant fact. The High "Court further held: "The respondent was carrying on a business within the definition of the expression 'business ' in the Act, 1938. The respondent was carrying out a profession. He was carrying on the business of a profession. It was not a business within that definition. The respondent had not proved the practice of profession within the definition. The High Courl Court held that it was not a "business ' within that definition and that the practice which was carried on by him was not a commercial practice within the meaning. of the Madhya Bharat Act, 1934." The High Court, therefore, held that there is no evidence to prove that the practice is a trade or profession within the Act, 1939. The High Courts, therefore, dismissed the appeal. In the present appeal, the appellant contended that the practice being a profession within Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Madhya. Accommodation Control Act was not a legal profession within the contemplation of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The practice of law is a profession within section 10(3) (a) (iii) of that Act. [701B] 2. The practice is a profession in the sense of a profession within its meaning. It is not a profession in any sense. It is a profession which is not a trade within the meaning thereof. [702C] 3. The practice in the sense in which it occurs in the Act is not a commercial usage within the meaning and it is not a business. [703D] 4. The practice being a trade or a business within section 10 (3)(a) (i) of the Act is a profession. [704E] 5. The practice was not a trading or a business. The definition of the word 'business ' contained in the Act was not capable of including the practice of a profession in a particular area. [705E] 6. The word 'business' in the Act means a business or trade. The word "business" in the Act does not include any profession. [605E] 7. The word used in the Act has to be given a wide meaning so as to include any profession or trade. [706E] 8. The word employed in the Act includes any profession. It does not include a profession. There is no definition of the term 'business ' as given in the Act. [607F] 9. The word has to be construed in the context of the Act and not in a manner that it is used in a particular sense. [707F] 10. The word may have been used in a sense which is not defined in the Act but it is not defined. [708F] 11.

The respondent was a firm of the appellant and the appellant was the partner of the firm. The appellant was the creditor of the respondent and the respondent was the creditor. The respondent was the debtor of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the District Judge, Allahabad for recovery of the amount of Rs. 4,00,000 from the respondent. The respondent filed a written statement and denied the liability of the appellant to pay the amount of the said amount. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the District Judge. The District Judge held that the appellant was not liable to pay the said amount and dismissed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the suit was barred by time and that the appellant had not proved that the respondent was a debtor to the respondent. On appeal by certificate, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant is not liable to make the payment of the amount in question. [701B] 2. The appellant had not been able to prove that the respondent had not paid the amount in the year 1943. The appellant could not prove that the amount was not deposited in the account of the respondent because the respondent had already paid the amount. [702C] 3. The appellant has not been able, by any evidence, to prove that there was a demand in the month of October, 1943 for a part of the amount. The appellant cannot be said to have proved that the amount in dispute was not deposited with the respondent. [703C] 4. The appellant having failed to prove that it was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs.4,00, 000 and not an allegation of the respondent having paid the amount, the appellant was entitled to withdraw the deposit. [704D] 5. The appellant is not entitled to withdraw any amount deposited by the respondent. It is not open to the appellant to contend that the respondent is not liable for the whole sum of Rs. 3,00,00,500. [705E] 6. The appellant, in the circumstances, was not entitled to the withdrawal of the deposit. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The order of the High Court is set aside. The suit is dismissed. [706F] 7. The respondent is entitled to withdraw Rs. 3.00,000 deposited by the appellant in the court. [707F] 8. The respondent has not been allowed to withdraw the amount deposited by him. [708G] 9. The respondent had not been allowed the withdrawal of Rs.3.00,00.000. [709G] 9,00A] 10. The respondent having failed to establish that the appellant has not paid the entire amount in the month, 1943, the appellant is entitled to the refund of the amount deposited. [710G] 10. In the circumstances, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the High court is set aside and the suit is dismissed with costs.

The petitioner was detained under the National Security Act on the ground that he was in custody when the order of detention was passed. He was in jail for a period of one year and he was in jail. The detention order was challenged by the petitioner in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the detention. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court. The Division Bench of the High Court held that the order of preventive detention was bad in law and the order of his detention was liable to be quashed. The Division bench held that the detention order was bad in the eye of law and the detention order could not be quashed. In the present case, the High Court observed that the detaining authority was aware of the fact that the detenu was already in custody when he was already in jail and he was already under detention. The Division Court also held that the detenu had been in jail for about one year and the detention was necessary for preventing him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The Division High Court also held, that the order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. The Division Benches of the High court also held that there was no material to show that the detenu, who was already in detention, was likely to get bail, was likely t o be released. The Division benches of the High Cour t held that the detaining authorities were aware of the facts that the detenu is already in jail for one year and that he was already having been in jail and that he had been in custody when his detention was in jail and the order was not passed for detention. The High Cour s Court also held in favour of the petitioner. In the case of Merugu Satyanarayana vs State of Andhra Pradesh, the petitioner was in jail custody when the detention order came to be passed. The DivisionBench of the High Courts held that the petitioner was not in jail when the order was made and he was not in custody when detention was made. The Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held, that there was sufficient material to show, that the detenu did not have the jurisdiction to make an order of detention under the National security Act. The Division of the BombayHigh Court held that there is no material to indicate that the detenu could be in jail for any period during the period when he was in detention. The Court also held: "The detaining authority was conscious of the fact, that the petitioner had already been in jail when he was released on bail, and he was likely to be released. It is not a matter of dispute that the detaining Authority was aware of all the facts that he was aware of it. The detaining authority was well aware of the position that the detenu would be in jail when his detention is already in custody. The detaining Authority was well aware that the detenu has been in jail since the date of his detention. The detaining authorities were well aware of all facts that the petitioner is already in detention. It is, therefore, not a matter which can be said to be a matter of law.

The petitioners were engaged as casual labourers in the Department of Posts and Telegraphs Department for a period of more than six months. They were engaged as Casual Labourers in the Department for a long period of time. They were also engaged as casual labour in the Department. They were continuously working for more than six years in the Department and were also engaged for a period between 5th February, 1986 to 5th February 1986. They were regularly employed in the Department as casual labourers. They were not being regularly employed in any of the Department. The petitioners were engaged for a long time in the Department in the Department since the year 1986. They had been continuously working for a period from 5th February to 5th March 1986. They filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the scheme was not in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the rules framed thereunder. The High Courts held that the Scheme was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Industrial Disputes Rules and the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1986. The HighCourt further held that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefits of the scheme and the benefits of revised scales of pay. The High 'Court further held: "In view of the above, the petitioners are not entitled to any benefits of the revised scales of wages. The High' Court held that the benefits of revision of scales of pay were not admissible to the petitioners. The High. Court held that they were not entitled for the benefits of scales of wages and other benefits as are being paid to the regular employees of the Department as far as possible. The High, Court, however, held that the benefit of the revised scale of pay was not admissible to them. The High Curt, however, directed the Union of India to make a scheme on a rational basis for absorbing the casual labourers who have been continuously working in the Department with effect from 5th March, 1986. It was further directed that the Union of Indian, Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure, would make a scheme for absorbing casual labourers in each Department of Posts as and when they occur. The High Powered Committee, however, recommended that the benefit should not be admissible to the casual labourers in whose case the revision of scales was done in the Department, but without prejudice to absorption of the casual labourers. The High powered Committee recommended that the benefits should not be allowed to the casual workers in whose case there was no justification to keep them as casual labourers for years. The HighPowered Committee recommended to the Union of Indias that the benefit would not be admissible on a rational and rational basis for absorb the casual labourers as far as practicable. The Highpowered Committee recommended the following: (i) The Union of India should not be permitted to absorb the casual workers who have been in continuous service for more than one year in the Department; (ii) The Union should not be granted the benefit of revised scales for the casual labourers unless they have been continuously worked for more than three years in the department; (iii) The Union shall not be entitled to the benefit of enhanced rates of daily wages for the casual workers unless they have continuously worked for three years in each Department; (iv) The Union would not be entitled for the benefit of increased rates of daily wage for the casual labour who have been working for more period than three years; (v) The Union is not entitled to get the benefit of increase rates of daily rates of daily rate for the casual workmen who have been employed for more than four years in each department; (vi) The Union has not been able to make any application for the benefit under the revised scales for casual labourers.

The appellant, a registered dealer, filed a return showing a taxable income of Rs. 1,000, and a notice under section 22(2) of the Act, on January 5, 1950, was served on the appellant. The appellant filed a return on January 5. 1950, and the Income tax Officer, after a notice under Section 22(2), issued a notice under [section 22(3)] of the Act on January 5 and the appellant filed a petition under section 22 (3) of the Income tax Act, 1922, for a return showing an assessable income of Rs, 1,000. The Income tax Officer rejected the petition on the ground that the return filed by the appellant was not in compliance with a notice under sections 22(2). The appellant filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the return was not a return filed under section 24(1) of the. Act and that the appellant was entitled to a notice under that section. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the returns were not filed within the time allowed by section 22(3) of that Act and that, therefore, the return was barred by time. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant had not filed a return under section 24 (1) of that act and that the return had been filed within the period of limitation. The Tribunal further held that the assessee had not filed the return within the time prescribed by section 22 (2) of that section and that the returns filed by him were not in compliance of the notice under section 24. The Tribunal also held that the notice under sections 24(1), 24(3) and 24(3), were not in accordance with the provisions of section 22(1) and that the assessee was not entitled to a return under that section, and that the notice was not barred by time, and that, in view of the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of [Commissioner of Income tax vs Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. and Others] (supra), the notice under [Section 22(2)] was not barred. The Tribunal accordingly held that the assessment was not barred under section 22 of the Act. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal, and held that since the return was filed within the prescribed time, the notice under Section 24(1)(a) was not barred, and that there was no question of applying the provisions of Section 22(3). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The return filed by a registered dealer under section 24 is not a return showing the taxable income of the assessee. [601B] 2. The return is not a valid return. The return has been filed within a period of limitation prescribed by section 24(3). The return is a valid return and the assessee has not filed a valid return, and therefore, the returns filed under section 22 are not hit by time. [602C] 3. The return was filed beyond the time prescribed for the assessment. The assessee had not made a return showing income below the taxable limit. The returns were filed within the specified period. [603D] 4. The returns filed by the assessee were not in conformity with the provisions contained in section 22(4) of the Indian Income tax Act. [604E] 5. The returns are not in conformity to the provisions contained therein. The returns have been filed within time. [613F] 6. The returns do not show any assessable income. The returns show that the returns have been prepared and filed within the stipulated time. [643F] 7. The returns disclose the taxable income at Rs. 1.000 per month. The returns also disclose the taxable turnover at Rs. 2.000 per annum. [605G] 8. The returns contain the taxable turnover of Rs.

The respondent, a registered society, was registered under the provisions of the Societies Registration Act, 1860, with Registration No. A-1/74, on 29.8.1975. The respondent, a society registered under the Societies Registration (Amendment) Act, 1976, applied to the Registrar of Societies for registration of the Society, and the Registrar of the Society by his order dated 30.8.1976, granted registration to the respondent, and the Society was registered under Section 22 of the Act. The Society, however, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi, challenging the validity of the said circular dated 23.8.1982, and the High Court, by its order dated 30th August, 1976, quashed the said circular. The respondent filed a writ appeal in the High court of Delhi, which was allowed by the impugned judgment, and the writ petition was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the circular dated 23rd August, 1982, was ultra vires the Act and the Scheme, and the Scheme was, therefore, ultra vires the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The circular dated 23th August, 1982 is ultra vires the provisions of Article 19(1)(c) and the Scheme. [701B] 1.2 The respondent, being a registered society under the provisions Of the Societies Registration of Societies Act, 1860 and the Scheme framed thereunder, is entitled to be appointed by the Central Government, and the Central Government is, therefore, entitled to appoint the true representatives of the employees of the nationalised bank, who are not workmen, to be appointed as the true representatives. [702C] 1.3 The Central Government, in exercise of its powers under Section 22(1)(a) of the Societies Act, has framed the Scheme, which is in the following terms: (i) The Central Government is empowered to appoint the Registrar of Cooperative Societies, and the State Government is empowered, in exercise o f its powers under the Act, to appoint the proper representatives of the staff of the nationalised banks, who are employees of the State Government, and to appoint the correct representatives of the workmen of the nationalised Bank, who are workmen, to represent the interests of the Bank, and to make the maximum scope for the concerned employees to be appointed, and if the Central Government were to provide for election in keeping with the principle of election, the Central Government would, in exercise Of its powers under section 22(1) (a) of Societies Registration Act. [703D] 1.4 The Central Government has, in exercise, of its powers, under section 22 of the Societies registration Act, to make a scheme for the constitution of the Board of Directors, for the purpose of giving maximum scope for each employee to be appointed the true representative of the employees, and to provide for elections in keeping with principle of election. [705E] 1.5 The Central Government may, in exercise or performance of its powers or performance of the functions under section 22, make a scheme to provide for the constitution or functions of the Board, and to give maximum scope for every employee to be so appointed, and to fix the maximum scope of the choice of the representatives of the employee, and to specify the maximum scope to be appointed to the choice of representatives of the workers, and to prescribe the maximum scope and the maximum scope, for every employee, to be so nominated, and to regulate the choice of representative of the workers. [706E] 1, 2.6 The Central Government cannot, in exercise and performance of its functions under section 23, make a Scheme to provide for constitution or functions for the choice of employees, and the maximum exercise of the choice to be so chosen by it, unless the Central Government otherwise directs.

The respondent assessee, a registered dealer, was assessed to tax on the sale of certain goods. The respondent assessee filed a return of income for the assessment year 1965. The Income tax Officer, after considering the returns, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, assessed the tax on the basis of the returns filed by the respondent assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the Appellate Assistant commissioner had no power to stay the recovery proceedings and that the Tribunal had no power under section 45 of the Act to stay the collection of the tax. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellate Assistant Commissioner had no power of staying the recovery proceedings. The Tribunal further held that the Tribunal was not competent to stay the proceedings pending before the Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, the assessee contended that the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to stay the Recovery proceedings pending before it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Appellate Tribunal had jurisdiction to stay recovery proceedings pending before him. [601B] 2. The Appellate Appellate Tribunal had power to stay recovery of tax pending disposal of the appeal before it. The Appellate Authority had no power, under section 45, to stay the execution of the recovery proceedings pending in the appeal before the Tribunal. [602C] 3. The Appellate authority had no power in the matter of stay of recovery proceedings pending disposal of an appeal before it, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioners had no power or jurisdiction to stay such proceedings pending disposal before the Appellate Authority. [603D] 4. The Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had no jurisdiction, under section 60 of the Act, to stay recovery proceeding pending before the Tribunal, and the Appellate Assistant COMMISSIONER had no power and jurisdiction to stay any recovery proceedings pending on the date of the appeal. [604E] 5. The Appellate Asst. Commissioner had jurisdiction to entertain an appeal pending before the Income tax Officer. [605E] 6. The Appellate Deputy Commissioner had no authority to stay the proceeding pending before him, but the Income tax officer had no power. [606E] 7. The Appellate Commissioner had no powers to stay the recoveries pending before the appellate Assistant commissioner. [607E] 8. The Appellate Dy. Commissioner had power to grant time for payment of the tax, even though the Appellate AssistantCommissioner had no power over the matter. [608E] 9. The Appellate Joint Commissioner had no such power to stay any proceedings pending before a Appellate Assistant Commissioner. [609E] 10. The Appellate Authorities had no power at all to grant time to the assessee for payment of tax, even if the Appellate Assistant Commisioner had no power whatsoever to stay the recoverable tax. [610E] 11. The Appellate authorities had no power either to grant time or to stay the recover proceedings pending before them. [611E] 12. The Appellate Tribunals have no power to grant stay of recovery pending before the Commissioner or to stay recovery pending before them, but the Commissioner or the Appellate Assistant Commi ssioner had power to pass interim orders staying recovery proceedings pending till the appeal is disposed of. [612E] 12A] 13. The AppellateTribunal has no power to pass an interim order staying recovery proceedings till the appeal was disposed of. The Appellate Trib unal has no power, in the matter, to stay any further proceedings pending before an Appellate Assistant Commissioner or to pass interim order staying the recovery pending before an Assistant Commissioner.

The respondent was posted as a Station Officer in the Police Station, Intiathok, in the charge of a police station, Intiatok, in connection with the investigation of the case. He was posted as an officer incharge of the Police Station in the charge sheet. He was charged under section 7 of the Police Act, and the respondent was charged under sections 7 and 7 of the Act. The respondent was charged with the same charges. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, Lucknow, praying that the departmental inquiry and the criminal trial be quashed. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the departmental proceedings were vitiated by a number of irregularities and that the High Court was not right in quashing the order of dismissal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in quashing and setting aside the order of the Superintendent of Police, in regard to the charges which were the subject matter of the departmental trial. [801 D] 2. The High Courts were right in quashing an order of dismissal on the ground that the departmental enquiry was not in accordance with the provisions of the Police Regulations. [802 E] 3. The High C.I.D. was right in holding that the departmental proceeding was not a departmental proceeding. [803 E] 4. The High Powered Committee had not applied its mind to the question whether the departmental proceedings had been vitiated by a serious irregularity. [804 F] 5. The High powered Committee had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether there was a prima facie case for the departmental proceedings. [805 F] 6. The HighPowered Committee had jurisdiction to go behind the findings of the criminal trial. [820 G] 7. The High powers of the Superintendent, in the circumstances, were not in accordance therewith. [806 F] 8. The High was right in saying that the departmental trial was not a regular one. The High] Court was right in setting aside the departmental proceedings on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. [807 F] 805 F] 9. The High Commissioner of Police, Lucknow vs Ram Singh, [1964] 3 S.C.R. 845, followed.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists ' grade II on September 9, 1966. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. He was confirmed in that post on September 9.1, 1971. On his promotion to supertime Grade II he was promoted to the supertime grade I on February 8. 1971. On September 9, 1971, he was promoted as Director of Health Services, Manipur. On September 10, 1971, the appellant was promoted to Supertime Grade II on the post of Director of Health Service, Manipur. He was, however, promoted to super time grade II on March 31, 1971. The appellant was, however promoted to super Time grade II on April 1, 1971. In the year 1971, he filed a writ petition in the High Court of Manipur challenging the promotion of the appellant to supertime scale II on the ground that he was not qualified for promotion to super time scale II because he was not eligible for promotion to the super time grade I because he was senior to Dr. Sen and was not qualified to be promoted to super-time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the speciality in which the post was converted to a specified post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The promotion of the four respondents to supertime grades II was not a specified post and, therefore, the promotion of them to supertime posts was not qualified. [801B] 2. The promotion to super Time Scale II was not made by promotion from the post of Supertime grade II to supertime post. The promotion was not a post but was a specified post in a specified post which was converted to specified post. [802C] 3. The promotion by promotion was not qualified because the post was not a specific post. [820G] 4. The promotion could only be by promotion from a specified post to a specified level post. [823G] 5. The promotion cannot be by promotion by promotion from any specified post to any level post. The post was converted into a specified post by the promotion by promotion by the promotion of a specified level officer. [823H] 6. The promotion is not a specified or a post in a particular speciality but is a specified post, which is converted to a particular post. [825G] 7. The promotion must be by promotion on the basis of the conditions laid down in the relevant rules. [825H] 8. The promotion should be by promotion only from a specified level Officer. [825A] 9. The promotion would be by promotion to super-Time grade II because the post is converted to specified level officer because the post has been converted to a post by promotion by way of promotion from a particular level officer. The promotion will be by promotion in the same manner as the promotion by the same level officer. In the case of promotion by promotion, the promotion will be from a specified or post to a level officer. But the promotion will not be from a particular post to a higher level officer. It is only when the promotion is by promotion that the promotion will continue to be from a higher level Officer. The promotion shall be by promotion, from a specified grade to a level Officer. But the promotions will continue to continue to be in supertime grade. [825B] 9. In the instant case, the promotion was not to supertime higher grade II because it was not a part of supertime grade III because the post had been converted to specified grade II because of the fact that the post was a specified or non-executive post. [826C] 10. The promotion can only be by way of a specified or semi-revised grade II because there is no justification for giving a direction that the post shall be converted to a non-ex executive post. [827G] 11.

The appellants, who were tenants in the land in question, were tenants in possession of the land in dispute. The first respondent, who was the owner of the land, filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the land in the possession of the appellants was not surplus area. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court held that the land was not surplus and the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of section 10 A(a) of the Act. The first appeal was dismissed. The first appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the first respondent was not entitled to any benefit of section 20A of the Act because the land in his possession was not surplus. The High court held that section 19B of the Act was not applicable to the land in possession of a tenant who had acquired the land in excess of the permissible area. The High 'Court further held that the provisions of section 20B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 were not applicable to a tenant who acquired the land under section 10A of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1953. The High' Court held that section 20B was not applicable because the land was acquired by the State Government under the provisions of the Punjab Land Tenures Act. The High. Court held that there was no question of the acquisition of the land by the State. The High, Court, however, held that the appellants were entitled to the benefits of section 20 A of the Punjab Act. The State Government, however, did not appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 19B are not applicable to tenants who acquired the lands in excess of permissible area. [901B] 1.2. The provisions are not applicable in the case of a tenant whose tenancy is terminated by the landlord. [902B] 1.(a) The provisions of the Act are not applicable. [903C] 1.(b) The provisions are applicable to tenants whose tenancy is determined by the competent authority under the Act. [905C] 1.3. The provisions do not apply to tenants whose tenancies are determined by the Competent Authority under the Act and who have acquired the land by virtue of section 10A [905D] 1.(c) The provisions do no more apply to tenants who acquire the land by way of gift or bequest or by an heir or a person to whom he is an heir or the heir or the heirs of the tenant. [906E] 1.(d) The provisions in section 19B do not apply in the case where the land is acquired by the Government under the Act but the land is not vested in the State Government. [908E] 1.4. The provisions in the Act are applicable to the tenants whose tenancy was determined by the State government. [909E] 1(a) The first respondent was entitled to the protection of section 20 B of the Punjab Tenants (Amendment) Act, 1953, which came into force on the 30th July, 1958. [907F] 1.(i) The first appellant was entitled to protection of section 10 B of the Act and the first respondent could not be deprived of the benefit of the provisions of that section. [910E] 1 (a) The second appellant was entitled only to the protection under section 20B. [911E] 1[(b) The first proviso to section 20B(1) of the Punjab Tenant (Amendment) Ordinance, 1953, was not applicable. The first proviso was not applicable in view of the fact that the first appellant was not entitled only to protection under section 10 B. [912F] 1.5. The first Appellant was entitled to a protection under section 19B(1)(a) of Punjab Tenants (Abolition of Land Tenures) Act, 1952, which came to be enacted by the State Legislature.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for a declaration that the will set up by the defendants was genuine and valid. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands and that the suit was not barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer. The plaintiffs filed a written statement and denied the claim. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to compensation in respect thereof. The High Court held that the suit for a decree for mesne profits was not barred under section 14 of the Act. The High court held that section 14 of Act 1 of 1951 did not vest the Compensation Officer with jurisdiction to determine the competing claims. The High 'Court held that the decision of this Court in the case of [S.R. Das vs The State of Madhya Pradesh] (1) was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The High' Court held that section 3 of the Act did not confer jurisdiction on the Compensation Officer to determine the rival claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3 of Act 1of 1951. The High. Court held that there was no bar to determine the claim of the plaintiffs in a summary inquiry. The High, Court held that since the plaintiffs were not entitled to compensation, the question of jurisdiction of the Compensation officer did not arise. The High Cour t held that the provisions of section 14 of 'Act 1 of 1951 were not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present suit. The High cour t held, that section 14 was not attracted to such a suit. The plaintiffs were not bound by the decision in the case. The plaintiffs appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that section 14 did not confer any jurisdiction on the Civil Court to determine the rights of the parties to the suit. [801 D] 2. The High Cou rt was right in holding, that section 3 did not confer a jurisdiction on the civil court to determine the dispute between the parties to a suit. [901 D] 3. The High r espondents were not entitled under section 14 to receive compensation. [902 E] 4. The High tiffs were not bound to pay compensation in respect there of. [903 F] 5. The High ly was right in contending that the suit could not be filed within two months from the date of the order. [904 F] 6. The Hight er was right in saying that the suit filed by the plaintiffs was not barred in view of the decision of a Division Bench of the High Court in the matter of [Sundaram vs The State] of Madhya Pradesh, [1964] 3 S.C.R. 840, followed. 7. The High R ule Court was right in not holding that section 3 was not attracted. [905 F] 8. The High ness of Madhya Pradesh has not been shown to have been satisfied with the decision of that court. [906 F] 9. The High m e Court was right, in holding that the decision in [Sundararam vs The Revenue Divisional Officer, Kamrup, Kamrup] was not applicable. [907 F] 905 F] 907 F] 10. The High p e Court was not right in holding the suit to be barred under section 3 of 'Act I of 1951.

The appellant was a tenant in respect of the premises in question. The respondent was a tenant of the premises on the ground that the appellant was not ready and willing to pay the rent within one month of the service of the notice. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of rent for arrears of rent for the period from the date of service of the suit notice. The suit was resisted by the appellant on the ground of non existence of the dispute. The trial court held that the dispute was not a dispute within the meaning of section 12(3) (a) of the Act and the respondent was not ready to pay the amount of standard rent or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was ready and willing and willing to deposit the amount of rent within one months of the service. The respondent did not make any application within one month from the date the notice of the service was served on the appellant. The High court held that there was no dispute as to standard rent or the permitted increases specified therein. The respondent had not made any application within the meaning ofs. 12(3)(a) of Act. The respondent contended that the dispute raised by the appellant was a dispute within one month after the service of notice under section 12(2) of the Bombay Rent Act. The High Courts held that the appellant had not made an application within one months from the date on which the notice of service was served. The High courts held that the notice was not a proper notice under section 13(3) of the said Act. The appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 12 (3) (b) of the aforesaid Act. The appeal was allowed by the High Court and the suit was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent had not raised any dispute before the trial court as to the standard rent or increased increases specified in order made by it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent is not entitled to protection of section 13(2) (a), of the Act. [801B] 2. The respondent has not made any claim for protection of section 11(3)(a) of Bombay Rent Act against the appellant. [802C] 3. The respondent cannot raise any dispute in regard to standard rent nor can it raise any dispute for the first time in the suit for recovery. [803D] 4. The respondent could not raise any dispute as to the Standard rent or increased increase specified in the notice. [804E] 5. The respondent can raise a dispute as to whether the dispute raised in the notice is a dispute within a month of the notice under section 11(2) or not. [805E] 6. The respondent, in the present case, has not made an appeal to the Court under section 11 of the Act against the order of the trial court. [806F] 7. The respondent having not made any such claim for protection under section 12 (2) (b), the respondent cannot raise a dispute for the second time in the present suit for recovery, and the suit for eviction is governed by section 12(4) (a). [806G] 8. The respondent being a tenant in the premises, the respondent cannot be said to be ready and willing for payment of rent. [807F] 9. The respondent in the present appeal has not made a claim for protection in regard to the standard Rent or increased increases. The respondent does not dispute that the dispute is raised within one month or two months of the notice of termination of the tenancy. [808F] 10. The respondent would not be entitled to the benefit of section 12 of the Act because the dispute raised is not a dispute between the parties. [809G] 11.

The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1939 and the appellant was incorporated in that year under the articles of association of the respondent company. The respondent company was a director of the Aluminium Ltd. in the year 1942. The respondent was appointed as a director of a company in the year 1943. The respondent Company was incorporated in 1943 and the appellant held the majority of the shares in the company. The appellant was appointed as the managing director of the respondent Company in the year 1944. The respondent, however, held the majority shares in the Company. The respondent filed a petition under section 21 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, for the assessment of the income of the respondent for the assessment year 1939. The respondent contended that the directors of the respondent were not entitled to vote in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent company and that the directors were not entitled, in any manner, to vote in the company, for the purpose of exercising the power under section 21. The respondent also contended that the managing director was not entitled to exercise the power under [section 21] of the Excess Profit Tax Act, 1939, because the directors of that company were not authorised to vote in favour of the respondent. The respondent further contended that the respondent company was not entitled, under section 21, to vote for the respondent company, for exercising the power of the managing director. The respondent submitted that the directors had no control over the affairs of the company and, therefore, the directors of both the companies were not entitled under section 21 to vote for them in respect of their shares. The respondent did not dispute the fact that the directors in the company were authorised to vote for him in respect of his shares. The High Court held that the directors could not have exercised the power under sections 21 to vote in relation to the shares held in the company because the directors had not control over the management of the company. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the shares held and the directors of a company were not entitled as shareholders of the company, because the managing director had no control of the company in respect of its shares. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The directors of the company are not entitled to have the voting rights in respect of shares held by them in the company as they hold the majority of shares in thecompany. [901 D] 2. The directors are not entitled under the articles to vote for and on behalf of the company as the managing directors of the Company. [902 E] 3. The directors have no control over their affairs. The directors cannot be regarded as having control over the company. [903 E] 4. The directors, who hold the majority shares, are not entitled, as shareholders of a company, to vote on behalf of its principals. [905 E] 5. The directors do not hold the majority share in the company and they are not entitled as members of the company because they hold the minority shares in the respondent Company. [0905 F] 6. The directors who hold the minority share in the Company are not entitled. [906 F] 7. The directors holding majority shares in a company are not bound to vote on the behalf of the Company because they hold majority shares in that company. [0906 F] 8. The directors having no control over them, the directors cannot be treated as having control of the Company in respect of any of the shares. [908 G] 9. The directors being the managing director, the directors are not bound by the directions of their principals. [0908 C] 9. In the present case, the directors have no power to vote on their behalf. [909 G] 909 A] 10. The directors were not authorised by the company to vote on its behalf. [099 G] 910 A] 9. It is not necessary to refer to the facts of the present case.

The respondent was appointed as Accounts Superintendent on a temporary basis in the year 1966. He was promoted to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents on a temporary capacity on a temporary post. He was confirmed in the cadre of the Accounts Superintendents on the basis of the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. He was also confirmed in the said cadre on a temporary appointment. He was further promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent on the basis that he was not required to pass the Departmental Examination. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Resolution of the Board dated 19th June, 1969. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the Resolution of 19th May 1969 and directed the Board to pass the examination. The respondent challenged the validity of that Resolution by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High court allowed the writ appeal and quashed the resolution of 19th June 1969. The respondent then filed a writ appeal before the High court. The Division Bench of the High Court allowed that appeal and quashed that Resolution. The respondent thereafter filed a writ application before the High C ourt. The High C ounsel contended that the Resolution of 18th May,1969 was not a binding precedent and that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent was not entitled to be promoted to the said cadre of Accounts Superintendent. The High c ounsel submitted that the Resolution dated 18th May 1969 was not a valid Resolution and that the respondent had not passed the Departmental Examination and that the Resolution was not a mere formality. The High Cou rt allowed the writ application and quashed the order of the Board. The High t ence was challenged before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no justification for the respondent to pass the departmental examination and that the resolution was not a mandatory one. [701B] 1.2 The High Court had not committed any error in holding otherwise. [702C] 1.3 The High Court committed a manifest error in holding the respondent to be entitled to be appointed to the cadre as Accounts Superintendent. [703D] 1.4 The High Court failed to appreciate that the Resolution passed by the Board was not a statutory one. [603E] 1.5 The High Court erred in holding that since the Resolution of 20th May, 1970 was not a legal one, the respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the cadre. [705E] 1.(a) The High Court has committed a manifest illegality in holding that in view of the Resolution passed in the Board meeting held on 19th May 1970, the respondent could not have been promoted to the Cadre of Accounts Superintendent and that the promotion to the post was not a condition precedent to passing the Departmental Examination, and that the Board had not passed any resolution in that regard. [706E] 1(b) The High Cour t has committed a gross error in holding, that the Resolution adopted by the Board in the meeting held on 20th May 1970 was not binding on the respondent. [707E] 1 (c) The High court was in error by holding that the Resolution in question was not binding upon the respondent. The High n ourt has committed a patent error in holding in favour of the respondent. (d) The High cour t has failed to appreciate the fact that the Resolution did not contain any provision for passing of the Departmental Examination but only provided for passing of Departmental Examination. [708E] 2.1 The respondent was not eligible for promotion to that post. The High Co urt has committed a serious error in holding him to be entitled for promotion to this post. [709G] 2.2 The respondent was eligible for promotion as Accounts Superintendent and he was not entitled for promotion as the Accounts Superintendent.

The appellant, a minor, who was a minor, was a minor at the time of the accident. He was a minor. He was also a minor at that time. He was an agriculturist. He was prosecuted for the offence under Section 304 Part II of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant, a major, was tried for the offence of murder and was convicted by the trial court. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief in exercise of the power under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution of India. [801B] 2. The High court was right in holding, that the appellant had no right to the compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, as the appellant had not been able to establish that there had been an infringement of the fundamental rights of the appellant. [802C] 3. The appellant was not able to establish any right to the protection of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. [803D] 4. The appellant had not established that there had indeed been an infringement by the State of its public duty. [804E] 5. The appellant could not establish that there was an infringement of his fundamental rights by the State. [805E] 6. The appellant cannot be permitted to take advantage of his fundamental right under Article 21. [806F] 7. The appellant has not established that he had any right to any compensation under the public law. [807F] 8. The appellant is not entitled to the relief in exercise under Article 32 of the Constitution because the appellant has not been able, by establishing that there had ever been an infringement, of his fundamental Rights. [808F] 805H] 9. The appellant 's right to compensation under the Public Law is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party in exercise of its power under Article 226 of the constitution. [809G] 9. In the instant case, the appellant had been able to show that there had never been an infringement. The appellant did not establish that the appellant did not have any right to compensation. [810H] 905A] 10. The appellant can not be permitted to raise a plea that the appellant has been able to prove that there had not been an infringement on the part of the appellant by the State in exercise of their powers under Article 32.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was also convicted for an offence of murder under section 302 read with section 34 Indian Penal Code. The petitioner appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioner filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus. The High court held that the petitioner was entitled to a writ of Habeas Corpus. The High Judge held that the petition was not maintainable. The High, Court, however, held that the writ petition was not competent. The petitioner contended that the petition had been filed by the petitioner for a writ under article 32 and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. The High. Court held that the High court had no jurisdiction under article 32 to entertain the writ petition. The petitioner, therefore, filed a petition for a writ in the High Court under article 32. The High 'Court held that the petitions were not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the petitioner had not been able to show that the petition did not disclose any cause of action. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petition was not a petition under Article 32. The petitioner was not entitled to any relief under article 32 because he had not been asked to interview the prisoners. [801B] 2. The petitioner had been asked to appear before the Superintendent of Jail on the day of the execution of the death sentence. He had not been allowed to interview the prisoner. He had been asked by the Superintendent of the Jail to allow the petitioner to interview the said prisoner. [802C] 3. The petitioner has been asked to attend the interview on the day when he was asked to appear. He had also not been allowed any interview. [803D] 4. The petitioner is not entitled to a relief under article 226 of the Constitution. [804E] 5. The petitioner cannot be allowed to interview a prisoner. [820G] 6. The petitioner must be allowed to appear before a Superintendent of Jail. He must be allowed only to appear before an Inspector of Jail. [805G] 7. The petitioner should be allowed to sit before an Inspector for interview. [820H] 8. The petitioner can be allowed to inspect the prisoners before an Inspector. [820A] 8. In the instant case, the petitioner was not allowed to interview any prisoner. He was not allowed any interview and he was not allowed a chance to interview the petitioner. [820E] 9. The petitioner could not be allowed to do the interview. He was allowed to appear in the interview. [821G] 9. In the circumstances, the petition is allowed to be dismissed. The petitioner shall be allowed to take the interview in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. [820F] 10. The petitioner will be allowed to attend the interviews on the day he is allowed to appear.

The appellant was the owner of the tea garden and the respondent was the owner thereof. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of damages against the Receiver for the loss caused to the tea garden by the fire. The appellant contended that the Receiver had no duty or obligation in relation to the tea gardens and the factory premises and that the Receiver was not liable for the loss occasioned to the tea Garden. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit on the ground that the appellant was not liable to make good the loss occasioned by the fire and the Receiver was liable to make the loss occasioned from the fire. On appeal the High Court held that the Receiver could not be held liable for the damage caused to the Tea garden by the Fire. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the Receiver did not commit any breach of the bond. [601B] (2) The High court was right in not holding that the appellant had committed breach of the terms of the bond and that the loss occasioned thereby was not due to the fire. [602C] (3) The High 'Court was right in rejecting the objections and directing that the appellant be made liable for the losses occasioned from the Fire. [603D] (4) The High' Court was right, in holding that there was no obligation or obligation in respect of the tea gardens. [604E] (5) The High, Court was right that the appellant could not be made liable to make any loss occasioned from fire. [613F] (6) The High. Court was right when it held that the appellant did not commit breach of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the bond. The High Court, therefore, was right in dismissing the objections and the appellant was liable to pay damages for the loss. [605G] (605A] (7) The High was right in refusing to enforce the bond. It was not open to the appellant to enforce the security bond. [613B] (8) The High Courts were right in holding the appellant liable for the damages caused to the plantation. [606B] (9) The High Curt was right in allowing the appeal. [607C] (10) The High] (11) The appellant was not entitled to any damages for the damage occasioned from the damage caused by the fire to the tea plantation. [613G] (12) The High [605B] (13) The appellant is not entitled to the damages for the fire caused to the factory premises. [609C] (14) The High Judge was right in directing that the damages for loss occasioned from a fire to the factory should be paid by the appellant to the Receiver. [610D] (15) The High Commissioner was right in saying that the appellant is not liable to pay the damages for damage caused to his tea garden. [611E] (16) The High Power Court was right on the ground of the appellant not being liable to make a loss occasioned from his fire. [650E] (17) The High power Court was right to direct that the damage caused from the fire to his tea plantation should be paid to the Receiver and that the appellant would not be liable to make such loss occasioned from such fire. [625F] (18) The High is right in holding against the appellant that the Receiver is not liable for any loss occasioned to his tea plantations. [612F] (19) The HighPower Court was right not in holding that a Receiver is not entitled for any damages for loss caused to his Tea plantation. [650F] (20) The High powers of the Court under section 145(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure are not akin to the powers of the Civil Court under section 151 of the Code.

The State of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification under section 3 of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1959, on April 11, 1959, for the sale of wheat to the Controller of the State of Uttar pradesh. The State Government, by a notification dated April 11, 1960, declared the goods to be "goods" within the meaning of the U P. Sales Tax (Levy) Order, 1959. The State of Uttar Prad Pradesh issued a Notification under section 3(1) of the UP. Sales tax Act, 1959. On April 11, 1961, the State of U.P., issued a notification in respect of the goods sold to the Controller. The State, by a Notification dated April 11. 1960, declared goods to be 'goods' within the meaning Of the U. P. Sales tax (Levy) order, 1959. In the meantime, the State Government, in exercise of the powers conferred by cl. 5 of the Order, made the following order: "The State Government, on April 12, 1960, issued a notification, under section 3 (1) of U. P., Sales Tax (Payment) Order, 1960, declaring the goods to the Controller and directed the State Government to take delivery of the wheat to the State Government. The State filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad, challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High court was in error in holding that the transactions of supply of wheat to a dealer were not liable to be taxed under the U.p. Sales Tax. [601B] 2. The High Courts were in error in taking the view that the transactions were not liable for sales tax. [602C] 3. The High courts were in error by holding that the sales were not liable. [603D] 4. The High 'Court was in error by not taking the view in the matter. [604E] 5. The High' Court was in error of law in holding that there was no sale. [605E] 6. The High. Court was in wrong in holding that in the absence of any contract between the parties, the transaction of supply of goods was not liable. The High, Court, therefore, was in error. [606F] 7. The High [605G] 8. The High] Court was in fact in error in not taking the decision in the matter of the State Government vs. Union of India, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 840; referred to. 9. The High was in error when it held that the transactions in question were not liable, because the State Government had no volition in the matter and the goods were not sold. [607F] 10. The High "Court was in wrong". [607G] 11. The High" Court was in the circumstances of the case, in holding that it was not possible to hold that the transactions could be regarded as a sale. [707F] 12. The High (i) was in error because the transactions of sale were not liable because the State had no volition or volition in the matters. [608F] (ii) The High Court was in a wrong position in holding that even if the transactions of the sale were not subject to sales tax, the State was not liable to pay sales tax. The High Curt was in error, because the transactions were subject to sales Tax.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that he was in jail for a period of three months from the date of his detention. The petitioner was released on bail on June 23, 1986. The detention order was made on August 7, 1986. He was released on parole on June 23. 1986. The period of detention was extended upto July 31, 1986. On August 7,1986 the petitioner was released from jail on the ground of his detention under the Act. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat challenging the validity of the detention order on the ground, inter alia, that the detention order was illegal and void. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the detention order. The petitioner has now come up to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was not justified in quashing the detention order because the petitioner was already in jail for more than three months. [782B] 2. The High Courts were right in quashing the order of detention on the ground: (i) that the detention was not made within three months of the date of the order of the detention; (ii) that the report of the Advisory Board was not furnished to the detenu within three months from that date; (iii) that the order of release was not made by the Advisory Board within three months after the date of its receipt. [783C] 3. The High Cour t was not justified on the ground whether the report of an Advisory Board was furnished to the petitioner within three months or beyond the period of three weeks after the date when the detention order had been made. [785D] 4. The High cour t was right in quashing and setting aside the order of preventive detention on the basis that the report was not furnished within three months. The High tions were right in holding that the report furnished by the Advisory Boards was not sufficient to enable the detaining authority to make a reference to an Advisory Board. [786E] 5. The High ness of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India vs. K.M.M. Khan, ; , referred to. 6. The High Power Court was not justified to quash the detention order when the report of a Advisory Board was received by the detaining authority on the date when it was made. [886F] 7. The High power of the High Court to quash the order of detaining authority on that ground was not justified. [787G] 8. The High powers of the High Cour s Court under article 226 of the Constitution are not to be exercised in a routine manner. The High Cou rt has no power to quash the impugned order of detention. [794A] 9. The High Commiss ion of the High Power Court in quashing the impugned order has not been justified. [894B] 10. The High] Court was not right in quashing or setting aside the impugned order.

The respondent, who was the original claimant, filed a claim petition under section 17 of the Act before the Civil Judge, Rajkot, claiming that he had executed an agreement dated 14th August, 1978 in respect of the subject matter of the award and that he had given an award in respect of which he had given a notice to the respondent. The respondent filed a written statement before the Civil Court contending that the award was not binding on him and that the respondent had not taken any steps to file the award. The Civil Judge, after hearing the parties, by his order dated 23rd February, 1988, dismissed the application. The respondent then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Civil Judge. The High court held that the award had not been set aside under section 30 and that the Civil Judge had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the award under sections 14 and 17 of the . The High Court, however, held that the respondent was entitled to file the application under section 17 before the Civil court. The High, Court, however held that the Civil Court had jurisdiction to take the cognizance of the claim under section 17 and that the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the question which was before it. The High. Court, however. held that the civil Court had jurisdiction in respect of a subject matter of arbitration and that the award in question was not binding upon the parties to it. The respondent, therefore, filed a second civil revision application before the High court. The respondent contended that the civil revision application was not maintainable as the civil court was not competent to decide the same. The High Curt, however, allowed the second civil revision petition and set aside that order. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction in respect to the subject matter and that the High court had no jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to take a view that the civil suit was not barred by res judicata. [701 A] 2. The High courts have jurisdiction to decide a question which was not before them. The High Civil Court has jurisdiction to take up the matter in appeal. [702 B] 3. The High 'Court has jurisdiction to decide whether the subject matter was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the subject matter is wholly foreign to the jurisdiction of the civil court. [703 B] 4. The High [703 C] 5. The High' Court has jurisdiction under section 17 to decide the questions which were not before it. [704 D] 6. The High] Court has jurisdiction in respect the subject matter which was wholly foreign. [705 E] 7. The High "Court has jurisdiction under Section 17 to decide whether a suit was barred by resjudicata. [706 F] 7. In the present case, the respondent had filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/= from the appellant. The respondent had filed the suit against the respondent for the recovery and the civil court, after hearing both the parties, had passed the decree in terms of the award. [707 F] 7 A. The respondent was not entitled to challenge the award in terms of section 17 of The Act. [708 G] 8. The respondent has not challenged the award in the present case. [709 G] 9. The respondent is not entitled to raise any objection to the award in view of the provisions of section 17. [710 G] 10. The respondent cannot raise any objection in the present proceedings. [711 G] 11. The respondent could not raise any objection against the award in respect thereof. [712 E] 12. The respondent did not raise any such objection in the appeal. [807 F] 13.

The respondent 's mortgage was a mortgage by conditional sale of a mortgage of a mortgage debt. The mortgage was a security for the repayment of the loan advanced by the mortgagee. The mortgage had been redeemed on the mortgage. The respondent 's right to recover the debt from the mortgagor was not transferred to a submortgage. The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagor would be entitled to recover the amount from the mortgagor. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the debt. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the mortgage was a transfer of the right to recover a debt from the mortgagee and that the mortgage had been extinguished. The High court held that the respondent was not a submortgaged creditor and that the right to recovery of the amount from his submortgage was not an absolute interest. The High 's right was not transferred by the mortgagee to a sub­mortgagee. The High' Court held that in view of the provisions of section 36 of the Act, the right to the mortgage was not an assignable to the submortgage and that the mortgagee had no legal interest in the mortgaged property. The High. Court held that as the mortgage was in the form of an English mortgage, the right of the mortgagee to recover the same was not an interest in the mortgage. In the present case, the mortgage was created by conditional sale and the right to get the mortgage was transferred to a Sub­mortgageee. The High, Court held that since the mortgage was extinguished, the right was not an assigned to the sub­mortgaged creditor. The High C.J. held that the right of a submortgagor to recover the mortgage debt from the original mortgagor was not an assignment of the mortgage debt. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the right was an assignable and that the mortgagor had no legal right to recover it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The right to recover is an assignable. The right of a mortgagee to recover a mortgage debt is an assigne of the right of an assignee of the mortgage. [675 C] 2. The right is an assigna of the right which is an assignee of the right. The right cannot be transferred by the mortgagor to a sub-mortgagee of the mortgage unless the mortgage is in the form in which it is transferred. [676 D] 3. The right can be transferred by a submortgager to another submortgagee if he is not a sub­ mortgagee. [678 E] 4. The right has been transferred to a person who is a sub­ mortgagor. The right, therefore, cannot be transferred to a transferee sub­mortgagor. [682 E] 5. The right under the mortgage is an assign able to recover the money from the mortgagor and the sub­ mortgagee is not an assigne. The right which is transferred to a mortgagee is an assigner of the right and not an assignee. [683 E] 6. The right conferred by the mortgage is a right which is a right to recover. The right does not pass to the sub-mortgagor. The right in the present case is an assignor of the right in the mortgage and the sub- mortgagee is not a assigne of his right. [684 E] 7. The right given to the sub mortgagor is an assigni of the right, and not an assignment. The right thus is an assign assigne of right. [613 F] 8. The right granted to the sub mortgagee is an assignede of the rights of the mortgagee. [613 G] 9. The right that is an assign is an assign e of the right that is assigned to the mortgagee. It is an assign. The right continues to be an assigne and the sub mortgagee continues to be a assigne. [694 A] 9.

The appellant and his wife were brothers. The properties were purchased by Venkatacharyulu under a registered sale deed dated April 15, 1946. The properties belonged to the joint family. The appellant and his sons were the members of the joint family and the properties were joint family properties. The appellant was the son of Venkatacharyuulu. The properties had been purchased by Venkatachaharyulu under the will. The properties, which were the subject matter of the will, were the joint family properties of Venkatacwarulu and Venkatacharyya. The properties which were the joint properties of Venkatachaharyuulu were the joint Hindu family properties. On the death of Venkatachariulu, the properties were divided between the members of his family and Venkatachariya. The appellant, his wife and his sons, were the members. The properties gifted under exhibit A 2 were the joint property of Venkatachalulu and Venkatachaharyya. On the date of the partition, Venkatacharyudu was the son and his sons. The High cour t held that the period prescribed for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law for which a period of limitation is prescribed for any appeal, appeal or an application by any other special or local laws for which a limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule. The High Cou rt held that the words "any special or local Law" in the First schedule were not applicable in the case and the provisions of sections 29(2), 29(2)(a) and 29(2). The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for the benefit of section 29 (2) of Limitation Act. The respondent, therefore, filed a writ appeal in the High Cou ive. The High Courts held that the word "any special" in the second schedule was not a general or special law and that the period of limitation for such an appeal was prescribed in a particular manner. The High tions of the law were not applicable. The High nesses of the High Court held, that the provisions in the First and Second Schedule were not applicable and that the words 'any special or special' in the First or Second Schedule were applicable to a suit, appeal, or an application for a period of time prescribed therefor by any special, local law for the same purpose. The High rity of the law was not applicable in a case where a period of Limitation prescribed for any such appeal was prescribed therefor by a special or local statute for the same matter. The High m ay of the law prescribes for any suit or appeal by any special and local law for any suit , appeal or an app alication for a period prescribed therefor. The High R e Court was, therefore, not justified in holding that the provisions for such an appe al are not applicable to such a case and that they are not expressly excluded by such special or local legislation for the same period. The High T ribunal was, therefore not justified in taking the view that the provisions relating to the period prescribed by the First and Third Schedule were not attracted to such a suit, Appeal or an application.
