The scheme, therefore, does not contain a provision for the amount of loss to the original plot and not the final scheme, and the amount of the compensation payable for loss to land has tobe determined on the principles laid down in section 71 of this Act. [77F] 6. The scheme has to be prepared by the town Planning Officer under section 68, and the Town Plan Officer has a duty under section 71 to calculate the amount of damages payable to the owner. [705G] 7. The scheme cannot be prepared by a Town Planning Officer under the provisions of the Act, and the scheme cannot be altered without reference to the improvement contemplated in the scheme. [706A] 8. The Town & Planning Officer has a statutory duty under section 70 of the Act to calculate the compensation payable under section 66 of the Act and the Town and planning scheme. [77G] 9. The Town Improvement Officer has a power under section 71, and the town planning scheme has to determine the amount of damage payable to the owners or the persons affected by the making a scheme. [78A] 10. The Town or Planning Officer has no power under section 70 to determine the compensation payable in respect of loss to land. [77B] 11. The Town Town Planning Officer has the power under section 73 to determine the market value on the basis that the compensation is payable on the basis thereof. [77C] 12. The Town Committee has the power to determine the value of the plot at the date when the declaration of intended to make a Scheme is made.

The testator was to select the house of the testator for the daughters and the children. The testator was to give the right of selection to the daughters and to make the selection. The testator made the selection and the selection. He was to select and appoint the daughters. The testator also made the selection. In the case of the widow, the testator made the appointment and the selection was made by the legatee. The testator, however, made the selection in the order in which he was to select his daughter. The testator then made the selection but the legatee did not choose to select the daughters. He was not to select the daughter. The widow, however, did not choose the right of the legatee to select the children. In the meantime, the testator, however made the selection of the daughters and made the selection by the legatee and made the appointment. The testator thereafter made the selection, but the legatee made the selection on the basis of the selection made by the testator. The testator did not choose his right of selection. The legatee made the appointment but the legatee himself made the selection without making the selection. On the construction of the will, the testator was to appoint the daughters and make the selection and appoint the daughter. In the circumstances, the testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to take them to the daughters. In the present case, the testator did not make the selection but he made the selection only on the basis that the daughters would get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The testator had made the selection after taking into consideration the good and good quality of the lands. The testator intended that each daughter would select the lands devised to take her to the daughters, but theamma would select the daughters and give her the right of appointment to the daughters; and the testator intended to give the selection and appointment to the daughter. It was, therefore, necessary that the testator intended the selection and appointing the daughters. It was not necessary that each daughter should get the areas of land devised for taking them to the daughter and to make her the selection. It was also necessary that each son should get the lands to be taken by each daughter. The object of the testator was clearly to select the sons and to make them the selection and to appoint the daughter to the daughters who would get their properties. The testator wanted to select the son and to make him the selection and he wanted to select his daughters. The legatee, however, was not to make the appointment. He was also to select the wife and to make it the selection and appointed the daughter. He was, therefore not to select his wife and to appoint his daughter. He, however, could not select the daughters because he had not made the selection or the selection. Held, that the testator had intended that each son would select the children and that the testator would give the right to select the mother and to make appointment to the children. It was open to the testator to select the nominees of the legatee and to make his selection and appointment. The proviso to section 89, which is in the form of an exception to section 89 of the Act, is in the nature of an exception. The testator has to select the wives and the children and to make their selection and appointment in the manner prescribed by section 89. The testator is to select the heirs and to make appointments in the manner provided by section 89, and to make such appointments. The testator cannot select the heirs or to make appointments. The proviso is in the same form and it is not necessary that the legatee should get the properties to be taken to the daughters or to make their appointments. The object is to select and make appointments in accordance with the provisions of section 89. It is not necessary to make the appointments in accordance either with the provisions contained in section 89 or section 89.

The appellant was the owner of the plots in dispute. He filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the plots. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the relief of partition and separate ownership. The High Court, however, held that the plaintiff was entitled to the reliefs of partition and joint ownership. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High court held that the trial court was right in holding that the appellant had not proved that the respondents were in joint possession of the lands and the plots in question. The High Curt, however, reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding in favour of the appellant. [901F] 2. The High courts were right in reversing the decision of both the courts below. [902F] 3. The High 'Court was right in reversing that decision. [903F] 4. The High' Court was right in not interfering with the judgment of the trial Court. [904F] 5. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was no evidence to prove that the respondents had practised a fraud on the consolidation authorities. [905F] 6. The High, Court was right on its finding that the appellant did not establish that the respondents are in joint possession and possession of the land. [906F] 7. The High] Court was right when it held that the respondents could not be said to be in joint possession. [908F] 8. The High was right in setting aside the judgment of both the Courts below. [0901F] 9. The High [905G] 9. In the instant case, the appellant had failed to establish that the partition proceedings were in his possession. The HighCourt was right when the appellant had produced a certified copy of the partition proceedings. [909F] 10. The High "Court was right, on its finding, that the appellant has failed to establish the fact that the partition was in his possession and that the respondents have acquired the rights of a co-sharer in the land. The High" Court was right that the appellant could not be deemed to be the owner of a part of the land and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to a decree for partition and joint possession. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The petitioner was elected as a Prime Minister of India in the year 1951. He was elected as the Prime Minister of the State on the basis of the oath register maintained by the Prime Minister. He was also a member of the Council of Ministers. He was appointed as the Prime Ministers of the State. He was a member of Legislative Assembly of the State and was also a Member of the Council. He was nominated as the Prime Minis ter of the State of Haryana. He was not a member of any political party. He was, therefore, not a member in the Council of States. He was disqualified to be a member of a political party. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Prime Minister. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner has filed this appeal by special leave. The petitioner contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the oath register was not the one prescribed by the Constitution and that the oath was not a part of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that a person who is a member of an political party is not a member thereof. [701B] (2) The High court was in error by holding that the petitioner was not a Member of a political Party. [702C] (3) The High Curt was in error. The petitioner was not entitled to any relief. [703D] (4) The High Courts were in error in not holding that the appellant was not a person who was a member in a political party and that the High Curt had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition on the ground that the appellant had not been a member of that political party. [704E] (5) The High cites of the Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Virji Ram Sutaria Premji Bhavadia & Ors. vs Nathalal Premji Bhavaria & Ors., [1977] 1 S.C.R. 848, followed. (6) The High Cou rt was in error when it held that the oath is a part of a constitutional document. [705G] (7) The High tions of the Constitution were not merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a Prime Minis ter but were merely descriptive of his person and of the nomination as a Minister. [706A] (7)(a) The High Power Committee had not been constituted for the purpose of examining the question whether the oath register is a part or not. The High Power Committees had not been appointed for the purpose. [707B] (b) The High power Committee had not acted in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and the Constitution. [709C] (c) The High Commiss ion of the Constitution was not a mere error or error in the descriptive part of the oath. [710E] (8) The High powers Committee had not taken into consideration the fact that the oath registers were not a part or a mere error in theksj of the oath and that the appellant did not take any oath as a Prime Ministers. [711E] (9) The High Commissioner of the State Government had not been impleaded as a party to the writ petition and the High Court had not committed any error in holding the appellant as a member of his Council of States and the High Power Committee was not a party to that writ petition. [712E] (10) The High Commission was in error because the appellant was a member thereof and the High Commissi on of the Constitution had not been described as a member thereof in the Constitution. The High Commis sion of the High Court, therefore, was not correct. [713G] (11) The High Se cial Committee was not competent to act as a Prime minister.

The appellant, a factory, was engaged in the manufacture of "strike" and the workers were paid holidays with pay under section 49 A of the Factories Act. The appellant was appointed as a "strike " in the factory " in the year 1948. The appellant, however, did not work on that night. The workers were not entitled to annual holidays with pay. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the award of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to annual holiday with pay under the rules of the Mills. [601 A] The appellant was entitled only to annual holidays and the workers had to work on that day. [602 B] The appellant had not worked on that day and the workers could not be treated as having completed a period of twelve months ' continuous service in the factory. [603 C] The appellant, therefore, was entitled to the annual holidays with wages at the rate of Rs. 4,000 per month. [604 D] The appellant could not be said to be in the employment of the workers on that day because of the strike. [605 E] The appellant did not work in the factory on that day, and the workers did not work for that night. [606 E] The workmen were entitled to annual hours of work on that date. [607 F] The appellant would be entitled to annual wages at the rates of Rs. 5,000 per annum. [608 G] The appellant is entitled to annual leave on the date of the strike and the workers would be entitled only to the annual hours of service on that day on the date on which they would have completed a periodof twelve months ' in the factory, and the appellant would be liable to pay the annual holidays at the rate applicable to the workers on the date when they would have complete a period of 12 months ' in that factory.

The appellant, who was working as a driver of a vehicle, was convicted by the trial court under section 5A(1) of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000. The appellant was convicted by a trial court under sections 5A(2) and 79 I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a term of one year. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the certificate granted under section 79 of the Act was invalid because it was not issued by the competent authority under section 79 and that the certificate was not issued under section 79. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The certificate granted under sections 79 and 79 of the Penal Code is valid and effective. The certificate is valid and operative. [601B] 2. The certificate issued under section 80 of the Penal code is valid and valid. [602C] 3. The certificate under section 79 is valid and enforceable. [603D] 4. The certificate was issued by the Central Board of Film Censors and not by the Central Government. [604E] 5. The certificate has been issued by the Board under section 79, and the certificate is valid. [613F] 6. The certificate does not contain any reason for the certificate being invalid. The certificate cannot be used as a substitute for the certificate. [605G] 7. The certificate must be valid and operative and the certificate must be accompanied by a certificate under section 80. [606F] 8. The certificate being a substitute for a certificate, the certificate must also be accompanied by the certificate. The certificate should be accompanied by an affidavit. [607F] 9. The certificate in question is valid and subsisting. [608G] 10. The certificate of the Board under sections 79 is valid, valid and operative, and the prosecution is unsustainable. [609G] 11. The certificate, therefore, is invalid and inoperative. [610G] 12. The certificate dated 19.9.1979 is valid and legal. [612G] 13. The certificate having been issued by an authority competent to grant the certificate, the appellant cannot be prosecuted for an offence under section 292 I.P C.P.c. and the prosecution being unsustainable, the appellant is entitled to the benefit of section 79 I. P.C.

The appellant, a Government Pleader, Madras, was appointed as a Government Pleader for the State of Bihar. He was appointed as an Advocate for the State. He was also appointed as an advocate for the State and was also appointed a Government Pleader. On the basis of the report of the Public Service Commission, the Government Pleader was appointed as the Advocate for the appellant. The appellant was appointed as Advocate for the High Court of Patna. He was a Government Pleader and was also a Government Pleader in the High Court. He was the Advocate for a High Court of Calcutta. He was an Advocate for a Government Pleader at the High Court and was also an Advocate for another High Court. The Government Pleader was also appointed by the Government Pleader. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court of Patna challenging the appointment of the Advocate for him as an Advocate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High Courts of Patna. The High court held that the Government Pleader had no duty to the Government Pleader to perform all or any of the functions and duties to be performed by him in the due exercise of that office. The High Courts held that the appellant was not a Government Pleader nor was a Government Advocate. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High 'Court of Patna for a writ of mandamus to the Government pleader to perform all the functions and functions to be performed in the due discharge of that office, and that the Government pleader was also appointed to perform all those functions and duties. The High 'Court held that the appointment of a Government Pleader was a public office within the scope of the quo warranto proceeding. The High [Court further held that the State Government Pleader was not a public office and that the appellant had no duty or duty to the public at all and all the functions were performed by him. The High "Court further held: "The Government Pleader was an agent of the Government Pleader and he was also a public officer acting in his official capacity. He was not a party to the writ petition and was not a Public Officer. The High, Court held that the act of the Government pleader amounted to a public office. The appellant had no right to the office of Government Pleader. He was, therefore, not a Government Advocate and was not entitled to the office as a public officer. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant is a Government Pleader who is a Government Advocate in the High Curt. The High Curt held that the office of the Government is a public office, and the Government Pleader is a Government pleader. The High Commissioner, in his order dated December 7, 1979, held that the post of Government Pleader was merely a public office; and that the High Court held that it was not a private office. The appeal was dismissed. The appellant thereupon filed a writ of certiorari under Article 226 of the Constitution. The HighCourt held that a writ of quo warranto was maintainable against the Government Pleader, who was a public officer, and that he was not a person who was a Government pleader, and that since the Government Pleader did not act as a public servant, the High Court was not competent to issue a writ of Mandamus. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Power Court was right in holding that the Government Advocate was not a "public servant" within the meaning of Article 21 of the Constitution and that the writ of quo Warrant issued by the High Court against the Government Advocate, was not maintainable. [782E] 2. The High power of the Government to issue a Writ of quo warranto is not a power of superintendence. The High powers of the Government are not a power which is not a matter of any kind. The HighPower of the Government cannot be exercised in a manner which is not in the interest of the public at large. [785A] 3. The High is not a Court of law.

The appellants were the shareholders of the Mills. The shares of the Bank of India were sold by the Bank of Baroda to the Mills. On the sale of the shares, the Mills sold the shares to the Bank of the Bank. The Bank of India, in turn, sold the shares in favour of the Bank, and the sale proceeds were distributed among the shareholders. The Bank, in turn sold the shares, to the Bank, in favour of its nominees. The Bank sold the shares on the ground that the shares were not distributed in the market. The Bank filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of the sale of shares. The High Court held that the sale of these shares amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income Tax Act and the sale of those shares amounted to a distribution of dividend. The High court held that the right to apply for the shares of the Mills amounted to distribution within the meaningof section 2(5A) of that Act and the right to purchase the shares was not a dividend within the ordinary meaning of that expression in section 2(2) of the Act. The High, Court, however, held that the distribution of the right to the Bank was a distribution of the dividend within the definition of "dividend" in section 2 (6A) and the right was not a "dividends" within the meaning Of section 2(8A) of Income Tax Act. The Bank appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The right to apply under section 2(3) of the Indian Income Tax Act is a right to apply to the Bank for the shares. The right to purchase is a right which had a monetary value. The right of the Bank to apply for shares is a right not a dividend. [701B] (2) The right of a Bank to apply to it for the shares is a "dicend" within the definition in section 2 of the Act and the distribution of dividend is a right of the shareholders. [702C] (3) The right is a right in the Bank of a share to sell the right to a shareholder. The right is not a dividend but a right to sell the shares. [703D] (4) The right under section 2 (5A) is a right that had a monetary amount of the value of the shares. It is a right flowing from the right to sell. The right under [703E] (5) The right cannot be taken away by the mere fact that the shares had a monetary consideration. [704F] (6) The right conferred by section 2(4) of the Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1922, is a right created by the Act. [705G] (7) The right given to the Bank to sell the share of the Bank is a right, which had a pecuniary value. [706F] (712A] (8) The right, which was conferred by section 3(6A), is a right given to a shareholder to sell the same share. The right conferred under section 3(5A), is not a right created in favour of a shareholder. [707F] (9) The right which was conferred under section 2 of The Bank of Baroda Act, 1922 is a right conferred by the Act and is a right acquired by the Bank. [709F] (10) The right was not an absolute one. The Bank was not entitled to sell the entire share of the shares of a company. [710F] (11) The right had not been taken away by a resolution for the sale of a share of the company. [809F] The right to sell was not an exclusive right to sell a share of a company but a right conferred on a shareholder. It was a right to transfer a share of company.

The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the order of the High Court refusing to examine the witness who was present in the Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order passed by the High Court. The petition was dismissed by the High court. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High High Court. During the pendency of the writ petition, the appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to refuse to examine the witnesses who were present in the court and that the High court had no jurisdiction under Order XVI Rule 1A to examine the persons who were present when the evidence of the witnesses was not material for the decision of the petition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court has no jurisdiction to decline to examine the person who is present in the witness who is present when the witness produced by the party is being examined. [801B] 2. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to reject the witness who has been present when the witnesses are called for the purpose of procuring the attendance of a witness by the Court. [802C] 3. The High courts have no jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure to refuse to examination the witness who are present when the examination of the witness is not material for deciding the petition. [803D] 4. The High Curt has no jurisdiction under Article 226 to refuse to examining the witness who may have been present when his evidence is not material. [804E] 5. The High Civil Court has no jurisdiction in refusing to examine a witness who is not present when the document is being examined by the Court and the Court has no power to refuse to summon a witness who may be present when the documents are called for. [805E] 6. The High Criminal Court has no powers to refuse to call a witness who has not been present when their evidence is not necessary for the decision. [806E] 7. The High Power Court has no authority to refuse to consider the witness who can be present when his statement is not material and that the witness who produced the document is not available when his evidence was not material. The High power of the Court to refuse to allow the witness to examine is not a power of the court to refuse to permit the witness to produce the document. [807E] 8. The High powers of the Court under Order XVI Rules 1A and 1A of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not available when the evidence is not relevant for deciding the application. [808E] 9. The High is not right in refusing to consider the witnesses who are present in the list filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1A of Order XVI. [809F] 10. The High Commissioner has no jurisdiction, under Order XVI, Rule 1A, to refuse to produce the witnesses who may have appeared in the list prepared under sub rule(1) of rule 1A. [810G] 11. The High Commission has no jurisdiction. The High Commision has no jurisdiction and the Court is not closed. [811G] 12. The High [811H] 12. In the instant case, the High Court has no Jurisdiction to refuse to exercise its discretion to examine the petitioner who is present before the Court. It is not open to the High Court to refuse the examination of a witness who can produce the documents under Rule 1A. The HighCourt has no jurisdiction over the matter. [812G] 13. The High Cou rt has no jurisdiction or power to refuse the production of the documents under rule 1A of Rule 1 A. [813G] 14. The High Se ction of the High Courts under Order XVI of the Code is not applicable to the facts of the present case.

The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College on April 27, 1981. He was appointed as a Principal of the college on April 27. 1981. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the appellant as Principal of that college. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the appointment of appellant as Principal was not valid and that the appointment was not made on April 27 1981. The High, Court, however, held that the order of appointment of the Principal was not invalid. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High 'Court. The High 'Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the salary paid to him as Principal of a College on April 28, 1981. The appellant contended that the order dated April 7, 1981 was not valid because the order contained in the radiogram had no effect on the validity of appointment of appellant. The High. Court, however held that the power to make the appointment was conferred on the Committee of Management under the Regulations and therefore the appointment of Principal was valid. The appellant thereupon filed a writ Petition in the High. Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High' Court held that the Selection Committee had no power to make appointment and therefore the order dated May 1, 1981 was invalid. The High Cour t held that the Committee of management had no power under the Regulations to make the selection on April 27 1982. The High cour t held, that the Selection Board had no power, under the Regulations, to make the appointments on April 27 1983. The High tions, therefore, held that there was no power of appointment on April 27 1984. The appellant then filed a writ peti tion in the High Cour cial Court challenging the selection on the ground that the Selection committee had no power or jurisdiction to make the Selection Committee under the Regulations. The High Cou rt held that the selection was valid and that it was not open to the Selection Committee to make the de cision of the Committee of the Management to make the ad hoc appointment. The High ny, however, dismissed the writ appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Selection Com mittee had no power and jurisdiction to make appointment on April 28 1983. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Selection Committee had power to make selection on April 28 1982. The Selection Board had power to cancel the appointment of a Principal on April 27 1980. [782E] 1.2. The Selection Com mmissioner had power to issue appointment order on April 27 1979. The Selection Commi ssion had power to do so. [783G] 1.3. The Selection Commission had power to appoint a Principal on May 27, 1981 and the Selection Committe sion had power under the regulations to make the appoint ment on April 27 1985. [784G] 1,3.1.2. In the instant case, the Selection Commit sion had no power. [785G] 1:1.3.1 The Selection Commit tee had power to select and appoint a Principal. [786G] 1.:1.3 The Selection Committ ee had power to suspend or rescind the appointment of an employee on April 27 1986. [787G] 1 :1.4.1.1.3 In the instant cases, the Selection Committee did not exercise power under the Regulation to make theappointment on April 27 1988. [794G] 1.(1)1.3 It is true that the Selection Commi sion had powers to make the Appointment on April 27 1989. But the Selection Committed had power to pass the appointment on April 29 1988. [894G] 2.1.4 The Selection Committed has power to make an appointment on April 30 1988.

The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, with effect from January 1, 1956. The appellant company was registered under the Indian Company Act, 1956. On September 8, 1988, the appellant company was transferred to the Labour Court, Dhanbad. The respondent company was registered as a case under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. The respondent Company was registered as Case No. 10 of 1988. The respondent was served with a notice under section 33 B of the Act on the appellant company. The appellant Company filed an application before the Labour Court for transfer of the case from the Labour Court to the Labour court, Dhanbad. On September 9, 1988, an application was made by the respondent company to the Labour Judge, Dhanbad, for transfer of case from the labour court, Dhanbad to the Labour 'Court, Dhanbad. It was contended that the respondent company had not been served with a copy of the order of transfer and that the respondent had not been given an opportunity of being heard before the Labour 'Tribunal. The Labour 'Tribunal, Dhanbad, by its order dated September 9,1988, allowed the application and directed the respondent company not to transfer the case from Dhanbad to the labour 'Court, Patna. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Labour ' Tribunal, Dhanbad, and directed the appellant company to transfer the matter to the Labour' Court, Dhanbad, on the ground that the respondent was not served with a certified copy of the orders of transfer. The respondent challenged the order of his transfer before the High court. The High court allowed the appeal, set aside the orders of the Labour Court and the Labour ' Tribuna l, Dhanbad, holding that the respondent Company was not served and that the order of transferring the case from Patna to the Labour, Court, Dhanbad was illegal. The High 'Court, however, allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that since the respondent company was not served, the order of termination was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The respondent is a workman and the order of dismissal is not vitiated by any illegality. [701B] 1.2. The respondent had not challenged the order passed by the Labour 'Trial Court, Dhanbad in the application filed by the respondent before the Labour'Tribunal, Dhanbad. [702C] 1.3. The respondent has not challenged the orders of termination in the application before the labour 'Tribunal, which was filed by the appellant company before the Labour, Tribunal, Dhanbad. Therefore, the order passed in the application is vitiated by illegality. [602D] 1.4. The respondent, therefore, cannot be allowed to challenge the order of discharge in the application. [703E] 1.5. The order of the High Court is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Labour. Court, Dhanbad to decide the application afresh in accordance with law. [705G] 1.6. The order passed by Labour 'Tribunal is set aside. The Labour Court, Ranchi, in the application, is directed to decide the matter afresh in accordance wit hin the order of reinstatement. [706G] 1,6. The Labour'Tribunal is directed to dispose of the application afresh, in accordance with the law. [607G] 1:1.7. The Labour, Tribunal is directed to consider the application afresh and dispose of the same in accordance with Law. [707G] 2.1.2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the respondent is directed to file an application before this Court for transfer to the Labour Courts, Dhanbad, within a period of four weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of this order.

The appellant company was incorporated under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant company was registered under the provisions thereof. The appellant was incorporated under section 10 (1) of the Act. The appellant Company was registered under section 10(1) of that Act. The management of the hotel was also registered under the Act. It was in the course of the investigation that the appellant company was apprehended by the management of the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi, and its workmen were also named as workmen. The appellant, however, did not make a reference to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant was not a party to the reference and that the reference was bad in law. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the reference made by the appellant was incompetent because it was not a dispute between the management of Hotel Workers ' union and its workmen. The High court, therefore, held that it was not necessary to refer the dispute to the Industrial tribunal for adjudication. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The reference made by it was not competent because it was a dispute between a management of the company and its workmen, and it was not an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Act, as the dispute was not a matter of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour, of any person. [801B] 2. The dispute was not an Industrial dispute within the definition of the Act and therefore, the reference made to the Industrial Court was incompetent. [802C] 3. The dispute between the appellant and its workmen was not a " industrial dispute " within the meaningof the Act. [803D] 4. The dispute, therefore, was not a ' industrial dispute " in the sense of the term " in the Act. In the present case, the dispute was between the management and the workmen, and the appellant company, and it is not a "industrial dispute " within that meaning. [804E] 5. The dispute is not a dispute relating to the conditions of labour. The dispute does not fall within the definition. The reference was made to the Tribunal for adjudication. [805G] 6. The dispute relates to the conditions which were mentioned in the order of reference. The dispute did not fall within that definition. The dispute could not be referred to the Industrial court for adjudication. It was not a case of a dispute relating only to the conditions mentioned in the reference. [806F] 7. The dispute referred to the Tribunal was not a industrial dispute within that definition, and therefore, it was not open to the Tribunal to refer the same to the Industrial Judge for adjudication. In the circumstances, the reference was incompetent. The Tribunal was not justified in holding that the reference to the industrial tribunal was incompetent. 8. The Tribunal had not given any reasons for holding that the dispute was an industrial dispute. [807F] 8. The dispute which was referred to the industrial Tribunal was not an " industrial dispute" within the meaning ofs. 10(1)(a) of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947, and therefore the reference was not incompetent. [820G] 9. The dispute as to the conditions to be satisfied by the management was not an ' industrial dispute within s. 10(2) of the [807C] 10. The dispute in the present case was not an industry within the meaning Of the Act. Therefore, the reference to that dispute was incompetent. 10. The Tribunal has not given any reason for holding that it was an industrial matter. [808D] 10. In the instant case, the Tribunal has not made any reference to the dispute as to whether the dispute is an industrial dispute or not. [809E] 11.

The appellant imported a rod bushes and camshaft bushes, which were imported by the appellant, from the Customs authorities, and the bushes, which have been imported by the Appellant, were parts of such engines, which have already been included under Heading No. 84.06. The appellant imported a rods bushes and cam shafts, which have also been imported by them, from the customs authorities, and they also imported the same, and the goods were parts of the engines, which were also parts of such engine. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 1st March, 1976, and prayed for a direction to the Customs authorities to grant exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and the camshaft stones, which have not been imported by him, and also for a direction that the bushes, imported by the appellants, should be parts of such vehicles, and not a few parts of such tractors, which have to be imported by the Appellants. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Notification No, 281 Cus./76, dated January 1, 1976, exempts parts of such motor vehicles, which have the same characteristics of internal combustion piston engines, and that the bushes imported by the assessee, are parts of such chassis, and not any parts of such machinery, and that they are parts of the engine, which have nothing to do with the engines, and, therefore, the exemption granted by the Notification is not applicable to parts of such machines, and that, therefore, they are not entitled to the benefit of the Notification. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The exemption granted by Notification No.281 Cus./ 76, dated 1 st March, 1976 is not applicable in respect of parts of such parts of such vehicle, and, consequently, the parts of such cars, which have no other characteristics of internal diesel piston engine, and, as such, the exemption is not applicable. [601 C] 2. The exemption is not available to parts of the motor vehicles, and, in the absence of any provision to the contrary, the parts imported by the petitioner, are parts, of such vehicles. [602 D] 3. The exemption under the Notification is only for parts of such Motor Vehicles, which have a characteristics of internal fuel piston, and not for internal combustion pistson engines, which are parts of a engine, and not parts of such diesel pistons. [603 E] 4. The exemption cannot be denied to parts of motor vehicles, because, as mentioned in the Notification, the bushes, and the cam shafts are parts of that engine, and the parts of that engines, which cannot be imported by any other person, and, if so, the exemption cannot be claimed. [604 F] 5. The exemption, therefore, cannot be denied, because, the bushes imported, by the appellant are parts of internal combustion Piston engines falling under Heading No 84.06, and, that, therefore the parts of the diesel pistones, which have all the characteristics of internal engines, and not of internal combustion parts of that motor vehicles, cannot be imported, by any other individual, and, on the other hand, the parts, which are imported by the other individual, cannot be said to be parts of the Motor Vehicles, because, they are parts, which cannot, therefore, be imported by a person, and the exemption cannot, therefore be denied. [605 F] 6. The Notification does not contain any provision to that effect. The exemption does not contain a provision to that extent.

The plaintiffs of Fathima Bee, who were the daughter of Sayed Gaffar Sahib, had filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the Dargah and for a declaration that the right of Fathma Bee had become barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the right to possession of the plaintiffs was barred by limitation and the suit was dismissed. The High Court held that the right was not barred by limitation as the plaintiffs had not claimed any right or interest in the Dargah and that the right had become barred. The High court held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that Fathima was a Bee and that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any share in the Dargah. The High Curt held that the rights of Fathida Bee had become extinguished by ouster of Fathua Bee and that Fathma was a Bee. The High ct. Court held that Fathida was a Bee who had lost his right and therefore the suit was barred by time. The High Cou rt held that Fahima Bee had no right to claim any share in Dargah and that Fahida Bee had no interest in the property. The High n otice of the High Court was set aside. The High tiffs appeal was allowed. The High l ights Court held that there was no evidence whatsoever to show that Fathua was a Bee or that the right got extinguished by ouster was a matter of fact. The High rict Court held that even if Fathima had not been given a share in the property, the right of the plaintiffs would be adverse to the inter est rights of Fahida Pe. The High f ile Court held that it was not a case of ouster of Fahima Pe. The plaintiffs had not proved that Fathia Bee had any right to claim a share in Dargah. The plaintiffs were not able to prove that the right stood extinguished by ouster. The High m e Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show that the right came into existence at any point of time when Fathima Pe had become barred, the plaintiffs were entitled to any right in the Dargah as well as the right of management and possession of Dargah. The appeal was allowed and the suit of the plaintiffs for partition and recovery of possession was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the right which Fathima has lost the right of ownership and possession of the property was not barred. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right of Fahua Bee to claim any right or claim in the Dargah is a right which has become barred by time and the right of possession of Fathia Pe is a right to claim such right or claim as is available to Fathima. [601B] 1.2 The right of the Fathima to claim any interest in the Fathua Pe is a vested right to claim the right of Management and possession of property. The right of management or possession of Dargah is a vested one. The right to claim ownership and possession is a vested interest in Fathima and Fathima is a vested rights in Fathua. [602C] 1.3 The right of ownership or possession of the Fahima is a right of management, possession of Dargah and the right to claim interest in the affairs of Dargah. [603D] 1.4 The right of Management or possession of Fahuja Bee to claim ownership or possession is a right vested in Fathma. The right is a vested in Fahuja Pe. The right cannot be denied to Fathma on the ground that Fathoma Bee had no rights in the Dargah or that Fathila Bee had no title. [605E] 1.5 The right of title of Fathila Pe is a statutory right vested in the Fahuja pe. The right can be denied to the Fathila pe.

The appellant was appointed as a casual labourer in the office of the 1st respondent on a monthly salary of Rs. 10,000/- and was paid a monthly salary at Rs. 10/- per month. The appellant was appointed on a monthly pay of Rs. 5,000/- in the office. He was also paid a monthly allowance at Rs. 5/- per month and was paid Rs. 5/-. The appellant was also paid Rs. 10/-. The 1st respondent was appointed on the post of a casual labourer on a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3/- per month, and was paid an allowance of Rs. 2/- per month for the period of his service. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to the house rent allowance as he had refused to occupy the quarters offered to him. The 1st appellant contended that the house rent allowances were not included in the terms of the contract between the parties and that the appellant was entitled to get house rent allowance. The 1 st respondent contended that the appellant had been allotted the quarters allotted to him and that the house Rent allowance was not included in his terms of the agreement between the parties. The 1St respondent contended that he was not entitled to the House rent allowance as the same was not included within the terms of contract between the appellant and the 1st appellant. The 1 St respondent contended that there was no binding contract between the 1st and the appellant and that the 1st respondents had no right to claim house rent allowance and that the said house rent allowance was not includible in the terms. Held, that the appellant could not claim house rent allowances as he had not been allotted the quarter allotted to him. He was not entitled under the rules to claim house Rent allowance. The appellant had been given house rent allowance in the office and he was not bound to occupy the same. The 1ST respondent was not entitled, under the rules, to claim house allowance. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant did not have any right to claim House rent allowance. In the circumstances, the appellant was not entitled for house rent allowance under the rules. The appeal is, therefore, allowed, the judgment and order of the High Court is set aside and the appellant is entitled to get House rent allowance at the rate of Rs. 4/- per month from the 1st Respondent. The appellant is entitled for house Rent allowance at the same rate as was granted to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 11nd, 11th and 11th respectively.

The detenu was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, by the State Government under Section 3(1) of the (for short 'the Act') on March 25, 1980. He was served with a show cause notice, dated March 25, 1979, under Section 3 of the Act, alleging that he had committed a breach of the provisions of the Act. The grounds of detention were served on the detenus on March 25. 1980. The detenus were informed that they had been detained under the Act on March 25 and that they had, on March 25,. 1980, been informed that they were supplied with the copies of the statements and documents relied upon or referred to in the grounds of detention. The detenus, however, did not make an effective representation at the earliest. The detenus filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the detention on the ground that the grounds of the detention were not served on them and that they were not supplied with the documents and statements relied upon or relied upon by them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the detenus that the grounds were not served upon them and that the copies of those documents were not supplied to them. The grounds did not disclose the details of the statements of those persons. [792B] 11. The State appealed to this Court. The High Court held that the trial court was right in holding that the trial was not maintainable and that the accused persons were acquitted at a joint trial. The High court, however, held that the joint appeal against the accused persons was competent and the State was entitled to prefer an appeal against the acquittal. The High 'Court further held that the State was not entitled to prefer a joint appeal against an order of acquittal at a joint appeal by the State. In the appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that a joint appeal could not be admitted only on a question of law and that the High 'Court was wrong in not holding that the joint appeals against the accused were competent. The High' Court was right in not holding the joint appeals to be incompetent because the joint appeal was not competent. [802C] 3. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was no bar to contain a bar to contain an order of admission. [803D] 4. The High, Court was right when it held that the appellant was not entitled, to the benefit of the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, to be heard on the merits. [804E] 5. The High was right in rejecting the appeal. [805F] 6. The High] 7. The High [805G] 8. The High is right in holding in favour of the appellant that the joint trial was not competent because the appellant was acquitted at a stage when the appeal was heard on merits. [820G] 805A] 805B] 9. The High Curt was right in dismissing the appeal. The High 1.I.R. 1960 S.C. 1422, followed. 9. The appellant was acquitted by the trial court and the High court was right when the appeal against the acquitted accused was heard on the question of sentence and so the High Court had no jurisdiction to admit the appeal. 10. The High "Court was right in accepting the appeal against acquittal at a stage where the appeal against an accused was heard and the High ' Court was right. [806B] 805C] 9.1. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the 1918 Act on the ground that the interest on securities was not chargeable to income tax on the rental income from the house properties owned by the foreign firm. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the interest was chargeable to income on securities and the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the assessee was not entitled to the relief under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act. In the appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the interest could not be charged under the 1918 act because the interest on security was not chargeable under the 1918 law. The Tribunal accepted the contention of the assessee and held that interest on securities could not be chargeable to income chargeable to income from the rental income because the interest was not chargeable on securities. The Tribunal also held that the income from the immovable properties owned by foreign firm was not chargeable in the year of account. The Tribunal further held that the amount of interest on securities on securities was chargeable to tax under the 1922 Act and the assessee had not been able to prove that the interest charged was not chargeable. The Tribunal, however, held that the Income tax was not chargeable as the interest was charged on securities. In the present appeal, the assessee has challenged the order of assessment of the Income Tax Officer. The Tribunal has held that the entire income of the foreign firm was chargeable to Income tax on the income derived from the immovable property owned by the assessee. The assessee has also challenged the order on the ground of limitation. The Tribunal found that the interest chargeable on securities was a part of the assessee 's business and was not chargeable with income tax on income derived from immovable properties owned and held by the foreign business. The Tribunal was of the view that the interest paid on securities was in relation to the rental income of the assessee. In the circumstances, the Tribunal held that interest was chargeable on securities and was not liable to tax on the interest on the securities. The assessee preferred an appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The assessee is entitled to the exemption under Section 25(3). The assessee is not entitled to any relief under section25(3) because the interest paid by the foreign company on securities is not chargeable to tax on income received by the assessee from the foreign business and the assessee is not liable to pay any tax on the securities as well. [612E] 2. The assessee was entitled only to the benefit under section 25 of the 1922 act because the foreign business was discontinued in the year account. [613E] 3. The assessee had not claimed any relief under Section 25 (3). The Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to grant the relief under Section25(3). [613F] 4. The assessee did not claim any relief under [613G] 5. The assessee could not claim any benefit under section25 (3) because interest on securities is chargeable to income of the previous year. [614G] 6. The assessee, being a foreign company, was entitled to relief under section 75 of the 1922. [615G] 7. The assessee being a foreign Company, was entitled only for the benefit under Section 25 of the 1961 Act. [616G] 8. The assessee having not claimed any benefit under Section 75 of the 1961 act, the assessee was liable to pay interest on securities. [617G] 9. The assessee cannot claim any benefit in respect of interest on security on securities. It is not a case where the interest on capital on securities is charged to income tax. [618G] 912D] 9.1. The assessee in the present case was not entitled for the benefit of section 25(1) of the 1961.

The petitioner who was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Jammu and K.S.J.T. challenging the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on March 25, 1975. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Proclamation of emergency was in operation on the date of the order of the President and the Proclamation of the Legislative Assemblies of the States was not in operation on that date. The petitioner filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. The petitioner has filed this appeal by special leave. The petitioner contended that the Proclamation issued on March 26, 1975 was not in force on the date on which the Legislative Assembly was constituted and the period of five years in relation to the Legislative Assembly had not been extended by the two Proclamations of Emergency. The High Courts dismissed the writ petitions on the ground of delay and laches. The petitioner contends that the High Court was in error in holding that the Proclamation was in force on March 25.6.1975 when the Legislative Assembly took over the session of the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 (Act 30 of 1976) and that the two Pro Clamations of emergency were not in force when the resolutions were passed by both the Houses of Parliament. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Proclamation of Emergency is in operation on March 25/26, 1975 when the Legislative Assemblies were constituted and the two Pro clamations of the Emergency were in force when they were in force. The two Proclamsations of Emergency were in operation on 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 when they were not in operation. The two Acts of 1976 and 30 of 1976 were not in existence on the date when the resolutions of the Houses of the Parliament were passed. [701A B] 2. The two enactments of 1976 and the two Acts of 1977 were not in the official Gazette. The two statutes of 1976 and 25th day of June, 1975 were not in accordance with the resolutions of both the Houses. [702B] 3. The two provisions of the two Acts were not in conformity with the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament and the two Houses of Parliament respectively. [703C] 4. The two acts of Parliament approving the two resolutions of the House were duly published in the official gazette. The two resolutions of both Houses of the two Houses were duly approved by both the House of Parliament and by the two Houses. [603D] 5. The two notifications of the two houses of Parliament approving both the Houses were duly published by both the houses of Parliament and both the Houses and the two resolutions were duly approved. [704E] 6. The two Notifications of the two House of Parliament approving two resolutions of Parliament approving one of the two resolutions are duly published in both the Houses by the two houses. The two decisions of both the House are duly approved by the two House. [705G] 7. The two circulars of the two house of Parliament approving each of the two Resolutions of the two Legislative Assemblies of two Houses of the States were duly approved and the two Resolutions were duly approved in the two Houses by both the two Houses and the both the Houses had not been published in the Official Gazette. [706G] 7A. The two Circulars of the two States approving both the two resolutions have been duly approved by two Houses of both the States. [707C] 8. The two Resolutions of both the Legislative Assemblies are duly approved and they are duly approved. The two Houses of each of the three Houses of Parliament approving either of the two decisions of the two respective Houses of Parliament are duly approved in both the respective Houses of both Houses. [807D] 9. The two subsequent resolutions of both of the Houses are duly approved both by both the respective House of Parliament.

The appellant was the owner of a public temple situated in the City of Madurai. The respondents were the owners of the said property. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the property was a public temple within the meaning of the Madras Act 19 of 195 1. The respondents filed a written statement denying the claim of the appellant. The trial court framed the following issues: (1) Whether the property was an alienable private property of the family of the appellant and whether the property was not a public temple. (2) Whether the appellant was entitled to a decree for a declaration as prayed for. (3) Whether the suit was barred by limitation. (4) Whether the respondents were entitled to a declaration as sought for. (5) Whether the properties were private property of a public religious or a public temple as defined by the Madras Act 18 of 195 1? The trial court held that the property in question was not a private property of any kind and therefore the appellant was not entitled to a relief under article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959. The High Court held that the appellant was a public religious and a public temple and therefore the property was incapable of valuation. The High court held that there was no question of valuation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the property is a public temple or a private property was a question of fact. The question of valuation was a question which was not a question of law. [701B] 2. The question was whether the property in dispute was a public or a private temple. The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent 's factory at Calcutta. He was paid a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month. He was also paid a salary in lieu of the cash allowance. The appellant was paid a cash allowance for the re employment of the employees of the respondent ' s establishment. The appellant claimed that he was not entitled to cash allowance for his re employment. The Tribunal held that the re employment was not a matter of policy and that the appellant was not entitled under the Factories Act to claim cash allowance for re employment. In appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowances for the reemployed personnel which was not a question of policy and was not a dispute between the parties. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant had not made any provision for the reemployment of the reemployed employees of the respondents. The Tribunal further held that the claim of the appellant was rightly rejected by the Tribunal. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the reemployment was not a proper or justified policy. The Tribunal was in error in holding that it was not a case of re employment. [801B] The Tribunal was not right in holding the appellant 's case to be rejected. [802C] The Tribunal had not given any reasons for rejecting the claim of re employment of reemployed employees. [803D] The Tribunal has not given any reason for rejecting the claims of the appellant. [804E] The Tribunal, therefore, was in error. [805G] The Tribunal did not give any reasons for rejection of the claims of re employment and the appellant was entitled to cash allowances for re employment of all the reemployed persons. [806E] The appellant was not bound to make any provision for re employment in respect of re employment which was not the case of reemployment. [807F] The Tribunal could not have given any reasons in support of the claim of Reemployment of the appellant for cash allowance for work done by the appellant. The appellant had not been able to show that the reemployed staff of the respondent had been appointed on a liberal scale. [808F] The appellant had been making provision for the payment of cash allowance for employment in lieu of cash allowance. [809G] The appellant could not have been denied cash allowance for that part of the work done by him. [810G] The claim of the respondent for cash allowance was not accepted by the Tribunal and the Tribunal was right, in holding that re employment was a matter of Policy and was not justified. [811G] The High Court was right in refusing to make a reference on the ground that the re employed persons had made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellant and that the reemployers had made an undertaking to the effect that they would not be entitled to cash Allowance for re employment unless the re employed person had made an Undertaking to the effect, that the re employes had made an assurance to the effect. [812G] The fact that the re employing employees had made an undertakings to the effect would not be decisive of the question whether the re employment had made an implied condition of service. [813G] The question whether the appellant was bound to make a provision for the same or not would depend upon the facts of each case. [814G] The facts of the present case are not in dispute. The appellant is not bound to accept the re employment. He was not bound by the practice adopted in the comparable concerns in the region. [815G] The present case is not a case where the appellant was required to make a proper provision for the said re employment.

The respondent, the Union of India, the Railway Administration, was the agent of the Railway Administration and the respondent, the agent of Browne, the respondent, and the Railway Administration was the agent for the payment of the amount standing to his credit in a Provident Fund Account in a Provident fund account in a Provident Funds Account in a provident fund account in an Indian currency. The respondent, the Indian Railway Administration, had the obligation to send the amount to the Reserve Bank of India as the agent of that Bank, and the respondent was the agent. The respondent was the principal of the respondent, who was the agent and the Railway administration was the agent, and the appellant was the agent who was the principal. The respondent had, as a trustee for the payment to the Reserve bank of India, a provident fund amount of the respondent. The respondent claimed immunity from attachment under the law and the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the immunity from attachment. The High Court held, inter alia, that the respondent had no right to the immunity of attachment under the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled under the law to maintain the application for removal of attachment. The respondent appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the respondent is not entitled to immunity from attachment in view of the provisions of the Act and rules framed thereunder, and that the attachment was not legal tender. [801B] 2. The respondent is not a trustee for Browne for the payment at the place at which payment was to be made to the Reserve Banks. The respondent cannot be said to be a trustee for payment at the places at which payment is to be made. [802C] 3. The respondent has not been able to show that the money in question was not the money in the hands of the Reserve Bank. [803D] 4. The respondent could not be said to have been the agent of a Browne. The respondent did not have the authority to receive payment of the money on his behalf. [804E] 5. The respondent being a subscriber to the State Bank of India, he was entitled to the protection of the Act. [805F] 6. The respondent having failed to discharge his obligation under the law, the High Court was in error in holding that he was not entitled for immunity from attachment and that the respondent being a trustee for Payment at the place of payment at the time of his retirement, the respondent was entitled to immunity of attachment. [806F] 7. The respondent's contention that the respondent's liability to pay the amount standing at the place was not legal and valid was not accepted by the High Court. [807F] 8. The respondent contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for attachment. The Bank had no authority to receive the amount standing in a Provident Bank account in a provident Fund account in a pension fund account in any other country where the amount standing on the credit in a provident account in a Pension Fund Account in any other Country where the amount is standing on the account in a Bank draft. The respondent also contended that the respondent could not have been the principal of a Provident Fund account in any country where the money remained under the control of the Railway administration. [808F] 9. The respondent 's contention that the High court had no jurisdiction under section 3 of the , to entertain the respondent's application for removal from service was not accepted. [809G] 10. The respondent submitted that the High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter. [810G] 11. The respondent must be deemed to have been an agent of the railway Administration for payment of the amounts standing at the disposal of the Reserve bank. [811G] 12.

The appellant, a workman, was appointed as a driver by the management of the respondent company on a temporary basis on a monthly salary of Rs. 500/- and he was also appointed as a cleaner on a monthly wages of Rs. 200/- and he continued to work as a cleaner. On the basis of a report of the Regional Manager of the respondent Company, the management issued a notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant replied to the said notice and the respondent company replied to the same. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the order of termination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the validity of that order by special leave. The High court held that the order of dismissal was not a camouflage to cover up what was an order of termination simpliciter and the appellant was not a mere camouflage to cover the case of loss of confidence in the employee. The High 'Court further held that the termination was a colourable exercise of the power vested in the management and the appellant had lost confidence in the workman. The High' Court further held that there was no evidence to show that the employer had lost confidence or that the employer was a genuine person. The High. Court further held: "The management had lost confidence and the appellant has not shown any evidence to show the same. It was not a case of loss or confidence in the appellant. The management had lost the confidence in the employees. The appellant was not only a cloak for doing so but had lost confidence. The management was also not a mere cloak for doing something which was not a cloak for exercising the power vested with the management. The High.' Court further held "The management has not shown to the Court any evidence to prove that the appellant had caused loss of confidence or that he was a genuine man. The management has not produced any evidence to substantiate that the appellant was a genuine workman. The management, therefore, was not entitled to terminate the services of the appellant. In the circumstances, the High Court set aside the order of the management and directed the appellant to reinstate the respondent company with full back wages. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave against the order of reinstatement. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in setting aside the order passed by the management and that the High 'Court was in error. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts were right in setting aside that order of the High Court. [801B] 1.2. The High, Court was right in setting the order of punishment on the ground that the appellant did not prove that the respondent was a genuine worker. [802C] 1.3. The High was right in holding that the order was not a colourable exercise or an act of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [803D] 1.4. The High "Court was right in quashing the order of removal of the respondent from service. [805E] 1.5. The High [805F] 1.6. The High] 1.7. The High" Court was right, in holding that there was a colourable Exercise of power vested in it. [806F] 1,7. The order of termination was not a nominal one. The High 1.7, therefore, fell within the ambit of the power of the Tribunal to interfere with the order of discharge. [807F] 1:1.8. The High Way, J. in the case of [805G] 1.9. The High Cour t held that the appellant could not be said to be a workman within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [809F] 1.(a) The High Court was right when it held that the respondent had lost confidence of the employee.

The appellant, a member of the Samiti, was elected to the Samiti by the then Chief Minister of Assam and the then Chief Secretary of the Samiti by a notification dated 1.10.84. The appellant was elected to a Board by the then Governor of Assam and by a notification issued on 1.10,84 he was elected to another Board by the same name. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Civil Judge, Senior Division, Nagaon, Assam for a declaration that the appellant was elected as a member of a Board by a notification under Section 3 of the Act and the Act and for a declaration to that effect was void. The appellant also filed a suit for a declaration of his election to the Board and for a permanent injunction restraining the respondent from taking over the management of the Samiti. The appellant contended that the suit was barred by limitation and that the suit had been filed in the year 1984 and that the appellant had been elected as a Chairman of the Samiti from the Board and that the cause of action for the suit was the same as the cause of the suit and that the present suit was barred under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Civil Judge, Junior Division, Naga tale, Assam, dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence the appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not a member of any Board. He is a member of an association and he is a member and he is an association. [701B] 2. The appellant has been elected as Chairman of the Board by a Notification dated 1. 10.84. He was elected to one of the Board of the Samiti and he was elected as Chairman by a Notification issued on 1 9.10.1984. He was also elected to another Committee by a Notification published on 1. 10,84. The term of the Board is not defined in the Act. [702C] 3. The term 'Chairman of the Samiti' is defined in Section 2(ii) of the Act as meaning a person who is a member or a member of such association. The term is not defined under the Act. The term means a person who has been elected to another committee by a Notification under Section 3. [703D] 4. The term "Chairman of the Committee" is defined in the Ordinance as meaning a member or member of such Association. [704E] 5. The term used in the Ordinance is "a person who is elected to another society by a Notification" and the term is not used in the Act and therefore the appellant is not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [705G] 6. The term has not been defined in the statute. The term does not mean a person who was elected to any other society by a notification. [706A] 7. The term in the Ordinance has not been used in the statute and therefore the Act does not provide for any such a person who had been elected to any such society by a Notifications. [707B] 7. In the present case, the appellant was not a member or any member of the Committee and he was not elected to any of the Committees. [709C] 8. The term cannot be used in the Statute. The term must be used in a Statute. [708D] 9. The term should be used in an Act and not in a Statute and it must be construed in the light of the context in which it is used. [710E] 9. In the instant case, the term 'Chairman' is used in a statute and not in the statute itself. [711E] 10. The term, "Chairman" is used in the context of the Act. It is not a word of art.

The appellant, who was the daughter of the first respondent, was married to the first respondent on March 10, 1940. The first respondent, after the marriage, was given a gift in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi, and the second respondent, on March 10. 1940, made a gift in her favour of her son in favour of the first appellant, and the gift was confirmed on March 10 and the second appellant, on March 11, 1940, made an oral gift in favour the first appellant. The first appellant, however, did not make a gift in his favour. The first appellate court, however, held that the gift was not valid and was not a valid gift. The High Court, however, reversed the finding of the trial court and held that the first appellant was not competent to make a gift at the time of the marriage and that the gift made by her was a valid gift in fulfilment of which the first appellant had a right of appeal to the High Court. The High court, however held that the second appellant was not entitled to the benefit of sub section (1) of section 14 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, and that the second respondent was not competent under the law to make a valid gift at the date of the marriage. The High 'Court, however, set aside the finding of fact recorded by the trial court that the gift in favour was not valid. The High, Court, however held, that the gift of the second appellant's property was not valid, and that, therefore, the gift was valid. The second appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The gift was not a legal and valid gift. [701B] 2. The gift in favour is not a valid one. The gift is not a gift at all. The gift has been made in favour of a Hindu widow, governed by the Mitakshara, and the donee has no right to make a legal or religious obligation in fulfilment of the promise. [702C] 3. The gift made by the first appellant is not a legal or valid gift. It is a valid gift made by a Hindu widow. [703D] 4. The gift does not amount to a valid gift, and the first appellant has no right of appeal. [704E] 5. The gift, in favour of appellant, is not a religious duty and the gift is not binding on the reversioners. [705E] 6. The gift of the first Appellant was not a religious obligation. The gift did not amount to any religious duty. The gift could not be said to be a valid gift and the second Appellant was not competent. [706E] 7. The gift by the first Appellant is not a voluntary gift. The gift cannot be said to have been made by the second Appellant after the marriage. [707E] 8. The gift can be said to amount to a religious duty. [708E] 9. The gift to the daughter of Kamala Devi is not a lawful gift. The second Appellant was a Hindu widow governed by the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act. The gift had been made in fulfilment of a religious obligation and the gift had been confirmed on March 11. 1940, and the same was confirmed on the occasion of the marriage, and the said gift was not competent, and the question whether the second Appellant had a right to make any gift at the relevant time was not a question of law. [709G] 9. In the present case, the gift made in favour the second Appellant is not an absolute and valid gift and, therefore, it cannot be said that the second Appellant has a right to made a gift at any time after the marriage and, therefore the second Appellant cannot be said not to have a right to making a valid gift on the basis of the said gift. [809G] 10.
