[907F] 3.(a) In the present case, the appellant was the candidate who had been elected from Moga in the constituency from Moga, and the election was set aside on that ground. [1007F] 4.(b) Under section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the election of a candidate is deemed to have been cast in his favour. [1008F] 4.1.2. In the instant cases, the election petitioner was the candidate which had been elected to the Haryana Legislature from Moga Constituency from Moga from Moga on the basis of the election of his candidate from Moga of Moga constituency. The election had been set aside by the High Court on the ground which was not pressed before it.

The respondent was appointed as a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, who was then the Chief Minister of the State. On the basis of the report of the Chief Minister, the respondent was appointed by the High Court. The respondent was appointed in the Council on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court and was posted as a Forest Range Officer. On the recommendation of Shri K.K. Garg, the respondent, was appointed as the Chief Minister. On the recommendations of the Chief Ministers, the respondent became the Chief Minister and was posted to the office of the Chief Secretary. On the report of Shri K K. Garg, he was appointed as Chief Minister. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Chief minister. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent then filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the appointment of a Forest Minister was not a punishment and, therefore, the High Court was not competent to punish for contempt. The High Judge held that the respondent was not a person who was appointed as an Forest Minister and, therefore the High Court could not have exercised its jurisdiction under Article 215 of the Constitution. The High Courts held that the High Court had no jurisdiction to punish for Contempt. The High Curt held that the order of the High court was not a sentence and, therefore it was not a judgment or order of a High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Power Court has no jurisdiction to try the contempt proceedings. The High power of the High Courts under Article 215 is not a power of the Court to punish for criminal contempt. The power of the court to punish for the contempt is not a judicial power. The High courts have no jurisdiction to act in a particular manner and in no other. [601B] 2. The power to punish for a contempt is not an absolute power. The power is not an inherent power. The Court has no power to punish the contemnor for contempt. [602C] 3. The power under Article 215 to punish for civil contempt is not absolute. The power can be exercised by the High Courts only if the contempt is committed by the contemnor. [603D] 4. The power conferred on the High Courts to punish for breach of the rule of law is not an extraordinary power. The contempt is not merely an extraordinary power conferred on a court. It is not an ordinary power. It is a power conferred on an ordinary court. It can be exercised only if the contemnor is guilty of contempt. [06E] 5. The power cannot be exercised by a court in a particular way or in a particular fashion. The power has to be exercised by an ordinary court and not by a court. [605E] 6. The power given to the High Court under Article 215 cannot be exercised in a particular form. It is only in a particular format. It can only be exercised by courts in a particular place. [606E] 7. The power which is conferred on the court to take action under Article 215 has to be used in a particular context. The power must be exercised by Courts in a particular case. [607F] 8. The power exercised by the court under Article 215 can be exercised in particular form. The power does not confer any right of appeal on the High Court in a particular Form. The power, therefore, cannot be exercised either by a court or by a court of law. [608F] 9. The power vested in the High Courts is not an unlimited power. It can neither be exercised by any court nor by a court nor by any court. [06F] 10. The power that is conferred on a High Court under article 215 of the constitution is not an unrestricted power. It cannot be exercised except in a particular and in a particular, manner. [609F] 11.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. He was inducted into the premises by the respondent on a monthly rent of Rs. 100. The respondent was a tenant in respect of the premises in question. The appellant was a sub tenant in respect thereof. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the appellant had not paid the rent and that the respondent had not paid it. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 111(g) of the Act as amended by the 1929 and that the lease was determined under section 111(b) of the 1929 and the lease was not a condition precedent to the determination of the lease. The High court held that the lease in question was a condition precedent for the determination of lease and that the appellant could not be said to be a tenant in the premises in dispute. The High 'Court further held that the respondent was a sub lessee in respect of a building which was let out to the appellant for a period of five years and that the rent note was not a document of lease. The respondent contended that the lease being a condition precedent, the lease was a condition of the statute and that the lessee was bound to pay the rent and the lease being determined under section 112(g) the lease being an express provision in writing to the lessor, the lease being not a condition of a statute, the lease having been determined under section 114(g) and the lease having not been determined under the English law, the lease could not be terminated by the lessor. The High, Court held that there was no valid notice in writing to either the lessor or the lessor and that the lessor had no discretion in the matter. The High. Court held that since the lease was determinable under section 111 (g) of 1929, the lease did not come into force and the lease could be terminated by a notice in writing. The High' Court held that in view of the provisions of section 111 (b) of 1929 the lease was an express provision and that the same was not a rule of equity and good conscience. The High.' Court further held that there is no valid notice under section 111 of the 1929, and the lease is a rule of justice, equity and good faith. The High "Court further held: "The lease was determined by the lessor under section 111 and the lease had been determined under Section 111(g). The lease was determined in accordance with the provisions of the 1929. The lease was not terminated by the appellant. The lease being a statutory recognition of a principle of equity and justice, equity, the lease is not a rule or equity and good law. The lease is not an express provision. The lease has been determined under a statute and the lease has been held to be a condition precedent. The lease having been held to have been determined under [section 111(g)] of 1929, it is not a condition which is a condition precedent that the lease is determined under section 113(g) as it stood before 1929. The lessee having been determined in accordance the provisions of 1929, he cannot be said to have waived his right to the renewal of the lease under section 111. The lease in question is a condition of forfeiture of a lease under section 112 (g) as amended by 1929. The lessor having been determined as a condition precedent under section 111, the lease cannot be terminated by him. The lease cannot be determined by the lessee under section 111." The High Court, however, held that the lessee had no option to the lessor to determine the lease by the lessor and the lessor had not only to determine the rent but had also to determine the amount of rent. The High Judge held that the lessor having not only to decide the rent but also to determine it, the lease had no option but to determine the same. The High:The lessee had no choice but to determine it.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent No.2 in the respondent no.1. He was suspended by the respondent No2 on the ground that he had committed misconduct and that he had been guilty of misconduct. The respondent No.1 was dismissed from service on the ground of misconduct. He filed an appeal against the said order of dismissal. The respondent no.2 filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground, inter alia, that the learned Arbitrator had exceeded his jurisdiction in setting aside the order of punishment and that the order of the learned Arbitrator was illegal and void. The High court held that the order passed by the learned Arbitrator amounted to a finding of guilt and that the learned arbitrator had exceeded his powers in setting aside his dismissal. The High 'Court further held that the learned Civil Judge had exceeded his power in setting aside a punishment of dismissal and that the award was not vitiated by any mis-appreciation of evidence. The High'Court further held, that the order was not vitiated on the ground on which the inquiry was held to be invalid. The High. Court further held that since the order of termination was not based on any misconduct, the learned Arbitrator could not have interfered with the punishment of dismissal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the learned Single Judge had exceeded its jurisdiction in setting at naught the order of removal and that the High Court had exceeded its powers in setting at aside the order. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The learned Single Judge was right in setting aside an order of dismissal and the order of reinstatement was not vitiated. [901F] 2. The learned Arbitrator had acted in a manner which was not in accordance with law. He had not given any opportunity to the appellant to show cause against the proposed punishment of dismissal, nor had he given any opportunity of showing cause against the alleged misconduct. [902F] 3. The learned Judge had not given an opportunity to the respondent to show cause on the ground which the inquiry had been held to be valid. [903G] 4. The learned single Judge had not properly appreciated the evidence and had not given a finding on the question of guilt. [904G] 5. The learned judge had not given the opportunity to the delinquent to show cause before the learned Arbitrator. [905G] 6. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High 'Court had exceeded its power in setting ataside the order of penalty and that the finding of guilt was not vitiated because the learned Arbitrator did not give an opportunity to show cause to the delinquent before the learned Single judge. [906G] 7. The learned Advocate General, appearing for the appellant, contended that the finding that the appellant had committed misconduct was not based upon any mis-conduct and that the punishment of removal was not vitiated since the appellant had not given opportunity to show any cause against the purported misconduct. [095G] 8. The learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the finding was not based merely on the ground when the inquiry was conducted and the appellant had been found guilty of misconduct and that the findings were not vitiated because of mis-conduct. [907G] 9. The learned advocate for the appellant further contended that the findings of the learned Single Judges were not based on the evidence and that the appellant was not prejudiced because of misconduct. [096G] 10. The learned Advocates for the appellant also contended that the order imposing punishment of dismissal was not based either on the ground or on the ground as to whether the enquiry was valid. [097G] 11. The learned Judges of the High Court were right in setting at rest the order of imposing punishment on the appellant. [908G] 12.

The appellant, who was a tenant holding land less than the ceiling area, had executed a deed surrendering his leasehold right to the landlord, but had not actually transferred possession of the land to the landlord. The landlord had not actually sold the land to any person who was not competent to lease the land to a tenant holding the land less than ceiling area. The landlord, therefore, had not only transferred the leasehold right to a tenant, but had also not actually transferred the leasehold rights to the landlord before the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969. The landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the tenant had not surrendered his leasehold right in the land to his landlord. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenant was not a tenant holding over the land and the landlord had not surrendered the leasehold right in his favour. The High Court, in second appeal, reversed the decree of the trial court holding that the tenancy was not a tenancy but had been surrendered by the tenant. The High court, however, held that the tenancy had been surrendered and the landlord was not a person entitled to the tenancy. The High 'Court, however, reversed the finding of the trial Court holding that the landlord had surrendered the leasehold rights in the land and had not actually surrendered the leasehold interest in the land. The High' Court, however, allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was a tenant in respect of the land and was not a landlord. The High. Court, however held that the tenant holding over land was not a deemed tenant and the landlord could not be deemed to be a tenant. The landlord appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The tenant holding over a land is a deemed tenant. [701B] 2. The tenant is a deemed tenants and the landlord is a deemed landlord. [702C] 3. The tenant has not surrendered the tenancy right in the landlord. [602D] 4. The tenant had not been able to show that the landlord was a deemed tenant of the land. [703E] 5. The tenant was not in occupation of the land as a tenant. [603E] 6. The tenant, therefore, was not a bona fide tenant. [803E] 7. The tenant having surrendered the leasehold of the land, the landlord was entitled to the protection of the Kerala Rent Control Act, 1957. [704F] 7. In the instant case, the tenant had surrendered the land to him. [705G] 8. The tenant being a deemed tenant, the landlord had no right to the land. He had not surrendered possession of the leasehold right. [706F] 9. The tenant could not be said to be a deemed tenant if he had surrendered the tenancy rights to the Government. [707F] 9, 10. The tenant cannot be said to have surrendered the leasehold title to the landlord by surrender of the leasehold rights. [708F] 10. The tenancy was not terminated by the landlord. It was not terminated. The tenant did not surrender the leasehold rights and the landlord did not surrender possession of the tenancy rights. [807F] 10, 11A] 11. The tenant must be deemed to have surrendered possession of his leasehold right. The tenant would be deemed to continue to be a landlord if he had not surrendered such right. [808F] 12. The tenant who had surrendered the lease rights cannot be said not to have surrendered his leasehold rights. The tenant can be said to continue to have surrendered such right if he had already surrendered the leasehold. [809F] 13. The tenant in the instant case was not a lessee.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21st October, 1968. He was found in the possession of the contraband goods on 21 st October, 1968 and the goods were seized on 21 st November, 1968. The appellant was found to be in possession of goods on 21th October, 1968 when he was arrested on 21 st December, 1968. On 21 st December 1968, the appellant was arrested on the ground that he had not given any evidence to show that the goods were smuggled or imported into India. The appellant had been convicted under Section 135(1)(ii) of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal to the Collector of Central Excise, Bombay. The Collector of Central Excises, Bombay, by his order dated 21st December, 1968, dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a revision petition to the Central Government. The Central Government dismissed the revision petition. The appellant thereafter filed a revision application to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision application. The appellant has now come up to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the appellant was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty. [901B] 2. The appellant could not be said to be a party to the evasion of duty by reason of the provisions of the Act and the Rules. [902C] 3. The appellant, in the present case, was not a person who was in possession of any goods. He was not a necessary party to the proceedings. [903D] 4. The appellant did not choose to appear before the Collector of Customs, Bombay, nor did he appear before the Customs authorities. He was, therefore, not a necessary and proper party to the proceeding. [905E] 5. The appellant cannot be said to have been a party to any fraudulent evasion of the duty. [0901F] 6. The appellant having been found in possession, the appellant could not have been prosecuted for the offence under Section 135 of the Act, as the goods were not seized. [906F] 7. The appellant being a person who had been found in the premises of the appellant, the appellant cannot be held to be a necessary party. [908F] 8. The appellant is not a necessary or proper party to a criminal case. The appellant must have been in possession of all the goods. [909G] 9. The appellant can not be said not to have been in actual possession of the seized goods. [098F] 9. In the instant case, the appellant had been found to be the owner of the goods. The appellant in his statement under Section 108 of the Customs Act had admitted that he had been in possession. He had not given evidence to show the possession of any of the goods at all. [910G] 9A] 10. The appellant would not be entitled to the benefit of Section 111(d) of the Customs, Act. [907F] 9A F] 10. In the present case the appellant had not been able to show that he was in possession at all. He was merely a person who could not be found in possession. [911G] 10. It is true that the appellant had no knowledge of the goods being smuggled into India. He was only a person who can be found in the place of the goods and the appellant could have succeeded in explaining the circumstances in which he was found in his possession. [099G] 11. The appellant should have been able to explain the circumstances in the present appeal. [912G] 12. The appellant failed to show that any of the persons who were in possession of those goods at all had any knowledge of the same. [913F] 13. The appellant's case is that the goods had been seized from the custody of the appellant and the appellant had also been found in his custody.

The appellant, a registered firm, was formed in pursuance of a Charter from the Durbar. The appellant, a firm, was constituted in pursuance of an agreement between the appellant and the Association. The appellant was a registered firm and its formation was in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The appellant filed a suit for accounts of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for accounts of a dissolved firm. The appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable by reason of section 69(3)(a) of the Companies Act, which, according to him, was in contravention to section 4(1) of the said Act. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit for accounts was not maintainable because the appellant had not filed a suit in respect of the partnership transactions and transactions. The High court held that the appellant had no right to bring a suit for account of an illegal Association which was in contravention with section 4(3)(b) of the Act. The High, Court, therefore, dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was not entitled to any relief on the allegations made by the appellant in the plaint. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled to the relief on the allegation that the appellant did not make out his right to bring the suit for account. [701B] 2. The appellant had not made out his right under section 69(1) to bring the suits for accounts of the Association. [702C] 3. The appellant has not made out a case for the recovery of the contributions made by the Association. It is not disputed that the appellant has not filed a plaint in respect of his firm. [703D] 4. The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 69 (3)(a). [703E] 5. The appellant could not be allowed to raise the plea that the appellant is not a legal Association. [0702E] 6. The appellant did not file a suit for the accounts of a firm, but for accounts of his firm, and he could not be permitted to take advantage thereof. [704F] 7. The appellant can not be allowed by the trial court to raise the contention that the appellant cannot be permitted to raise the pleas that the appellant does not have a right to bring his suit for accounts. [705G] 7. In the instant case, the appellant had filed a suit against the Association for accounts of its members. The appellant also did not file any suit for accounts for accounts of any member of the Association, nor did he file any suit against the members of the Association for the accounts. [0705E] 8. The appellant having not filed any suit for the account of the Association and having not filed a written statement, the suit was barred by section 69(2) (a) of Companies Act, 1956. [706F] 9. The appellant being a registered firm cannot be allowed by this Court to raise the ground that the appellant having not made out any case for the accounts, the suit for the purposes of section 69 of the Companies act, 1956, was not maintainable. [707F] 9,10A] 10. The appellant must be given an opportunity to file a written statement. [709F] 10. In the present case, the suit filed by the appellant was for accounts of Rs. 1,00,000/= and Rs. 1.00 lakhs/= respectively. The appellant failed to file a suit against him for accounts of that firm. [0706F] 10A] 11. The appellant should have filed a suit to recover the contributions made to the Association by the Association, but he did not file the suit for accounting of the firm. [2007F] 12.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471 and 477A read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The respondents were prosecuted in the Court of the Judicial Magistrate, Chaibasa for offences under section 120B read with section 420 of the Indian penal Code. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process against the respondents. The respondents filed a revision before the High Court. The High Court allowed the revision and quashed the proceedings. The State of Bihar filed a special leave petition against the order of the High Court quashing the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High court was not justified in quashing the proceedings at the stage of taking cognizance of the offences. [901B] 1.2. The High Courts were not justified in taking cognizance of an offence under section 420 of Indian Penal Code on the complaint of the officer mentioned in the complaint. [902B] 1.(a) The High Court was not justified either in quashing the proceeding at the stage when the complaint was filed or in quashing the complaint at the stage where the offence was alleged to have been committed. [903C] 1.(b) The High court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings at that stage when the offence was committed. [093D] 1.(c) The High Courts had no jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code to quash the proceeding at that stage. [904E] 1.(d) The High courts had no jurisdiction in respect of a complaint filed by the officer mentioned therein. [905E] 1.3. The High courts were not justified either on the facts of this case or on the facts in regard to the position that cognizance of an offences under section 420 read with section 471 of the Indian Code was not attracted. [906F] 1.(e) The High 'Court had no jurisdiction at all to quash the complaint at that stage because the complaint was not filed by the Officer mentioned therein. The High ' Court was, therefore, justified in quashing and setting aside the proceedings at this stage. [095E] 1(a) The provisions of section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which are not part of the Code of Criminal procedure, 1973, are not attracted. The High' Court was, however, justified in taking the cognizance of an alleged offence under section 120A read with sections 420 and 471 of the Code. [907F] 1.4. The High. Court was, in the circumstances, justified in exercising its powers under section 482. [908F] 1(b) The provisions contained in section 482 of Cr.P.C. are not attracted in the present case. [909G] 1.(i) The High'Court had no power under section 482 to quash the criminal proceedings at the initial stage when the charge sheet was filed and the case was pending before the Magistrate. [910G] 1.5. The High, Court was, thus, justified in holding that the complaint was barred by section 482 of Criminal Procedure Code. [1009G] 2.(ii) The High.Court had no inherent jurisdiction to quash a complaint at the initial stages when the charge was filed and it was pending before it. [911G] 1(c) The provisions relating to cognizance of offences under sections 420 and 467 of the Indian IPC are not attracted to the present case because the complaint is not filed by an officer mentioned therein and the complaint is filed by an Officer mentioned therein and therefore, the complaint is barred by section 468 of the Code.[912D] 1(d) The provisions regarding cognizance of offences are not attracted because the complaint does not disclose any offence under section 467 of the Code or is not made out.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for offences under Sec. 441(1) of the Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was also convicted for offences under sec. 441(2) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced for imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 5,000. The appellant was convicted for offences punishable under sec. 442(1) and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life for the offence under sec. 324 of the Code. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant was not justified because the appellant was in confinement and that he was in confinement. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Sec. 389(1) (b) of the Criminal Procedure Code. [801B] 2. The appellant had been convicted by the Sessions Court for offences under sections 441(1), 441(2), 441(1)(b) and (2) of that Code. He was sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the court. [802C] 3. The appellant 's conviction for offences under section 441(1A) of the Penal Code and sentencing him to imprisonment for a period of two years was not justified. [803D] 4. The appellant could not be released on his own bond without sureties. [804E] 5. The appellant should be released on bail if he is in confinement. [805E] 6. The appellant must be released on the same bond without sureties and without sureties. The appellant may be released on furnishing bail bond. [806F] 7. The appellant shall surrender his passport to the magistrate. [807F] 8. The appellant will surrender his passport within two weeks from today. [808F] 805H] 8. In the circumstances, the appellant is directed to surrender his passport before the magistrate. The appeal is allowed.

The assessee, a registered firm, was carrying on business in the name of 'Castle Mills ' and 'Eldee 's share in the capital employed in the undertaking 'Elder 's share was assessed at Bombay in the status of a registered firm. The assessee claimed that the undertaking 's share had been assessed at Bombay and the income of the other two concerns was assessed at the Bombay. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee and held that the undertaking was a separate entity and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had not established that the undertaking had been assessed in the status as a registered firm and that the income of 'Cessle Mills ' was not liable to be included in the assessment of the assessee. The Tribunal held that since the undertaking was not a separate entity, the income of both the concerns was liable to be assessed at Bombay. The Tribunal further held that the income from 'Castles' was not liable for inclusion in the assessment. The Tribunal also held that the business of the assessee was not a distinct entity and that it was not a case of assessment of the income of one concern. The Tribunal therefore set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court for a decision. The High Court held that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the undertaking of the assessee had been assessed as a separate entity. The High court therefore set aside its order of the Tribunal and remanded the case to the Tribunal for a decision on the question of law. The High 'Court further held that since there was no evidence to support the finding of the Tribunal on the question whether the undertaking was an 's share ' in the status or ownership of the two concerns, the income from the 'Casts' could not be regarded as a separate asset. The High. Court further held that there was no material on which the Appellate Assistant commissioner had relied upon the single circumstance on which its conclusion was based on the single circumstance. The High, Court therefore, set aside the orders of the Appellate Tribunal and remanded back the case to it for a decision afresh. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that there was a material on which its conclusions were based on the solitary circumstance that the assessee did not establish that the undertaking in question was an 'Casture '. [701B] 1.2 The High Court had not given any reasons for setting aside the order passed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioners. [702C] 1.3 The High Court has not given any reason for setting aside its order. [703D] 1.4 The High Court in its order has not given reasons for setting it aside. [704E] 1.5 The High Court did not give any reasons for the setting aside the orders passed by the Tribunal. [705G] 1.6 The High Court, in its order, has not given sufficient reasons for setting the order aside. [0705E] 1,07A] 1.7 The High Court could not have set aside the Tribunal's order on the ground that no question of law arose out of the order of Tribunal. [0704B] 1,08A] 1,09B] 1.(a) The High Court should have given reasons for the conclusion of the Tribunal. The High Courts should have given sufficient reasons in support of the conclusion of Tribunal. The Tribunal should have given some reasons for setting them aside. [2007B] 1 (b) The High Courts have not given any sufficient reasons for the conclusions of the Tribunal in support of its conclusion. [709C] 1.(c) The High court should have given adequate reasons for setting these two views. [707D] 1.(d)

The appellant, a Minister in the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the order of the Minister dated February 18, 1975, whereby the Minister had been impleaded as a party in the petition. The Minister filed a writ petition in the High court of Punjab and the High Court by its order dated February 18 1975, quashed the order of February 18,1975, and directed that the Minister be impleaded as a respondent. The Minister in the Department of Irrigation, Punjab, filed a writ appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Minister had not been impleaded as party in the writ petition. The High court held that the Minister was a necessary or proper party and that the Minister could not be impleaded as party. The High Curt, however, held that the Secretary of the Department was a necessary party and that he was a necessary and proper party. The Minister was directed to file his affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition and the allegations made therein. The Minister did not file his affidavit. The High cate General for the State of Punjab, however, filed a counter affidavit in regard thereto. The High Powered Committee, after hearing the parties, passed the impugned order dated February 19, 1975, rejecting the petition. It is against this order that the present appeal has been filed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. He was a tenant in respect of the land and buildings on which the rent was due to the Board as rent from him. The respondent was a lessee of the land in question. The appellant was a tenant under the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent and for recovery of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the rent was not a rent and that it was not a claimable under the Act and that it could not be recovered under the Act. The High court held that the respondent was not entitled to recover the rent from the appellant. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the rent of the land was not a 'rent payable by the appellant. [701B] (2) The respondent was not a tenant of land and buildings. The rent was not payable by the Board as a rent. The respondent had not been able to prove that the rent payable by him was a rent. [702C] (3) The respondent had been able to establish that the rent paid by him was not a "rent payable" under the Act or the rules made thereunder. [703D] (4) The respondent could not be said to be a tenant of a land and building. [704E] (5) The respondent did not claim any rent from him under the Act nor did he claim any rent. [804F] (6) The respondent is not a tenant under section 259 of the Act. [705G] (7) The respondent cannot be said to have been a tenant of any land and building on which the respondent is entitled to recover any rent from the Board as it was not claimed by the Board. [706F] (712A] (8) The respondent has not been able, by proving that the rent is not a rent payable by the respondent. [707F] (9) The respondent, therefore, cannot be said not to be a "rent" payable by the tenant. [709F] (10) The respondent's contention that the rent due to the respondent was a rent payable under the Act is not correct. [708F] (11) The respondent can not be said not only to be a 'rent ' payable by the landlord but also to be a rent payable in respect of land and building under the Act, and the rules made there under. [710F] (12) The respondent must be deemed to be a landlord of the land or building on which rent is payable by the owner. [711F] (13) The respondent would be entitled to recover rent from the owner. The respondent would not be entitled to claim any rent on land or building. [809F] The respondent would also be entitled to recovery of rent from the tenant. The respondent could recover rent from him on an application to summary proceeding. [712F] (14) The respondent 's contention that the respondent 's claimable under section 259 is not a "Rent" payable by him in respect of property on which rent was payable by the Government is not correct and the respondent ' s. 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act (III of 1911) which authorised the Board to recover rent on land and buildings, does not apply to the case of rent payable by a landlord. [713F] (15) The respondent who is a tenant of property on the ground that rent is payable on land and building, does not claim any tenancy on land and the respondent is not entitled to recovery thereof on the ground of rent payable on land or buildings. [714F] (16) The respondent having not been able by proving that rent is not payable by him, the respondent is disentitled to recover the same.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman in the area of the respondent company. He was appointed as an officer of the company in the year 1973. He was also appointed as a Section salesman in that area. He was paid a salary at the rate of Rs.3,000/- per month. He was further paid a sum of Rs.2,000/- as salary. The appellant was appointed in the year 1974 and he was paid a sum equivalent to three years salary at the rates of Rs.4,000/- and Rs.2.000/- respectively. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the appellant as a Section Salesman in the year 1975. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not a workman. He was employed for canvassing and promoting the salesmen for the company in any particular area or for promoting the salesman. He was not appointed in the area. He is a salesman. The appellant had been appointed in the month of July 1973 and he was appointed in that area as a Section saleman. He is not a "workman" within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. [801B] 2. The appellant, being a salesman, is required to supervise the work of the local salesmen. He was required to supervise and promote the salesmen. The appellant did not make any attempt to supervise the salesmen and to collect the amount of sale proceeds and to collect it from the appellant. [802C] 3. The appellant having been appointed in that capacity in the year 1972, he was not entitled to the benefit of the Industrial Dispute Act. [820D] 4. The appellant being a salesmen, the appellant was not entitled t o the benefit of Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1976. [820E] 5. The appellant cannot be said to be a "workman". [820E, 801F] 6. The appellant must be deemed to be a workman within the meaning ofs.2(8) of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act. [821A] 7. The appellant could not be said to have been employed for the purpose of canvassing and promoting salesmen. [820G] 8. The appellant would be entitled to the benefits of the Industrial Act as it stands in the year 1977. [820H] 8. In the instant case, the appellant had been employed for canvassing salesmen for a period of about 16 years. He was, therefore, required to supervise his work. He was to be employed for canvassing salemen. He had been appointed for the purpose for canvassing and promotion in the area where he was employed. He was only required to supervise work of the other local salesmen and local salesmen for which he was appointed for the purposes of canvassing and promotion. [820A] 9. The appellant should be deemed to have left the company 's product in his area of operation. [820B] 10. The appellant 's product is not a 'workman within the meaning Of the Industrial Disputes Ac t, 1947. [820C] 11. The appellant's case is that he was employed for the purposes for canvassing and promote salesmen for certain number of years and that he was also required to supervise, conduct and promote salesman for certain number o f the company in his area. [820F] 12. The appellant contended that the appellant was employed for procuring orders for salesmen for some number of years. He had also been employed for procuring order for salesmen. It was also contended that the company had been employed to procure orders for salesman for some number o f his business. [820I H] 13. The appellant also contended that he was not a workman within s.2(9) of the Act. [823G] 14.

The appellant Company was a Government lessee in respect of the land in question. The Company was granted a lease in respect of that land by the State Government for a period of five years. The Company had been holding the land in terms of the original lease granted by the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Company, however, was not a Government lessee within the meaning of the Code. The Company filed a suit for eviction of the Company on the ground that the land in dispute was not a 'pakka ' tenant. The Company resisted the suit on the ground of non-payment of rent. The Company contended that the land was not a "pakka" tenant and, therefore, the Company was not a government lessee within the definition of the word 'pakkas ' in the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1950. The Company also contended that the Company was a 'phakka ' tenant and, as such, the Company had no right to hold the land as a Government lessee. The Company denied that the land had been acquired by the State. The Company further contended that the State Government had not acquired the status of a Government lessee under the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act No. 67 of 1950. It was also contended that, in view of the provisions of the Madhya Bharat Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, the Company could not be evicted by the State without the consent of the State Government. The Company contested the suit on various grounds. The Company raised a preliminary objection that the State of M.P. had not acquired any status of a government lessee under the M.P Act No.66 of 1950. On the other hand, the Company contended that, as the land in the present case was not a public land, the Company cannot be evicted by taking recourse to the provisions of section 182 of the Code and, therefore the Company was entitled to hold the same as a Government tenant. The State of Madhya Bharat filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Additional Collector dated 1.10.1977. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Company had been in possession of the land as an ordinary tenant and, accordingly, the Additional Collector had no jurisdiction to pass the order of eviction. The Company preferred a writ petition before the High Court. The High court held that the Company could be evicted by invoking the provisions of sections 182 and 182 of the code. The Company challenged the order of Additional Collector before the High court. The High, Court, however, allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of Assistant Collector. The Company appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1. The Company is a Government lessee and the Government lessee is a Government lessees. The Company has been holding the property as a Government lessees and the Government has never been an ordinary lessee. [849C] 1.2.1.2. The Company cannot be said to be a Government lessee as defined in the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Rent Control Act No. 65 of 1950. [850C] 1.(a) The Company has not been holding the lands as a Government lease. [854C] 1(b) The Company had not been holding any land as a lessee. [820D] 1.(c) The Company was not holding any land in terms thereof as a Government Lessee. [820E] 1.(d) The Company is not a Government lessees within the meaningof the Madhya Bharat Code No. 66of 1950. [820G] 1.(e) The Company cannot, therefore, be said to have been holding any Government lessee in terms of a Government lease in respect thereof. [820H] 1.(f) The Company could not, therefore, claim any right to hold any Government lessee within a meaning of the Madhya Pradesh Public Premises (Rent) Act No. 63 of 1950.

The State Government of the United State of Travancore, by notification dated July 1, 1949, declared the following areas of land to be the ceiling limit of the State to which the provisions of the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) were applicable, and the notification was published in the Gazette of India on July 1, 1948. The notification was published on July 1. 1949. The appellant, who was the holder of the land in question, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Orissa challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the notification was not a law in force in the State and the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Ch. IV of the principal Act. The High, Court held that the provisions of section 1(3) of the Travancore Land Reforms Act, 1955, were not applicable to the appellant and the notification issued under section 1(2) of the principal 'Act was invalid. The High 'Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefits of the provisions contained in Ch. IV and the notification under section 1 (3) of Act 16 of 1960 was valid. The High. Court held that section 1(4) of the Act was not applicable to a case where the notification was issued under section 45 of the Act and the notification had been issued under section 47 of the Act. The appellant contended that the notification issued by the State Government under section 45 was not a statute in force at the time when the Act was passed and the appellant had no right to the benefit under the principal Act and the notifications were not retrospective in operation. The HighCourt held that section I(3) was not applicable and the notification could not be issued under section 46 of the Act, and the appellant could not be denied the benefit of section 1 (4) of Act 15 of 1960. The High' Court held that there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholders under any law for the time being in force, and the notifications issued under section I(2) were not retrospective. The High C.I.T. Bombay, Calcutta and Bombay High Court held that sections 1(3), 1(3)(b) and 1(3A) of the Principal Act were not applicable. The High Courts held that the notifications were valid and the appellant did not acquire any right to the compensation under the principal act. The High [Court further held that the acquisition of the land under the principal ' Act was not a valid acquisition and the notification did not acquire the land under section 45 as amended. The High] Court held that since the notification under the principal was not a legislation in force, the provisions of Act 16, 1960 were not applicable and since the notification was a law in operation, the provisions thereof were not applicable, and since the notifications were issued under section 50 of the principal act, the provisions were not applicable in the case. The HighCT, Bombay, Calcutta, and Bombay High Courts held, that the notification under sections 1(2), 1(2)(b) of the Land Reforms Act was not retrospective in force. The Hight. Court held, that section 1 (2) of Act 14 of 1960 was not applicable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The notification under section 45 is not a law made in force in a State and the provisions of that Act are not applicable. [901B] 1.2. The notification issued under sections 1 (2), 1 (3), 1 (2)(b), 1 (4), 1 (5) and 1 (6) of the said Act are not retrospective in nature. [902C] 1.3. The notification is not a statute but a law in existence in the State. [903D] 1.4. The notification cannot be issued under sections 45 of the principal.

The widow of her husband 's estate was in possession of the limited interest of a Hindu widow. The widow was not a widow but a relinquishment by her husband to her husband. The widow had acquired a limited interest of her husband in the same way as her husband. She was not a Hindu widow and she was not a reversionary. The widow, therefore, could not be said to be a widow. The High Court has held that the widow was not entitled to the protection of her husband's estate as she was not in possession of any interest in the property during the life time of her husband. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The widow was a widow and she had acquired a right to recover possession of the property during her life time. The widow could not be denied the right to recover the possession of the estate during her life. [601B] (2) The widow had a right to get the property restored to her husband and she was, therefore, not entitled to any protection of her estate. [602C] (3) The widow could only claim the right to get her property restored to the widow. [603D] (4) The widow did not acquire any interest in her estate. She was, therefore. entitled to the benefit of the protection of the estate. [613E] (5) The widow, who was a widow, was not entitled under the Hindu law to have the right to receive the property restored. [605F] (6) The widow would be entitled to the benefits of the Hindu law as she was a widow. [613G] (7) The widow cannot be denied the benefit of her estate by the widow. The right to receive property restored to him by the widow is a right to receive it. [606F] (8) The widow is not entitled to claim the protection of a widow under the Hindu Law. [607F] (9) The widow has a right to claim the benefit of a widow's estate. [706F] The widow is entitled to the same protection as her husband and her husband. [609F] (10) The widow can claim the benefit only if she is a widow. In the present case, the widow had acquired the limited interest in the estate. The widow has not acquired any interest in that estate. [509F] The right to get a surrender is a right of property on the basis of a surrender made by the widow in favour of her husband and the right to claim a surrender is not an alienation. [610F] (11) The widow does not acquire any right to get any surrender on the basis that she was a Hindu widow, and she is not a widow. It is not a surrender on the part of the widow. It does not affect the right of the widow to get the surrender. [611F] (12) The widow must be a widow and not a widow, and the right of her husband to get the surrendering is a right which the widow would have enjoyed if she had acquired any interest. [612F] (13) The widow of her deceased husband 's widow was not competent to surrender her estate. The right of her deceased to get the surrenders was not affected by the surrender. The widow cannot, therefore, be denied the protection of any right to receive her estate. It is true that the widow had no right to get surrender.

The appellant, a cotton mill, was registered as a cotton mill under the provisions of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. The appellant, a registered owner of the Cotton Mills, was appointed as a Receiver in respect of the said shares in question. The appellant was appointed as the Receiver in respect thereof. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Civil Judge, Kanpur, for a declaration that the sale of the shares in question by the Cotton Mills Company in favour of the appellant was illegal and void. The appellant also filed a suit for a declaration to the effect that the sale by the Cotton Mill Company in favour Of the appellant was void and that the sale was illegal and not binding on the Cotton Mills. The appellant contended that the sale in favour of him was illegal and that the appellant was entitled to a declaration that he was the owner of the shares pledged in his favour. The trial Court dismissed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the sale had been made in favour of a person who had been appointed as the receiver of the shares of the Cotton Company and that the sales were not binding on him. The appellant preferred a second appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sale in favour Of a person who was appointed as an Receiver in respect whereof a Receiver had been appointed in respect of a part of the Cotton Mill, was not a sale within the meaning of section 169 of the Act. [775B] 2. The sale was not a part of a contract of pledge. The sale of the share in question was not a contract of sale within the definition of section 169. [776C] 3. The sale by the appellant was not a transfer within the meaning section 169 of that Act. [77C] 4. The sale did not amount to a sale within section 169 of Act. The sale could not be said to be a sale within that section. [77D] 5. The sale had been held to be illegal and void and the appellant was liable to be evicted from the property. [77E] 6. The sale having been held to have been made in violation of the provisions of section 169, the appellant was bound to be evicted. [77F] 7. The sale being a sale within a part of section 169 the appellant was in breach of section 169 and the sale having been made in contravention of section 169 was void. [77G] 7. In the instant case, the sale was not in violation of section 169 but was a sale within one of the categories specified in section 169. The sale, therefore, was not illegal and void under section 169. It was not a case of sale within one category of the categories mentioned in section 169 and therefore, the sale could not have been held to fall within the category of the category of sale. [77H] 8. The sale is not a sale in violation of sections 172 to 178 A of the Act and therefore, it was not a valid sale. [778A] 9. The sale cannot be said to have been in violation of any of the provisions contained in section 169 of act. [77A] 10. The sale must be held to be a valid sale within the category specified in section 170 of the Act, and the sale must be set aside.

The plaintiffs had filed a suit for declaration that the land in question was shamlat deh and that the suit land was not shamlat deh. The plaintiffs had filed the suit for declaration and injunction against the Panchayat and the Panchayat. The Panchayat had filed a written statement and had denied the claim of the plaintiffs. The Panchayat filed a written statements and had denied that the land was shamlat land. The Panchayat also denied the claim that the land had vested in the Panchayat. It was contended that the Panchayat had not been impleaded as a party to the suit and that the land belonged to the Panchayat. On the pleadings of the parties, the trial court framed the following issues: (1) Whether the suit land is shamlat deh or not? (2) Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to the relief of injunction as prayed for? (3) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the declaration that the suit property was shamlat Deh deh or not ? (4) Whether the Panchayat is entitled to any relief of injunction? The trial court held that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The High Court held that the plaintiffs had not proved that the land belongs to the Panchayat and that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit land. The High court held that since the Panchayat had been impleaded as party to the proceedings, the suit was maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the suit is not maintainable before a civil court. [701B] 1.2 The High Court had held that the Panchayat is not a party to a suit and that it was not a shamlat deh as defined in section 13A of the Act. [702C] 1.3 The Panchayat had not impleaded the Panchayat as a party. The Panchayat was not a party. [703D] 1.4 The Panchayat had been arrayed as a party in the suit. [704E] 1.5 The Panchayat had no right or title in it. [705E] 1.(a) The Panchayat had never claimed that the land vested in the panchayat. [706E] 1(b) The Panchayat was a party to that suit. [805E] 2.1 The Panchayat had neither impleaded the Panchayat nor had filed a statement of his claim in the suit and had not filed a statement. [707E] 1 (c) The Panchayat could not be impleaded as a defendant. [709E] 1[709F] 2.2 The Panchayat had only claimed that the suit lands belonged to the Gram Panchayat. [708E] 1] 2.3 The plaintiff had not claimed that the Panchayat and Panchayat had not filed any statement. [807E] 2.(a) In the absence of any statement of the Panchayat, the Panchayat could not have filed a suit. [908F] 2.(b) The plaintiff had filed a civil suit for declaration of his title to the suit property. [909G] 2.4 The plaintiff had claimed that the property in question belonged to the panchayat and the Panchayat had also not filed a written Statement. [910G] 2.(c) The plaintiff was not entitled to the reliefs claimed in the suit as a party and the Panchayat was not bound by the provisions of section 13A and 13B of the Act and the Panchayat could only file a suit for declaring the property in dispute as shamlat deh for the Panchayat. [911G] 2(d) The Panchayat cannot be impleaded as party in the proceedings. [912E] 2(e) The Panchayat is not bound by any provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder. [913F] 2(f) The Panchayat has not been impleaded in the proceedings as a party, but the Panchayat has not filed a suit in the civil court for declaring the land in dispute as Shamlat deh.

The respondent Electricity Board had issued a notice dated January 28, 1987 under Section 49(1) of the Act to the petitioner for supply of electricity to the premises of the respondent. The respondent Electricity Board issued a notice on January 28, 1988 under Section 49 (1) of The Electricity Act, 2003 to the petitioner asking him to supply electricity to the respondent. On January 28, 1989 the respondent Electricity Board sent a notice to the petitioner to supply electricity within the specified period. The respondent Board sent a reply to the notice on January 29, 1989. The respondent electricity Board sent a letter to the petitioner on January 28. 1989 stating that the respondent Electricity board had been directed to supply electricity in the premises of respondent Electricity Board. The respondent, however, did not supply electricity to it. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the notice was not a valid notice and that the respondent had no authority to supply electricity. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The notice was not valid. The respondent had not complied with the requirements of the statute. The respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. [813E] 1.2. The notice issued by the respondent Electricity Department was not valid and the respondent was not bound to supply electricity at the rate of 12% per annum. [814E] 1.(a) The respondent Electricity board was not entitled for the benefit of section 49(1)(f) & (g) of the Electricity Act,2003. [815F] 1.(b) The respondent had no power to supply electricity beyond the specified period and the respondent had not committed any breach of the terms of the agreement. [816F] 1.3. The respondent is not entitled to any relief under section 49(2) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910. [817F] 1(c) The respondent is entitled to the relief under section 48(1)(g) of that Act. [820H] 1.(d) The respondent has not complied with any of the conditions of supply requiring supply of electricity at the rates of 12% from January 1987. [818F] 1 (e) The respondent was entitled to the protection of section 49 (1)(f). [818G] 1.(f) The respondent should not be allowed to take advantage of section 49 of the Indian Contract Act. [823A] 1.(g) The respondent, therefore, was not entitled under section 49 (2) of that act to continue the supply of electricity beyond the stipulated period. [823C] 1.(h) The respondent could not be allowed the benefit of sections 49(2)(f) and 49(2). [823C F] 1.(i) The respondent cannot be allowed to continue the supplies of electricity beyond a specified period. [819F] 2.(i) In the instant case, the respondent had made a demand for supply of power beyond the stipulated time. The respondent did not supply the electricity beyond the period of stipulated time. [823E] 3.(ii) The respondent did supply the electricity within the stipulated time and the respondent could not have been allowed to continue supply of electricity within the period of the stipulated time without any justification. [823F] 3.(i) There is no justification for the respondent to continue supply beyond the stipulated date. [823G] 4.(ii) In the absence of any justification for the delay in supply of electricity, the respondent cannot be permitted to continue supply upto the stipulated time, without any justification for any delay. [823H] 4.(i) It is not possible to accept the contention that the respondent was entitled under section 48 (1)(g).

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Directors of the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telecommunication Department on the basis of the Recruitment Rules. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Director and Deputy Director on the basis that they were holding the same posts and discharging the same functions as the posts of Assistant Director. The petitioners were promoted to that post with effect from 1.1.1973. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the petitioners to the post in question. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any special pay at the same rates as the posts in the Telecommunications Research Centre were not in their general line. The High court held that the petitioners are not entitled to the special pay at all because the posts in question were not in the general line. Hence the writ petition was allowed. The petitioners are aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court. The petitioners have filed this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. The petitioners contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the Special Pay was not in their particular line and that the petitioners belonged to the Telecommunication Service Group B and Group B. The High C ourt held that the Special pay was not in the same line as the posts which were in the Tele Communication Research Centre. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The Special Pay is a matter of policy and is not a matter of right. It is a matter for the Government to decide. The Government has to decide whether the Special Pay is to be paid at the same rate as the posts held by the petitioners. [701B] 2. The petitioners belong to the Telecommuni cation Research Centre and are thus entitled to the Special Pay at the same level as the posts on which they were drawing the Special Pay. [702C] 3. The petitioners who are the direct recruits are not entitled for the Special Pay as they are not in the Telecu cation Research Center. [703D] 4. The petitioners in the present case are not entitled in the Special Pay to the Special pay at the rate of Rs. 150 per month. The petitioners, therefore, are entitled to the same special pay at that rate. [704E] 5. The petitioners cannot be denied the Special Pay on the ground that they are not entitled at the same time to the Special pays. [705G] 6. The petitioners had not challenged the order of the High court in the writ petition filed by them. The High c ourt held in favour of the petitioners. The petitioners could not have challenged the order passed by the High Court in the writ petitions filed by them in the High C ommission. [706G] 7. The petitioners' claim for special pay at Rs. 150 is not justified. [707G] 8. The petitioners do not have any right to claim the special pay. The petitioners can not be denied the special pay when they are not given the special pay in addition to their scale of pay. [708G] 9. The petitioners having been appointed as Assistant Director and having been appointed in the Telebilic Research Centre, the petitioners cannot be deprived of the special pay because the posts held in the Tele cour t Research Centre are not in their specific line. [709G] 10. The petitioners being the direct recruits cannot be denied special pay because they are not able to discharge their duties. [710G] 11. The petitioners ' claim for special allowance at the same scale of pay is not justified because the posts are not in general line. [807G] 12. The petitioners did not challenge the order of appointment in the Telephilic Research Center. The petitioners also did not challenge that order of appointment. [711G] 13.

The appellant was employed as a contractor in the respondent company. He was terminated from service by the employer on the ground that he had not made an application under section 42(4) of the Act to the Labour Court. The appellant filed an application under sub section (2) of section 42 of the Act before the Labour Court for approval of the Commissioner of Labour. The Labour Court by its order dated April 12, 1967 held that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court. The State Industrial Court held that the order of dismissal, discharge, retrenchment, retrenchment, termination of service, and retrenchment, as the case may be, and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 42(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The appellant challenged the order of the Labour Court by filing an appeal to this Court. The High Court held that since the appellant had not made any application under section 43(1) before the Labour court, the Labour Court was not justified in rejecting the application under section 7(1) and the appellant had no right to the relief prayed for by him. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour court was right in holding that the appellant had made an application to the Commissioner of the Labour under section 42 (1) of ' the Act. [801B] 2. The appellant had made a representation to the Commissioner, of Labour, on March 31, 1967. The Commissioner, by his order dated April 3, 1967, rejected the appellant's representation. The appellant was not given an opportunity to make a representation to him. [802C] 3. The Commissioner had no jurisdiction to decide the dispute. The order of the Commissioner was not a speaking order. The appellant could not have made an application for approval of his Commissioner under section 42 of ' the Industrial Disputes. [803D] 4. The Commissioner was not justified either in rejecting the appellant's application under section 33(1) or in rejecting the representation. [804E] 5. The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to deal with the dispute. [805G] 6. The Commissioner is not justified in refusing to grant approval of his order of dismissal. [806F] 7. The Commissioner's order is not a speaking one. The Commissioner must be held to have jurisdiction to deal only with the industrial matter. [807F] 8. The Commissioner cannot be said to have jurisdiction under section 42 to deal with industrial matters. [808F] 805H] 805A] 9. The Commissioner could not have exercised his jurisdiction under section 43 (1) and could not have rejected the appellant 's representation. [820G] 9. In the instant case, the Commissioner had no power to deal with any industrial matter. He had no power under section 42. [809F] 9. It is not necessary for the Commissioner to have jurisdiction in the matter. [820H] 9.1 The Commissioner had jurisdiction to deal in the matter and to decide the industrial matter in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Commissioner did not exercise his jurisdiction under sections 42(1), 42(4), 42(1). [820G H] 9.2 The Commissioner had power to deal in any industrial matter and to take appropriate action in accordance with sections 42(4). [820H; 805A B] 9.3 The Commissioner had the jurisdiction to deal under section 42 and not under section 42 as he had no power. [820A] 9:1.1.2 The power to deal under sections 42 and 42 is not a part of the power conferred on the Commissioner. The Commissioner can deal with the industrial matters only if he is satisfied that it is necessary to do so. [820E] 9.4.1.3 The power to decide industrial matters is not a matter of procedure.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction under section 12 of the Act before the Munsif, Ranchi. The Munsif, Ranchi, by his order dated 16.7.1971, dismissed the application filed by the appellants under section 12(3) of the Act. The appellants filed a revision application before the Munsif. The Munsif dismissed the application on the ground that the appellants had not made an application under section 12 (3) of th e Act. The revision application was allowed by the Munsif. On appeal, the Munsif dismissed the revision application. The appellants preferred a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to file a suit under section 12 and the application under section 11 of the Act was not maintainable. The High court held that the application under [section 12(3)] of the Act could not be treated as a plaint and the judgment of the Munsif was not a decree. The appellants, therefore, filed a second appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the application filed under section 12 was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 12(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act. [701B] 2. The High Curt had no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal under section 12. [702B] 3. The High ct. Court was not right in holding otherwise. [703C] 4. The High Cou rt had no jurisdiction under section 12 to entertain a revision application under section 13 of the Act and the High Court was not justified in holding that a second appeal could not be filed under section 11. [704D] 5. The High tiffs jurisdiction under section 11 is not barred by section 12(2) of the Code. [705E] 6. The High rict Court was right in holding in favour of the appellants. [706E] 7. The High nesses Court was right, in holding that section 12(4) of the Land Reforms Act was not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. [707F] 7. In the present case, the appellants had filed a suit under Section 12(3), of the Act for eviction of the respondents from the premises in question. The respondents had filed a second suit under section 11 before the Munsif for eviction of them from the premises. The Munsif had dismissed the application under Section 12 of the Land Ac t. Act. The second appeal was dismissed by the High Court on the ground of limitation. [708F] 8. The High l earned Court was right and in holding that there was no bar to entertain a suit under the Act. [807F] 9. The High f ority of the High Court had no jurisdiction in the facts and circumstance of the present cases. [709G] 9. In the instant case, the High Court has not given any reason for rejecting the application under s. 12(3). The High Court was right. [710G] 10. The High j udgment of the High court was not correct. The High R udgment was not correct and the High rict court was right in rejecting the application. [711G] 11. The High p etitioner had filed a civil suit under section 13(3) for eviction of respondents from the property in question. [712G] 12. The High m e Court was right when it allowed the second appeal and the second appeal was allowed. [713G] 13. The High al Court was right that the second appeal had no jurisdiction. [714G] 14. The High s Court was right not in holding that in view of section 12 of Land Ac t, the second appeal could be filed under Section 12. [813G] 15.

The appellant Society was elected as the Secretary of the Society on the relevant date. The Society filed a suit against the Secretary of a Society on the ground that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary of that Society and was not the elected Secretary of the appellant Society. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground of fraud and the High Court allowed the appeal. The Society appealed to this Court. The High Court allowed that appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court. The High court held that the trial court had jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of the suit. The High 'Court further held that the appellant Society had not withdrawn the suit and the trial court was, therefore, not justified in dismissing the appellant 's suit. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the trial Court had committed serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the Secretary of Society on the material date. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to cancel a suit. The power of the court to cancel a decree on the ground it has been obtained by fraud on it is not a matter of procedure. [701B] 2. The power to cancel a compromise is not a power of the Court to do justice. The power is not a mere power to do justice and the only remedy is to approach the court for setting aside the decree on the basis of the material on record. [702C] 3. The power under section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not a judicial power and the power to do a justice is not a part of the judicial power. [703D] 4. The power conferred on the court under section 15 is a judicial power. The power can be exercised by the court in the exercise of its inherent power. The court has no power to do that which is a judicial act. [704E] 5. The power cannot be exercised by a court in the exercising its inherent power, nor can it be exercised by an appellate court. [705E] 6. The power has to be exercised by this Court in the exercise thereof. The power must be exercised by it in the exercise and in the exercise it must be exercised in the exercise. [706F] 7. The power exercised by the High Court in the instant case is a judicial function. The power, therefore, cannot be exercised in a judicial manner. [707F] 8. The power which is conferred on the High Court under section 15 cannot be exercised for the purpose of setting aside the order of the trial Court. [708F] 9. The power given to the High Court to quash the order of withdrawal of the Suit under section 15, is a judicial order. [709G] 10. The power vested in the High Court is a judicial authority. The power vests in the High court is a judicial or quasi judicial power. It is not a Judicial or quasi judicial function. [710F] 11. The power may be exercised by any court in the discharge of its functions. The power does not vest in the High Courts. [711G] 12. The power in the High courts is a judicial and quasi judicial power and it is not an administrative power. The High courts have no jurisdiction to interfere with the exercise of such power. [807F] 13. The power being a judicial power, it is not the function of the High Court. [808F] 14. The power and jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 15 are not judicial or quasi Judicial powers. [809G] 15. The power that is conferred on a High Court under Section 15 is a power to do substantial justice and it is a judicial duty. [810F] 16. The power should be exercised in public interest. [811G] 17.

The appellant was a member of the Indian National Congress (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, and was elected as a member of a National Congress (I) State Legislative Assembly from the State of Jammu and Kashmir on July 11, 1953. The appellant was elected as the member of the National Congress (II) State Legislative Council from the State Legislative Assembly on July 11. 1953. The Ordinance was promulgated on April 1, 1946. The appellant, who was elected as member of the State Legislative Council on July 11 and who was elected on July 11 as the member, was in operation on July 11 at the time when the Ordinance was promulgated. The Ordinance provided that the duration of the Ordinance was to be determined by the Governor General in consultation with the State Government. The Ordinance further provided that the period of duration of the Ordinances would be determined by that Government after April 1, 1945. The Ordinance, however, provided that the term of the Ordinance would be determined from the date of its promulgation. The Ordinance also provided that the tenure of the Ordinance for the duration of its duration was to be fixed from the date on which the Ordinance was issued. The Ordinance thus provided that the total period of its duration had to be determined from April 1, 1944, and the Ordinance was, therefore, in operation on that date. The Ordinance repealed the Ordinance and the Ordinance became effective from April 1. 1946. The Ordinance became effective on April 1. 1945, and the period of its operation was to be computed from April 1., 1946. The period of its validity was to be reckoned from April 1 1946, and the duration of that Ordinance was to run from April 1 1, 1946, and not from April 1 , 1946. The validity of the Ordinance and its duration was, therefore not limited to the space of not more than six months from its promulgation. The High, Court was not wrong in holding that in the case before it, the death sentence could be awarded to any of them. [704E] 5. The High Courts were not justified in holding that since the death sentence imposed on the two appellants was not warranted, the death penalty could not be awarded to the two appellants under section 354(2) of the code. The High] Court was not in error in holding that it was not necessary to specify the special reasons for awarding the death sentence. [707B] 7. In the present case, the High Court has not given any special reasons for the imposition of the death sentence on the two accused. [709G] 8. The High [709H] 9. The High Judge was right in confirming the sentence of imprisonment imposed on the appellants. [809H] 10. The High Powered Committee had not given any reasons for the award of death sentence to the two accused, and the High Court had not given special reasons for such imposition. [710G] 9. In the instant case, the appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P..C. and sentenced to imprisonment for the same. [711G] 10. In the case before this Court the appellants were sentenced to imprisonment of life and a sentence of imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 10,000/- under section 302/34 I.P., 1860.

Court was right that the departmental Enquiry was not invalid because the appellant did not appear before it. [708G] 9A] 10. The High "Court was right when the departmental enquiry is held to be null and void because the appellant has been acquitted of all the charges. [710G] 10. In the instant case, the appellant was acquitted of all charges. [807E] 11. The High] Court was right. The departmental Enquiry was held to be invalid because the charges were not proved. [711G] 12.
