The appellant was appointed as an Inspector of Consolidation of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. He was appointed as a Consolidation Officer by the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda, and was posted as an Assistant Consolidation Officer. The Settlement Officer, who was the appointing authority, passed an order of termination of his services on March 17, 1955. The appellant was appointed on probation for a period of one month and was confirmed on March 17. 1955. He was, however, confirmed on March 31, 1955. On March 17, 1956 the appellant was appointed to the post of Consolidation Officer. On March 31, 1956 the Settlement Officer passed an order terminating his services. The appellant filed an appeal to the Settlement Officer. The settlement Officer dismissed the appeal. The appellant appealed to the Settlement Commissioner. The Settlement Commissioner held that the order of termination was not in accordance with the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the order terminating his service was in violation of article 311 (2) of Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was not a probationer and that the order was not a punishment. The appellant also contended that the termination of his service was not in violation of the provisions of the Constitution and that the termination was not a dismissal. Held, that the order passed by the Settlement Commissioner was in violation, of article 311 of the Constitution, and that the appellant had no right to hold the post. The order of termination is not a punishment and the appellant was a temporary employee. The order was passed in violation of Article 311(2). The order of dismissal was not a termination of service. The order is not a penalty. The order does not give any indication that the termination is a punishment. It is only a termination of the service. The termination of the appellant was in violation either of article 311 or 311 of the constitution. The order cannot be said to be a termination of his employment. The order, therefore, is not a termination simpliciter. The appellant had no opportunity to show cause against the order of dismissal. The order passed by Mr. Justice Bishan Narain was not a penalty and the appellant had a right to hold his post. The appellant, therefore, was not a temporary employee and the order of his termination was not an order of dismissal but was a termination of employment. The appellant could not be said to have been a probationer, because he was not a permanent employee. The appellant cannot be said that the order is a termination of services.

The appellant, a University, was established in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, by the Jammu and Kashmir State Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred to as the Commission) in the year 1971. The Commission was constituted under section 3 of the Jammu and Kupwara University Act, 1971, and the Government of Jammu and Kangra, by notification dated July 22, 1969, appointed the Commission. The Commission, after consultation with the Commission, recommended the names of four Lecturers, who were appointed as Professors in the colleges, and the names of five Lecturers were sent to the Government for their recommendations. The Commission recommended the names for appointment of four Lecturers in the colleges. The Commission submitted its report to the Government on June 2, 1969, and the Commission recommended the name of four Lecturers for appointment as Professors in various colleges. The Government, however, recommended the name for appointment of five Lecturers, who had been appointed as Professors, in the colleges in the State. The Commission also recommended the names to be recommended for appointment as Professor in the colleges and the names for promotion as Professors were sent to it. The Commission forwarded the recommendations to the Government. The Government approved the recommendations of the Commission and the Commission, after consulting the Commission, approved the recommendations to be made to the State Government for the appointments. The Government thereafter approved the recommendations made by the Commission. In the meanwhile, the Government, however issued a notification dated July 23, 1969, appointing the five Lecturers, and the name of the five Lecturers was sent to the Commission for their recommendations to be approved by the Commission for the appointments to the posts of Professors. The Government thereupon approved the recommendations and the Commission forwarded the recommendation to the Government, and the State Government, on June 2/7, 1969, approved the recommendation to be made by the Government. On June 2, 1970, the Government approved the recommendation of the Commission. On June 3, 1970, a Committee was constituted by the Government to consider the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professor and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 of the Constitution, and the Chairman 's note dated June 2,1969, and the President 's note on June 2. 1969, and recommended the names recommended by the Commission to be made for the appointments of the Professors. The Commission after consultation with it, approved the list of the names recommended for the appointments as Professors in different colleges. The appellant State Government, however recommended the names in the list of Professors for the posts of Professor in various colleges, and it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, and the appellant State Government was therefore consulted on the suitability of candidates for promotion to the posts. The appellant, however, contended that the Commission was not consulted in regard to the suitability of candidate for promotion as Reader in various colleges and that the Commission had not consulted in respect of the suitability of persons for promotion as Readers. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petition and quashed the notification dated July 21, 1969, on the ground that the Commission did not consult in regard to suitability of candidates, and that the selection made by it was invalid for the reasons that the Commission could not consult in respect of suitability of candidates to the posts, and that it was not open to the Commission to consult in regard thereto. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Commission has not consulted in the manner required by section 133 of Constitution. [875 A] 2. The Commission had not been consulted in regard thereto, and the selection made was invalid for reasons that the Government had not consulted, and that there was no need for consultation in regard thereto and that the Government was not consulted. [878 B] 3.

The petitioner was elected as a member of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. He was elected as the Chairman of the House. He was removed from the membership of the House by the Speaker of the House, and he was removed from that membership. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad, challenging the validity of the order of removal of the petitioner from the membership. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner appealed to this Court. The High court held that the petitioner was not entitled to the protection of article 19(1) of the Constitution, because the petitioner was elected to the House of Lords, and the House of the People of the United States of America, and the members of the committees of the House were not entitled to protection of article 194(3) of the constitution. The petitioner contended that the House of Parliament had no power to prevent the publication of its proceedings, and that the petitioner had no right to prevent the publications of its proceedings. Held, that the petitioner is not entitled to any protection of article 195(3) because the House of People of the State of America, which was a State, had no power, to prevent the publishing of its proceedings without the authority of the House to be a breach of privilege. The petitioner is not a citizen of India. The petitioner has not been able to show that the House had no power or authority to prevent the published of its proceedings by the Speaker. The petitioner was not a citizen, and, therefore, the House of Speaker had no power and authority to prevent publication of its Proceedings. The petitioner cannot be denied the protection of the article 19(2) of the. Constitution, because it has no power or jurisdiction to prevent the publish of its proceedings in the House of a State. The petitioner, therefore, cannot be denied that the House was not a State within the meaning of article 19 (1) of article 19. The petitioner 's fundamental right under article 19(l) of the, Constitution, is, therefore, not available to the petitioner. The petitioner's fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) is preserved despite the provisions of article 194 (3) of Constitution. The petitioner can, therefore, be denied the right to prevent publication by the Speaker, if he has no power, or authority to prohibit the publication of the proceedings. The petitioner could not be denied the fundamental right under [article 19(1)] of the Constitution. The petition is, therefore dismissed.

The State Transport Authority, the Regional Transport Authority, Kanpur, issued a notification under section 68C of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, for the grant of temporary permits to the appellants for plying the vehicles on the route in question. The Regional Officer had no authority or power to grant permits for plying on the route and the Regional Transport Officer had no power or authority to grant permits on the basis of such permits. The Regional Director, Kanpur, was not competent to grant temporary/permanent permits to any individual or class of persons in respect thereof and, therefore. the Regional Transport authority had no authority. The appellant was charged under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed the murder of Ebrar Ali with the intention of committing the murder of the deceased. The prosecution case was that the appellant had committed the murder and the dagger was used by him in furtherance of the common intention of all. The trial court found that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant was guilty of murder and convicted him under section 302 of the Indian penal Code. The High Court, however, convicted the appellant under section 302 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High court was not right in holding that the charge under section 302 was not proved. [601B] 2. The High 'Court was not right, in holding that there was no evidence to show that the appellant committed the murder. [602C] 3. The fact that the appellant did not use the dagger in the commission of the offence was not proved by the prosecution. [603D] 4. The fact, that the appellant used the dagger in his own hand, was not proved, and so, the conviction of the appellant under sections 302 and 307 read with section 149 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code was not sustainable in law. [604E] 5. The fact of the case that the appellant and the other accused were acting jointly in furtherance of their common intention of committing murder of the victim, clearly shows that the appellant is guilty of murder. [613F] 6. The fact is that the appellant has used the dagger on his neck as if he had committed the offence of murder. The fact remains that the appellant, who was acting in furtherance of his common intention, had used the dagger, in furtherance of which he had caused the murder of his deceased. [605G] 7. The fact in the present case that the dagger was not used by the appellant in furtherance of any of his common intent is not in any way inconsistent with the common intention or with the common intent of all. [606E] 8. The fact as to whether the appellant had used the knife in furtherance of a common intention of the other accused to kill the deceased is not in dispute. The fact which is not in controversy is that the dagger used by the accused was used by the other accused in furtherance of common intention of his common object. [607E] 9. The fact whether the appellant was acting in pursuance of the common object of all or not is not in doubt. The fact however remains that the accused was acting in the furtherance of the object of all. It is not in question that the appellant acted in furtherance of that object. [613G] 9. In the present case, the appellant was not acting in furtherance or in furtherance of its common intention. He was not acting as a member of the unlawful assembly. He was merely acting in furtherance and in furtherance of such common intention. [609E] 9A] 10. The fact about the commission of murder of the appellant by the other two accused is not in issue. The fact regarding the commission of offence of murder of EBrar Ali with his common intention is not in the matter of the commission of crime of house trespass. [608E] 10. In the instant case, the prosecution has not proved that the appellant assaulted EBrar, Ali with the dagger on the neck of EBrarar Ali with a dagger on the person of EBrrar Ali. The prosecution has not established that EBrar was used by EBrar in furtherance of this common intention. The prosecution had not proved that EBrray Ali was used by them in furtherance of an unlawful assembly. [610E] 11. The fact relating to the commission of an offence of house trespass is not in connection with the commission of any offence of house breaking.

The appellant and his daughter were governed by custom. The respondent was a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly and the appellant was a member thereof. The respondent claimed that he was a member in the Punjab Legislative Council and the appellant had no right to succeed to the self acquired property of the father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not a collateral of the father and that the respondent was not a member of Punjab Legislative Assembly. The High Court, however, reversed the decree holding that the respondent had failed to prove that the appellant had not been a collateral of his father. The High court, however, held that the respondent could not succeed to the property in preference to the collaterals. The High 'Court further held that the appellant could not succeed in preference to his daughter. The High. Court, however held that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act and the respondent was entitled to succeed to his father 's property in preference. The High, Court, however. reversed the decree of the trial court holding that the suit for a declaration of his title to the selfacquired property of the appellant was maintainable in view the provisions of Section 2 of the Indian Evidence Act and the appellant could succeed to the collateral's self acquired property. The High' Court, however,. reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the trial court had not properly appreciated the evidence and that the appellant did not prove that the respondent did not belong to the family of the father, and that the High 'Court was in error. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that there was no custom in the Gurdaspur district of Gurdaspur which was the only custom in the Punjab State. [901 A] 2. The High Curt was right in holding, that the appellant 's right to succeed in preference was not a reliable or trustworthy document. [902 A] 3. The High] 4. The appellant was not entitled to succeed in the suit because the custom in the district of Gurdaspurtpur was not a conclusive or reliable document. [093 B] 5. The High was right in rejecting the appellant ' s appeal. [903 C] 6. The Hight. Court was right in reversing the decree of trial court. [904 D] 7. The High Riwaji ams of the same village Kingarian was not a ancestral and self acquired property and the appellant ' Sarswat Brahmins of the village Kingarian were not ancestral and selfacquired property. [905 E] 8. The High riwaji is not a reliable and trustworthy document. The High ted Court was right, in holding that it was not a valid and reliable document. The appellant 's case was not a� and reliable document and the High Court had no jurisdiction to reverse the decree of this Court. [906 A] 9. The High Ted Court was wrong in holding that this was a reliable and reliable document because the High Court has not properly appreciated that the appellant's father was not a coparcener. [908 C] 9. In the instant case, the High Court, in the first instance, was right in relying on the evidence of the appellant. [909 D] 9. It is well settled that the High Courts have no jurisdiction to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact. [907 A] 10. The High Cou rt was right in setting aside the decree of t he trial court. The High cour t was right in upholding the decree of th e trial court.

The appellant, a registered owner of a plot of land, purchased by him, from the respondent, on the basis of a sale deed executed by him in favour of the respondent, and the respondent, by a registered deed of sale, sold the same to the appellant, and the appellant, in turn, sold the plot to the respondent, for a consideration of Rs. 1,000. The respondent, by an agreement of sale, agreed to sell the plot to him, and the sale deed was executed by him, in favour of his wife, and the latter, on the terms of the agreement, was to sell the property to the appellant. The respondent executed a sale deed in favour of her husband, and the same was registered in the office of the appellant. On the basis of the sale deed, the respondent executed a registered sale deed in her favour, and the title of the appellant was transferred to her husband. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract, and the trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the decree of the trial court, and decreed the suit, holding that the instrument in question was not a single instrument, and that the instrument was not capable of performing any one of the acts which could be done by the donor himself, and that, therefore, the instrument in the hands of the donor, was not capable to perform any one of those acts, and that it was not capable only of performing some one of those act, but was capable of performing some other acts which could not be done by him, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys, and that he could exercise all those powers, and that therefore, the instruments in question were capable of performing all those acts which could properly be done by his wife, as trustee or administrator, and that since the instrument in favour of respondent was capable of perform all those acts, the instrument was capable of doing all those acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The instrument in question is a single instrument consisting of several acts, and the instrument in respect of each of those acts is capable of performing one of those duties, and that is the position, which the donor is capable of doing, whether in his individual capacity or in his individual capacities, and that can be done by a general power of attorney, and that could be done only by the donor, and that cannot be done by any general power of Attorney, and that too, by a general powers of attorney. [849B] 2. The instrument is capable of performance by the donor and the same can be performed by a general Power of attorney. The instrument does not comprise any other acts which can be done either by the donor or by any general powers of Attorney. [850C] 3. The instrument, in question, does not comprise all acts which can properly be done either individually or collectively. The instrument cannot be split up into separate instruments, and thus, the instrument cannot be divided into separate instruments. [852D] 4. The instrument can be split up in separate instruments, but it cannot be split into separate instruments and can be split into two separate instruments. The instrument has to be split up and separate instruments. It cannot be split together. [853E] 5. The instrument must be split up, and separate instruments must be split into different instruments. [820H] 6. The instrument may be split up or separate instruments. But it cannot be divided in separate instruments. There is no question of split up or split up into two separate instrument. [854E] 7. The instrument should be split up as separate instruments. If the instrument is split up or consolidated, it cannot be converted into separate instruments because it is capable of being split up or divided into two separate Instruments. [855E] 8. The instrument would be split up if the instrument is divided into two different instruments.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the basis of the written down value of the assets. The Income tax Officer, however, disallowed the depreciation allowance on the written down values of the assets on the ground that the depreciation allowed under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was not allowable under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the depreciation allowance to the assessee on the ground of the written off value of the written-down value of the asset. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the written down Value of the assets was not allowable as deduction under the Indian income tax Act, 1961. The High Court held that the depreciation allowance was allowable under the Bhavangar War Profits Act and the written down price of the assets could not be deducted in computing the written down fair value of the depreciation allowance. The High court, however, held that the assessee was entitled to the depreciation allowance under the Bhavsar War Profits Act. The High ' Court, however, took the view that the written off values of the asset on the basis that the depreciation allowable under the Act was in force in the past were not allowable under section 10(5)(b) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 and the written off price of the asset was allowable under section 13(5)(a) of the Act. The assessee, therefore, appealed to the High Court. The High, Court, however held that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was right in disallowing the depreciation allowance and the written- down value of assets on the basis thereof. The High. Court, however. held that the interest on the written off Value of the asset could not be allowed to the assessee under the Bhavgar War Profits Act as the written down amount of the written up value of the property was not allowable. The High' Court, however,. held that the working capital allowance was allowable as deduction in computing the depreciation allowance in computing the Written down value of asset on the ground the written down valuation of the asset had to be taken into account in computing the write down fair value. The HighCT. Court, therefore, held that in computing thewritten down fair value, the written down of the writtendown value of assets was allowable under sections 10(5) (b) of The HighCT, therefore, allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the written-off value of the fixed assets was not deductible under section 10 (5)(b), of the Indian Incometax, 1922, because the written down cost of the assets had to be computed in computing the income tax on the written-up value of the movable assets. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The written down value is the written down which is the written-out of the written cost of the asset and the written up cost of the written out of the written back value of the immovable assets. [601B] 2. The written-off values of the written assets are not allowable under sections 13(5) and 13(5). [601C] 3. The written off value is the depreciation allowance which is allowable under section 12(5) of the Income tax Act. [602D] 4. The written up value is the depreciable value of the depreciables which are allowed under section 12 (5) (a) of Income tax Act and the depreciation allowance allowed under section 13 (5) of that Act. [06E] 5. The written back value is the capital allowance which is allowed under section 10 of the Income Tax Act. [2006E] 6. The written forward value of the capital asset is the depreciated value of the securities. The written out of such written down value, is the deprecation allowed under section 11 of the Income TAX Act. [ 2006E] 7. The written return of the depreciated assets is the deprecated value of the security.

The appellant was a contractor for the construction of a building for the construction work of the K.P.C. The appellant was awarded a contract for the construction contract. The respondent was the contractor for the K. P.C. for the construction. The appellant submitted that the contract was awarded to the respondent for the construction and that the respondent was entitled to be awarded the contract. The appellant contended that the contract had been awarded to the contractor for construction of a new building and that the contractor had not been given the contract in the manner in which the contract was executed. The High Court held that the contract did not satisfy the requirements of para I and V of the N.I.T.s. and that the appellant was not entitled to the contract. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the contract in question was not a contract for construction of the new building and, therefore, the High Court should not interfere with the decision of the learned single Judge of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no violation of the conditions of the NIA. [801 D] 1.2 The High Court had rightly held that the appellant had not complied with the conditions of para I of the NAC. [802 E] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that there was a violation of the condition of the NCC. [803 E] 1.(a) The High Court should have interfered with the decision in the matter of the tender process.

The appellant was appointed as Custodian of Evacuee Property under the Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 (XXVII of 1949) and was appointed as the Custodian of Evacuee Properties under the Administration Of Evacuee Property Ordinance 1949 (XXVIII of 1949) on the date when the Act XXXI of 1950 came into force. The Custodian General made an order of confirmation of the order of confirmation passed by the Custodian General under section 27 of the Act. The CustodianGeneral made an order under section 27(1) of the Act XXXIof 1950 and the order of the Custodian General made under section 27 (1) of Act XXXI of 1949. The Custodian of Evacuee properties passed an order of the Additional Custodian under section 27 on the basis of the order passed by the Additional Custodian. The Custodian also made an order on the basis that the order of his confirmation was not a judicial order. The Custodian, Additional Custodian and an Authorised Deputy Custodian, acting under section 27, passed an order under that section on the basis thereof. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of Additional Custodian before the Custodian General. The Additional Custodian, acting on the basis the order passed under section 27 held that the order passed in the exercise of revisional power was not a quasijudicial order. The appellant challenged the order of Assistant Custodian and the Additional Custodian before this Court. The appellant contended that the order was not a quasi judicial order and that the order had to be treated as a quasi judicial one and that the Additional Custodian had no jurisdiction to pass the order of confirmed. Held, that the order under section 28 of the Act XLVIII of 1950 was not a purely administrative order and that it was not a case of quasi judicial order. It was not a matter of quasi judicial nature. The order of the Assistant Custodian was not a decision of quasi judicial character. The order was not an administrative order. The order passed by him was not a judgment of quasi judicial or quasi judicial nature and that it had to be decided in accordance with the provisions of the Act XXXVII of 1950. The order is not an administrative one. The order has to be treated in accordance with law and not as a quasi Judicial order. The appeal was not competent. The order had to operate as an administrative order and the order was a quasi judicial act. The order could not be treated as an administrative one and the order passed was a quasi Judicial one. The appeal had to be disposed of under section 27. The order did not amount to an administrative order, nor was it an administrative one, nor was an administrative one nor was an order passed by a quasi judicial authority. The order, therefore, was not an order passed in exercise of the powers conferred by or under the Act XXXI Of 1950.

The appellant, a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was a registered company under the Indian Company Act, 1956. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, was a company incorporated in the year 1965. The appellant was a registered Company under the Indian Trade Act, 1956 and was a registered firm under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The appellant claimed that the bonus payable to him was a customary bonus and that the payment was a customary or customary bonus. The appellant contended that the bonus was a customary and traditional bonus and that it was a customary right and that the bonus paid was a customary one. The appellant also contended that the claim for bonus based on the customary bonus was not a customary or traditional bonus and so, the claim for payment of bonus based on customary bonus was barred by the provisions of the Bonus Act. The appellant disputed the claim for the bonus based on a customary or contractual bonus. The Tribunal held that the claim was not a ' customary or traditional' bonus and so the claim for wages based on the custom or the customary bonus could not be based on the terms of the bonus. The High Court held that the bonus based upon the customary or traditional customary bonus was a recognised or customary bonus and so it could not be said that the claim of customary bonus based on custom or the custom or customary bonus was based on the principles of customary or traditional Bonus. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to claim any bonus based on any customary or traditional or customary bonus, because the claim for customary bonus based upon custom or customary or traditional remuneration was based on custom. The appellant challenged the decision of the High Court on the ground that the claim based on custom was not a " customary or traditional" bonus and so that the claim could not be founded on any customary bonus. Held, that the claim in the present case was not a valid claim for bonus and so was not a claim based on any custom or customary rights. The claim for bonus was based upon a customary or ordinary bonus. The claim was based on a custom or customary right and so it was not a recognised or traditional bonus. The question of customary or customary rights based on custom and customary bonus was, therefore, not a matter of dispute with regard to the claim for compensation based on the basis of custom or customary relationship. The claim based on the principle of customary or ordinary rights based on the conditions of service of the workmen was not a matter which could be decided on a proper or customary bonus based only on the terms and conditions of service. The claim of customary or contractual rights based on customary or traditional wages was based on customary and traditional wages. The claim, therefore, was not a dispute arising out of the customary or customary right or customary bonus which was based on any other customary or customary or customary relationship, and so it did not fall within the scope of the definition of customary or natural bonus. The decision of the Tribunal was affirmed by the High Court. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the decision of that Court. The High 'Court held that the decision of this Court in the case of [S.R.T.C. vs The Bombay Co. Ltd. & Ors. ; , followed. The Bombay Co.'s case (supra) was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The High Courts held that the payment of bonus was a ' customary bonus and it was a ' usual or customary bonus" and so it would not be a customary or normal bonus. The Bombay High Court held, that the payment must have been at a uniform rate throughout the relevant period and so it cannot be said that it was customary or customary. The HighCourt held that there was no evidence to show that the payment had been at a lower rate throughout the period. The High. Court held that there had been no evidence to establish that the payment at a uniform rates throughout the relevant periods was customary or traditional.

The respondents were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab on the basis of the orders of the High Court dated April 1, 1970. The High Court issued a notification fixing the seniority of the respondents and others who were appointed to a post in the Superior Judicial service on or after December 31, 1976. The respondents were appointed on the basis that they were appointed to that post on the basis on the basis the dates of their confirmation. The High court, however, held that the seniority of all the respondents was to be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation and not with reference to their dates of confirmation. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification fixing the inter se seniority of the direct recruits and direct recruits. The HighCourt held that the inter se inter se seniority between the direct recruits, respondents and others was to be fixed with reference to dates of confirmation, and that the seniority list was to be drawn up on the basis thereof. The High Courts, however, dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the High Court had erred in holding that the seniority was to be reckoned from the date of confirmation and that the respondents were entitled to be confirmed in accordance with the amended rule 12. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Power Court was right in holding that there was no rule of rotation at the time of confirmation. [801B] 2. The High power of the High Power Court to issue a notification fixing seniority of the promotees and direct recruits is a part of the rule of rotation and in accordance with Rule 12. The HighPower Court was right, in holding that it was not open to the High Power court to issue a Notification fixing the interse seniority of the officers appointed or promoted to the Superior judicial service prior to December 31,1976. [802C] 3. The High powers of the High court are vested in the Governor of Haryana and the Governor of Punjab and the Governor is vested in the High Power. [803D] 4. The High Commissioner, Haryana, in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, is vested in him and the Governor, in consultation with the High Court, is vested with the power of confirmation. He is also vested with the powers of confirmation. In the exercise of the said powers, the Governor is also vested in the State Government. [804E] 5. The High Commission has the power to issue a Circular fixing the inter seniority of the members of the Superior Judicial Services in accordance with rule 12. The power of the Governor to issue a circular fixing the inter inter se seniority is vested in a High Power Court. [805E] 6. The High is vested with a power of confirmation and the High Power is vested in it. [806E] 7. The High was not right in holding the inter se Seniority of the direct recruit and direct recruits to the Superior Civil Service of Punjab. [807E] 8. The High courts were right in holding inter se seniority in the Superior Civil Services of Punjab. The High Curt was right in not holding that the interse inter se seniority was to the Superior Curt. [808E] 8, The High Court was right when it held that the rule of seniority was applicable to the members of Superior Judicial Service who were appointed on probation on or after the date of the initial appointment. [809E] 9. The High] Court was right that the seniority in the Higher Judicial Service was to be taken into account for the purpose of determining the inter se merit of the members in the Superior judicial Service. [810E] 9, 10A] 10. The Highness of the High Courts was right in the view that the seniority should be determined with regard to the dates from which the confirmation was to be made. [811E] 10.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, who were appointed as Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants in the State of Andhra Pradesh, filed O.A. No. 1259 of 1987 before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad, challenging the order dated October 6, 1989, issued by the State Government in R.P. No. 2403 of 1987, contending that the State Government had no power to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts in any department, and that the State of Telangana had no power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) of the Order, to organise a new cadre in respect o f any category of civil services of, and class or classes of civil services, under the State. The Tribunal dismissed the O.A., holding that the State had no power, under proviso to Paragraph 3(1), to organise a single cadre in respect thereof, in respect of a category of posts, in any department. The State Government filed a revision petition before the Andhra High Court. The State of Andhrapradesh filed a revision before the Andhra State Administrative Tribunal, which allowed the revision, and set aside the order of the Tribunal. The State filed a revision against the order of Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the State was competent to organise a cadre in respect to any category of persons, and that it was not necessary for the State Government to have the power under proviso (1) to paragraph 3 (1) of G.O.Ms. No. 23 dated October 6. 1989, to organise classes or classes of posts in a department, and therefore, the State Government was competent to convene a separate cadre for the purpose of recruitment, seniority, promotion etc., as the case may be. The State was aggrieved by the order of tribunal. The State preferred a revision before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1. The State is competent to organise classes and classes of posts, under the Government, in a department. It is only for the purpose o f administrative convenience, not for the purpose for which a local cadre has been organised, in respect ov er of civil services. [701B] 1.2.1.2. The State has power under proviso(1) to para 3(1)(e) of the order, to organise any class or classes or classes or posts in a Department, and therefore the State Government is competent to convene such a separate cadre, in respect thereof. [702C] 1.3.1.3. The State had power under proviso.(1) to Para 3(1). The State Government had power under the proviso to para 3 (1). The power under proviso is only to organise a local cadre in respect whereof a local cadre is organised, in relation to any class or class of posts in the civil services of the State. [703D] 1.4.1.4. The State Legislature has power under the Proviso to para 3 of the Order to organise a special cadre in respect thereto. [704E] 1.5.1.5.2.3.3.4.4.5.4. In the present case, the State Legislature has not power under the said proviso to para 2(1) and therefore the power under the second proviso to para 4(1) is not available to the State Government. [705E] 1.(1) The State Legislature had power under Article 3(1); and therefore the powers under the second Proviso to para 4 (1) are not available to it. [706E] 1(2) The State Government has power under Article 4(1). It is only in respect of the category of posts which are in the civil service of the State, that the State Legislature can make a special cadre.

The plaintiff was a mortgagor in possession of the mortgaged property in the usual course of management by the mortgagor. The mortgagor had mortgaged the property in the ordinary course of management. The mortgagor was a mortgagor and the mortgagor had mortgaged his property in the normal course of management and the mortgagor was not entitled to the permanent lease. The mortgagor, however, had a right to redeem the mortgage. The mortgagor filed a suit for a declaration that the sale of the mortgaged properties in the usual way of management by him was illegal and void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the mortgagor had no right to redeem and that the sale was not binding on the mortgagor. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the mortgagor was entitled to the temporary lease in question. [601 A] (2) The High court was right in its conclusion that the sale in favour of the defendants was not binding upon the mortgagor. [602 B] (3) The High was right in the view that the sale by the mortgagor in favour of Wazir Narayan Singh was not binding. [603 C] (4) The High 'Court was right in not holding that the sale deed in favour of defendants was not valid and operative against the mortgagor. (5) The High'Court was right, in holding that a mortgagor in the usual manner of management by his father had no power to grant a permanent lease in respect of the mortgaged land. [604 D] (6) The High. Court was right, on the facts of the case, in holding, that the sale did not take place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage. [605 E] (7) The High, Court was right that the sale made by the mortgagor was a mortgage in the usual form and that the mortgagor could not have exercised his right of redemption if he had not exercised his right to redeem. [606 F] (8) The High Courts were right in holding, on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties, that the mortgagor did not exercise his right of redeem. [706 F] The High Court had rightly held that the sale could not be held to be invalid on the ground that the mortgagor in possession had not exercised the right of redemption.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the petitioner on May 27, 1978 for the execution of the work of construction of a bridge at the cost of Rs.2,000/- and the petitioner agreed to execute the work of the construction of a new bridge at the expense of the respondent. The respondent agreed to execute a work of construction at the cost and cost of Rs,2,000/-. The respondent agreed that the work of constructing a bridge at its cost would be completed within a specified period of time. The respondent filed a suit in the Calcutta High Court for a declaration that the arbitration agreement dated May 27,1978 was void and not binding on the petitioner and that the arbitration was void and inoperative. The respondent contended that the arbitration clause in the agreement was void and unenforceable and that the arbitrator was not competent to give the relief sought for. The trial court dismissed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the arbitration Clause in the agreement did not cease to have effect in respect of any matter required by the agreement and that the dispute or difference referred to in the notice of the petitioner and the respondent was not to be brought within the meaning of section 14 of the Limitation Act. The High court held that the arbitrator had no power to give the arbitration agreement in respect of the dispute or differences referred to in notice of the respondent and that the respondent had no right to ask the arbitrator to rescind the arbitration agreement and that he had no right of action or dispute to give the arbitrator a notice of the dispute to the Engineer in the first instance seeking reference of it to arbitration within 15 days from the date when the claim accrued. The HighCourt further held that the respondent was bound to give notice of the disputes to the Engineer within 15 days of the receipt of the notice of arbitration. The High Courts held that the time of the receipt was not to expire and that the time for completion of the work was not to end with the expiry of the specified number of years from the date on which the cause of action accrued. The respondent also contended that the time taken for completion of work was not the date on the date when it would have accrued but for the purpose of limitation. The High Curt held that the period of limitation was not to commence from the date of the notice and that the delay in completion of the contract was not to have accrued in respect of a matter required by law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The arbitration clause in an arbitration agreement cannot be construed as an arbitration agreement. The arbitration agreement is an arbitration agreement and it is an arbitration clause in a contract. The arbitration is an arbitration one. The arbitration Clause in an arbitration contract cannot be construed to have accrued to the party in respect of an arbitration agreement which has accrued but for its purpose. [849C] 2. The arbitration clauses in an arbitration document cannot be construed in a manner that the arbitration shall cease to have accrued but to the party who has entered on the reference or a sole arbitrator. [850C] 3. The arbitration proceedings are not an arbitration agreement but an arbitration agreement as defined in section 2(3) of the Arbitration Act. The arbitration agreements are not an agreement in writing and the arbitration clause is an arbitration document. The arbitration procedure is not an arbitration clause. [852D] 4. The arbitration provisions are not an Arbitration agreement. The Arbitration clause in an agreement is an agreement in terms of the arbitration agreement. [853E] 5. The arbitration provision is an arbitration contract. The Arbitration Clause in an agreement in a contract is an arbitration award. The arbitration award is an arbitration order. The arbitration terms are not an award. The Arbitration agreement is an award. [854F] 6. The arbitration contract is an award and the arbitration agreement is not an award and it is not an agreement. The agreement is an arbitral award. The agreement in writing is an arbitration Award.

The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of an estate, had mortgaged the same to the State of Bihar for a sum of Rs. 1,000. The mortgage was not in respect of the entire estate. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to the State. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the appellant had not paid the amount due under the mortgage decree. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 4(d) of the Act because the mortgage was not a mortgage decree. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in section 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, are not applicable to the facts of this case. The appellant was not a mortgagee in the possession of the land. [601 B] 2. The appellant had not been able to prove that the mortgage was a mortgage decree and that the appellant could not be proceeded against in execution of a mortgage decree against the estate of the debtor. [602 C] 3. The appellant could not prove that the mortgagee had not paid any amount due under a mortgage decree to the State and that the mortgage decree was not a decree. [603 D] 4. The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of section 4 (d) of Act 94 of 1959. [604 E] 5. The appellant is entitled to the protection of section 4 of the Act. [605 F] 6. The appellant has not been able, by any evidence, to prove that he had not paid a sum due under a decree. The High court was in error in holding that the appellant is entitled only to the protection under section 4(c) of the Land Reforms Act. [613 F] 7. The appellant, therefore, is entitled to a decree in the sum of Rs, 1,000 in view of the provisions contained in sections 7A and 4 of the Land Reform Act. [643 F] 8. The appellant can not be allowed to raise the plea that the mortgage is not a mortgage. [606 F] 9. The appellant having failed to prove that a mortgage decree had become unexecutable in view of section 4A of the LandLR Act, the appellant cannot be permitted to take advantage thereof. [607 F] 916 A] 10. The appellant being a mortgagee in a mortgage decree, the appellant is not entitled to any protection under section 5 of the Land LR Act. [707 F] 10. In the instant case, the appellant had failed to prove the execution of the mortgage decree by the mortgagee. [608 G] 11. The appellant failed to prove his case that the mortgage had become uneximutable in view the provisions contained therein. [609 F] 12. The appellant did not prove that he was entitled to the relief claimed by him. [610 G] 13. The appellant also failed to prove any other fact that the mortgage in question was not a security. [611 H] 14. The appellant in his written statement admitted that the mortgage deed was not a document of mortgage. He also admitted that the mortgagee was not a mortgagor. [612 F] 15. The appellant admitted that the mortgagor had not paid rent. He also denied that the mortgage money was not a part of the mortgage. He admitted that the appellant did not pay rent. He admitted the fact that the mortgagee did not pay the rent. He further admitted that the land was not part of the mortgaged property. He admitted his liability to pay rent. [613 G] 15. In the present case, the mortgage was executed by the appellant in favour of the State of West Bengal. The mortgage deed was executed by him in favour of his predecessor.

The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, by the order of the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated 25th November, 1986. He was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the Preventive Detention ACT, 1950. The grounds of detention were served on the appellant on 25th November 1986. The grounds were served on him on 25th December, 1986. The appellant was served with the grounds of detention on 25th January, 1986. On 25th November 1987, the appellant was served a notice of detention on the ground that he was not a friend of the detenu and that he was also a friend of Sundararajan. The grounds served on the detenu were not considered by the Advisory Board. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the order of detention on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has come to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention is vitiated by the non-application of mind. The order is vitiated by non-application by the Advisory board. [792 E] 2. The order was passed by the Government of Tamil Nadu on 25th October, 1986. It was not challenged by the appellant. The order has been passed by the State Government on 25th September, 1986. [793 A] 3. The order passed by the Advisory Boards on 25th July, 1986 is vitiated by violation of the principles of natural justice. [794 B] 4. The order dated 25th July 1986 is vitiated because of non-application on the part of the Advisory Board to permit the appellant to be represented by a friend of Sunderarajan. [795 C] 5. The order does not show that the Advisory Board was not satisfied with the request of the appellant to permit the assistance of a friend of a friend. The order also does not show the application of mind. [796 D] 6. The order cannot be sustained on the ground of non-compliance with the principles of Natural Justice. [797 E] 7. The order must be set aside on the ground on which the appellant has been denied the assistance of an advocate. [798 G] 7. In the present case, the order of rejection of the appellant's request for assistance of a lawyer is not challenged by him. [799 G] 8. The order, therefore, cannot be sustained. [791 A] 9. The order in question is vitiated because the appellant had no right to appear through a legal practitioner in the proceedings before the Advisory Board and the Government of Madras had no right, if a similar facility is denied to the detenu. [782 A] 10. The order therefore cannot be sustained in the present case.

The respondents were the owners of the goods and the goods were requisitioned on September 30, 1946. The goods were requisitioned by the respondents on September 30 and the goods had been delivered to the Government of India on September 30. 1946. The respondents were the managing agents of the mills. The goods had been requisitioned on September 29, 1946. On September 30, the respondents were the owner of the goods. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the goods were validly requisitioned and the orders of requisition and requisition were valid and binding on the mills. On September 29, the respondents filed a written statement and contended that the goods had not been requisitioned and that the goods could not be said to have been validly requisitioned. The trial court held that the goods in question were validly requisitioned on September 31, 1946 and that the respondents were not entitled to the declaration. The High Court held that the respondents had not been able to prove that the goods which were requisitioned were validly requisitioned. On appeal by the Union of India, the High Court held: (1) that the goods, in question, were validly requisitioned under the provisions of the [Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879] and (2) that the respondents could not be held to be the owners of those goods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The goods were validly acquired and the orders were valid and enforceable. [701B] (b) The goods had not passed to the Government and the respondents were, therefore, not liable to be acquired under the provisions. [702C] (c) The goods could not have been validly acquired under the Act. [703D] (2) The goods, in the present case, were validly acquired under s. 18 of the Act. The goods could be validly acquired under ss. 18 and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act. [603E] (3) The goods in question had been requisitioned under the Act and the orders had been validly passed. [704F] (4) The goods did not pass to the Government. The goods in the present cases were validly acquired. [705G] (5) The goods which were validly requisitioned were validly acquired by the respondents under the provisions Of the Act. They were validly acquired, and the orders issued by the Government of india were valid and legal. [706F] (6) The goods passed to the respondents were validly acquired in the present appeals. [707F] (7) The goods remained in the custody of the respondents and the respondents could be said to be the owner of those goods and the orders could not be questioned in the present proceedings. [709G] (712A] (8) The goods having been requisitioned, the respondents could no longer be said to acquire them. [708F] (9) The goods being requisitioned, the authorities could not be served on the respondents. [710F] (10) The goods are validly acquired and they are validly acquired. The goods having not passed to Government, the authorities were validly acquired on September 30/30, 1946. [713F] (11) The goods have been validly released and the orders have been validly passed on September 30 or September 30, 1947. [712F] (12) The goods cannot be said to belong to the mills. [714F] (13) The goods must be deemed to have been requisitioned under s. 3(1) of the Act and they must be deemed as validly acquired under that provision. [715F] (14) The goods can be said to vest in the Government of Bengal only on September 30 the goods are validly requisitioned. [716F] (15) The goods would be deemed to be validly acquired only on September 31 the goods are duly requisitioned.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee filed an appeal against the order of the Tribunal relating to the assessment year 1964 65. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the order of assessment relating to the year 1964 65 and the assessment relating to assessment year 1964 66. The assessee appealed to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922 and the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee had not made any provision for the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23A) and that the assessee could not be said to be a reserve. The Tribunal further held that the provisions of Sections 23A and 23A were not applicable to the assessment years 1964 65 and 1964 65. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that since the assessee had been assessed to income Tax under the provisions relating to the relevant assessment year 1964 67, the assessee was not entitled to the exemption under Section 23A. The Tribunal also held that the provision for the estimated liability of tax was not a reserve and, therefore, the assessee could be said to have been assessed to tax under the provision relating to the chargeable accounting year 1964 65, and the assessee was liable to pay additional tax under Section 23 A. The Tribunal, however, held that the amount set apart for contingent liability of tax under Section23A was not a provision and not a reserve. On appeal to this Court, it was contended that the assessee did not make any provision for anticipated liability of the tax (under section 23A) for meeting the anticipated liability for tax (under the provisions relating thereto). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any provision" in the section means a provision made by the assessee in its books for meeting the actual liability of tax. [601B] 2. The expression 'any provision" is not a reserve but a reserve. It is a reserve. Therefore, the provision made by it in its books is a reserve and not a reserves. [602C] 3. The expression used in the section is "any provision". It is a provision made for anticipated liability for taxes". Therefore, the expression "any provisions" in the explanation to section 23A is not a provision. [603D] 4. The expression reserve and not reserve is a reserve in commercial accountancy. It is not a part of the business. It is only a reserve. [604E] 5. The expression has been used in the explanation and not a provision for anticipated liabilities of tax. The expression is not a reserves but a reserve in the business. Therefore, it is a reserve which is a reserve for the purpose of business. [605F] 6. The expression reserves is a reserve but not a reserve in business. Therefore the expression "all provision" in explanation to section23A is not an reserve. It does not call a reserve. In the present case, the assessee had admittedly been assessed to Income tax under the Act. [606F] 7. The assessee had been maintaining books for the year 1964 67 and 1964 65 and had been maintaining the books for the years 1964 65, 1964 65 and 1965 65. The assessee was not a party to the proceedings. The assessee could not have been said to be the assessee in the absence of any provision in the explanation. [607F] 8. The assessee, therefore, was not entitled for the benefit of Section 23 A of the Act. The assessee is not entitled to any relief under Section 23AA. [608G] 9. The assessee has not been able to show that the provision in the Explanation to Section 23A was not applicable to his case. [609F] 10. The assessee cannot be said to not be a party to any provision in his books for the purpose. [610F] 11.

The petitioners were appointed as Engineers on the cadre of Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and they were appointed as Temporary Assistant Officers on the cadre strength. They were appointed as temporary Assistant Officers on a permanent basis. They were absorbed in the Indian Railways on the basis of the results of the competitive examinations held by the Union Public Service Commission. The petitioners were appointed on the cadre posts of Engineers in different capacities. They were confirmed in the Indian Administrative Service on the basis that they were appointed on a permanent post in the Indian Forest Service of Engineers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the rules framed by the Central Government in exercise of the power under Article 309 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court. The High court held that the rules framed under Article 309 were not ultra vires the Constitution. It was further held that the rule of constructive res judicata was not applicable to the case of the petitioners. The High Courts held that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The petitioners appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The rule of constructive Res judicata is not applicable to cases of recruitment to public services and appointments to public services. The rule is not applicable in the case of recruitment to the public services. [801B] 2. The rule does not apply to the case in hand. The rule has no application to the case before it. [802C] 3. The rule applies to the case when the recruitment is made by selection. The rule cannot be applied to the case where the recruitment is by selection. [803D] 4. The rule in question is not applicable. The rule merely provides for a quota of five years for the direct recruits to be absorbed in the service. [804E] 5. The rule provides for a separate channel of service and provides for a different channel of service. The rule also does not provide for a separate source of recruitment. [805E] 6. The rule, therefore, does not apply. [806F] 7. The rule clearly provides for a distinct channel of service for the direct recruitee to be absorbed into the service. The rules do not provide for any separate channel of recruitment. The rule only provides for a single channel of recruitment and does not provide that the quota of five year for direct recruits to the service shall be reckoned from the date of absorption. [807F] 8. The rule further provides for a uniform channel of service to be absorbed. [808F] 9. The rule itself provides for a special channel of service, and provides for an isolated channel of service in the cadre. [809G] 9. It is not open to the State to create separate channel of appointment in the cadre, and the rule does not provide any separate channel for recruitment. [820G] 9 A. The rule would not apply to cases of direct recruits to a cadre. [820H] 9. In the instant case, the rule does provide for a uniform method of recruitment and the rule would not be applicable to the cases of direct recruitee. [820A] 10. The rule will not apply to a case of direct recruitor. [820B] 11. The rule which provides for a suitable channel of appointment to a cadre is not a valid provision for the reason that the rule does confer a special channel for recruitment and does confer a right of equality in matters relating to employment. [820C] 12. The rule confers a special channel and provides for the same kind of appointment. [820D] 13. The rule makes no distinction between direct recruits and promotees. [820E] 14. The rule deals with a situation where direct recruits are not available for appointment. The rule lays down a general channel of appointment and provides for appointment to a post. [820F] 15.

[782 E] (6) The Special Bench was not competent, in the facts and circumstances of the present cases, to decide the case of the offences charged under section 5. [779 E] (7) The Special Special Courts Act does not violate against the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution. [787 B] (11) The Special Secretary to the Government of West Bengal, Home Department, Government of West Ben. vs The Special Secretary, Home Department and Ors., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 840, referred to. (12) The Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was a special statute. The Special Police establishment Act, 1946 was a special Act and the Special Police Establishment was a special enactment. The appellants were charged for the offence under section 396 I.P.C. and the learned Sessions Judge convicted them for the offence of murder and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. Hence the present appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.-2 is corroborated by the evidence of P W.2 and the other circumstances of the case. The evidence is corroborated by P.W., 7 and 8 who were injured in the occurrence. The evidence does not show that the appellants were seen by P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 in the house of the deceased Mauji Lal. [601B] 2. The evidence clearly shows that the appellants had been seen by P W. 2 and the other witnesses to the occurrence. [602C] 3. The evidence shows that the deceased Maui Lal was found broken open and the locks were found open. The evidence also shows that the doors of the house were found open and the keys were found open, that the boxes were found broken open. [603D] 4. The evidence further shows that the door of the house was found open and that the boxes had been found broken open, that it was found broken, that the doors were found open in the verandah of the house. [604E] 5. The evidence on record shows that the house of Mauji Lal was found open in a verandah of the houses of the deceased. The evidence, therefore, clearly shows that it was the appellant who had been seen in the verandah and that the doors had been found open. [613G] 6. The evidence in this case clearly shows that P.W, 7 and the other members of the family had been seen at the time of the occurrence. There is no evidence to show that the appellant had been seen with the deceased Mauja Lal. [613A] 7. The evidence indicates that the appellants and the deceased Mautiji Lal were seen by the deceased Maujji Lal in the verandah. The evidence establishes that the appellants could not have seen the occurrence. They were seen by them at the time when the occurrence had taken place. [605E] 8. The evidence discloses that the appellants did not have any intention to kill the deceased Mauwala Lal. The evidence therefore clearly shows that they were seen by all the appellants at the time the occurrence had took place. [613F] 9. The evidence thus clearly shows that there was no intention to kill Mauji Lal and that the appellants must have been seen by them in the verandah at the time and must have taken all reasonable steps to prevent the occurrence. It is not possible to accept the evidence of the witnesses that the appellants might have been seen at that time. [606E] 9. In the instant case, the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 clearly shows that when the occurrence took place, the appellants were found in the verandah, that the door was found open. There is nothing to show that they were found in any other place. [706E] 10. The evidence that the appellants saw the deceased Mauzi Lal and the deceased UPji Lal in their respective houses is corroborated by evidence of P,W. 2 and P.Ws 1, 7, 8 and 8. [607E] 11. The evidence cannot be relied upon for the purpose of proving the presence of the appellants at their respective houses. [608E] 12. The evidence which is corroborated by other evidence is corroborated from the evidence of PWs 1, 7 & 8. The presence of the witnesses at the time, and the place of occurrence, is corroborated by their evidence. [609F] 13. The evidence has been corroborated by the other evidence. The evidence corroborates the evidence of these witnesses. [610G] 14.

The appellant was a dealer in the business of selling scrap and unserviceable materials. The assessee was a dealer within the meaning of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The assessee, a dealer in scrap and unserviceal materials, was a dealer under the Bengal Finance Sales Tax Act, 1941, and the assessee was a "dealer" for the purposes of the Bengal Sales Tax Act. The assessee claimed that the goods were not liable to assessment under the Act. The Commercial Tax Officer, Commercial Taxes, West Bengal, by his order dated 17 June, 1960, held that the assessee was not a "dealer " for the purposes Of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941 and the Commercial Tax Officer was not a dealer within that Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, by his judgment dated 17 June 1960, set aside the order of the Commercial Tax officer and remanded the case to the Commercial Tax Tribunal for fresh disposal. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court of Calcutta challenging the order of remand. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of assessment. The assessee appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was in error in holding that the assessee is a dealer in scraps and unserviceable material lying with it. [901B] 2. The High 'Court was in error by holding that the activity of the assessee was incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the goods. [902C] 3. The High' Court was in error when it held that the activity was incidental or incidental to its business. [903D] 4. The High. Court was in wrong in holding that since the assessee was an "dealer" under the Bengal Sales tax Act, 1941 the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Bengal Act. [905E] 5. The High, Court was in a wrong position in holding that in the case of the assessee South Eastern Railway, the assessee was liable to be assessed under the Act and the Commercial Taxes Officer was not the dealer. [906F] 6. The assessee had not been able to show that the activity carried on by the assessee was ancillary or ancillary to the business of the assessee. [908F] 7. The assessee is a registered dealer under the Act, and the Commercial tax Officer was not competent to assess the assessee under the Act as a dealer. [0901F] 8. The assessee in the present case was a dealer and the Commercial TAX Officer was not an "dealer". The assessee was not an 'dealer" under section 2(c) of the Bengal Income Tax Act, 1942. [909F] 9. The assessee did not claim any exemption under the Bengal Act, and therefore the Commercial Tax Department was not entitled to assess the appellant under the Act on the ground that the activity did not amount to "business" within the meaning ofs. 2(c). [909G] 9. In the present case, the assessee had not claimed any exemption under section 56 of the Bengal Agricultural Income Tax Act. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, with effect from September 16, 1955. The appellant, a Company incorporated under the [Companies Act, 1956], was incorporated under a special Act, 1956. The appellant was a company incorporated in the year 1956, and the appellant was incorporated under that Act. The appellant had entered into a contract with the Union Agencies for the purchase of the securities. The appellant entered into a special contract with the Corporation of India, Bombay, on September 16, 1956, for the purchase and sale of the securities and for the sale of the same to Bharat Insurance Company Ltd., Bombay, on the terms and conditions set out in the contract. The appellant paid the amount to Bharat Insurance Co. Ltd., Bombay. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Delhi, for a declaration that the contract was a contract for the purchase, sale and delivery of the securities, and for the delivery of the same, to Bharat Insurance Companies Ltd., Bombay and for a declaration to that effect. The trial Court decreed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the contract had been entered into by the appellant with the Corporation and that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The appellant contended that the contract between the Corporation and Bharat Insurance Co., was a contract of the Corporation and, therefore, the contract was not a contract for sale and that the contract could not be enforced by the Corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract between the appellant and Bharat Insurance Company was a contract between the corporation and the Corporation. The contract was a works contract and the Corporation was not bound to make any payment to the Corporation. [701B] 2. The contract had been made by the Corporation and the Corporation had not made any payment to Bharat Insurance. The contract did not contain any stipulation that the Corporation would make payment to Bharat insurance. The contract, therefore, did not contain a stipulation that the appellant would make payment of the amount to the Corporation and deliver the same to the Corporation, and that the Corporation was bound to make payment to the appellant. [702C] 3. The contract in question was a works contracts and the Corporation could not make any payment in cash. The contract contained a stipulation that if the Corporation had made any payment in respect of the securities it would be open to the Corporation to make payment in cash to the Corporation without any further stipulation that the securities would be delivered to Bharat Insurance, and that if the securities were not delivered to Bharat insurance, the Corporation would be entitled to make payment of such securities. [703G] 4. The contract is a works contract. The contract contains a stipulation that unless the Corporation makes payment to the corporation, the Corporation shall make payment to it. The contract does not contain any condition that if the security is not delivered to the Corporation the Corporation would pay to the Corporation a sum of money to the Corporation in cash. [704G] 5. The contract also contains a stipulation in that behalf. The contract further contains a stipulation to the effect that if the amount is not paid to the Corporation within a period of six months from the date of the contract, the Corporation will pay to the appellant the amount to be paid to the appellant within a period not exceeding six months from that date. [705G] 6. The contract clearly shows that the Corporation had to make payment within a period specified in the contract and that the amount was to be paid within a period which was specified in the agreement. [706G] 7. The contract expressly shows that the appellant had to make the payment within a specified period. The contract specifically shows that the payment was to be made within a period set out in that clause. [707G] 8.

The appellants were appointed as the ministerial staff in the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were appointed as ministerial staff in various districts in the State of Saurashtra and Kutch. They were transferred to the Secretariat of Gujarat State. The appellants were appointed in the Secretariat and were posted in the Secretariat. The State of Gujarat was competent to transfer them to the Secretariat. On the basis of the provisions of section 115(7) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, the appellants were transferred to and were posted to the Secretariat in the State. The State Government, however, by a notification dated August 19, 1966, appointed the appellants as ministerial staff of the Secretariat of Saurashtra and Saurashtra States. The appellants challenged the validity of the order of transfer of the appellants to the Secretariat and the High Court held that the order of the Central Government was illegal and void. The appellants filed a petition in the High Court of Gujarat challenging the validity of that order. The High Court held, inter alia, that the order was illegal and invalid and that the appellants were entitled to the protection of section 115 (7) of that Act. The High court held that the appellants had no right to be absorbed in the Secretariat, and that the order did not amount to absorption in the Secretariat under the Absorption Rules. The High Courts held that the transfer of the respondents was illegal and that the respondents were entitled to be absorbed into the Secretariat. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the State Government dated August 19. 1966 was not illegal and void and the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of section 115 of the Bombay Reorganization Act. [701B] 2. The order dated August 19/January, 1966 was not valid and the appellants could not be absorbed in any other department of the State. [702C] 3. The order was not valid. The appellants could not claim any protection of section 116(7) as they were not absorbed in any department of the Government of Gujarat. [703D] 4. The order did not create any right in favour of the appellants. The appellants had no vested right to be considered for absorption in any other Department of the Government. [704E] 5. The order does not create any vested right in favour the appellants. [705G] 6. The order is not valid. [706G] 7. The order cannot be held to be invalid merely because the appellants were absorbed in the Department of the State in the Secretariat in which they were posted. [707A] 7. In the present case, the appellants had been appointed in the Department in the Secretariat as ministerial staff. They were not absorbed into the Department of Gujarat. The order merely created a legal right in favour them. [709G] 8. The order clearly shows that the appellants could be absorbed in some other department of Gujarat. It was not open to the appellants to challenge the authority of the Government to appoint them in the Secretariat to perform the duties of the ministerial staff. [708G] 9. The order also does not create a legal right to be absorption in any department or department of the government in which the appellants were posted. The order further shows that the Government had no right in favour to the appellants. It was open to the Government to adopt any other method of recruitment to the ministerial service of the Secretariat. [710G] 9 A. The order, therefore, cannot be held as invalid merely because it was not passed by the Government. The order must be held to have been passed by the State Government in exercise of the power under article 309 of the Constitution. [711G] 10. The order has been passed by way of an administrative order. The order itself shows that the State Government had no power to appoint the appellants in the Secretariat but it was open to it to adopt any one of the methods of recruitment to ministerial service of its Secretariat.

The appellant, who was the decree holder, filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the decree.
