Court held that the compromise decree holders were entitled to have their debts scaled down under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, 1938, and the decree holder 's application could not have been allowed to have the benefit of the decree holders under the Act, as he would have to refund to his vendor the entire amount due under decree. The High, Court, however, held that the amount payable under the decree was a part of the mortgage decree and the amount payable thereunder was a part and parcel of the mortgage. The High Cour t held that the suit was not maintainable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the compromise decrees were not binding on the parties and the High Court was wrong in holding that the compromise was not binding on them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise decrees are binding on the appellant and the decree debtors. [701B] 2. The compromise was binding on the respondents and the decree Holders. [704E] 5. The compromise in the present case was not binding upon the appellants and they were bound by it, and the compromise decree was binding on them, and the appellants were bound by the compromise decree. The Andhra Pradesh Act, which came into force on 2nd May 1972, was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature to provide for the ceiling area to the family unit in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted by a State Legislature to provide that the ceiling area shall be liable to be aggregated with the lands of other members of the family unit and by reason of section 4(1)(A) of the Andhra Pradesh Act the ceiling area would be liable tobe aggregated with lands of other member of the family. The Andhra State Legislature enacted the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Land (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, which came to be known as the Andhra Pradesh Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The Andhra Area (Ceiling on Land Holdings) Act was enacted to provide for ceiling on land situate in all the other areas of the State of the State. The Andhra Land (Ceiling) Act, 1956, was enacted to regulate the ceiling on land situated in all the areas of the States of Andhra Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh. Section 4(1) of the Act provided that the ceiling on the land situated in any other area of the State shall be liable for acquisition of the ceiling area. Section 4 of the Act empowered the State Government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. Section 4 provided that the State Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act and for carrying out those provisions. Section 4 empowered the State to make rules to carry out the purposes and for carrying into effect the provisions of that Act. Section 5 provided that the provisions of this Act shall not apply to any land situated in the State. Section 6 provided that the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for regulating the ceiling on any land situated within the urban agglomeration of the State and for carrying on the provisions of any other law for the time being in force. Section 7 provided that the rules made under the Act shall be published in the Official gazette and on such publication shall be conclusive evidence that the land is required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Section 8 provided that the land shall be deemed to be the ceiling area for the purposes of this Act. Section 9 provided that the extent of land held by a person in excess of the ceiling limit shall be determined by the State Government in the manner provided in section 9. Section 10 provided that the total extent of land acquired by a person shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of section 9. The State Government, however, made rules for the determination of the ceiling on such land. Section 11 provided that the maximum ceiling area for a person shall not be less than one lakh and the ceiling area so determined shall be deemed for the purposes for which it is acquired. Section 12 provided that the excess land shall be taken into account for the purpose to which it was so acquired. Section 13 provided that the surplus land shall be used for the purpose specified in section 9 and the excess land so taken shall be deemed as if it was acquired under section 3(f) of the Central Act. Section 14 provided that the amount of compensation payable to a person for the acquisition of the land shall not be more than one lakh. Section 15 provided that the compensation payable to the person for the land acquired shall be determined on the basis of the principles laid down in section 9(1) and (2) of the Land Acquisition Act. Section 15(1) provided that the market value of the land acquired for the purpose shall be determined under the provisions of sections 9 and 10. Section 15A provided that the value of the excess land acquired shall not be greater than one lakh but the ceiling area determined under section 3 (f) shall be liable only to be aggregised with the lands so acquired.

The development was not in accord with the development planning plan prepared by a local authority under the Act and that it was not in conflict with the development scheme. [820H] 7. The development is not in accord With the development plan but in accord with section 17. The development has to be done in accordance with sections 4 to 16 of the Act which are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder. [820A] 8. The development in accordance with law is not in conflict therewith. [823E] 9. The development can be done in the manner provided in section 17 of that Act. [823G] 9. In the instant case, the development was not done in accordance therewith and the development was in accordance with a proper planning plan. [823F] 10. The development could not be done in a manner which is not in accordance With the development plans.

The appellant, who was the mortgagee in possession of the mortgaged property, filed a suit on July 12, 1946, for recovery of the mortgage money. The trial Judge decreed the suit on July 13, 1946, and the appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the mortgage money was not barred by the law of limitation and that the suit was barred by the Law of limitation. The High court held that the suit filed on July 12 was barred by limitation. The appellant filed a second appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that in view of the provisions of section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act, the suit was not barred. The High Courts held that the appellant was entitled to recover the mortgage money under section 68 of that Act. The appellant then filed a second suit on July 14, 1946, in the Court of the Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad, for recovery the mortgage money and the suit was filed on July 13. 1946, within the period of limitation. On July 14, 1947, the appellant filed a suit for recovery of mortgage money. On July 12, 1947, he filed a suit in the Court for recovery of a mortgage money. In the suit, the appellant contended that the mortgage was not barred under the law of Limitation. The trial Court held that there was no bar of limitation for the suit to recover the money. The HighCourt held that the mortgaged property was not barred from the date when the mortgage money is payable. The appellant contended that there was a mortgage in the year 1937, and that the mortgage amount was not barred in view of section 68(1) (b) of the Transfer Act. The High 'Court held that there could be a mortgage in respect of the mortgaged properties and that the appellant could not enforce the mortgage in respect thereof. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the mortgage in question was not barred because the mortgage was created on the mortgagor 's interest in Mauza Bansjora, and that there was nothing in the mortgage deed to enforce the mortgage. [601B] The mortgage was not a mortgage in favour of the mortgagee. The mortgage was a mortgage by conditional sale. The mortgage deed was not a conditional sale. [602C] The mortgage deed did not create a mortgage in terms of the mortgage. The mortgage did not create any mortgage in favour. The mortgage in question did not create an interest in the mortgaged property. The mortgage created by the mortgagor was a mortgage. The mortgagor was not entitled to recover any mortgage money from the mortgagee. [603D] The mortgage in the present case was not a simple mortgage. The mortgagee was not entitled under the law to recover the amount. [604E] The mortgage money was a mortgage and the mortgagor was not bound to enforce the claim to recover the same. [605G] The mortgage had been created by the mortgagee in favour of his heirs and the mortgagor had parted with his interest in the property. [607F] The mortgage created in favour of a mortgagee was a mortgage of the mortgaged land. The mortgage had not been created by a mortgagee in favour. [609F] The mortgagee was entitled to enforce the mortgaged property against the mortgagor. [608F] The mortgagor was entitled to redeem the mortgage money in accordance with the provisions of the mortgage deed. [610F] The mortgaged property was a mortgage which was not a security. [611F] The suit was not maintainable. [612G] The suit for recovery was not maintainable because the mortgage money had not been recovered by the mortgagee. It was not a suit for redemption. [613F] The appellant was not entitled for the relief claimed in the suit. [615G] The appellant had not claimed any relief in the suit for recovery. [616F] The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit.

The appellants were engaged in the business of transport of passengers. They were registered as a transport vehicle under the provisions of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The appellants were registered as transport vehicles under the provisions thereof. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not a public service vehicle within the meaning of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act did not provide for the levy of a tax on passengers carried by a stage carriage. The High court held that the Act does not provide for a tax on the passengers carried by stage carriage. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Act is a general law and the tax is not a tax on goods carried by a public service vehicles. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Act does not create any difficulty in the way of the appellants being able to pay the tax on passengers carrying by stage carriage, and therefore, the tax is a public service tax. [982 C] 2. The Act is a special Act and the tax on the passenger carried by stage carriages is a public tax. The Act provides for a tax at the rate of Rs. 2 per month. The Act also provides for a special status, namely, the transport facilities provided to the employees by the company. [983 D] 3. The Act, therefore, does not provide any difficulty in giving transport facilities to the employees of the company. The Act cannot be said to be a general law. [984 E] 4. The Act has been enacted to provide for the imposition of a tax at a rate of Rs 2 per month on all passengers carried by road, and for the transport facilities to be provided to the staff of the company, and for providing transport facilities to them. [994 G] 5. The Act makes a special provision for the levy and payment of a tax. The rate of tax is not fixed by the Act. [995 C] 6. The Act gives a special status to the employees and it does not provide that the transport facilities should carry the passengers by road, or that the employees of a private company who are given facilities as not members of the public, but as a holding a special status. [996 D] 7. The Act further provides for a levy and payment to the State Government a tax on all passengers carrying by road, but not on passengers carried on a public service. [997 E] 8. The Act clearly provides for a general law, and the tax must be levied on all passengers, whether carried by road or not, and whether carried by a private service vehicle. [998 D] 9. The Act nowhere provides for a rate of tax on passengers, whether carrying by road or otherwise, and does not provide a rate of a tax for passengers carried by public service vehicles, and therefore the tax is leviable only on passengers carried in stage carriages. [999 E] 9. In the instant case, the appellants were not carrying any passengers on a public services vehicle. They were not carrying passengers on a private service vehicles. They were carrying passengers on the public service vehicles and therefore the provisions of section 3 of the Act were not attracted. [901 D] 901 E] 901 F] 901 G] 901 A.I.R. 1962 Bom. 901 A, referred to. 901 C] 901 D] 1001 E] 1001 F] 1001 A.2. The Act was enacted to provide a special status for the transport of passengers carried by the public service vehicle. The Act provided for a special type of transport facilities to employees of the public service. The Act did not make any special provision for a special kind of transport facilities provided for the employees of public service vehicles to the employees. [902 D] 902 A.2 A.2 B] 901 C.

The appellants, who were the local residents, applied for a licence for a cinema house in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The licensing authority refused to grant a "no objection certificate" to the appellants. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh challenging the grant of a "no objections certificate" to them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The grant of a cinema licence is a matter of policy and is not a matter of right. [601B] 2. The grant or refusal of a cinema license is a matter for the licensing authority to refuse a cinema licence. The grant is not a question of policy. The grant, however, is a matter which is not a policy. [602C] 3. The grant was not a policy but a policy. The licence was granted to a person who had objected to the grant of the cinema licence. [603D] 4. The grant had been refused by the licensing authority and the order granting the licence was passed on the same grounds. [604E] 5. The grant in question was not a "no" certificate. The grant did not amount to a "no Objection" certificate. [605G] 6. The grant made in favour of the appellants was not a 'no objection certificate'. [605F] 7. The grant by the licensing authorities was not a matter for which the appellants could not have been permitted to challenge the grant of an "no objection" certificate. It was not a question which was not a part of the policy. [06F] 8. The grant to a person is a matter not of policy. [613G] 9. The grant does not amount to an "no" licence. [613H] 9. In the present case, the grant was not in respect of a cinema house. The grant could not be said to be a policy. It was a matter of fact. [607F] 10. The grant cannot be said to have been made in violation of the principles of natural justice. [609F] 11. The grant itself was not a licence. The licence had been granted to a cinema house and the grant was in respect of the same grounds which the appellants had objected to. [608F] 12. The grant being a policy, the grant of no objection certificate is not a "No" certificate. In the absence of a valid objection certificate, the grant cannot be held to be a "no".

The appellant, who was the lessee of the mining lease, filed a suit for specific performance of the contract on the ground that the respondent had agreed to assign the mining lease to the appellant. The respondent filed a suit in the Court of the Civil Judge, Junior Division, Bangalore for specific performance. The trial court decreed the suit. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the contract was concluded by an oral application for shares and the acceptance of the offer was communicated to the appellant and that as the respondent did not accept the offer, the appellant was not entitled to remain in possession of the mining area. The High court held that the respondent was not entitled for the relief claimed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that the contract between the parties was concluded by a written communication of the acceptance of an offer by the respondent and that as there was no concluded contract, the respondent was entitled to remain the in possession of mining area. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The contract between the appellant and the respondent was concluded by the communication of the offer by the appellant to the respondent. The respondent was not bound to accept the offer. [782B] 2. The contract was concluded on September 2, 1957 and the respondent had not applied for and obtained the consent of the Central Government to assign the lease to the respondent and the acceptance was communicated to him. [783C] 3. The respondent had not complied with the terms of the contract. The respondent could not be compelled to accept the offers. The contract, therefore, could not be unilaterally terminated by the respondent. [785D] 4. The respondent did not make any offer to the appellant before the expiry of the period of the contract and the acceptance by the Central Government was communicated to it. [786E] 5. The respondent, in the present case, had not complied therewith. The respondent cannot be compelled to take the offer. The respondent has not made any offer to it. The respondent is not entitled to continue in possession of any mining lease. [787G] 6. The respondent's offer was not accepted by the Central government. The respondent having accepted the offer, he cannot be compelled by the respondent to accept the same. [794G] 7. The respondent can not be compelled by his own conduct to accept the highest offer. [894G] 8. The respondent must be deemed to have accepted the offer. He cannot be compelled either by the respondent or by the appellant in the present suit to accept the bid. [795G] 9. The respondent 's case is that the appellant had not accepted the offer and the acceptance thereof was communicated to her. [796G] 9,10A] 10. The respondent failed to make any offer before the expiry date of the lease. The respondent made an offer to the appellants. The respondent accepted the offer after the expiry date. The respondent also failed to make an offer to her. The respondent therefore, cannot be compelled from the offer. It is not possible to say that the respondent did make an offer before the expiration date. [798G] 10. In the present case the respondent had accepted the offer before the commencement of the contract, and the acceptance had been communicated to her before the expiry. [799G] 10A] 11. The respondent should have made an offer before November 1, 1957. The respondent would have made an application for and obtain the consent of November 1,1957. The respondent may have made an oral application to the appellant for and obtain a consent of November 2, 1957. [797G] 12. The respondent does not have any right to file a suit for the specific performance of contract. The suit for specific Performance of the contract is not a suit for a specific performance of a contract. [793G] 13.

The appellant was a sugar factory manufacturing sugar. He was manufacturing sugar at the relevant time. He was also manufacturing sugar at a factory at a factory. The appellant was manufacturing sugar in the year 1965. He was selling sugarcane at a factory in the year 1966. The appellant purchased sugarcane at a price of Rs. 1,000/- per quintal. The appellant sold sugarcane at a higher price. The appellant filed a complaint before the police alleging that he had purchased sugarcane at the factory at a price higher than the price of sugarcane purchased by him. The police registered a case under section 7 of the Act and the appellant was prosecuted for the offence under section 7(1)(f) of the Act. The appellant contended that the complaint was not maintainable because the complaint was filed after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by section 3(2)(b) of the Central Act. The High Court held that the complaint did not disclose a Cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of the complaint. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 3(1)(b) and the complaint was liable to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The complaint was not competent. The power conferred on the Government under section 3(3) of the Bihar Act is a part of the legislative power of the State and the same is a part and parcel of the field of legislation. [701B] 2. The power of the Government under the Act is a legislative power and the same cannot be exercised by the State Legislature. The power to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs is a part, of the Act, and as such it is a part. [702C] 3. The power under section 3 (3) of Act is a power to legislate on the same subject matter. The power is a legislative function and the same can be exercised by a State Legislature. [703D] 4. The power given to the State Legislature under section 3 of the Act is not a legislative power. The power can be exercised only by the State Government and not by the State. [704E] 5. The power cannot be exercised in respect of the production, supply, distribution and supply of foodstuffs. The power has to be exercised by an authority subordinate to the State Government. [705E] 6. The power, therefore, cannot be exercised on the basis of the complaint made before the police. [706E] 7. The power which is conferred on the State Government under section 2(3) is a legislative one and it is a legislative authority. The power must be exercised by that authority in accordance with the provisions of the Act which are in force at the time when the Act was enacted. [707F] 7. In the instant case, the power conferred on it under section 3 is a legislative and not a legislative one. The power exercised by the Government under Section 3(3)(b) is a power which is a legislative body and not a part of agriculture. [708F] 8. The power in respect of sale and purchase of sugarcane is a legislative head of the State. The power does not include the power to regulate the sale and purchase. The power thus conferred on the Central Government is a legislative field and the same has to be construed as a legislative power in respect to the sale and the purchase of sugarcane. [709G] 9. The power so conferred on the Parliament under section 3 cannot be exercised to regulate the purchase of the sugarcane by the State legislature. [710G] 9 A. The power that is conferred on Parliament under section 2 (3) is not a part and it is not a matter of legislative power. [711G] 9A.

The appellant was a manufacturer of sugar and was manufacturing sugar. The appellant was a dealer in sugar. The State Government issued a notification under Section 8A of the Act on 30th June, 1969, which was published on 30th September, 1969. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Karnataka challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court held that the doctrine of promissory estoppel could not be regarded as good law in view of the subsequent decision of this Court in Usha Martin Industries Ltd. (supra). The High Court held that the principle of promissory estoppel was not applicable in the present case. The appellant contended that the doctrine was not applicable to the facts of the present case because the appellant had not filed a writ application in this Court and that the doctrine could not be treated as good law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory estoppels cannot be regarded as a good law in the present context. [801B] 2. The doctrine is not a good law. It is a rule of law and not a rule of practice. It is an authority for the proposition that a person who has been granted a certificate under the provisions of the Act, must be held to be entitled to the benefit of the same. [802C] 3. The doctrine cannot be regarded to be a good law because the conditions of the grant of a certificate are not prescribed in the Order. [803D] 4. The doctrine has no application to the facts in this case. [804E] 5. The appellant had not produced any material to show that the grant of the certificate was in the nature of a concession. The appellant could not be said to be a dealer in the manufacture of sugar. [805F] 6. The appellant, therefore, could not be granted the benefit of a concession under the order dated 30th June 1969. [806F] 7. The appellant is entitled to the refund of sales tax paid by a new industrial unit on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production. [807F] 8. The appellant has not produced any evidence to show that any concession was given by the earlier order dated 30 th June, 1969. [820A] 9. The appellant cannot be said to have any right to the refund. [808F] 9. In the circumstances, the appellant is entitled for the refund of the sales tax paid on raw materials. [809F] 10. The appellant should be granted the refund of tax paid on all sales tax paid in the year 1969.

The appellants were charged for offences under Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. and Section 302 read with section 149 I. P.C. The trial court convicted the appellants under Section 148 I.P..P.C., and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court, however, acquitted the appellants of all the charges. The High court, however, convicted the appellants of the offences under Sections 147 and 302 read. The High Cou rt, however, found that the appellants had not committed any offence under Section 302 read. In appeal, the High Court, on a consideration of the evidence, found that there was no evidence to show that the appellants were guilty of the offences charged. The High C ourt, however, held that the appellants could not be convicted under Section 302 I.P, I.P., and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the appellants did not commit any offence under Sections 147, 148 and 302 I. P, I. P., and that the High C o f Sessions Judge had erred in convicting the appellants under Sections 148, 302 and 149 I. PC. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in convicting the accused under Section 148 and 302, I. PC, and sentencing them to imprisonment. [701B] 2. The High c ourt had erred in upholding the conviction of the appellants under [Section 302] read with Section 34 I.P.; and sentenced them as aforesaid. [702C] 3. The High t rial Court had erred by holding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants assaulted the deceased with the spear and the injuries on the person of the deceased were caused by the appellants. [703D] 4. The High rict Court had erred on the basis that the appellants, who were the aggressors, had not committed the offence under Section 148, I.PC. [704E] 5. The High f ile Court had erred, in holding that there was a long standing enmity between the parties. The High n ourt had also erred in holding the appellants guilty under Section 302, I PC. [705E] 6. The High l e Court had erred while holding that the accused had not committed an offence under Section 149 I PC. The High m e Court had also erred, in upholding the convictions of the appellants. The High j udgment of the High Court was, therefore, set aside. [706E] 7. The High R e Court had found that the prosecution has failed to prove the offence under Sections 148 I. P; and the appellants were convicted under Section 148 read with Section 302 read, I.p. PC. [806E] 8. The High al Court had also found that the accused were guilty under Section 148 IPC. The High Al lice Court had also held that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [707E] 9. The High, Court, however had found that there were no eye witnesses to the occurrence. The High e Court had further found that the eye witnesses to t he occurrence were the persons who had assaulted the deceased and the injuries were caused by them. The High Crl. A. No. 469 of 1981 Court had also acquitted the appellants under s. 302 read with s. 34 I. P.; and the High Court convicted them under Section 148 of the I. P.. The State of Assam has preferred this appeal. 10. The High Criminal Appeal No. 469/1981 was filed by the State of Assam against the acquittal of the appellants by the High Court. The High Co urt has convicted the appellants for the offences under Section 148.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had entered into a partnership with the Indian National Bank, a registered firm, and had obtained a loan from the Indian National bank. The assessee had obtained a certificate from the Income Tax Officer, and had also obtained a certificate of registration from the Income tax Officer. The Income Tax Officer had issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, to the assessee, and had asked him to show cause why the certificate should not be cancelled. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, and the Appellate Assistant commissioner, after hearing the assessee, confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal, after hearing both the parties, held that the certificate of registration was not valid and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 147 of the Income TAX Act, 1961. The Tribunal held that the assessee had not produced any evidence to show that the certificate was not genuine and that the certificate had been issued in the name of the assessee. The Tribunal further held that the income of the assessee was not taxable under the provisions of the IncomeTax Act, 1961 and that the income was not taxable. The Tribunal also held that the Income Tax Department had not produced the certificate of Registration and that the Income tax Department had not furnished the certificate of the Incometax Officer. The Tribunal accordingly held that the certificates of registration were not genuine and the assessee was liable to pay tax under the provisions. The Tribunal observed that the assessee did not produce the certificate ofregistration and that the Department had not been able to prove that the certificate issued by the Income tax Office was genuine. The Tribunal therefore held that the Department was entitled to take the fair market value of the capital asset as on the date of the transfer. The Tribunal however held that the transfer was not genuine. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Tribunal. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the transfer of the capital assets was not genuine, but was only a device to avoid the tax liability. The Tribunal was of the view that the transfer did not amount to a gift and that the transfer amounted to a gift. The Tribunal did not accept the contention of the assessee that the transfer had not accrued to the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the transfer could not be regarded as a gift. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The transfer of the assets was not a gift. [601B] 2. The transfer was not a sale. The transfer did not result in any amount being taxed. The transfer could not amount to gift. [701C] 3. The transfer had not taken place in the course of the business. The transfer, therefore, was not a transfer of the asset. [702D] 4. The transfer is not a sale but a transfer of a capital asset. The transfer does not amount to sale. [703E] 5. The transfer cannot be regarded as an amount received by the assessee or in other words, the transfer is not an amount received in respect of the consideration in respect of transfer. [704F] 6. The transfer can not be regarded to be an amount received as a gift and the transfer can not amount to an amount received for the transfer. [605G] 7. The transfer may not amount to the transfer of a part of the capital account. The transfer must be regarded as one of the transfer of an asset. [606G] 7A. The transfer would not amount to transfer of an amount received or to the transfer. It is only a device for avoiding the tax liability and not a transfer. [805G] 8. The transfer has to be regarded as the transfer of capital asset. [806G] 9. The transfer should be regarded as transfer of an income. [807A] 10.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence under Section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. He was convicted by the trial Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months. He was also convicted for the offence of having kept adulterated food for sale. He was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for two years. He was further convicted for the offences under Section 7 (i) of Prevention of Food Act, 1954 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was also convicted under Section 7 of the Prevention Of Food Adulteration Act. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and the sentence. The appellant has come up in this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the evidence of the Food Inspector was not reliable and that the appellant was guilty of the offence under section 7(i). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was in error. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not reliable. The evidence was not reliable because the Food Inspector had not stated that the appellant had kept adulterated food in his shop. He had not stated in his evidence that the appellant kept adulterated food. [701C] 2. The Food Inspector had clearly stated in his statement that the appellant did not keep adulterated food in the shop. He was not a person who had kept adulterated article for sale. The Food inspector had clearly stated that the food was meant for human consumption. [702C] 3. The Food Inspectors had clearly stated the appellant 's version that the appellant sold the food to the Food Inspector. The Food Officer had clearly stated, in his evidence, that the appellant used the food for human consumption and not for human consumption, and that the Food Inspector did not state that the appellant intended to keep adulterated food for human use. [703C] 4. The Food Controller had clearly stated "that the appellant had sold the food for consumption". The Food Inspector did state that the food for the purpose of being sold for human consumption was meant for a special use. [603D] 5. The Food Analyst had clearly stated: (i) that the appellant purchased the food for commercial purpose. (ii) that the food in question was meant for commercial purpose and not for any other purpose. [704E] (iii) that the Food inspector had not stated the appellant to be a person who sold the food in a shop. [705E] (iv) that the sample was not sent for analysis to the Food Analyst. [706E] (v) that the report of the Food Analyst was not supported by any evidence. [707E] (vi) that the High court was not right in holding that there was no evidence to prove that the food sold for human use was meant for any other purposes. [709G] 6. The Food Adulteration Act does not provide for any other matter. The Food Act does not prescribe any other matter for which the Food Inspector can be prosecuted. [708E] 7. The Food Rules do not prescribe any particular matter for which a Food Inspector can prosecute. [710E] 8. The Food Commissioner had clearly stated 'that the food for sale of food for human purposes is meant for human use and not for a special purpose. [809G] 9. The Food Authority had clearly stated so in his evidence. The Food Court had clearly stated as under: (i). The Food Inspector has clearly stated that he had written on the cash memo that the appellant has told him that he had told him that the food is meant for a Special purpose. [908E] (ii). The Food Authority has clearly stated in the evidence that the food which was meant for the special purpose was meant for public use and not meant for human food. [909G] (iii).

The appellant, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh, was dismissed from service by an order dated 13th of January, 1966. He filed a second appeal before the High Court against the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the second appeal on the ground that the order of the State Government was not an order of dismissal but was an order of punishment and, therefore, the order of reinstatement was not an effective order. The appellant filed a second special leave petition before this Court. The High court dismissed the appeal on the view that the order passed by the State Government on the ground of limitation was not an operative order and, therefore the appeal was not maintainable. The appellant then filed a second writ petition before this court. The High 'Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground, inter alia, that the order dismissing the appeal was an effective order and, as such, the appeal was maintainable. The High' Court held that the order was an effective one and, therefore it was not an appealable order. The High. Court held that since the order of termination was an effective and operative order, the appeal could not be entertained. The appellant, therefore, filed a second civil appeal before this Court which was dismissed on the ground 's maintainability. The appellant thereafter filed a second revision before the High court which was dismissed. The appellant has now come up to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court dismissing the revision petition is an effective order, and, therefore. the appeal was competent. [701B] 2. The High Courts have not committed any error in holding that the order dated 13 th of January,1966 was an effective, and operative order. [702C] 3. The High, Court, in the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 226 of the Constitution, could not exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the constitution. [703D] 4. The High Curt had no jurisdiction to entertain the second revision. [704E] 5. The High] Court had no jurisdiction under article 227 of the Constitution to entertain the revision. [77F] 6. The High [704F] 7. The High Commissioner, in the present case, was not competent to entertain the first revision. [76G] 7. In the present case the order of removal was passed on 13th of Jan, 1966. The order was passed on 31st August, 1966. Therefore, the order passed in the second revision was an effective. [705G] 8. The order passed in appeal was an order passed in exercise of the jurisdiction under article 136 of the Constitution. [706G] 9. The order in appeal was passed on 30th August, 1966 and the order in appeal had ceased to be operative on the expiry of six months from the date of the original order. [77G] 9,10A] 10. The order dated 31st August 1966 was an effective interim order and, thus, the order in the second appeal was an operative order. The order had ceased to exist on the expiry thereof. [707B] 10. In the instant case, the order dated 31 st August, 1966 was an operative one and, thus the order in revision was an operative on the date when the second revision came into force. [709G] 10. It is true that the order in question was an operative and operative order and the appeal was pending at the commencement of the Constitution and the order was not an interim order. But the order in this case was an operative interim order and the order had ceased. [710G] 11. The order did not cease to be operative because the order in that case was an interim order and it was an operative. [711G] 12. The order could not be said to be an operative one. [712G] 13.

The appellant who was the decree holder of a decree for affirmance of the decree passed by the trial court, filed a suit for recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/. The appellant contended that the decree was a decree for the amount of interest and the High Court was in error in holding that the variation was made in regard to the amount of costs. The High Court held that the variation in the decree was not a part of the decree and the variation was not a decree. The High court held that the decree of affirmance was a decree of affirmances and the variation in respect of the decree was of affirmance and the variation made in regard thereto was not a substantial variation in the decision of the trial court. The High. Court held that there was a variation in the judgment of the trial Court and the variation of the decree in regard to interest was not a variation in regard to it. The High 'Court held that the modification in regard to costs was not a modification in regard thereto and that the variation made was not a condition of the decree. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that a variation in respect to the decree was made in the decision or the decree which is a part of a dispute between the parties. [601B] (2) The High ' Court was right, in holding that there was no variation in the decisions of the trial courts. [602C] (3) The High court was right in not holding that the modification was made in respect of costs. [603D] (4) The High' Court was right when it made the variation in regard thereto.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act. The appellant, a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1959. The appellant filed a petition under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, for the revision of the order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, against the revisional orders of the District Judge under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Court Act, 1950, which were pending before the District Court. The appellant contended that the revisional order of the High Court under section 115 of the Code, was not maintainable because the revisional order under section 25 was not a decree passed by the District Court and the revisional order was not a judgment passed by the High Court. The High Court rejected the revision petition under section 25 and dismissed the revision petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contends that the revisional orders passed by the courts below under section 25 are not appealable under section 115. The High court has not given any reasons for rejecting the revision petition filed by the appellant. The High Courts have not given any reason for rejecting the petition under section 50, Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Curt has not given reasons for rejecting it. The High, Court has not given sufficient reasons for rejecting a revision petition under [section 115, Code, of Civil Procedure]. The High Court has not applied its mind to the question whether the revisional order passed under section 25 is a decree passed under section 115 or section 115, as amended by the Amendment Act, 1976. The High. Court has not exercised the revisional power under section 25. The High 'Court has not given a reason for rejecting a petition under [Section 115, Code], of Civil Procedure. The revisional order of a District Court under Section 25, Provincialised Small Cause Courts, is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High court under section 115 and the revisional orders under section 25 were not maintainable. The High [Court] has not given the reasons for rejecting an application under section 25 for consideration as a revision petition. No. 2844 of 1979) that the revisional power of the District Courts under section 25 would vest in the High Court, was not a case of revision under section 115 C, Code of civil Procedure. The revision petitions filed by the company were not maintainable against the revisional order. The High Power Court has not granted any reasons for rejection of the revision petition Under section 25, Code of the Civil Procedure. No. 9752 of 1979) was, therefore, competent to entertain the revision petitions under section 115 against the revisional authority under section 25 or section 115.

The respondents were owners of the land in question. The State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Act for acquisition of the notified land for the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur. The respondents challenged the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52 (1) of Rajasthan Act. The State of Rajasthan filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification issued under section 52 of the Act was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the notification issued thereunder. The State filed a special leave petition against the judgment of the High Court. The High court dismissed the special leave petition holding that since the notification issued in the year 1984 under section 52 was not in conformity with the provisions contained in section 52(2) of the Rajasthan Act, the respondents were not entitled to challenge the validity of notification issued by State Government under sections 52(1), 52(2), 52(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification issued by Government under section 53(1) is not in conformity to the provisions of section 52(l) of the Land Acquisition Act. [605B] 2. The notification under section 53 (1) is in conformity with section 52(3) of the said Act. [705C] 3. The notification is in conformity to section 52(4) of the State Act. [805D] 4. The notification dated February 8, 1984 under section 53 of the Act is in conformity only with the provisions relating to acquisition of the land under section 52. [606E] 5. The notification in question is in conformity of section 52 (2) of Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [607F] 6. The notification was issued under section 53 and the State Government issued the same under section 52, which is in conformity therewith. [608F] 7. The notification has been issued under section 54 of the Act. The notification does not disclose the purpose of the acquisition of the lands under section 52 and the State has not been able to show that the purpose of acquisition of the said lands was not bona fide. [609G] 7. In the instant case, the notification issued on February 8,1984 under section 52 is in conformity and the State is not able to show the purpose of acquiring the lands under sections 52 (1), 52 (2), 52 (1). [609F] 8. The notification itself discloses the purpose of taking possession of the lands. The State has not filed any appeal against the order of the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 52 or the Act. [613G] 9. The notification merely discloses the purpose for taking possession of lands under section 53. The State is not entitled to file any appeal against such order. [610F] 9. In the present case, the State Government has not filed appeal against the notification issued for acquisition of notified land under section 53, nor has filed any appeal challenging the validity of such notification issued by it under section 52.(1) or the State Government of Rajasthan under section 52 has filed any petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the Rajasthan High Court at Jaipur Bench. [611G] 10. The notification of the State Government dated February 8 1984 under section 54(1) or section 52(i) of the Jaipur Bench of the Rajasthan High court, Jaipur Bench, is quashed and set aside. The respondents are directed to file a petition under article 227 of the Constitution in the High court at Jaipur Bench, within a period of two weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of this judgment.

The appellant was assessed to house tax under the old Rent Act on the basis of the assessment of the house tax and water tax. The appellant filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the building was constructed in 1968 and the building was not completed on the date of the suit and, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of s.39 of the new Rent Act. The appellant contended that the building had not become ten years old on the date when the revision came to be decided by the High Court and, therefore the appellant was entitled to the protection of the new Act. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the decree for eviction on that ground. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the building in question was not a new building and, therefore it was not a building within the meaning of the new rent Act. [801B] 2. The High Courts were right in holding, that the building which was constructed in the year 1968 was not a newly constructed building and, consequently, the appellant could not get the benefit of the new lease. [802C] 3. The High 'Court was right in setting aside the decree of the trial court and remanding the case to the trial court. [803D] 4. The High' Court was right in reversing the decree of eviction on the basis that the building is deemed to have been completed on the first day of the assessment year 1971. [804E] 5. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was no change in the cause of action and, therefore there was no question of giving the benefit of section 39 of the newRent Act. [820E] 6. The High, Court was right when it held that the building could not be deemed to have become ten years of old on the first date of the assessment. [805E] 7. The High was right in the view that the building having been constructed in 1968, the appellant would be entitled to the benefits of the new [805F] 8. The High [805G] 9. The High] Court was right that the building being constructed in 1968 the appellant would not be entitled to any protection of the old Rent Acts. [806F] 9. In the present case, the building was admittedly constructed in 1968. The building was constructed on the date on which the assessment was made. The building had been constructed in the years 1968 and the appellant had been assessed to house taxes on the date immediately after the assessment. The building having been completed on 1st October, 1971, the appellant had become ten years ' old on the day when the revision was decided by the Additional District Judge. [807F] 9,10A] 10. The High Curt was right in taking the view that there was a change in the date of assessment and, therefore no protection of the New Rent Act could be given to the appellant. [808F] 10. In the instant case, the appellant has not been able to show that the building has been constructed in 1967. The High Commissioner was right in not taking the view in the absence of any report, record or assessment. [820G] 11. The High Commission was right in rejecting the appellant's contention that the building did not become ten year old on the basis on which the first assessment was made and, therefore. the appellant was disentitled to the benefit under section 39 of that Act. [823G] 12. The High Powered Committee was right in accepting the appellant's case that the building constructed in 1968 was not ten years old and, therefore was exempted from the operation of the new Municipal Rent Act. [825G] 13.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1956. The appellant was incorporated under section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Ranchi, for a declaration that the agreement dated February 6, 1948, was null and void and that the arbitration agreement was null and invalid. The appellant contended that the arbitration clause in the agreement was not a part of the original agreement and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to make the award. The Subordinate Judge, however, dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the arbitration was not a valid arbitration agreement and that it was not a contract relating to the execution of the agreement. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The arbitration agreement was not an instrument relating to the arbitration agreement. The arbitration clause in that agreement was not in force at the relevant date. The arbitration was not an arbitration agreement. [601B] 2. The arbitration proceedings were not a valid agreement. The agreement was not one relating to the original agreement. The arbitrator had no power to make the original agreement, and the arbitration agreement could not be said to be an instrument relating only to the execution. [602C] 3. The arbitration could not be held to be an agreement relating to the executing of the contract. The arbitration had no jurisdiction. [603D] 4. The arbitration did not amount to an instrument relating merely to the execution, and that the agreement was an instrument relating thereto. [604E] 5. The arbitration is not a valid contract relating to execution of the contract, and the arbitrator had jurisdiction to make an award. [605G] 6. The arbitration cannot be held to have been completed by the time the original agreement was executed. The arbitration does not amount to a valid arbitration. The arbitration can only be held to fall within the entry 12, in which case the arbitration agreement would be valid. [606E] 7. The arbitration has no jurisdiction to execute the agreement. [06E] 8. The arbitration in the present case was not a proper arbitration agreement. It was not a document relating to the contract. It was a document relating only to execution of a works contract. The agreement did not amount merely to a valid reference to arbitration. [607E] 9. The arbitration being a valid arbitration, the arbitration agreement cannot be held as a valid arbitration clause. [608E] 10. The arbitration having been completed by a valid arbitration and the arbitration having been made in accordance with the provisions of section 35 of Stamp Act, the arbitration was a valid arbitration within the meaning of section 35. [609G] 11. The arbitration, therefore, was not a "arbitration agreement" within the meaning ofs. 35 of the Stamp Act. [610E] 12. The arbitration proceeding was not a 'arbitration agreement' within the meaning Of section 35 of Indian Stamp Act. The arbitration itself was not a formal arbitration agreement. Therefore, the arbitration proceedings were a valid arbitration under the Indian Stamp Law. [611E] 13. The arbitration Act does not provide for the levy of any penalty on an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document. The arbitration under the Stamp Act is a valid arbitration in the sense that it does not provide any limitation on the power of the court to make an order for the enforcement of any right or liability.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was placed under suspension by the State Government on the ground that he was not given the benefit of the provisions of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules. The respondent was served with a charge sheet on the basis of which he was prosecuted and punished in the judicial proceedings. The respondent filed a criminal appeal in the High Court challenging the order of the State Government. The High Court allowed the appeal and quashed the First Information Report. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court. The High court set aside the order of acquittal and quashed the prosecution of Mangal Singh Minhas for the offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The State of Punjab preferred an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence. The High Judge allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this court, the High Court set aside the acquittal of Mangal Singh and directed the State Government to reconsider the case afresh. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts have committed a manifest error of law in taking the view that the respondent was not entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (b) of Rule 2, as for the benefit of a government servant, the conditions stated therein are satisfied. [928 A] 1.2. The High Curt has committed a manifest illegality in taking the contrary view. [929 B] 1.3. The High Powered Committee has not applied its mind to the question whether the respondent was entitled to exercise his right conferred on the government under the substantive provision of Rule 2 or not. The High power of the State is not to be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general prohibition against prosecution of a government employee for any offence committed by him. [930 C] 1.4. The High powers of the State are not to be construed as laying down a rule regulating the conditions of service of a government Servant. [931 D] 1.5. The power to frame a rule under Article 309 of the Constitution is not tobe interpreted as layingdown an absolute or a general prohibition against the prosecution of a Government servant for any offence which took more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High Court to be a rule regulating conditions of service. [932 E] 1.6. The power of the High Court under Article 309 is not to lay down a rule prohibiting the prosecution of any Government servant for an offence which took less than four years after such institution. [933 A] 1, 2.7. The power under Article 309 cannot be construed as to lay down an absolute prohibition against the institution of judicial proceedings for prosecution in respect of a cause of action which took more or four years after the institution of the departmental proceedings. [934 A] 1:1.8. The power conferred on the High Court by Article 309 of Constitution is not a rule regulating or prohibiting the prosecution for an offence committed by a government servant for any period which took more at four years after institution of the disciplinary proceedings. [ 934 A] 2.9. The power given to the High Court in the matter of quashing the prosecution of an employee for any period is not a part of the power conferred on it under Article 309. [935 B] 1:2.9.1.2.2.3.3.1.3.2.1.4.1.1.

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913, with effect from April 1, 1956. The respondent company was registered as a public limited company under the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1956. On April 28, 1956, the respondent company acquired and carried on the business of manufacture and sale of "paints" and "painting" shares of the company. The respondent Company acquired and carried the business of manufacturing and selling "paintons" and "Paints" of the company, and the respondent company was entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of the provisions of section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and prayed for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Income tax Officer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1922 were not applicable to the respondent company, and that the provisions were not applicable, because the respondent company had not acquired and carried out the business of sale and purchase of "pinner" and "participated" shares of that company. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, are not applicable to a company in which the public are substantially interested. [775B] 2. The provisions are not applicable in the case of a company in whose public are substantially interest. [776C] 3. The provisions do not apply to a company which is substantially interested. The provisions in the Companies Act do not apply in the case where the public are not substantially interested. It is only where the public have substantially interested. In the case of companies which are substantially interested, the question is one of fact to be determined in each case, whether it is a company in whom the public are interested. [77C] 4. The provisions relating to the holding of shares by the public are materially interested.

The appellant, a registered dealer, filed a suit against Dwarkadas Khetan & Company for recovery of the goods from the first appellant on the ground that the goods were delivered to him as the agent of the Mills. The trial court decreed the suit and the suit was decreed. The first appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. The first respondent appealed to this Court. The first question that arises for consideration is whether the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the suit was not barred by limitation, and the suit must be dismissed. The suit was not filed within the period of limitation. The suit must be held to be barred by limitation and the suit should be dismissed. In the present case, the suit was filed within the prescribed period of limitation and the first appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed. The suit should be held to have been filed within the time prescribed by the Act. The suit is barred by limitation as the first appellant had not filed the suit within the prescribed time. The suit could not be dismissed on the ground of limitation. [834 C] The suit was barred under the provisions of the Act. [835 D] The suit must fail. The suit had been filed within a period of six months from the date of the delivery of the goods. The suit, therefore, was not barred under the Act. It was open to the first appellant to take the plea that the suit had been barred by limitation in view of the provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act. [934 D] The High Court was right in holding that the suit must fail because the suit was within the period prescribed by the Limitation Act and the suit had not been filed within six months from that date. [935 E] The suit should have been filed beyond the period of six month from the date the delivery of goods was made. [937 E] The High court was right in not holding that the goods had been delivered to the Mills. [938 E] The goods had been sent to Dharsi Moolji for delivery in the same truck as the goods had passed. The suit filed by Dwarkadas mills was within the prescribed limitation. [939 F] The suit had not at all been filed within time. The period of limitation prescribed by the law had not been exceeded. [940 F] The High Courts were right in holding, that the suits were not barred by time.

The appellant was appointed as a lecturer of the Government College on a monthly salary of Rs. 500 per month. He was appointed as an examiner of the Government college on a monthly pay of Rs. 300 per month. The appellant was appointed to the post of a lecturer of Government College on an ad hoc basis. He was also appointed as an Examiner of the Government Colleges on a monthly remuneration of Rs. 200 per month. On the basis of the report of the Public Analyst the appellant was appointed a lecturer of a Government College on the pay of Rs, 300 per month and he was also appointed to the said post. The appellant challenged the appointment of the said lecturer by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court. The State contended that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code and that the appellant had not committed any offence under section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High court held that the appellant could not be said to be a public servant when he accepted an illegal certification. The High 'Court further held that the offence under section 161 of the Indian penal Code was not made out. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant did not commit any offence under the Prevention of Criminal Law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is not a public officer. He was not a person in the service of the Government and he was not a Public servant. He was merely a public servant. [813E] 2. The appellant had not been appointed as an analyst of the Government colleges on a monthly emoluments of Rs. 400 per month. It was not a case of corruption. The appellant did not hold any public servant. He had not been paid any remuneration by the Government as a public servant, nor was he ever in the service. [814E] 3. The appellant, therefore, was not a Government servant. [914E] 4. The appellant could not have been held to be a Public servant when he was acting as an examiner. [915F] 5. The appellant cannot be said to have committed any offence in the discharge of his official duties. [916F] 6. The appellant having been appointed as a public prosecutor, he was not entitled to be prosecuted under section 5(1) (a) of the Act. [917F] 7. The appellant being a public servant was not a civil servant within the definition of section 2(d) of that Act. [815F] 8. The appellant's case was that he was not an officer in the service and he was a public servant and that he was also not a public Servant. [918G] 9. The appellant has not been able to show that he was a civil servant. [1018F] 9. In the instant case, the appellant was a public Servant and he was appointed as the examiner of the University. He was a public prosecutor. He was, therefore, not a public prosecutor within the meaning Of section 2(c) of the Code. [919G] 918A] 9. It is true that the appellant is a public servant but he was not in the service as a public Prosecutor. He was neither a public servant nor a public servant who was a public Prosecutor within the meaning thereof.

The petitioners were engaged as casual labourers in the open line of the Construction Department of the Railways. They were engaged as Casual Labour in the open Line of the Construction department of the Railways on completion of 360 days of continuous employment. They were appointed as Casual Labour on completion of 180 days of continuous service. They were also appointed on completion of 240 days of continuous engagement. The petitioners were appointed on completionof 360 days of service as temporary employees on completion of 120 days of continuous engagements. The petitioners, who were appointed on temporary basis, were appointed on regular basis. The petitioners filed applications for being absorbed in regular cadre in the Railways. The Railway Administration, after considering the applications, rejected the petitioners' claim. The petitioners approached the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the orders of the Railway Administration. The High court held that the petitioners were entitled to all the privileges as applicable to regular railway servants as per the scheme framed under orders of this Court. The petitioners challenged the orders of absorption in the High Court by filing writ petitions. The High Courts allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of absorption. The HighCourt held that the scheme framed by the Railway Administration was not in accordance with the directions of this Court and, therefore, the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme framed by this Court under orders of 1st June, 1984, was not in accord with the directions issued by this Court. [901B] 2. The scheme formulated by the Railway administration was not in conformity with the directions given by this Court and the High Court had not given effect to the same. [902C] 3. The scheme was not in conflict with the directions contained in the order of 1st July, 1984. The petitioners had not been able to show that the scheme was not consistent with the directions. [903D] 4. The scheme is not in accord With the directions of the Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters. The petitioners are not entitled to the same pay as is admissible to other employees. [904E] 5. The petitioners have not been able enough to show that they are entitled to the benefits of the scheme framed in the open lines. [905F] 6. The petitioners cannot be denied the benefits of pension. [906F] 7. The petitioners should be entitled to all benefits of pension as applicable to open line. [908F] 8. The petitioners would be entitled to the benefit of pension as per the existing rules. [909G] 9. The petitioners shall be entitled to get the same benefits as are applicable to open lines. The petitioners may be given the same benefits. [907F] 9. In the circumstances, the writ petitions are allowed. The impugned orders of the High Court are set aside. The writ petitions are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant, a registered association, was formed by the Association under section 12 of the Act with the object of regulating the conduct of its business in the Association. The objects of the Association were to regulate the conduct of business in the association. The objects were to regulate its conduct in the Association and to regulate its business in its own. The objects included the following: (i) to regulate the business in its members; (ii) to regulate its own business in its affairs; (iii) to regulate and control the conduct of the business in the associations; (iv) to regulate, control and regulate the conduct in the associations and to regulate the affairs of the Association; (v) to regulate or control the conduct in its members and to regulate their own business in the affairs of such associations; (vi) to regulate their business in the Associations; (vii) to regulate all other business in the members and to control the conduct and regulate the affairs in the Association; and (viii) to regulate such other business in its meetings and to regulate such manner in which the members may be present. The appellant, a member of the Association, was a member of a recognised association. The appellant was a member in the Association, and the Association was a member. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the bye laws of the Association. A learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The bye laws of a recognised Association are not to be construed as statutes of the Association and the Association is not a body corporate. [743A] 2. The power of the Central Government to make a bye law is not a power to make a Bye law. The power to make bye laws is not a legislative power. The power is not a judicial power. [744B] 3. The power conferred on the Central Government under section 12(1) of the Act is not a delegated legislation. The power under section 12 (1) of Act is not an administrative power. [844C] 4. The power given to the Central Government by the rules made under the Act is a power to frame bye laws. The power has been conferred on the Commission under section 12 and the power conferred on it under section 12 is not a delegation of power. [944C] 5. The power can be exercised by the Central Government only in the case of a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The power cannot be exercised by a body corporate, but it can be exercised only by a body which is a body corporate and not a body which has been constituted by the Central or a State Government. [945D] 6. The power which is conferred on the State Government under section 11 of the Act cannot be exercised in the case where the power is conferred on a body corporate or a body which was constituted by the State Government. The power, therefore, cannot be exercised for the purposes for which the power was conferred on the body corporate or body which was a body corporate under section 12. [946E] 7. The power exercised by the State is not a regulatory power. The State Government has power to make rules under section 12 which are framed by the Central and a State Government under the Act. [948G] 8. The power vested in the Central Government is not a statutory power. The powers conferred on the Government under section 13 are not a power conferred on a State Government and the power to make the bye laws is a power conferred by section 12. The power in the State Government is not an executive power. [1049G] 9. The power that is conferred on an executive authority under section 12 cannot be exercised to make a rule under section 12 or to amend any bye laws made by such an authority under section 11. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. The appellant was a shareholder of the Company. The shares of the Company were acquired by the Ukhara Estate. The appellant acquired the right to receive compensation for the acquisition of the land compulsorily. The compensation received by the Ukhra Estate was not capital gain. The appellant claimed that the compensation received by it was capital gain. In the first instance, the appellant claimed that it was not liable to tax under section 12 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the compensation was capital gain and not capital gain and the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 12 of that Act. The High court held that the amount of compensation received by a shareholder of a company was capital gain, and the appellant had not acquired the right of receiving compensation for the acquired land compulsorily. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the amount received by the appellant was capital gain because the acquisition of land compulsorily was not part of the fixed assets of the Company, and the interest which is payable on compensation received by him was capital gain within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian income tax Act, 1961. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the amount attributable to the acquisition of lands compulsorily was capital gain in the hands of the assessee. [701B] (2) The High court was right in not recording the answer to the questions in the negative on all the questions in favour of the assessee and against the assessee. The High 'Court was right in rejecting the appellant's contention that the receipt of compensation for the land compulsorily acquired was capital gain as the income of the Company was not part and the interest was not capital gains. [702C] (3) The High ' Court was right, in holding that, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the amount attributable was capital gain which was taxable. [703D] (4) The High' Court was right when it held that the receipt was capital gain under section 12(6A). [703E] (5) The High. Court was right that the amount was capital gain arising after 31st March, 1948, and the amount attributable thereto was capital gain on the date of the acquisition of that land. [704G] (6) The High, Court was right. [705G] (7) The High was right in the view that the amount payable to the appellant was revenue gain. [706A] (712A) (8) The High Courts were right in holding, that the amount paid by the appellant to the Ukhali Estate was capital gain for the purpose of section 12(5A) of Income tax Act. [707B] (9) The High Curt was right in its view that the interest was capital gain incurred by the Ukra Estate on the date when the Act came into force. [709C] (10) The High Income tax Officer was right in treating the interest as capital gain under the Act as capital gain. [909D] (11) The High Commissioner was right in taking the view that, the interest was income earned by the UTI Estate from the fixed assets. [910E] (12) The High Commission was right in answering the question in favour of respondent No. 1. [911E] (13) The High Powered Committee was right in deciding the question in the negative. [912F] (14) The High powered Committee was not right in holding the interest to be capital gain. It was not right to hold that the amount earned by the appellant from the fixed asset was capital gain or capital gain. There was no question of law arising in the present appeals.
