The assessee was carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, and the business of the firm was settled on March 31, 1939. The firm was dissolved on March 31. 1939, and a fresh partnership was entered into between the partners on March 31 1939. The assessee was, however, dissolved on March 30, 1939, and on March 31 1938, the firm was dissolved. The assessee filed a petition under section 25(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, for the assessment of the firm for the assessment year 1939, and for the assessment for the assessment years 1939, and also for the assessment in respect of the assessment year 1942, for the relevant assessment year. The High Court held that the firm was not carrying on business in the timber which was allotted to it at the time of dissolution of the firm, and that the partners were entitled to relief under section 25 (4) of that Act. The High court, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to relief in respect of that assessment year. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the firm had been dissolved on March 1, 1939, because the firm was a separate and separate entity from the firm of Hakam Mal Tani Mal TaniMal Tani Mal, Tani Mal Mal Tani, Mal Tani and Mal Tani. The HighCourt held that the partnership was not a separate and distinct entity and that the firm of M/s Hakam Mal Mal Tian Mal Tani was a separate entity from that of Hakam Tani Mal. The High 'Court further held that the business of Messrs Hakam Mal, T. Mal Tani amounted to a separate and independent partnership of the assessee, and that it was not entitled to relief. The High. Court, therefore, allowed the appeal, and held that the assessment of firm for the relevant year was not correct. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the firm constituted to carry on the timber which were allotted to it, at the time when the partnership was dissolved, was a separate firm and that the partnership of HakamMal TaniMal Mal Tani Tani Mal was a separate partnership of the firm of the assessee. [601B] The firm was a distinct and separate entity and the partners were, therefore, entitled to relief on the dissolution of the partnership. [602C] The firm of Hakm Mal Tani Lal Tani Mal had been dissolved in March 1943, and the firm of Messrs Hakm Mal Mal T. Mal had been reconstituted in March 1943. The firm of M. Mal T.Mal Tani was dissolved on April 1, 1939. [603D] The firm had been reconstituted on March 31 and 1939, and, therefore, the partners were not entitled to the benefit of section 25(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. [604E] The firm, Hakam Mal had been constituted to carry out the business of timber which was settled on April 1. 1939, upto March 31, 1938, and the partners had become separate from the firm. [605E] The partnership of HakmMal Tani Lal Mal Tani Chand Mal Tani Ram Mal Tani Dass Mal Tani Das Mal Tani (supra) was not applicable to the case of the assessee as the firm of Shri Hakam Mal was a distinct entity. [606E] The assessee was not carrying business at the time the firm of Sam Mal Tanimal Mal Tani had been dissolved. [607E] The business of the assessee was not carried on at the commencement when the partnership of the partnership of M. T. Mal was dissolved.

The State transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grant of the permits and directed the permit to ply the stage carriage on a route Devenegere to Shinoga. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of Transport Authority granting permit in pursuance to the earlier resolution of Regional Transport Authority. Datar, had no powers to grant a stage carriage in pursuance of a resolution of the State Government. [907 F] 9. The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Shimgarh, had no statutory authority to grant permits in pursuance of any earlier resolution of a Regional Transport Authority which had been affirmed in appeal by the State Transport Tribunal. Datar, was competent under section 64 to grant the certificate. The appellant filed a petition under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (in short 'the Code') for a declaration that the election of respondent Prakash Vir Shastri was void and for a declaration to declare that the election was void. The appellant also filed a petition for a declaration of the election of the respondent Prakash Vir Gandhi Shastri to be void. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant filed a second appeal before this Court. The High court held that the publication of the newspaper was not proved to be published with the consent of the respondent and the supporters of the appellant. The appellant contended that the publication was not proved as to the truth of the contents therein. The High 'Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir had committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant and that the appellant was not guilty of any corrupt practice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The publication of the news item in the scriptures of the appellant was a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The publication was not in the scripture of the appellant but was in the scripty of the respondent. [801B] 2. The publication in the script scriptures of respondent Prakash was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The publication is not in the language of the scriptures. The publication does not disclose the name of the appellant as having been assaulted or chased or chased or assaulted or chased. The publication also does not disclose that the appellant made any complaint to the Election Commissioner. [802C] 3. The publication did not disclose the names of the appellant or any of the witnesses who were examined by the Election Commissioner to prove the contents therein and the appellant did not disclose any complaint to him. [803D] 4. The publication made by the appellant in the script sheets of the respondent was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act. [804E] 5. The publication by the appellant was in the language which was not in consonance with the provisions in the Act and the Rules. The publication clearly disclosed the name of respondent Prakash. The publication further disclosed the name as having been attacked or chased or attempted to be chased or chased. [805E] 6. The publication, therefore, was not in compliance with the provisions relating to the personal nature and conduct of respondent Prakash and the supporters. [806F] 7. The publication itself disclosed the name and the name of appellant as having assaulted or chased the supporters of respondent Prakash with the consent. The publication disclosed the name, character and conduct as having been done by the appellant. [807F] 8. The publication had not disclosed the name or character of the appellant, as having been chased or chased by the supporters of Prakash Vir Shastri. The publication could not be proved to be a corrupt practice in the sense that the appellant did make any complaint to that effect. [808G] 9. The publication merely disclosed the name which was the subject matter of the election petition. The publication has not disclosed the names of respondent Prakash, Vir Shastri and his supporters. The publication therefore, was in conformity with section 123(2) of the Act and was not in violation of section 123 (1) of. The publication cannot be proved to the truth. [809G] 10. The publication must disclose the name and character of the candidate as having been subjected to the corrupt practice in connection with the personal character, conduct and conduct of candidate Prakash Vir Shastri and the supporters thereof. [810H] 11. The publication would not disclose the identity of the candidate or his supporters. [908F] 12.

The Division Bench of that Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the learned Single Judge and dismissed the application. The respondent then filed a second appeal to this Court. The Division bench of the High court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order of dismissal of the second application for setting it aside. The respondent thereafter filed a second application for restoration of the second appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed that application on the ground that the application for restoration was made after the sale was confirmed. The respondent thereupon filed a second revision before the High Court which was dismissed. The respondent, therefore, filed a second special leave petition before this Court. The application could not be filed within the period as prescribed by the Limitation Act, but it was within the time prescribed by Article 133 of the Limitation, and the period prescribed under Article 136 of t he Limitation Act cannot be computed from the date of the dismissal. [805E] 6. The application has been filed within the prescribed period of limitation. The period of limitation prescribed by Article 138 of the Limitation is not applicable to the application for condonation of delay. [806E] 7. The application must be accompanied by a certified copy of the order rejecting the application for the setting aside of sale. [807E] 8. The application should be accompanied by an affidavit in support of the application. [808E] 9. The application cannot be treated as an application for setting the aside of the auction sale. [820G] 9. In the instant case, the application for re spondent decree holder was made within a period of one month from the date on which the decree was passed. The application did not contain any such averment. [809E] 10. The application, therefore, was not maintainable. [810E] 11. The application had been filed within one year from the date when the decree was put into execution. The application ought to have been filed within a period o f one month from that date. [811E] 12. The application in the present case was not within a period prescribed by the Code of the Civil Procedure. [812E] 12A] 12. In the present case, the respondent decree holder had purchased the property on July 17 1980. The application of the respondent decreeholder for delivery of the possession on July 18 1980 was made within two years from the date the decree was made.
