The respondent No. 5 was granted permission to develop a hotel on the land in question. The respondent No. 1, the Municipal Corporation, had applied for permission to develop the land in the year 1966. The respondent no. 1, however, granted permission to the respondent No. 2 to develop the said land. The respondent NO. 1, on the basis of the sanctioned plan, had applied to the Municipal Corporation for permission to construct a hotel on it. The Municipal Corporation, however, refused to grant permission to the petitioners. The Municipal Commissioner, by his order dated April 30, 1984, granted permission for the construction of a hotel on a portion of the land in dispute. The Municipal Council, however, rejected the application of the respondent No, 5 for permission to build a hotel on his land. The Municipal respondent No. 4, however, by his letter dated April 30. 1984, informed the respondent No 5 that the proposal for the construction was not approved by the Municipal Corporation. The Municipal Board, however, did not accept the proposal for construction of a Hotel on the land. The petitioners, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Municipal Corporation rejecting the application of respondent No. 3 for permission to establish a hotel on its land. The High Court, by its judgment dated April 30th, 1984, allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of exemption granted to the respondent no. 5. The Municipal appeal filed by the Municipal Council was allowed by the High Court by its judgment and order dated April 29, 1984. The Municipal Appeal filed by the respondent No 4 against the order of grant of exemption was allowed by this Court. The Municipal Appeals filed by the petitioners against the order granting exemption were dismissed by this Court by its order dated April 31, 1984. In the appeal filed by respondent No.4, the Municipal Council, in its appeal, contended that the High Court had committed a serious error in holding that the respondent No 2 had no sufficient quantity of land for park and recreation ground. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High court was not justified in holding that there was no sufficient quantity for park and open ground. [701B] 1.2. The High Courts were right in holding that a proper area was kept for park and reserve for park and for recreation ground. [801C] 1.3. The High courts were right in rejecting the application for approval of the plan submitted by the respondent no 5 for the construction. [802D] 1.4. The High Powered Committee had approved the plan submitted for the construction by the respondent NO. 5. It was not open to the respondent NO 5 to challenge the approval of the revised plan. [805E] 1.5. The High powered Committee had not approved the plan of the respondent no 1 for the construction and had not considered the same. [806E] 1,6. The HighPowered Committee had, therefore, rightly rejected the application for sanction of the revised development plan. [706E] 2.1.2. In the present case, the respondent No 1 had not approved any revised development plan submitted by it. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 had not approved such plan. [820G] 2.2.3.1.3.2.1.1. In the circumstances, the High Court was not justified to interfere with the order of granting exemption to the respondent Nos. 2 and 3. [820H] 2.3.3.4.1.4.2.2.4.3. In the instant case, the High Powered committee had approved the revised development plans submitted by the Respondent No. 5 for the purpose of granting exemption. The High powersed Committee had also approved the revised plan submitted by Respondent No. 2 for the construction on the land and had not recommended the revised development Plan.

The appellant union was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of various products. The appellant union was registered under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant company was engaged in a business of manufacturing, selling and selling of certain products. The workmen were reemployed in the same undertaking. The appellant Union was reemployed in a different undertaking. The workmen had been reemployed in different undertakings. The appellant employer had been re employed in different undertakings and the workmen were re employed in the same undertakings. The workmen, who were reemployed, were reemployed. The appellant management, however, terminated the services of the workmen on the ground that they were reemployed and that the workmen were not reemployed. On the ground that the employer had not established that the workmen had been retrenched, the Industrial Court held that the employer was guilty of unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court held, that the employer, in order to determine whether the employer had committed an unfair labour practice, must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the employer was not guilty of unfair practice or not. The Industrial court held that the employers had committed an act of unfair labour practices and that the employer did not impose a lockout or had closed down the industrial undertaking. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant union was guilty of an unfair labour practices. The Industrial Courts held that the workmen, who had been reengaged in the same Undertaking, were re employed by the employer and that the appellant Union was not guilty. The Industrial Disputes Act was amended by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1976. The Industrial Tribunals held that the termination of the services of workmen was illegal and that the employers were guilty of unfair trade practice. The industrial Court held that there was no evidence produced before the Industrial Tribunal to show that the employer has closed down the undertaking and that the management had not closed down the same. The Industrial Appellate Tribunal held that there had been a closure of the undertaking and the employer had closed down its undertaking and that there was a closure of its undertaking and the management had closed down it. The Industrial appellate Tribunal held that since the employer had failed to establish that the workmen have been reemployed and had closed down, the Industrial Tribunal was justified in holding that the employer could not impose a closure of an industrial undertaking. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The employer is not guilty of an offence under the Industrial Disputes act. [601B] 2. The employer has to establish that there was an unfair labour Practice. The employer can only establish that the employer is not the guilty of an act of victimisation or unfair labour practice and that the workman has not established that he has closed down or has closed down. [602C] 3. The employer cannot impose a lock out or has closed the undertaking and has closed down, or has closed it. [603D] 4. The employer, in the present case, has not established the fact that the employer in the present cases has closed down and has closed the industrial undertaking and has not closed down or had closed the undertaking. [604E] 5. The employer in the instant case has not established any fact that the workmen in the present appeals were reemployed or had closed their undertaking. [613G] 6. The employer had not proved that the workmen are reemployed or have closed down or have closed their undertaking and that they have closed down and that they had closed down or that they have reemployed or were closed down. The employer could not therefore be said to have established that the employer would not have closed down the Undertaking and that the undertaking was closed down or was a closed down. It was not open to the employer to say that the employer should not have closed the undertaking or that the undertaking should not have been closed down or closed down. In the present case the employer has not established either that the workmen who were re employed or have closed the Undertaking were closed down or were closed. [605E] 7.

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924, as an investment company. The assessee company was incorporated in the year 1924, as a dealer in investments and properties. The assessee Company was incorporated on June 29, 1924. The assessee was a dealer in shares, securities and securities and properties. In the circumstances of the case the assessee company was a dealer and not an investor. The assessee filed a petition under section 66(1) of the Act before the Appellate Tribunal for a reference of the questions framed by it. The Appellate Tribunal after hearing the parties and after hearing the arguments of the parties, by its order dated March 2, 1966 held that the assessee company had not been a dealer in securities and properties and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities, securities and properties were not a question of law. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Income Tax Officer had not been able to prove that the assessee had incurred losses or profits made by the sale of the shares, securities or securities and properties of the assessee company. The Appellate Appellate Tribunal held that the profits of the assessee Company were not a business profits and that the assessee was a person in investments and property and that the Income tax Officer had not committed any error in holding that the assessee Company was a dealer. The Appellate Commissioner held that there was no material on the record to support the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the assessee did not have any investor. The Appellate Court held that the income of the assessee was not a dealer in investment and properties and the profits arising from the sales of shares, security and properties of that company were not a matter of fact. The Appellate Authority held that the facts and in the circumstances of this case were not a mixed question of law and fact and that the facts found on the basis of the materials on record were not a pure question of law, and that the question as framed at present was a mixed question as framed by the Appellate Tribunal in its order dated June 15, 1952. The AppellateTribunal held that the question of law as framed at this stage was a mixed questions of fact and law and that the questions were not a mere question of law but a mixed question. The Appellate tribunal held that the questions framed at this late stage were not a substantial question of law because the facts and the evidence on record were different from the facts found by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and that the Appellate Tribunal had not committed an error in holding the assessee company to be a dealer in the investments and properties of E.D.D.L. and properties of M/s. E.D.'s case. The Appellate Tribun al held that the Appellate Assistant commissioner had not been right in holding that there was material on the basis that the assessee is a dealer in Investments and properties of its own funds and properties. On the question of income, the Appellate Tribunal held in favour of the assessee and against the assessee company holding that the profits were not a trade profits and losses. The Appellate Collector held that the profit of the assessee had not been assessed as business profits and losses and that the profit had not been made by the assessee company in investments and securities and that the losses arising from sale of shares and securities and other properties of the company were not the same as profits and losses made by the company. The High Court held that there were no material on record to support that the profits or losses arising from sales of shares and other properties were not the income of that company. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding the income of a dealer in a investments and properties and securities and securities that the profits arising therefrom were not a trading profits and losses but were a trading profits. [601B] 2. The High Courts were right in holding in favour of a dealer holding shares, securities etc. of the assessee. [602C] 3.

The appellant, a Judicial Officer, was appointed as a District Munsif in the Madras Presidency, and was posted as District Munsif, in the Madras District. He was posted as a District Munsiff in the Madras City, and was transferred to the Madras Presidency. He was appointed as District Munsif in 1955, and was confirmed in the service. He was then posted as a Subordinate Judge in the Madras State. He was transferred to Madras Presidency, but he was posted as the District Munsif in Madras. He was later transferred to Madras, and was then posted to Madras, but he continued to work as District Munsif. On April 28, 1954, the appellant was transferred to Hyderabad, and was later transferred as District Munsif to Madras, on April 28, 1955. The appellant was then posted in Madras, and he was transferred to Bombay, and was further transferred to Madras. The appellant challenged the order of suspension before the High Court of Madras, and the High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court, and obtained a certificate of fitness from the High Court. The High Court dismissed that petition, and the appellant filed a petition in the Supreme Court, under Article 226 of the Constitution, challenging the order of the Government. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally, and that the order of transfer was bad, and that, therefore, the order of dismissal was bad, as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The High court dismissed the petition, and held that the order passed by the Government was bad, because the High Court did not decide the matter properly, and that it was not open to the Government to pass the order of punishment, because the order of removal was bad, since the order of termination was passed by the High Court on January 28, 1954. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under article 226 of the constitution, challenging the validity of the order of his suspension. The High, Court, dismissed the petition on the ground that the order was bad, but the order of retirement was bad, inasmuch as the order of compulsory retirement was passed by it on January 28. 1954, and that there was no fresh question of law, and that no fresh question was raised, and that since the order was not passed by the Governor, the order was void, and that as the order was passed by him, the order could not be challenged, and that he was not entitled to any relief, and that in any case, the order passed was bad, the order must be set aside. The appellant filed a writ appeal in the High court, and the learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition, and dismissed the writ petition. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is bad, because it was passed by a competent authority, and the order of discharge was bad, though the order of appointment was passed by itself, and the Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry and decide for itself whether the charges were well founded or not. [849B] 2. The order passed by a Government is not a punishment, and the question whether the order of reinstatement is bad, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [850C] 3. The order is not a penalty, and the mere fact that the order is passed by a government authority, does not necessarily mean that the order has to be passed by a court, and that a court has no jurisdiction to go into the question whether it has jurisdiction to decide for itself. [852C] 4. The order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice, and the principles of law, laid down in the case of [852D] 5. The order, therefore, is bad, and the writ petition is liable to be dismissed. [853D] 6.

The appellant, a legal representative of a deceased person, filed a suit for assessment of income tax on the basis of the income received by him from the estate of the deceased. The appellant contended that the income received from the estate was not liable to be taxed in the hands of the legal representative of the deceased person, and that the Income tax Officer was not entitled to levy tax on the income received or of the loss sustained by him or of the death of the deceased, and that, therefore, the Income tax officer was not entitled, to levy tax in respect of the income of the deceased on the basis that it was the personal income of the legal representatives of the deceased and that, in view of the provisions of the Act, the Income Tax Officer was not competent to levy tax. The High Court held that the Income Tax officer was not competent under section 24B of the Act to assess the income received and income received by a legal representative from the estate after the death of a deceased, and, therefore, he was not liable for assessment of the income. The High court held that the income was not liable in accordance with the provisions of section 24B and the Legislature had not made any provision for assessment of tax on the personal income received by the legal representative from such estate. The High 'Court further held that the provisions of sections 24B and 24B were not applicable to the income received in the hands or of the legal Representatives of the deceased persons, and that they were not liable to pay the tax on the death of such deceased person, as the personal income was not received by such legal representative of deceased person, but was received by such deceased person. The High' Court held that section 24B was not applicable to income received by legal representative of an individual, and that section 24BB was not applicable, and that it was not open to the Legislature to levy tax under section 24A on the personal Income received by a Legal representative of a person, who died, and that income received by such person was not liable, and that such income was not chargeable to tax in the hands on the death, of such person, and the Legislature did not provide that the income which was received by a person by whom income was received by the Legal representative of the estate of a deceased deceased person, was to be regarded for the purpose of assessment of income of the estate. The appellant, a Legal representative, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay, challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not applicable in the case of the appellant, and that there was no provision for assessment on the personal assets of the deceased or of the deceased of the deceased in the hands, and that no tax could be levied on the personal properties of the deceased if he had not died, and, as such, the income received was not liable. The High, Court, held that the Act did not authorise the levy of tax on personal properties of a deceased assessee, and that since the income received on the death was not liable under section 24 B, the income which could be deemed to have been received by a legally representative of the Estate of the deceased could not be deemed to be received by alegal representative of the legal Representative of the estate, and that in view of section 24 B of the Act the income received could not be treated as income of the personal income. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High. Court held that there was nothing in section 24B to suggest that the income of a deceased can be deemed to represent the personal income, and that if the income is received by aLegal representative of the family, the income would be deemed to constitute income of the family. The High Courts, therefore, held that section 23A was not applicable.

The appellant was a Ruler of a State. He was a Ruler. He was appointed as a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was also a Ruler of Madhya Pradesh and was a Ruler under the Government of India. He was, therefore, a Ruler of State. He had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. He was not a Ruler of any State. He, therefore, was not a citizen of India. The appellant was a maufidar and was a citizen of Madhya Pradesh under the Constitution. He was an ex Ruler of Madhya Bharat. He was recognised by the Government of Madhya Pradesh as the Ruler of Madhya Madhya Bharat. The appellant, therefore, could not be regarded as a Ruler. The appellant filed a suit in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh for a declaration that the villages in question were not liable to be assessed to land revenue. The trial court held that the appellant was a citizen and was not a maufiidar. The High Court held that the villages were not liable for assessment to land revenue and that the appellant had no right to recover the rent or revenue. The High court, however, held that the village in question was not a "Maufidar" and that the villages had not been recognised by the government as the private property of the appellant. The High ' Court, however, found that the appellant could not be treated as a mauidar under the Constitution and held that the villagers in question were entitled to recover rent and revenue from persons who held land in their villages. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a Ruler of an Indian State and the appellant was not a person holding land in his villages. [701B] 2. The appellant had not been able to show that he was a Ruler and that he was not a naufidar. He was neither a mauiidar nor a Ruler of Indian State. [702C] 3. The appellant could not establish that he was an ex- Ruler of Madhya State. [602D] 4. The appellant cannot be regarded as an ex-Maufidars. The appellant has not been able, in the circumstances, to establish that he had a right of recovery of rent or revenue or that he had no right of recovery from persons holding lands in his villages in his villages, nor was he a mau fidar. [703E] 5. The appellant did not establish that the villages held by him were not "Mau fidar" within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Constitution. [704G] 6. The appellant does not establish that there was any dispute as to the title of the appellant to the villages in his village. [705G] 7. The appellant having failed to establish that the village held by him was a "Mou fidar" and therefore, the appellant was an ex emploadidar within the meaningof article 366( 22) of the constitution, the appellant cannot be treated as an ex em ploadidar. [605G] 8. The appellant being a Ruler of Gwalior State, the appellant is not a moufidar within the definition of the word 'proprietor ' in the Act. [706G] 9. The appellant's contention that the villages of the appellant were not "mou fidar", is not correct. [707G] 10. The appellant 's case is that the villages which were notified as "Mau gidar" were not "maufidar" and, therefore, the villages in the villages in which the appellant was "maufidars" were notified as 'Mau gidars'.

The respondent was posted at Shillong in the office of the Director of Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. He was transferred to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Directorate of Botanyical Survey of Indian, Eastern Circle. He was posted at Pauri (U.P.) by the Senior administrative Officer, office at Pauri. He was allowed to continue at Shillong for a longer period, but was posted at different places. He was also allowed to continue in Shillong for a period of one year. He was again posted at P.O. Pauri (West) by the Director of Mines and Geology, Government of India, Ministry of Mines and Mines, Government of Indias, New Delhi. He was relieved from Shillong on January 29, 1991. He was not allowed to continue till he was posted at the same place. He was, however, allowed to continue until he was posted in Pauri (East) by the Directorate of Mines and Minerals, Government of Bengal, Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of Indian, Ministry of Finance, Government of india, New Delhi, and he was posted to Pauri. The respondent was posted to Shillong in the Office of the Director, Botanic Survey of India. He was promoted to the post of Director, Botsanic Survey, Eastern Circle on January 29. 1991. He filed O.A. No. 33 of 1991 in the Central Administrative Tribunal, Guwahati Bench, praying for quashing the order of transfer. The Tribunal allowed the O.A., and quashed the order of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Guwahati. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the impugned order of transfer and quashed the same. The respondent has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the Tribunal is not an order of transfer but is an order of punishment. [801B] 2. The respondent is not a Government servant. He is a Government servant and he is not entitled to any relief. He is not entitled for any relief. [802C] 3. The respondent cannot be transferred to a place where he is working. He is entitled to continue till the Government servant is transferred to a particular place. [803D] 4. The respondent, in the present case, is not a government servant. He was appointed to a place which is not a place where the respondent is working. The respondent had no choice but to continue till his posting at the same station. He was given a posting at the place where he was posted. He was working at the same post. He was retained at the same location. He was sent to the office of Director, Mines and Geology at Pauri, but he was not allowed. He was kept in the same place where he had been posted. He had been posted at Pouri. He was asked to report to the Director, Mines & Geology at Pouri, but he did not report to the Directorate of Geology at Pure. He was informed that he was posted there at Pouri and he was asked to join at Pauri where he was working. He was further informed that he would join at Pouri where he was transferred to Shillong. He did not report at Pure and he was informed that the respondent was posted in Shillong. He could not join at Pure where he was sent to Pure where the respondent was working. The Tribunal held that the respondent had no option but to continue at Pure, but he could not join in Pure where his transfer was made. He was directed to join at Shillong. He joined at Pure on January 29 and he was relieved from Pure where it was made. The Tribunal further held that the transfer was not in violation of any statutory provisions.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with Section 149, I.P.C. and were convicted under Section 302, I. P.C. read with Section 34, I.PC. The appellants were sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 7,000 each. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The High court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants had committed the offence of murder. The appellants filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellants contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the prosecution failed to prove the charge under Section 302/149, I. PC. The High C ourt set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High c ourt set it aside. The High Courts were right in holding that there was no evidence to prove the offence under Section 302 of the I.P.. The High Court was right in holding the appellants guilty of the offence under Sections 302/149 and 304, I.p.c. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment of five years. [701B] 2. The High Cou rt has rightly held that the appellants were not guilty of the offences under Section 302 and 304, Part I, I.Ps. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High rs Court has rightly held the appellants guilty under Section 302 I.P., I.P, I.e. P.S. and sentenced each of them to undergo rigorous Imprisonment for five years and to pay fine of Rs, 21,000 each, in default, to undergo rigorous imp ugned sentence of imprisonment for five months. [702C] 3. The High tution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution had failed in proving its case beyond a reasonable doubt. [703E] 4. The High nesses have failed to prove their case beyond a period of five years and the appellants were convicted under Sections 302 and 149, I PC. 5. The High f ority has not been shown to be a case of any evidence. The High l ourt has not given any finding in respect of the commission of offence under Section 149, IPC. The High m e Court has not given a finding in respect thereof. [704G] 6. The High j udgment of the High Court is based on the evidence of the eye witnesses. The High p e Court has given a finding that the prosecution has failed to establish its case beyond any reasonable doubt. It has also not given any reason for not accepting the evidence of eye witnesses. [705G] 7. The High R e Court has also not shown any reason for accepting the evidence. The evidence of eye witness is not reliable. The High e Court has failed to give any reason for rejecting the evidence of PW 1. The evidence is not reliable and the High Court has not shown any reasons for accepting the same. [706G] 8. The High Crl nesses were acquitted by the High Court and the High rs court has not given reasons for accepting their evidence. [707G] 9. The High Co urt has not given sufficient reasons for accepting t he evidence of eye wit nesses. The High Cr eution has not shown sufficient reasons for rejecting the testimony of eye witnesses, particularly, when the High Court was of the opinion that the prosecution was not able to prove its cases beyond a reasonable doubts. [708G] 10. The High w e Court has rightly not given any reasons for rejecting t he evidence. [807G] 11. The High CR e Court has wrongly given reasons for rejecting evidence of eye l witnesses. [808G] 12.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1913. The appellant Bank was established under the Banking Company Act, 1913 and was registered under the Banking companies Act, 1913, and was registered as a banking company under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The appellant bank was constituted under a special Indian law. The Banking Companies Act was enacted by the Indian Legislature and not by the Parliament. The Banking Company Act was enacted to protect the British economy and to provide for the regulation of banking business. The Banking companies Act was enacted in the interest of the general public and for the protection of the interests of the general economy of the country. The Banking company Act, 1913 was enacted to provide for certain special laws relating to banking business. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969, shall apply to the Banking Companies as if it were a Central Act. Section 4 of the Act, which is relevant for the purpose of this case, provides that the provisions of the Act shall apply to a banking company as if it was a Central Act and not a banking company. Section 4 (e) of that Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the Banking Companies Acts, other than the Banking Companies, Act, 1949, shall apply in the case of banking companies. Section 4 provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the provisions of this Act. Section 5 provides that the rules made under the Act shall be published in the Official gazette. Section 6 provides that the Government may, from time to time, make rules to carry out the provisions thereof. Section 7 provides that the State Government may, after previous publication, make rules in respect of any matter relating to banking companies. The State Government has framed rules under the Act. Rule 3 provides that the Reserve Bank of India shall, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, make rules regulating the procedure to be followed by the Reserve Bank in respect of banking companies and for the purpose to be specified in the rules. Rule 4 provides that every rule made under the Reserve Bank shall be laid before each House of Parliament. Rule 5 provides that every rules made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after they are made, before each House. Rule 6 provides that every such rule shall be laid as soon as it is made before each House, and if it is not so made, before the expiry of the session in which it is so laid or the session immediately following. Rule 7 provides that every notification issued under the Act by the Reserve bank shall be laid on or before each House and if it relates to a matter not specified in the notification, it shall be published by the Reserve Government in the Official Gaziological Gazette. Rule 8 provides that every order made by the Reserve Board under the Act and every rule made thereunder shall be laid in the Official Gazettee. Rule 9 provides that every direction issued by the Reserve board under the Act or the rules made thereunder shall, in the case where it is not made, be published in such manner as may be prescribed. Rule 10 provides that every application for revision of any order made by a Reserve Board under section 4(e), shall be made in the form prescribed in Appendix I. Rule 11 provides that every revision application shall be made by a person who is aggrieved by any order made under section 4 (e). Rule 12 provides that every person aggrieved by any such order shall, within a period of thirty days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Rule 13 provides that every appeal shall be heard and disposed of by the Appellate Tribunal in accordance with the provisions of section 4 (a) and (b). Rule 14 provides that every memorandum of appeal shall be accompanied by a copy of the order appealed against and shall be accompanied with a copy of such memorandum.

The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad, challenging the validity of the impugned notification issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that the impugned notification is violative of the fundamental rights of the appellant and the appellant is not entitled to any relief. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the impugned notifications are violative of the rights of the appellants and the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is not violative of the right to trade and commerce guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. [601B] 2. The impugned notifications are not violative of Article 19(2) of the constitution. The impugned Notification is not violative either of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution or is violative of Article 14 of Constitution. [701C] 3. The impugned Notifications are not violative either Article 14 of Part III of the Constitution and are, therefore, void. [702D] 4. The impugned orders are, therefore void. [602E] 5. The impugned order is, therefore, bad in law. [703G] 6. The impugned Government Order is, therefore void and is, therefore. void. [803G] 7. The impugned judgment of the High Court is, therefore set aside and the writ petition is allowed. The impugned Order is quashed and the writ petitions are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act. The appellant, a public limited company, was incorporated on June 30, 1956. The appellant was a company incorporated on June 31, 1956. On June 30, 1957, the appellant was incorporated under section 3 of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1956. In the year 1957, the Company was incorporated under a special statute. The appellant filed a petition in the High Court of Calcutta under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that there was a substantial increase in the working class cost of living index. The Tribunal was right in holding that it was not justified to increase the working class of living index in the year 1957. [813 A B] The Tribunal was not right in holding the appellant to be a member of the Indian Administrative Service. [814 B] The appellant was not a member of any of the Indian Civil Service. He was not a Government servant. He was a member of a service of the Indian Government. He was appointed to the Indian Administrative Services on a temporary basis. He was paid a salary of Rs. 2,000/- per month. He was also paid a salary in the scale of Rs. 3,000/- in the scale. The appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in holding that he was not a government servant. The High court held that the Tribunal erred in holding the respondent to be a Government servant and that the Tribunal committed an error in holding the respondents to be a government servant and that he was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Courts held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefits of the provisions contained in article 14 of, the Constitution. [815 C D] The Tribunal had not given any reasons for holding that the appellant had not been able to establish that the working class was not a part of the service of the Company. [816 D] The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that the working classes were not part of the Service of the Company and that the working conditions of the Company were not such as to justify the increase in the cost of living. [817 E] The Tribunal has not given any reason for holding that there were substantial increase in working class cost. [818 E] The appellant did not produce any evidence to establish that there was substantial increase in his working class cost in the year 1958. The Tribunal has given no reasons for holding the appellant not to be a part of his service of the company. [819 F] The Tribunal did not give any reasons for the holding that the working condition of the Company was not a whole of the service. [820 F] The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for the benefits of article 14. [821 G] The Tribunal, therefore, erred in holding, that the appellant did not have any substantial increase in its working class cost and that the appellant could not be said to be a person who was a member thereof.

The appellant, who was appointed as a "Modified" in the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh, was appointed as "Modification" in the year 1939. The appellant was appointed as the "Modifications" in the State of Andhra. The scheme was framed under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act. The appellant, who is the Executive Officer of the Mutt, was appointed by the Government as "Modeatory Officer" in the former State of Andhra, and was appointed as such on the basis of the scheme framed under the provisions of the former Act. The scheme provided for the appointment of "Modatory Officer" and "Modicory Officer" in respect of the "Modeal Officer" in place of "Modetal Officer". The scheme provided that the "Mhodatory Officer" would be appointed as "Nodatory Officer". The appellant was, however, appointed as "Todatory Officer " in the erstwhile state of Andhra Pradesh" in the then State of Andhra and was appointed on the basis thereof. The appellant challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(f) and 19(1) (f) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the scheme was not valid when it was framed and the scheme was framed. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of this scheme on the grounds that the scheme framed by the Government was not consistent with the provisions of section 103(d) of the Act and that the scheme had been framed under the Act. The High court held that the schemes framed under the earlier Act were not consistent with section 103(D) of the Andhra Pradesh Act and that they contravened the provisions contained in the latter Act. The State of Andhra filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High 'Court held that the appellant was entitled to seek the protection of article 19 (1)(f). The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. HELD: 1. The scheme framed by Government under the earlier enactment was not consistent and was not binding on the appellant. [601B] 2. The scheme is not consistent with any of the provisions of any of the said Act. The schemes framed under section 63 of the earlier enactment are not consistent with either of the provisions contained therein or of the provisions thereof. [602C] 3. The scheme under section 63 is not consistent or inconsistent with any of those provisions. The scheme has been framed under section 68 of the Act. [603D] 4. The scheme does not contain any provision for the appointment or transfer of the "Nodal Officer" and the "Nedal Officer" as the case may be. [604E] 5. The scheme, therefore, does not violate the provisions of Article 19(1). [604F] 6. The scheme cannot be held to be inconsistent with any provision of the Constitution and the Act. It is not inconsistent with any other provision of the Act or the rules made thereunder. [605G] 7. The scheme must be read in the light of the provisions in the Act and the rules made there under. [606F] 8. The scheme should be read in its entirety and the scheme should be construed in the light thereof. [06F] 9. The scheme in question is not consistent and is not inconsistent. The scheme itself is not consistent. The scheme can be construed in its entirety. [607F] 9(i) The scheme is consistent with the relevant provisions in the earlier Act and the Rules made thereunder. The scheme may be read in a different manner. [609F] (ii) The scheme cannot, therefore, be held to have been consistent with the earlier Act or the Rules made there under and the scheme cannot be said to be inconsistent therewith.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi teacher in the school with effect from July 12, 1982. He was appointed as a Hindi teacher in that school with effect on July 12,1982. He was also appointed as a teacher in that School with effect from January 12, 1982 and was working with the approval of the authorities for the period from July 12 1982 to July 12, 1983. He was further appointed as a Sanskrit teacher in that post with effect from August 12, 1982 on ad hoc basis. He was continued to serve as Hindi teacher till he was appointed as such on July 12 1982. He continued to serve till he was replaced by a candidate from the select list. He was, however, appointed as Hindi Teacher in that school on ad hoc terms and conditions of service. He was confirmed in that post on July 12 1983. He continued in that post till he was re-appointed as Hindi teacher. He was re-employed as Hindi teacher on July 12 1984. He was again re-employed on July 12 1985. He was paid salary and other emoluments due to him as a result of the termination of his service. He continued as Hindi teacher from July 12 1984 till he was again reemployed on July 13, 1983. The appellant was re-engaged as Hindi teacher by the managing committee on July 12 1986. He was absorbed in that school by the managing Committee on July 12 1987. He was given the salary and other allowances for the period between July 12,1983 to July 12 1987 and he was reemployed on August 12, 1983 on ad hoc and on ad hoc on July 12 1988. He was then re-employed in that school. He was thereafter re-employed by the managing body on July 12 1989. He was continuing to serve as a Hindi Teacher in the school till he was selected by the managing authority for 89 days. He was subsequently re-employed at that school on July 12 1991. He was selected by a selection committee for 89 days and he was appointed on July 12 1992. He was regularly appointed on July 13 1992 and he was continued to work with the approval and approval of the managing committee. He was finally re-employed after July 12, 1984. He continued till he was given the pay and allowances for the periods from July 12 to July 12 1988 till he was redeployed as Hindi teacher with effect from June 12, 1982 till he was employed on July 12. He was regularised as Hindi teacher w.e.f. July 12, 1988. He continued upto July 12, 1992 and he continued to serve on July 12 1993. He was thus re-employed till he was retrenched on July 12 1994. He was not re-employed until he was re­employed on July 14, 1983. On the other hand, he was re re-employed only on July 12 and he continued till he retired on July 12 1995. He was retrenched on August 12 1995. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Validation Act on the ground that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised in the post of Hindi teacher. The High Court held that the appellant had been re-employed and he was entitled to be regularisation in the post. The appellant, therefore, filed a special leave petition in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1.2. The High court was in error by holding that the appointment of the appellant as Hindi teacher was not in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Education Act. [813E] 1.2.3.1.3.3. The High Courts were in error in allowing the writ petition. [814E] 1.(a) The appellant was not re­employed and he continued in that school till he retired from service on July 12 or July 12, 1986. He continued until he was replaced.

The appellant was elected as a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti by a resolution of the Panchayat Samiti dated March 31, 1967. The appellant was elected to a Panchayat Samiti on March 31, 1968. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the Chairman of a Zila Parishad. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was disqualified under r. 7 of the Rules and that the High court was in error. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant had not been able to establish that the allowances payable under r. 3 to 7 were in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance under rule 3 to 7. [801 A] 2. The appellant, who was elected as Chairman of a Samiti, was not entitled to any mileage allowance. The appellant could not establish that the allowance payable under rs. 3 to7 was in addition to his daily allowance. [802 B] 3. The appellant having failed to establish that he was disqualified under the rules, the High Court rightly held that the appellant had failed to establish the fact that the allowances were in addition or in addition to what was required to be paid to him. [803 C] 4. The appellant did not establish that he had been disqualified under rs 3 to 7 of the rules. [804 D] 5. The appellant failed to establish any fact that he was not disqualified under r, 3 to 7, because he was treated as a member of a Panchayat Samitis. [805 E] 6. The appellant cannot be said to be disqualified under r., 3 to 7 because he was not a member of the Panchayat Samitis. The appellant is not entitled to the mileage allowance under r. 8 of the Rules. [806 F] 7. The appellant being a member of Panchayat Samiti, the appellant was not entitled for any mileage allowances. [807 F] 8. The appellant must be deemed to be disqualified for being a member under r. 4 of the Rules, if he is a member of any Panchayat Samiti. [808 G] 8. In the instant case, the appellant had not established that he was a member of Zila Parishad. [809 G] 9. The appellant 's case was that he was entitled to mileage allowance for the day of departure from the place of residence of the Chairman and Members of the Panchayat. [810 G] 9 A. The appellant should have been given mileage allowance at the rate of Rs. 100/ per day for the day when he was treated. [811 G] 9A. The appellant's case was that the Chairman of the Panchayat had no reason to doubt the correctness of the allowances paid to him by the Chairman of Panchayat Samiti. The appellant also did not establish any fact in this case that he was treated to be a member of Samiti. [820 A] 10. The appellant can not be said to have established that he had not been disqualified under the Rules. The appellant may be deemed to have been disqualified under s. 7 of, the Rules if he is not a member under the rules. The appellant would be entitled to mileages allowance at the rates prescribed by the Rules.

The appellant was inducted into the disputed premises by the respondent on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondent was inducted into a building by the appellant with the consent of the landlord. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had constructed a tin shed on the open land adjacent to the disputed tin shed and the respondent had constructed a shed on the disputed tin sheds. The appellant contended that the disputed tin structure was constructed by the respondent without any alteration in the structure or the structure of the building. The trial Court held that the disputed structure was not a material alteration in the accommodation and the structure was not altered in the manner or structure of the disputed tin roof. The High Court held that there was no material alteration in any structure or structure of a building. The High court held that the respondent had not made any alteration in any building or structure of his own. The High CDGH held that the structure was constructed on the open plot adjacent to the open land adjoining to the disputed structure and the respondent was not entitled to file suit for eviction. The High ctions held that the appellant was not entitled for the protection of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the disputed construction was not a permanent structure. [701B] 2. The High Cou rt was right in holding, that the disputed wall was a material alteration and the structure of a shed was a material alterations. [702C] 3. The High tions were right in not interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the First Appellate Court. [703D] 4. The High rity of the disputed structure had not been proved by the respondent. [704E] 5. The High ness of the disputed wall had not been established by the respondent by producing any evidence. The High f rom the Court was right in not relying on the observations of the Full Bench in Sita Ram 's case (supra). [704F] 6. The High R e Court was right, in holding that there was material alteration in a structure or structure which did not affect the question as to whether the construction was permanent or temporary in nature. [705G] 7. The High ly Court was right when it held that the construction was temporary in nature and the same was not a substantial alteration in the ti tions. [706G] 7A] 8. The High m e Court was not right in holding the disputed structure to be permanent in nature. The High p ersons case (Supra) was not right. [707G] 9. The High al Court was right. The High j udgment of the High Court was not correct. [708G] 9: The High Court was right that the disputed structures were permanent in nature and they were not put to any alteration in their structure or structure. [807G] 10. The High Co urt was right when the disputed structure or structure was put to any permanent structure or structure and the same had been constructed on the disputed structure. [907G] 8. In the instant case, the disputed structure is a material alteration which could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation.

The respondent company had filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 28,479/. The company had filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside the ex parte decree. The company filed an application for setting aside an ex parte decree on the ground that the summons were not served on the company. The company also filed an application in the High Court for setting aside a decree on the grounds that the summons was not served on its behalf. The High Court allowed the application and set aside the ex p parte decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the summons served on the respondent company was not served in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The summons served on a gentleman who is described as an office Assistant, on 17 1975 at 3.40 P.M. and on the date of the filing of the suit, the summons was duly served on the defendant company. The summons was duly signed by the defendant company and the address of the person who was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. The summons were duly served on its address. The summons did not bear the seal of the company. [701A B] 2. The summons sent to the defendant company was duly served by the company on its address and the address. The defendant company had not filed any rejoinder to the counter affidavit filed by the company. It was not the case of the defendant company that the summons sent to its address was duly served. [702B] 3. The summons issued to the defendant was duly served and the address was duly affixed. The defendant had not filed an affidavit of the defendant. The summons had been duly served on his address. The notice sent to the plaintiff was duly served upon the defendant company on its registered office. The defendant was not served with the summons on its address nor was it the case of its service on the defendant. [703C] 4. The summons in the present case was duly served in accordance therewith. The defendant did not file any rejoinder to its counter affidavit. The summons which were duly served upon its address were duly served. The defendant Company had not filed a rejoinder to its written statement. [704D] 5. The summons for service of the summons on the defendant was not duly served on it. The summons, therefore, were duly served and it was left at the registered office of the company at the registered address. [705E] 6. The summons must be served on the address of a person who is entitled to be served on his behalf. The summons should be served on a person who has been identified and in his presence the address of his person who is bound to accept summons on his behalf, or where the defendant is not a person who was not a person entitled to be serving on his behalf in accordance with sub clause (b), of Rule 2. The defendant must be served with the notice on his address and the name and address of the defendant, or where he is not a company, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of summons on his address or where the company is not a registered office, and there are no agents empowered to accept summons. [706E] 7. The summons cannot be served on any person who is not a party to the suit. [707E] 8. The summons is not served on a firm or a firm. The summons does not bear the signature of the firm or a partner. The summons may be served on an individual or a firm or on the firm or on a firm. [708E] 9. The summons has been served on the firm and the firm or the firm or partners. [709G] 9. In the present case, the summons served upon the respondent company on its behalf was not served. [807E] 10.

The appellant was the owner of the land in dispute. He filed a suit for declaration that he was in possession of the land and the respondents were in possession of it. The respondents filed a written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint. The trial court framed a preliminary issue that the dispute was a breach of peace and that the respondents were not in possession of any land. The trial Court held that the dispute had ceased to exist and that the dispute could not be said to be a breach of the peace. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the dispute existed at any stage of the proceedings and that the breach of peace existed at any time when the order was passed. The High court further held that the order of the Magistrate was not a final order and that the Magistrate had no power to take proceedings under section 145, Cr.P.C. for a breach of a peace. The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Court. The High Judge allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of Magistrate. The High 'Court held that the Magistrate was justified in holding that the dispute having ceased to exist at any stage when the order of preliminary order was passed, the order of magistrate was not a nullity. The High, Court, therefore, allowed the revision application. In the present appeal, it is contended that the High Court was in error in holding that there was a breach on the part of the Magistrate to mention in his final order the finding that there was an apprehension of breach of peace. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts were right in holding that a breach of law exists when the order is passed. [701B] 1.2. The High was right in holding, that the dispute did not exist at any time and that the order was not a decree. [702C] 1.3. The High is right in holding in favour of the appellant that the dispute which was pending between the parties was a breach as contemplated by section 145, Criminal Procedure Code. [703D] 1.4. The High Curt was right in setting aside the order passed by the Magistrate. [704E] 1.5. The High Power Court was right in quashing the order of a Magistrate. [77F] 1.6. The High power of the Magistrate under section 145 is not a curable irregularity which is not sufficient to vitiate the order of an Magistrate. [78F] 1,6. The order of the High Court is set aside and the revision application is allowed.

The appellant, a non resident, was assessed to income tax on the sale of his goods in British India. The appellant claimed that the profits of the business were apportioned to the manufacture of the goods in British Indian States, and that the profits were apportioned to his business in British India, and that, therefore, the profits were liable to be taxed on such portions of the profits as apportioned to the business in British Indian India. The Income tax Officer, who heard the appellant, held that the profits had accrued to it in British India and that the appellant was not liable to tax on such portions. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the profits accrued to it, and that they were not liable to be assessed to tax on the sales of the goods. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no evidence to show that the profits belonged to the appellant, and that it was not liable as it had not been treated as profits by the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and held that the income of the appellant was liable to be included in the profits of British India, but the question was whether the profits were assessable to tax on those portions of the income of British India. In appeal to the Tribunal, the appellant contended that the profits must be assessed to income Tax on the sale or purchase of the goods, and that since the profits were apportionable to the manufacture, the profits must also be assessed to the tax on the goods. Held, that the appellant could not be assessed to sales tax on the profits of business, because the profits were divided into two parts, and that there was nothing to show that they were liable to tax, because the appellant had been able to show that there was any connection between the profits of a business, and that he was not liable, because the income of that business was apportioned to the manufacturing business. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 42(1) and the appeal must be dismissed.

The assessee was appointed as a Manager of the mill at the initial stage and he was paid a sum of Rs. 75,465 as commission to the General Manager. The assessee was appointed by the General Manager as a Manager. The remuneration of the employees was fixed at Rs. 75.465 and the rate of commission was fixed at 25% of the commission. The assessee claimed that the commission paid to him was not wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and that the rate of 25% was fixed for him. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the commission was not paid wholly for the purpose and not for the purpose. The Tribunal, however, held that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee holding that the commission had been paid to the General Managers and the commission was paid to them for the purpose, of the business and not for any purpose. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Tribunal. The High court held that the amount of Rs.75,465 paid to theGeneral Manager was not a revenue expenditure and that the assessee had not made any profit. The High 'Court further held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively in the business of a trader or it was not laid out or exclusively for the purposes of the business. The High' Court, however held that the expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose for the purpose which the assessee was able to secure an order from the account of the General Manager and the commission paid for the purpose was not wholly or exclusively for any purpose of the assessee, and that the amount laid out or spent wholly and exclusively was exclusively for the business of that assessee. The High. Court, however found that the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out and exclusively for carrying on business and that the same was not incurred by the assessee in the character of a trader. The High, Court, however. held that the said amount was laid into consideration for determining the remuneration of the employee of the assessee in fixing the remuneration of his employees. The HighCT. Court, therefore, held that it was not a case of commercial expediency for determining the amount of commission paid to the general Manager. The Hight. Court, on appeal, held that though the commission was laid out, it was not an expenditure wholly and exclusively to the business of an assessee and therefore the allowance was reasonable and the allowance was not a part of the business, but was only a part of business. The assessee, therefore, appealed to the High Court. The High Courts held that the allowance was unreasonable and the allowance had been rightly restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee. In the present case, the High Court held that the rate was reasonable and not a part or exclusively for carrying out business and that it was a part of its business. The appellant, therefore, contended that the High Court was right in taking the view that the rate fixed for the assessee was reasonable and that the allowance had to be fixed for the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Power Court was right, in holding that a sum of rupees 75,465 paid by the assessee to the General manager was not a expenditure wholly and solely for the purpose or exclusively for his business of the business or profession of the assessee as required under section 10 (2)(xv). [749B] 2. The High power of the Tribunal to come to a conclusion whether an expenditure was wholly or exclusively laid out or solely for the purposes and exclusively for his purpose of the profession of the business is not correct. [749C] 3.

The appellant was employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, and was working as a workman in the Dighas factory of B. Bata Sho Company (Private). The appellant was employed as a workman under the Dighas Factory of Bata Shri Bata Shu Company (Private), Limited, a registered trade union of which the appellant was a member. The appellant was appointed as a workman by the management of Bata Bata Shila Company (Private); and the management of the appellant was authorised to appoint the appellant as a workman. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Patna praying for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Tribunal dated March 11, 1957, and for a direction to the Tribunal to give a fresh representation to the Secretary of the Union. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had committed a serious error in rejecting the appellant 's application for a writ. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had committed an error in rejecting a petition under Article 226 of the constitution. [701B] 2. The Tribunal was not right in rejecting the petitioner 's application under article 226. The High court was not right, in rejecting the petition under article 227 of the Constitution. [702C] 3. The Tribunal has not given any reasons for rejecting the petitioner's application under article 227. The High Courts were not right in holding that the Tribunal was not justified in rejecting the application under article 228. [703G] 4. The Tribunal did not give any reasons for rejection of the petitioner ' s application under article 136 of the Constitution and the High Court was not right. [704G] 5. The Tribunal's order was not correct. The Tribunal could not have rejected the petitioner ' 's application on the ground that the Tribunal did not record reasons for rejecting his application under article 133 of the Constitution, because the Tribunal had not given any reason for rejecting the application. [705G] 6. The Tribunal, in the present case, had not given reasons for rejecting appellant 's representation. The Tribunal failed to give any reasons. The Tribunal also failed to give reasons for rejecting petitioner 's representation, because the petitioner 'S union had made the complaint against the appellant ' s union. [706G] 7. The Tribunal in the present appeal had not given sufficient reasons for rejecting applicant 's representation and the High court was right in rejecting appellant ' s application. [806G] 8. The Tribunal committed an error by rejecting the appellant's application under Article 226. [707G] 9. The Tribunal erred in rejecting the applicant 's application without giving any reasons. [708G] 9(i) The Tribunal was right in holding the appellant ' 's representation to be rejected. [709G] 10. The Tribunal ought to have given reasons for rejection. [710G] (ii) The Tribunal had not applied its mind to the facts of the case and had not given a proper reason for rejecting appellant's application. [907G] (iii) The Tribunal did give reasons for rejection and the appellant 'was not entitled to any relief. [712G] (iv) The Tribunal has failed to give sufficient reasons for rejection, because the appellant 'S union was not a member of any trade union. [807G] 10(i) In the present case the Tribunal had given reasons for not rejecting the appellant' s application under Article 227 of the constitution, because the High Court had not given proper reasons for rejecting it. [713G] (v) The Tribunal failed in giving reasons for rejecting respondent 's application.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in dispute. The respondent No. 1, who was the tenant of the appellants, filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the ground that Kedar Nath had died during the pendency of the appeal. The respondent filed a written statement and denied the allegations made in the plaint. The trial court framed a preliminary issue on the basis of the pleadings of the parties and held that the suit was not maintainable. The trial Court held that the appellants were tenants in the premises and, therefore, the appeal was not maintainable and dismissed the suit. The respondent preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that Kedar Nath was not a tenant of the appellant and, therefore the appeal was incompetent. The respondent, therefore, filed an appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appeal was not competent. The respondent was not a party to the appeal. [901 A] 2. The respondent had a right to remain in occupation of the premises on the basis that Kedar Nath, one of the persons having a joint right to remain as a tenant of one of the landlords and not as a tenant. The respondent could not have been ejected from the premises when he had a right of being a tenant of all the other persons who had a joint right. [902 A] 3. The right to remain the tenant of Kedar Nath was a joint right and, therefore could not have ejected him as a tenant if he had a joint interest in the premises. [903 B] 4. The right of the respondent to remain in possession on the basis on the basis as a tenant was a joint and separate right. [093 C] 5. The right under O.XXII, r. 4 of O.XXI, r. 3 of O.XXXII, r, 3 of OXXII, was not a joint right but a joint right, and, therefore. the right to remain a joint right was not a separate right. The right was not an independent right. [1001 D] 6. The right conferred by O.XXIII, r. 5 of O. XXXII, r., 3 of OXXXII, was a joint tenancy and, therefore,. the right to continue as a tenant could not have accrued to the respondent. [904 A] 7. The right given to the respondent to continue as tenant of the premises was a joint one and, therefore a joint right could not have devolved on the appellant. [905 B] 8. The right granted to the respondent under O.XXXI, r., 4 of OXXI, was a right to continue the appeal as a tenant and, therefore it was not a competent appeal to the respondent, and, consequently, the appeal could not have taken to be an appeal to which the provisions of O. XLII, r.. 4 of OXXXI, were applicable. [906 C] 9. The right which was conferred on the respondent under r. 4 was a joint interest and, therefore there was no question of the respondent being a tenant. [907 D] 9. In the present case, the respondent was not the tenant of a joint Hindu family. The right, therefore, to continue as an owner of the premises, was a separate right and, consequently the respondent was entitled to continue as the tenant of that premises. [094 E] 9. It is true that the right to be a joint Hindu property is a right to be exercised in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants, if all the plaintiffs and defendants, if any, have a common right to remain and to be entitled to continue in possession on that basis. But the right to hold the joint Hindu family property on the basis thereof is a right which is a joint Hindu right. [995 E] 9, 10.

The appellant, a tenant, filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the ground that the respondent had terminated the tenancy in terms of the lease deed dated January 28, 1952. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment on the ground of default in payment of rent. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a tenant and that the notice was not a notice under section 111(g) of the TP Act. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the notice under section 112(g) was not a valid notice and that the respondent did not have the requisite notice. The High court held that the respondent could not be said to be a tenant and the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 111(h) of the Act. The High 'Court further held that the appellant was a tenant and was not a landlord. The High' Court held that there was no requirement in English law of a written notice to the lessee of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground in regard to the requirement of the written notice. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled, in view of the principles of justice, equity and good conscience, to have the effect of a written statement of the respondent. The High. Court held that since the notice was a notice under Section 111(g), the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the protection of Section 111(h). The High Court, therefore, held that the provisions of the TP act were not applicable to the lease of 1952 and the appellant had no notice under section 106 of the TP. Act. The appellant was not a 'tenant and was not entitled under section 111 (g) of that Act to have the protection of the rent control law. The High, Court, therefore held that the lease of the appellant was valid and binding on the respondent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the lease was not a lease of 1952 but was a statutory recognition of a principle of justice, good conscience and good conscience. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The lease of 1952 was a statutory recognized lease of 1952. The lease was not in existence at the time when the lease was executed. The lease deed was not a statutory recognition. The lease had been determined by efflux of time limited thereby in terms of section 111 (h) of that act. [819C] 1.2. The lease is not a statutory recognized tenancy. The lease has been determined by lapse of time limited by efflux of period limited by efflux. The lease cannot be said to have been determined by a lapse of time. [820D] 1.3. The lease in question was not a legal lease. The lease having been determined by the efflux of time, the lease having been held to be valid and binding, the lease being a statutory recognition, the lease was rightly determined by efflux. [821E] 1.4. The lease being a legal lease, the lease cannot be held to be a valid one. [822F] 1.5. The lease, being a statutory recognized licence, is not a lease. The lessee having been determined, the lease is not an ordinary lease. [823F] 1,5. The lessee had been determined to be a statutory recognized tenant. [824F] 1:1.6. The lease does not create a lease. It is a statutory recognition and the lease is a statutory recognized one. [924F] 2.1.7. The lease can be terminated by efflux of the time limited by lapse of period limited. [825F] 1.:1.8. The lease would be a statutory recognition if the lease is determined by efflux and the lease has been held to have been held to take effect from the date of the lease.

The appellant, who was dismissed from service, was dismissed from the service on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The appellant, who had been dismissed from service on the basis of the findings of the enquiry officer, was dismissed. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal on the ground, inter alia, that the Governor had not given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action proposed to he taken in regard thereto and that the order of the Governor was not in accordance with the provisions of the unamended clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Court, on a consideration of the evidence adduced before it, came to the conclusion that the Governor was satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it was not expedient to hold the inquiry under the principal clause, that the Government was satisfied that it was expedient to hold such inquiry. The High court, on a reference, held that the Governor, had not given the opportunity of showing an opportunity of show cause against his action proposed to him. On appeal, the High Court, HELD: 1. The Governor had to arrive at the conclusion that it was not reasonably practicable to hold the enquiry under the principal clauses, that the government servant was satisfied that the Government had to arrive for some reason to be recorded by that authority in writing. [801 E] 2. The Governor, in exercise of his powers under article 311 of Constitution, is satisfied that in order to give an opportunity of explaining the circumstances, he had to be given an opportunity, of showing cause. [802 F] 3. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Tribunal was dismissed. The Tribunal held that the loss was not determined in pursuance of a return filed under Section 139 and set off under sub section (1) of Section 74A of the Act. The Tribunal further held that the claim of set off was admissible in view of the provisions of sub section (2A) of Section 80 of the Act and the loss was rightly set off under the provisions of the Act, and set off was rightly set aside. The Tribunal also held that the appellant ' s loss was not set off under Section 80 of 1922 Act and set off in accordance with the provisions of Section 80 was rightly set Off. The Tribunal, however, held that the losses were not set off in the computation of the loss and set off. The High Court, however, set aside the order of assessment and allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the loss had not been determined in pursuance o f the provisions of section 80 of the Income Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The loss was not assessed in pursuance of the provisions contained in sub section (3) of section 80. The loss was rightly held to be not set off. [701B] 1.2 The loss was assessed in pursuance o n the provisions of subsection (3) and sub section (4) of section 73 of the Act respectively. [702C] 1.3 The loss was correctly set off under section 80 of 1922. [703D] 1.4 The loss was set off under subsection (3). The loss was computed under the Act and set Off. [704E] 1.5 The loss was determined in pursuance to the provisions of sections 80 of the 1922 Act. [705G] 1.6 The loss was to be set off under sections 80 of 1922 and section 80 of 1961 Act. [605G] 2.1 The losses were to be set Off. It was not set Off. In the circumstances, the loss was tobe set off under [705F] 2.2 The losses were set off under Sections 80 of the 1961 Act. The loss had not to be setoff under Sections 80 and 80 of the 1962 Act. [805G] 3.2 The assessee had not set off any loss under Sections 80 or 80 of the 1963 Act. The losses were not to be carried forward under Sections 80. [706G] 3.(a) The loss was thus set off under Chapter IV of the 1961 and the loss had been set off under that Chapter. [707A] 3.(b) The loss had been computed under the provisions contained under Chapter IV and the loss has been set off in respect of the loss. [708A] 3.3 The losses were computed under the Income tax act, 1961. [709B] 3.4 The losses were assessed under the provisions relating to set off under Part IV of the 1922 and the loss under Part IV was set off in Part IV of that Chapter.
