The respondent was recruited to the Defence Science Service on October 12, 1966. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Airport) (Deptt. of Defence) and was posted in that service. He was promoted to the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and was posted to the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Development and production (Airport). He was posted to that service. On the basis of the recommendations of the 6th Central Pay Commission, the respondent was promoted to that service on October 12. 1966. The respondent was promoted as Senior Scientific Officer on October 12 and was posted as Senior Scientific Officers on October 12 1966. The services of the respondent were governed by the Service Rules. The respondent retired from service on October 13, 1966. The service conditions of the respondent as a Senior Scientific Officer were governed by Rule 12(a) of the Service Rules and the respondent was appointed to the Defence Training and Research Development Organisation (Dept. of Defence), and was promoted to those posts on October 12 1967. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Tribunal and the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent challenged the validity of Rule 12(b) of the Rules before this Court. The High court held that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the enhanced age of superannuation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent is entitled to the benefits of the enhanced superannuation age. [801B] 2. The respondent had been recruited to the defence Science Service on the basis of a competitive examination held by the Defence Research & Development Organisation (DODO), and he was posted to those posts in the Defence Science Services. He was appointed to those posts by the Defence Science service. He had been promoted to those post by the Defence Training & Research Development Organisation, and was posted on that basis. [802C] 3. The respondent, therefore, was not entitled for the benefit of enhanced age of retirement. [803D] 4. The respondent could not be said to be a member of the other unit. He was not entitled either to the enhanced age or to the members of the other units. [804E] 5. The respondent cannot be said to have been appointed to the defence science Service on the ground that he had not been retired. [805F] 6. The respondent did not opt for the revised age of superannuation and he was not entitled, therefore, to the benefit under the enhanced age. [820G] 7. The respondent having been recruited to Defence Science Service, he was not governed by the service rules. [806F] 7. In the circumstances, the respondent is not entitled to any benefit under the revised age. [823G] 8. The respondent being a member of one unit, the question of his retirement benefits does not arise. [823H] 8. In the instant case, the respondent had been appointed to Defence Science Services on the basis that he had been recruited in the Defence Research Service. He was, therefore, not entitled to get the benefit of revised age of retirement on the basis on the basis whether he had been retired or not. [823E] 9. The respondent has been recruited to defence Science Service and he was, therefore entitled to the enhanced retirement age. [825G] 10. The respondent would be entitled to the revised age on the basis either of the two units or of the two unit. [823F] 8.1 The respondent was not a member of any other unit. The respondent's services were governed by different set of Rules and the service conditions of his employees were governed by separate set of Rules. [823A] 8.2 The respondent was appointed in the Defence Training Service on the recommendation of the 6 th Central Pay Commission. The respondent continued in service till he attained the age of 58 years.

The appellant was a member of the Municipality and was elected as a member of a Municipality. He was elected as the Chairman of the Municipality. He challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the appellant had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 21(1) of the Act. The learned Judge held that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practices under section 21 (1) of Act. He, however, held that the charge of corrupt practice was proved against the appellant and the appellant was found guilty of corrupt Practice. The learned judge, however, found that the appellant could not be held guilty of corrupt conduct under section 21 of the Act and, therefore, he was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 21(2) of the Representation of the People Act. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant has now come up before this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the appellant did not have any right to be heard in the matter. [775B] 2. The High Courts were right in holding, that the appellant 's election to the Sangli City Municipality was not liable to be set aside on the ground of corrupt practice. [776C] 3. The High 'Court was right in setting aside the order of the learned Judge. [778D] 4. The High' Court was right in quashing the order of dismissal of the appellant. [782E] 5. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was no evidence on which the Judge could have come to the conclusion that the appellant committed corrupt practice. The High, Court was right. [786E] 6. The High] 7. The appellant was not entitled under section 21 to have the election set aside. The High was right in rejecting the appellant's application for issue of summonses to him when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968. [787G] 7. In the present case, the appellant was not able to show that he had been guilty by corrupt practice. He was not able, to show that the appellant himself had been guilty. [785G] 8. The High "Court was right, that the evidence of the two witnesses was not satisfactory. The evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient to come to the finding that the appellant and his election agent had been guilty for corrupt practice. There was no evidence to show that they had been guilty under section 21.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1913], and the appellant was registered as a dealer under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant was assessed to sales tax in respect of the sales effected by it to its dealers. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad, challenging the validity of the impugned notification, and the High Court quashed the same. The High Court held that the impugned notification was ultra vires the powers of the legislature under which the tax was levied and that the impugned Act was not a law in respect of tax on the sale of goods, and that the State legislature had no power to impose a tax on the occasion of sale of goods. The High court held that the State Legislature had no power under entry 54 to enact a law with retrospective operation, and that it was competent to the legislature under the impugned Act to enact a tax on sale of goods and that the legislature had no competence to enact a valid law with retrospective effect. The High, Court held that there was no power in the legislature under entry 54, to enact a retrospective law with retrospective force, and that there was a valid law in respect to sales tax, and that no tax could be imposed with retrospective operation. The High ' Court held that a tax on sales effected by the dealer to its dealers was a tax on those sales, and that since the State legislature did not make a law with prospective operation, the impugned notification could not be held to be invalid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is not a law within the meaning of entry 54, and as there is no other entry in the State List, the impugned Act is not a valid law. [701B] 2. The impugned Act is a law in the sense that it is a law made by the legislature under Entry 54, and that, therefore, the impugned Notification is not a tax on transactions which are not within the purview of the State legislature under entry 52. [702C] 3. The impugned Notification is a law which is not a statute in the sense in which it is made by the Legislature under entry 54. [703D] 4. The impugned notifications are not a law made under entry 54 and are, therefore, not a law under entry 54 in List II. [704E] 5. The impugned Notifications are not a tax in the sense of a tax on goods which are not known as goods. The impugned orders are, therefore liable to be quashed. [705G] 6. The impugned order is, therefore, quashed. The appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment is set aside. The writ petitions filed by the appellant are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court, Ambala for offences under Section 376(2)(f) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. He was also convicted for the offence under Section 376 (2)(f). The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The prosecution case is that the appellant was married to one Smt. Pushpa Devi on the date of the incident. The appellant was married on the date when the incident took place. The appellant had a child. The appellant married to Smt. Pushpa on the date the incident took places. The appellant and the victim 's husband were living together. The appellant, however, did not return to his house. The appellant is a young man. He was a young man and was a young boy. He was not a young man, but a young man who was a young girl. The appellant also did not return. The appellant did not return and he was a young person. The appellant filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant had been falsely implicated in the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant must be given the benefit of doubt. [701B] 2. The appellant should be given the benefits of doubt. He should be given all the benefits of the doubt. [801C] 3. The appellant 's husband was a young lady and was a good man. He had a good career and had a good reputation. He was in a position to maintain his family. He was an old man. He could not have been convicted for the offences under Section 354 of the Indian penal Code. [802D] 4. The appellant could not have committed the offence of rape. He was, therefore, entitled to the benefit of the doubt and the High Court was right in setting aside the conviction and the sentence. [803E] 5. The appellant cannot be given the advantage of the sentence. He must be given all his benefits. [804F] 6. The appellant can hardly be given the same benefits. He must, therefore, be given the said benefits. [820G] 7. The appellant would be entitled to the benefits of Section 354 of Indian Penal Code. [820H] 7. In the instant case, the appellant was a young woman and was a hard criminal. He was convicted for the murder of her husband. He was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. [820A] 8. The appellant's conviction and sentence are, therefore, liable to be set aside. [820B] 9. The appellant shall be given the full benefits of Section 376(1) of the Code. [823G] 10. The appellant will be entitled to all the benefits under Section 354(1) and 354(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1956. The appellant, a public limited company, was incorporated on April 25, 1956. The assessee was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The assessee, a company registered under the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1956. It was registered under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1913. The assessee claimed that the compensation received by it related to the acquisition of land and the amount of compensation payable to it related to that amount of compensation. The assessee contended that the compensation was not a receipt of a revenue nature and, therefore, a receipt of compensation was not an offer or tender of the compensation determined by the Collector. The High Court held that the compensation payable to the assessee was not a payment of compensation and, therefore the assessee was entitled to an additional compensation. The High court held that the amount of the compensation received was not a consideration of the compensation and, consequently, the assessee was liable to pay the additional compensation. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the amount received by the assessee was a consideration of compensation and the amount to be determined in accordance with the decision of the High Court was not a mere offer or tender. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'consideration of the compensation" in section 18 of the Act is a term of art and it is not a question of merely quantifying the amount to the assessee. [601B] 2. The expression "consideration of the amount to which the right to receive payment" is in dispute is a term which is in dispute and it is a question of fact whether the amount to whom the right to compensation accrued or accrued is determined is a consideration of an offer or tendering of the compensation. [602C] 3. The expression is of wide import and is not confined to the amount of an offer. The expression must be understood in the sense that it is not confined only to the amount towhich the right to the compensation accrued or is determined. [603D] 4. The expression has to be understood in its ordinary sense. It is not confined merely to the amount which the right has accrued or is deemed to accrue or is deemed not to accrue. [604E] 5. The expression does not mean that the amount to Which the right has been determined is left to be determined by the final court. [605F] 6. The expression, 'consideration of an offer" in section 19 of the Act means that the amount which has accrued or has been determined by the decision of a court. [06F] 7. The expression cannot be confined to the amounts which the right had accrued or has accrued or had been determined by a court. The expression may be confined to a particular amount of compensation which has accrued but has not been determined by any court. [ 605F] 8. The expression should be understood in a sense that it should be confined to something which the right actually has accrued or was determined by a Court. [606F] 9. The expression would be confined to only the amount which had accrued or had accrued or was deemed to accrue. The expression will be confined to any amount which had been determined as payable by the Collector to the assessee as compensation. [ 605G] 9. In the present case, the amount of Rs.7,36,190 payable to the appellant was not a sum payable to the respondent. [607F] 10. The amount of compensation received by the respondent was not a part of the compensation payable. [608F] 11. The amount payable to the company was not a capital receipt. The amount was not a revenue receipt. The respondent was not entitled to any compensation. [06G] 12. The amount paid was not a money receipt. The payment was not a commercial receipt. The money was not a profit.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant from a shop in dispute on the ground of personal necessity. The tenant filed a suit against the landlord for eviction of a tenant from a building in dispute on two grounds, namely, (1) that the landlord was entitled to possession on one or other of the statutory grounds mentioned in Section 12(1) (f) of the Act, and (2) that the tenant in question was entitled to protection of a tenant based upon public policy. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the landlord had withdrawn all his defence to the suit and the decree for eviction was accordingly passed. The tenant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the compromise decree was not binding on the landlord and the tenant in the absence of any specific provision in the Act or any other law for the protection of a tenancy based upon public Policy, the compromise decree could not be passed. The High court also held that the compromise was legal and was in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the compromise decree. The High 'Court further held that the landlord could not be permitted to withdraw all his defence in the suit and that the compromise could not be executed in accordance with law. The High' Court further held that there was no material before the Court to come to the conclusion that the compromise had been arrived at in accordance with Section 12(2) (f). The High ' Court further held: "The compromise decree was binding on the parties and the tenant was bound to make out a case for eviction in accordance with provisions of the law. The compromise decree was, therefore, binding on the tenant and the landlord. The compromise was not binding upon the parties and was in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act and any other law. The tenant in question had withdrawn all the defence to the eviction of the appellant. The compromise had been accepted and the case was accordingly decreed in accordance with condition of the compromise. The tenant had withdrawn all her defence to the proceedings. The landlord had filed a suit in the Court for eviction of her tenant from a room in dispute on one or more of the grounds mentioned in section 12(1)(f) of The landlord had withdrawn her defence to that suit and the compromise was binding on her. The tenant also filed a suit on the basis of the compromise decree for eviction. The tenant contended that the compromise in the suit was not binding between the parties and, therefore, the compromise was not valid and binding on the tenants. The High. Court held that the decree for ejectment was not binding and the compromise had not been binding on the landlords. The High, Court, however, held that the consent decree was binding between the landlord and her and the tenant had no right to get the decree for possession. The High Curt, however, reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise in the present case was not binding. The compromise is binding on the appellants and the tenants. [901B] 2. The compromise has been arrived at after a full and complete satisfaction of the terms of the compromise and the decree has been passed. [902C] 3. The compromise does not affect the rights of the parties. The compromise cannot be binding on the appellant. [903D] 4. The compromise can be binding on both the parties and it cannot be binding upon the appellant. It is not binding on him. [904E] 5. The compromise, therefore, cannot be binding between the appellant and the tenants, because the compromise is binding between the appellants and their tenants. [0904F] 6. The compromise could not have been binding on both parties and it could not have be binding on them. [905F] 7. The compromise would not affect the right of the parties to get the suit decided on the basis that the compromise is not binding between them.

The assessee company, a public limited company, had a business of manufacturing and selling shares in the relevant accounting years. The assessee company had a business in the relevant previous year and the profits were distributed in the relevant year. The assessee Company had a business dealing in the relevant assessment years. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the loss incurred by the company in earlier years was a capital loss and not a capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, set aside the order of the Income tax Officer and held that the losses incurred by the assessee company in earlier year were not capital losses. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the loss was a capital expenditure and not a revenue loss. The High Court, however, reversed the order of assessment. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the loss suffered by the company was a capital asset and not a trading loss. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The loss incurred by a company in earlier previous year was a capital gain and not a profit. [701C] 2. The loss was incurred by the Company in earlier years and the profits made in earlier years were not capital loss. [702C] 3. The loss suffered by a company was a revenue loss and not capital loss incurred by it. [703D] 4. The loss could not be said to be a capital loss because the company had incurred losses previously incurred by it in earlier years. [704E] 5. The loss had been incurred by the appellant company in earlier period and the profits had been distributed in the previous year. [705E] 6. The loss, if any, incurred by the respondent company in earlier two years was a revenue expenditure. [706E] 7. The loss did not result in the loss incurred in earlier years because the company did not declare dividend in earlier years but only in the case of a company whose business consists wholly or mainly in the relevant Accounting years. [605E] 7A. The loss arose in earlier years when the company declared dividend in earlier year. The loss in earlier years had been incurred in earlier year and the profit had been distributed. [707E] 8. The loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ was not a capital gain. The loss therefore was a capital receipt. [708E] 9. The loss which was incurred in earlier two year was a revenue receipt. [807E] 10. The loss sustained by the company could not be considered to be a revenue loss because the loss incurred was a capital item.

The High 'Court further held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was not barred by section 37 of the Act. The High, Court, therefore, held that the decision of the Civil judge was not a decision of the arbitrator under section 12(6) of the Act and that the decision was not a final decision of the civil court. The High.' Court further held that section 37 was not applicable in the present case. The appellant, therefore, filed a second revision before the High 'Court. The High Curt allowed the second revision and set aside the order of the Civil 'Court. In the present appeal, the appellant has challenged the correctness of the High ' Court 's decision. The High Courts have held that the provisions of section 37 of 'the Act are not applicable to arbitrations under section 12 of the Act, and that the High 'court was not justified in holding that the Civil 'court had no jurisdiction, and that section 37 applied to arbitrations under the Act. In the result, the High ' court was right in holding that section 37 applies to arbitrations under sections 46 and 47 of the Act." In the present case, the High Court held: "Section 37 of the .Act provides for the appointment of an arbitrator by the State Government. The High "Court" has no jurisdiction to make the applicable to the arbitration under section 12 (6) of 'the .Act. The High" Court held that section 12(4) of the . Act applies to arbitrations and that section 39 of the .the Act applies to all arbitrations under section 13 of the .The High 'Court held that section 13 of 'the ,Act applies to arbitrations other than those under section 13(4) and that section 13(6) applies to arbitrations not covered by section 12(5) of the ,Act. The appellant has filed this appeal against the order of Civil Judge modifying the award made under section 12. The appellant contended that section 37(1) of the 'Act applies to all arbitration under section 13 (4) and section 37 of . The High Court, in its judgment, held that section 36 of the . The Act applies to the proceedings under section 12 and section 37(4) to the proceedings which are pending before the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings. The High [Court] held that section 39 applies to arbitrations which are pending in the court before the arbitrator and that section 36 applies to arbitrations pending in the Court before the arbitrator, and that Section 37(1)(b) applies to all proceedings pending in the arbitrator as they emerge after appropriate proceedings." The High Court further held: "...The High Court has held that section 38 of the . .Act applies to the arbitration proceedings pending in court before the Arbitrator and that section 38 applies to all pending proceedings in the arbitrator. It is true that section 38 does not apply to arbitrations pending before the Arbitrator. But section 38 does apply to arbitrations which have been pending in the courts before the arbitrator but section 38 does no apply to arbitrations under Chapter III of the .

The respondent Corporation issued a resolution on the basis of the resolution passed by the respondent Corporation in 1988. The respondent Corporation issued an order dated 30th September, 1988, which was challenged by the petitioner in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the resolution. The respondent corporation challenged the validity of the resolution by filing a writ petition in the High court. The High court allowed the writ appeal and quashed the order of the respondent corporation. The High 'Court held that the resolution passed in 1988 was not a valid classification and the classification made by the respondent corporation was not a proper classification. Hence, the writ petition was allowed. The High' Court held that the classification made in 1988 was valid and the classification was valid. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The classification made by respondent corporation was valid and was not in accordance with the law. [901B] 2. The respondent was appointed as Enquiry Officer under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi particle Settlement dated 19th October, 1966. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition. The respondent preferred a writ appeal before the Division Bench of the High court. The Division Bench of that Court allowed the appeal and quashed the order of the learned single Judge. The Division bench of the High Cou rt held that the respondent was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The Division Benami Banking Co. Ltd. vs The State Bank of India, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. The respondent had been appointed as Enquiry Officers by the Bank in the year 1964 and he was appointed as a Enquiry Officers by a de facto order dated January 9, 1979. The respondent challenged the appointment of a Enquiry Officer by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The Division Court dismissed the writ appeal. The respondent appealed to this Court. The High Cou iction of the High Courts in the impugned order of punishment was not justified. [879D] 4. The High Courts were right in holding, that the respondent did not raise any objection to continuance of the Enquiry officer by the said Mr. U.B.'s order. [882E] 5. The High Cour t was right in saying that the respondent could not raise any objections to the continuance o f the Enquiry Officer by the said U.B., Menon as an administrative officer. [883E] 6. The High cour t was not justified in holding that a second or a second enquiry was not justified and that the respondent 's order was not justified, because the High Court was not justified either in holding that there was an appointment to the office which was defective or that the respondent himself was not entitled t o the benefits to which he was entitled to. [884F] 7. The High tions were right in quashing and setting aside the order of penalty. [885G] 8. The High rity of the High Cour s Court was not correct in holding that an enquiry was not warranted. [886F] 8. In the instant case, the respondent was appointed a Enquiry Officer and he was not entitled for any relief. [887G] 9. The High ness of the High cour s Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of removal. [890G] 9, 10. The High Co urt was right in setting aside the impugned order. [982A] 10. The appellant No. 1 was the Secretary of the appellant No. 2 and the appellant No 1 was the District Magistrate. The appellant No. I was the Secretary and the appellant Nos. 2 and 3 were the District Magistrate and the appellant no. 1 was a member of the judiciary. The appellant Nos. 1 and 2 were the District Magistrates. The appellant no. 2 was the Secretary. The appellant was the District Magistrates and the appellant nos. 1 and 3 were also the District Magistrate, and the appellant were the District Judges. The appellant nos. 2 and 4 were the District Judge and the appellant was the Sessions Judge. The prosecution case was that the appellant No, 1, a member of a judicial service, was the District Judge. The appellant contended that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try the case and that the District Judge had no jurisdiction. Held, that the District Court had no jurisdiction in the matter. The District Magistrate had jurisdiction to try a case and that he had no jurisdiction, and that the High Court had no power to try the appellant No., 1. The District Court had jurisdiction to entertain a case. The District Judge had jurisdiction to hear a case. He had jurisdiction to decide a case. In the present case the District Magistrate was not the District Judge, and the High Court was not the Sessions Judge, and therefore the Sessions Judge had no power, and the Sessions Judge was not the High Court. The District judge had no jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to entertain a complaint. The District and Sessions Judge had jurisdiction, and the complaint was therefore not maintainable. The District & Sessions Judge had therefore no jurisdiction to entertain the complaint. The High Court was therefore not right in holding that the District & Sessions judge had no power under section 482 to entertain a criminal complaint. The appeal of the appellant Nos 1 and 2 was therefore dismissed. The appellant filed a special leave petition against the order of the High Court quashing the complaint. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court had no jurisdiction and the complaint could not be entertained. [701B] 2. The District Judges had no jurisdiction over the complaint. [702C] 3. The District Courts had no jurisdiction or power to try a complaint. [602D] 4. The District Magistrates had no jurisdiction of the Sessions Judge to entertain a Criminal complaint. [802E] 5. The District Sessions Judge had the jurisdiction to try such a complaint. He had no jurisdiction as the Sessions Judge did not have jurisdiction to try it. [703G] 6. The District Judicial Magistrate had no power or jurisdiction to try an offence. [704G] 7. The District Munsiff had no jurisdiction at all to try the complaint. He was not the court of Sessions. [705G] 7A] 7. Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not confer any power on the High Court to entertain a petition for quashing the complaint and the High court had jurisdiction to deal with the complaint. It is only in cases where the complaint is not maintainable, the High Court can entertain a criminal petition. [707C] 8. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to deal in a complaint. It was not competent to entertain a civil complaint. [783A] 9. The District Munsif had no jurisdiction but he had no power and jurisdiction to try and try the complaint and therefore the complaint was not maintainable. [709G] 9. In the instant case the District & Session Judge had no such jurisdiction. [708G] 10. The District Collector had no jurisdiction nor power to try an accused. [706A] 11. The District Probation Officer had no jurisdiction except to try a Criminal complaint and therefore it was not competent for the District Magistrate to entertain a 'complaint.

The plaintiff was serving the State Police as a constable in the Police Department. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of acquittal. The State filed a second appeal before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the order of the Additional District judge was illegal on the ground that the order was passed by an authority not competent. [801B] 2. The High Cour t was right in setting aside the judgment and decree of the first appellate court. [802C] 3. The High tiffs judgment is clearly illegal and void. [803D] 4. The High cour t was not right in setting it aside. [804E] 5. The High r ef Court was right in reversing the judgment of both the courts below. [805E] 6. The High Cou rt was right in dismissing the second appeal. [806E] 7. The High Courts were right in setting the judgment of two courts below. The High n ourt was right in confirming the judgment of conviction and the decree of the trial Court. [807E] 8. The High R ef Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the judgment of t he first appellate court, and the High Court was right, in setting aside that judgment. [808E] 804F] 9. The High Tr ibunal was right in rejecting the second appeal in limine. [809G] 9. In the instant case, the High Court had no power to interfere with t he judgment of the first Appellate Court. [908E] 10. The High Co urt was right, and the second appeal was rightly dismissed.

The respondent assessee, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea garden tools, requisites and also acts as agents for sale of tea garden tools. The respondent assessee, who is a private limited Company carrying on business, is a private company carrying on the business of selling tea garden tool tools and requisites. The respondent company is a private Limited Company carrying on the trade of selling tea gardens tools and requisites, and also acting on behalf of the respondent company. The respondent is a private Company carrying on a business in tea gardens tools, requisites, and other goods. The respondent was carrying on the trading business in tea plant tools and requisites in the tea garden tools in the tea gardens tools. The assessee was carrying on business of selling the tea gardens tool tools and the requisites. The assessee carried on the business in tea plantation tools and requisites for the sale of tea gardens tools in the Tea garden tools. On the other hand, the respondent company carried on the trading activity in tea gardens tool and requisites. On the sale of the tea gardens, the respondent assessee carried on business in the tea plantation tools in the business of sale of tea bushes tools and requisites which were not completed by actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips. The respondent carried on the trade in tea gardens, requisites and other goods in the tea estate tools and requisites on the sale of such tea gardens tools to the respondent company and the sale of those goods to the respondent assessee was speculative. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the validity of the explanation to sec. 24(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the explanation to section 24(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act was not relevant for the purpose of the case and that the transactions entered into by the respondent assessee were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24 (1) of that Act. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High court held that the explanation was not relevant and that the transaction entered into by it was speculative transactions within meaning of explanation 1 to section 24 of the Act and that the explanation did not violate the provisions of section 24(2) of the said Act. The appeal was allowed and the order of the High Court was set aside. The respondent 's appeal to this Court was allowed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The explanation to section 25(1) is not relevant for determining the question whether the transactions entered in the tea plantations were speculative transactions or not. The explanation does not violate the provision of section 24 of Income Tax Act. [901B] 2. The explanation is not relevant and does not violate section 24(3) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [902C] 3. The explanation merely states that the transactions were speculative transactions and not speculative transactions. The explanation cannot be said to be vague. The explanation states that the transaction was speculative transactions and that the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transaction. [903C] 4. The explanation further states that the loss in speculative transactions and the loss in a trading activity cannot be set off against the income, profits or gains in any other head of business. [905D] 5. The explanation makes it clear that the loss is a speculative transaction and not speculative transaction. The explanation also does not violate any provision of section 25(3) which permits the setting off of a loss in speculative transaction. It does not violate Section 24(3). [905E] 6. The explanation reduces the loss in the speculative transactions and does not contravene any provision of Section 24(1). [906F] 7. The explanation provides that the loss has to be a speculative transaction, and does not affect any transaction of sale which is otherwise speculative in a speculative manner. [906G] 8.

The appellant, a candidate for the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the Punjab Legislative Council. He was elected to the Punjab Vidhan Sabha on the basis of a nomination paper completed in the prescribed form and subscribed by the candidate himself. The appellant was elected to that Assembly. The Returning Officer rejected the nomination paper on the ground that the appellant had not signed the nomination paper as proposer himself. The Returning officer rejected the nomination papers on the ground of the improper acceptance of the nomination paper. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the rejection of his nomination paper on two grounds, namely, (1) that the nomination paper was not signed by the proposer himself and (2) that the Returning Officer had not given any reason for rejecting the nomination paper of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Returning officer had not given reasons for rejecting the nominations of the appellant and that the rejection of the nomination papers was not in accordance with the requirements of the Act and that the Returning Officers had not given the reasons for rejecting his nomination paper. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Returning Officers had no power to reject the nomination paper when there has been a failure to comply with any of the provisions of the Act. [901 A] 2. The Returning Authority had no power under section 36 to reject any nomination paper on any of the grounds mentioned in section 33. [902 A] 3. The Returning Office had no power of rejection of any nomination paper when the appellant had signed the nomination papers. [903 B] 4. The Returning Authorities had no power at all to reject any of the nomination forms on any of these grounds. [905 C] 5. The Returning authority had no power in rejecting the nomination papers of the appellant on the ground ' that the Returning Authority had not given reason for rejecting his candidature on any of those grounds. [093 D] 6. The Returning authorities had no power, in rejecting the nominations on any of such grounds. [1003 E] 7. The ReturningOfficer had no power or jurisdiction to reject any candidate on any of grounds. [1103 E] 8. The Returningofficer had no power and jurisdiction to reject the nominations on the ground "that the Returning Officer has not given any reasons for rejecting any nomination paper". [905 F] 9. The Returning officers had no power nor jurisdiction to reject a nomination paper when it was made by the candidate.

The appellants were employed as "Skilled Workers" in the Company 's establishment in the year 1972. They were terminated by the Company on September 20, 1972. The Company filed a complaint against the appellants and others alleging that the appellants had abandoned the service of the Company and had abandoned the services of the Company. The Company denied the allegations and claimed that the appellants were not entitled to reengage the services of their workmen. The Company also denied the allegations of abandonment of service and alleged that the appellants did not intend to abandon the service of their workmen and that they had abandoned the employment of the Company during the pendency of the industrial dispute. The Company alleged that the workmen had abandoned the Service of the Company without their consent and that they were not entitled for reengagement. The Company contended that the appellants could not be said to have abandoned the service and that the workmen were not entitled, as the Company had abandoned the work of the Company, and that the appellants should be deemed to have abandoned their service. The Company further contended that the workmen concerned had abandoned the job of the Company in the year 1971 and that the Company had not abandoned the service. The Labour Court held that the appellants' case was not covered by the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case and that the termination of their services was not justified. The Company preferred an appeal to the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal held that the termination was not justified and that the services of workmen were not terminated by the appellants. The Company appealed to the Industrial Court. The Industrial Court held that there was no abandonment of service on the part of the appellants and that the action on the part that the appellants abandoned the service was not justified, and that there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the appellants in the surrounding circumstance or the conduct which had been communicated by the Company to the appellants. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants were not justified in terminating their services. [601B] 2. The appellants had abandoned their service and had not abandoned their service during the pendency thereof. The Company had not terminated the services of its workmen. The appellants could not have abandoned their services during the pendency. [602C] 3. The appellants did not voluntarily abandoned the service during the period of their absence. The Company was not entitled to retrench the services of any workmen. [603D] 4. The appellants, in the circumstances of the case, were not entitled either to retrench or to retrench their workmen. [613E] 5. The appellants having not abandoned their services, the Company was not justified in removing them from their rolls. [605E] 6. The appellants have not been able to show that the Company was in any way abandoned their services. The appellants are not entitled to any retrench their services. They were not entitled under the Standing Orders to retrench them. [606E] 7. The appellants cannot be said to be in any way guilty of abandonment of their services. It is not a case of abandonment of services. The Company has not been able, at any rate, to retrench its workmen. [706E] 8. The appellants' case is that the Company has abandoned the service for which they were entitled to retrenching them. [613G] 9. The Company 's case is that it had abandoned the contract of service and had abandoned it. The Company, therefore, cannot be said that the appellants have abandoned the services. [613F] 9. In the circumstances of this case, the appellants were entitled to re-engage the workmen. [643A] 10. The Company cannot be said not to have abandoned service of its workmen during the pendency or after the termination of the industrial disputes. [607E] 11. The Company is not entitled to retrenchment of its workmen in the circumstances mentioned in the letter of the Company dated September 7, 1972.

The appellant, a public trust, was a public trust. The trust was registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The appellant was the trustee of the trust. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a second appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal and that the High court had no jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court had jurisdiction to entertain the second appeal. [701B] 2. The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain second appeal. The High courts have jurisdiction to try the second appeal and the High Court has no jurisdiction to try it. [702C] 3. The High 'Court has no jurisdiction in a second appeal. It is only in a case where the High Court exercises its jurisdiction under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, that the High 'Court can entertain a second suit. [703D] 4. The High' Court has no power to entertain a third appeal. [603E] 5. The High. Court has no inherent jurisdiction to entertain an appeal. The jurisdiction of the High Court is not limited to the question of jurisdiction. [704G] 6. The High, Court has no such jurisdiction. The High [704A] 7. The High is not bound to follow the decision of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court. [705B] 7. In the instant case, the High Court was not justified in holding that the appellant had no jurisdiction in the matter. [707C] 8. The High was not justified by the fact that the appellant was not a public trust and that the mortgage was not a mortgage. [709G] 9. The High] Court was not right in holding that a second appeal could not be entertained. [708G] 9, 10A] 10. The High "Court has no inherent power to entertain an second appeal. But the High Court can entertain a third suit if it is satisfied that the earlier decisions of the High ' Court were not warranted by the fact of the case. [706B] 10. In the present case, the appellant had not filed a suit to set aside the sale held in execution of a decree. The High Curt had no jurisdiction under section 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950 to set aside a sale held in the execution of a warrant of sale. [710G] 10. It is not necessary for the High Court to go into the question whether the appellant had any right to apply to the Court for setting aside the sale. [807C] 10. Section 36(a), of the Bombay public Trust Act, 1951, provides that the Court may, if it is of opinion that it is of the opinion that it would be in the interest of justice and for the public good, order that the sale be set aside. [711G] 11. The High Commissioner was not justified either in holding that he had no jurisdiction or in the matter of setting aside the auction sale held in favour of the appellant. [712G] 12. The High Power Committee had no jurisdiction and the question whether a second appeal would lie against the order of the Commissioner was not a matter which could be decided by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [713G] 13. The High power Committee had no power to set aside an auction sale held by the appellant. The High Commission had no jurisdiction, and the question of setting aside an auction sales held in favour the appellant did not arise. [714G] 14.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935 and was promoted to the post of Senior Clerk on June 4. 1935. He was promoted to a post of Senior Assistant on June 4 and was posted as a clerk in the office of the Chief Engineer, Northern Railway, Lucknow. He was posted as an Assistant Engineer in the office on June 4 in the year 1935. He retired from service on June 4 on attaining the age of 55 years. He was given a notice of not less than three months in writing to the Chief Engineer on June 4 for retirement. He was retired from service in the year 1964. He was served with a notice of retirement on June 4 but he was not given a notice in writing to his higher authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of retirement was passed by the Chief Engineer in exercise of his discretion and the same was not in accordance with the rules. The High court held that the order was passed by way of punishment and the same is not in accordance therewith. The appellant also contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the order is in violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of retirement is in accordance with law and the same cannot be interfered with by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [801B] 2. The order is in accordance therewith and the same does not violate any of the principles laid down by this Court in the case of [Union of India vs P.N. Menon and Others] [1964] 3 SCR 886; State of M.P. vs P.K. Sharma and Others, [1964] 4 SCR 886, followed. 3. The order passed by the High court is in accordancewith law and the said order is in conformity with the principles of law. [802B] 4. The order was passed in accordance with rules and the same has no parity with Rule 2(1) of the Rules. [803C] 5. The order dated June 4, 1934 was not in conformity with rules and was in accordance with rule 2(2). The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in the mills at Raichur, had been carrying on business at Raichur in the manufacture of oil in their mills at Raichur. The assessee had been carrying out business at Raichur for the manufacture of the oil in their Mills at Raichur. During the accounting period ending March 31st, 1943, the assessee had been paying income tax on the basis of the turnover of the business at Raichur. In the assessment proceedings for the relevant accounting period ending on 31st March, 1943, it was contended that the assessee had not suffered any deficiency of profits during the chargeable accounting period ending 31st March 1943 and that the assessee was not entitled to set off the said amount of profits during that period. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee could not be said to have suffered any deficiency in profits during the relevant accounting periods and, therefore, set off the amount of profits at the chargeable accounting periods ending on 31 st March, 1943. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the amount of the profits at Raichur was not liable to be set off in computing the chargeable accountingperiod ending on 31 March, 1944. The assessee thereupon filed an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was no deficiency of profits at Raichur and that the amount was not liable for set off in computation of the chargeable accounting Period ending on 31 St March, 1944 and that the deficiency of profits was not liable. The assessee then filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and contended that the deficiency in profits was not attributable to the manufacturing activity at Raichur and the deficiency of profit was not liable as the assessee had incurred any deficiency in the chargeable accounting. The Appellate Court held that the deficiency was not attributable either to the manufacturing activities at Raichur or to the manufacturing operations at Raichur and, therefore the question whether the assessee was entitled to set the amount of profit at Raichur was irrelevant. The assessee contended that the amount at Raichur was liable to be included in the chargeable chargeable accounting period and, therefore was not liable in computing the profits at the relevant accountingperiod. The Appellate Appellate Tribunal held, that the assessee carried on business atOUT at Raichur and was not liable under section 7 of the Act. The assessee, therefore, appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that there were no deficiency of profit during the chargeable chargeable chargeable accounting periods and that the profits were not liable to set off in respect of the chargeable chargeable business. The assessee thereafter filed an appeal against the order of the Appellate Assistant commissioner. The High court held that the question whether there was any deficiency of profit in the chargeable business was irrelevant for the purpose of computation of the profits under section 7. The HighCourt held that the profit was not chargeable to income tax under section 7 and, therefore set off was not allowable. The assessee filed an appeal in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the amount paid by the assessee was liable to set Off in computation of chargeable accounting period. [701B] 2. The High 'Court held that there could be no deficiency of business in the chargeable period ending on or before 31st March 1944. [702C] 3. The High' Court was right in holding, that the amount payable by the assessee to the assessee was a part of the chargeable period and, consequently, set off in the chargeable account period ending on the 31st March 1942. [703D] 4. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was a deficiency of profits in the chargeable year ending on 31St March, 1942. [073E] 5. The High] 6.

The appellants were appointed as Civil Engineering graduates on the basis of the results of the two tests held by the Kerala Public Service Commission. They were appointed as Engineering graduates on a temporary basis. The KPSC prepared the two rank lists for Engineering (Civil) for Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering. The appellants were appointed on a temporary capacity basis. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the judgment of the Kerala Public Services Commission. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. The appellants challenged the validity of their appointment on the ground that the KPSC had not prepared a common list for Civil Engineering graduates and the other for Mechanical Engineering graduates. The High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the K.PSC had prepared a common seniority list for Civil engineering graduates and the Engineering graduates. Hence the appellants are before us. The appellants contended that the KAAC had prepared a separate seniority list for the Engineering graduates and that the KPISC had prepared separate seniority lists for Civil Engineering (Civil). The High Court held that the KMPSC had prepared the two separate lists for Civil engineering and Mechanical Engineering and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. The High Courts dismissed the writ appeals. Hence the present appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The KAAC was not directed to prepare a common list of Civil Engineering graduates for Civil Engineering. [801B] 2. The K.P.SC prepared a common gradation list for Civil Engg. graduates and Engineering graduates. It was not open to the KP.SC to prepare a separate seniority lists. The KMPSC prepared a separate list for Civil Engineers and Mechanical Engineering graduates and it was open to the appellants to prepare a combined seniority list for civil Engineering graduates and Engineering Graduates. [802C] 3. The KPISC prepared a combined seniority lists for civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineers. The KPsSC prepared a seniority list for Engineering (Electrical) for Civil Engg., Engineering and Mechanical engineering. The KGPSC prepared a consolidated seniority list for Electrical Engineering and Mechanical Engg. graduates. The KNPSC prepared a revised seniority list for Mechanical Engineering and Mechanical Engineer. The KPPSC prepared a fresh seniority list for Commercial Engineering and Mechanical (Civil) Engineering. The KEB prepared a common Seniority list for Civil Engineer and Mechanical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Electrical Engineering. The appellant filed a writ appeal in the High court. The HighCourt dismissed the writ appeal holding that the seniority list prepared by the KPTC was not a valid one. The KPLSC was directed to prepare separate seniority lists of Civil Engineering and Electrical Engineers. The Highcourt dismissed the writ. Hence the appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.(i) The KPTC prepared a common merit list for Civil and Mechanical Engineering for Civil Engineering, Mechanical and Mechanical Engineering of Civil Engineering. The High courts have held that the seniority lists prepared by the Public Service Commission for Civil Engineering Engineering and Mechanical and Mechanical Engineers were not valid. [803D] 2.(ii) The KMPTC prepared a combined Seniority list for civil engineering graduates and Engineering Graduate Engineers for Civil Engineering for Civil Engg, Engineering and Mechanical. The KPMSC prepared a Seniority list for Electrical Engineers and Mechanical Engineers for Civil Engg and Mechanical Engineering in Civil Engineering. On the basis of a common seniority lists prepared for Civil Engineering Engineers and Mechanical engineering, the KPET was directed to prepared a common rank list for Civil, Mechanical Engineering. [820E] 3.1 The KPET prepared a common ranking list for Civil Mechanical Engineering and Engineering graduates for Electrical Engineering. It was open to KPSC to prepare separate Seniority list for Mechanical Engineers and Mechanical Engineer in Civil Engineering and Engineering. The Kerala Public Service Tribunal, which had the jurisdiction to prepare a Common Seniority list for the Civil Engineering and Civil Engineering graduates, had no jurisdiction to prepare separate merit lists for Civil Engg./ Mechanical Engineering.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for dissolution of partnership accounts and valuing at Rs.150 for his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department, inter alia, for a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum of Rs,1,26.796. 72 besides another sum. The plaintiff respondent filed an application under section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act for a sum equivalent to the sum of Rs1,26.,796.73. The trial court rejected the application. The plaintiff filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the trial court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken a view that the valuation put by the plaintiff in the plaint is not correct and that the valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction. [701B] 2. The plaintiff has not been able to show that the valuation given by the plaintiff is not correct. The valuation put by him is not correct, and that the plaintiff has not established that the valuation made by him is correct. [702C] 3. The plaintiff is not entitled to the relief claimed in the suit. [703D] 4. The plaintiff in the suit has not shown that the valuation has been correctly made by him. The plaintiff, therefore, cannot be permitted to challenge the valuation put in by the plaintiff. [704E] 5. The plaintiff cannot be permitted by the court to put a tentative valuation on the suit. The plaintiff can, therefore, put a tentative value on the suit and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. It is not possible, therefore, to give an incorrect valuation of the plaint. [705G] 6. The plaintiff was entitled to the reliefs claimed in the plaint. The plaintiff could not have been permitted to challenge valuation put by it. [706A] 7. The plaintiff had not shown that he had any interest in the business. The plaintiff did not show that he had taken any interest in business. The valuation was not correct. [605B] 7. In the present case, the plaintiff has clearly stated that the valuation was not correctly made by the plaintiff and the valuation put was not correct and the valuation was correctly made by it. The plaintiff 's objection to the valuation put on the plaint by the plaintiff was not correct, but was rejected by the trial court. [707C] 8. The plaintiff must also state a valuation which need only be approximately the correct amount payable by one party to the other. [709D] 9. The plaintiff should also state a true valuation of the accounts put by him on the plaint. If the plaintiff is entitled to the amount claimed in the plaintiff, he must state a valuation of the account put by him. [708E] 10. The plaintiff may have the right to put a provisional valuation on the plaint, but he cannot be permitted either to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for the purpose of court fees or to put a final valuation on the plaintiff. The plaintiff would be entitled to the costs of the suit, but he must state the exact amount payable by him.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of various kinds of "traditional industries" and had set up the industries in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant company was granted a certificate under section 12(1)(i) of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The State of Madhya Bharat filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the notification was not retrospective in operation and that the appellant company was entitled to the exemption under section 12 of the Act and the notification was accordingly quashed. The High ' Court held that the exemption granted by the notification was prospective in operation and the appellant company could not be denied the benefit of the exemption under the notification. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the notification did not set out the conditions on which the exemption was granted and that the conditions on the basis of which the exemption had been granted were not set out in the notification itself and all that the Director of Industries had to do was to comply with the conditions on whom the exemption was to be granted. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The notification does not set out any condition on which the concession of deferment of tax is to be granted to a dealer. The condition on which exemption is granted to a registered dealer is that the dealer should have availed the facility of deferment of payment of tax under the rules framed for the purpose. [601B] 1.2. The condition regarding the exemption is that the certificate should have been issued to the dealer. The exemption is granted only to a registered person and not to a dealer and not to any other person. [602C] 1.3. The condition relating to the exemption is not available to the industries mentioned in rule 14. The exemption granted by rule 14 is only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for the exemption. [603D] 1.4. The exemption under rule 14 is not available in respect of the industries mentioned by it. [604D] 1,4. The conditions on which exemption was granted to a company are set out in rule 14 and the exemption is available to the units listed in rule 14, and the exemption under rule 15 is available to those industries who opt for the scheme of deferment of the scheme of exemption. [613E] 1.5. The exemption from the provisions of the Act is available to all the industries mentioned therein. [605F] 1.6. The exemption cannot be denied to the units mentioned in rule 15. [607F] 1, 4.1. In the present case, the exemption granted under rule 14 was not available to those units who opt for a scheme of deferment or deferment of payment. [609F] 1,.4.2. In the instant case, the appellant company had set up a new industrial unit which was not eligible for exemption under rule 12(1) of the rules framed under the Act. [608F] 1..2.3.1.2.1.3.2.2.3 In the present cases, the exemption under Rule 12(1), as it stood prior to the amendment, was not available. [606F] 1 .3.2 The exemption under Rule 14 was available to those industrial units who opt to a scheme of exemption under rule 13(1) and the exemption was available to such units who opt under rule 14. [610F] 1.,4.2,4.3.3.4.1.1.4.2., the exemption under clause (1) of section 12(2) was available to the industrial units who opted for a scheme under rule 14 and they were eligible for exemption from the operation of the scheme.

The petitioners were appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judges on the basis of the recommendations of the High Court. They were appointed as District & Sessions Judge on the basis that they were regularly appointed as Additional Judges of the Delhi Judicial Service. The High Court, by its judgment dated April 21, 1981, held that the petitioners were not fit for promotion and that they were not fit to be promoted as Additional District and Sessions Judge. The High court, however, held that they were entitled to be promoted to the post of Additional District & Session Judge on the ground that they were appointed regularly in accordance with the qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) of the Rules. The High Curt, however, set aside the judgment of the High court and directed that the petitioners should be promoted as District & Session Judges on the ground of their having not less than ten years of service in the judicial service. The petitioners were promoted as Additional Judges on the recommendation of the High Curt. The High Courts, however, directed that the seniority of the petitioners should not be fixed on the basis on the basis whether they were fit for promotion or not. The High courts, however, did not interfere with the judgment of this Court. The petitioners, who were appointed as Assistant District & Sessions judge on the recommendation made by the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order of the High Courts. The HighCourt, however, dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the Full Court of the High 9 Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Power Court had no power to interfere with an order of the Tribunal. [701B] 2. The High power of the Tribunal is not a judicial power. It is a judicial power and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the petitioners were fit for being promoted as Additional Judge or not. [702C] 3. The High powers of the Tribunal are not judicial powers. The High jurisdiction of the Tribunal cannot be equated with the power of the High Power Court to interfere with a judgment of the Tribunal unless it is shown that the Tribunal has exercised its jurisdiction not vested in it by law. [703D] 4. The HighPower of the Tribunal to interfere with its judgment is not a Judicial power. [704E] 5. The High is not a Court of appeal. The High appellate jurisdiction of the High appellate Court is not a power of the Supreme Court. [705E] 6. The High Judicial Service Rules, 1954, which are statutory in character, provide for recruitment to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. Rule 7(b) provides for recruitment to Delhi Higher Judicial Services. Rule 7 (b) provides that the seniority in the service shall be governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post in accordance with qualifications laid down in Rule 7(c). Rule 7(d) provides for appointment to the Delhi Judicial Services. [706E] 7. The High Civil Court, therefore, was not justified in holding that the petitioners are not fit for being appointed to the Delhi Superior Judicial Service. [707E] 8. The High] Court was not justified either in holding that there was no justification for the petitioners to be appointed to the post in accordance to the qualifications laiddown in Rule 7 (a) or Rule 7(e) of the said Rules. [708F] 9. The High was not justified by the High Power of the Tribunal in holding that Rule 7(aa) of the aforesaid Rules was not applicable to the petitioners. [709G] 10. The High, Court, in the circumstances, was not right in holding that rule 7(aa), as it stood at the relevant time, was applicable to the appellants. [710G] 11.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to tax in the hands of the Ambala Flour Mills. The Income tax Officer, Ambala Flour Mills, assessed the income of the Ambala Rice Mills in the hands Of the appellant. The Income Tax Officer, Ambala, on the basis of the assessment of the income of Ambala Flour Mills held that the income of a family of which the appellant was a member was liable to be assessed in the handsof the family of the Ambala Sugar Mills. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on the view that the income belonged to the family of which Parshad was a member, held that the Income tax Officer was competent to make the assessment. The High Court held that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was competent to assess the income of an association of persons under section 31(3) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The High court held that the assessment of income of the appellant was not barred by the law of Limitation. The High 'Court further held that the appellant was liable to pay tax on the income of his family. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High. Court was right in holding that the income was liable to tax on the basis that the income had been assessed in the names of the members of the association of persons. [882E] 2. The High' Court was right, in holding that since the income of family of which appellant was a partner was liable to assessment, the Income tax officer was competent to direct the Income tax to assess the appellant. [883G] 3. The High, Court was right when it held that the order of the Appellate Assistant commissioner was not a direction or an order of assessment. [884G] 4. The High Courts were right in holding, that the Income Tax Officer was competent under section 31 (3) of Income tax Act to assess the Income tax of the appellant. He was not competent to assess his income in the hands o the family of whom he was a member. [894G] 5. The High Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to direct the income in the assessment of his income in respect of the income in question. [895G] 6. The High Commissioner was right in directing the Income tax authorities to assess the assessee in the hands off the income of their family. [896G] 7. The High Power Court was right that the Incometax Officer was competent in law to assess the family of a person in the hands on the ground that the income in respect thereof was liable to income tax on the ground of the income being assessed in the name of the family of such person. [897G] 8. The High power of the Appellate Tribunal to make the order of assessment is not a power of the Income Tax officer to direct the assessment of such income. [898G] 9. The High] Court was right. The Incometax Officer had no power to direct the assessing of the income. [998G] 10. The High Curt was right in setting aside the direction of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner to make the re assessment.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the plaint schedule properties. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to a share in the properties of his father and that he was a member of the joint family. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to the value of his share at the rate of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value of the plaint schedule property. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the valuation of the plaint was not correct and that the valuation was not correct. The High court held that the appellant had not proved that the valuation made by him for the purposes of court fee was correct. The appellant contended that the valuation for the purposes Of court fee was not correct as the valuation was made by him on the plaint schedule and that the value of plaint schedule properties was not correct or that the valuation should be taken as the value for the purposes for jurisdiction. The High Judge held that the value was not correct but that the valuation could be taken as a valuation for the purpose of court fee. The High judge held that the plaintiff was entitled to have the value of her share at the rates prescribed by the valuation for court fee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The valuation of the suit properties for the purposes mentioned in section 7(iv)(b) of the Act is the value of their share at the time of the valuation. [701B] 2. The valuation for the valuation of plaint schedule property is the value for jurisdiction and the valuation for jurisdiction purposes is the value to be taken as to the value for purposes of court fees. [702C] 3. The valuation is the value which is to be taken for the purposes specified in section 7 (iv)(b). The valuation for jurisdiction and valuation for the said purpose is the value that is to be adopted for the purposes set out in section 7. [703D] 4. The valuation made by the appellant for the purposes referred to in section 7 is the value at which he seeks to amend his plaint and the memorandum of appeal should be taken to be the valuation for purposes of jurisdiction and the value for purpose of court fees and it provides for the determination of the value for a purpose set out in the plaint and the plaint and on the memorandum of appeals should be taken for determination of the valuation for purpose of jurisdiction and to be taken to the valuation for determination of value for jurisdiction. [704E] 5. The valuation to be adopted is the value in respect of the plaint and plaint and the valuation to be taken is the value prescribed for the purposes to be taken. [705G] 6. The valuation should be adopted for determining the value for court fee and it should be taken at the rate prescribed for the purpose to be adopted in respect of plaint and plaint. [706G] 7. The valuation must be taken as per the valuation made for the purposes stated in section 7 of the Suits Valuation Act. [707G] 7A. The valuation has to be taken at Rs. 15000 per share. The valuation cannot be taken at this rate. [708G] 8. The valuation can be taken at a rate higher than the rate prescribed by the court. [709G] 9. The valuation in respect of a plaint cannot be taken as it is on the basis of the valuation made in the plaint. [807G] 9A. The value of the suit schedule properties is the value fixed for the purposes laid down for the purposes. [710G] 10. The valuation, therefore, cannot be taken to have the valuation made at Rs.15000 per share and it is on that basis that the valuation has to been taken. [808G] 10A. The plaintiff is entitled to have his claim for partition of the plaint Schedule properties. [713G] 11.

The appellant, a public authority, issued a notice under Section 16(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, to the NDMC, calling upon it to stop the construction of the building within a period of 15 days from the date of the notice. The NDMC, however, did not give any reply to the said notice. The appellant, however, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the NDMC had not given any reply to it. The High Court, however, dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the NDMC was not justified in refusing to grant the sanction to the plans submitted by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The NDMC had not applied its mind to the relevant provisions of bye law 16.4.8.1 and the requisite sanction was not a condition precedent for the grant of sanction. [601B] 1.2. The NDMC was not entitled to refuse the sanction to plans submitted by it. [602C] 1.3. The NDMC could not have refused the sanction to such plans. [603D] 1.4. The NDMC did not have the requisite sanction to the plan submitted by it, and the High Court, therefore, committed a manifest error in refusing to sanction the plans submitted to it by the NDMC. [605E] 1.5. The NDMC has not given any reasons for refusing the sanction to it. [613G] 1.6.1. In the instant case, the NDMC had applied its mind and the requisite sanctions were not available to it. It was, therefore, not open to the NDMC to refuse the sanctioned plans submitted by them. [604G] 1, 2.1.2. In the present case, the appellant had not given a written undertaking before the NDMC that they would commence the construction work according to the plans. The NDMC failed to give any reply thereto.
