The plaintiff, who was the owner of a motor business, purchased a motor car from the defendants on April 1, 1946, for a sum of Rs. 1,000. The defendants were the owners of the motor business. The plaintiff purchased a motor vehicle from the defendants. The defendants purchased the motor car from them on April 1. 1946. The plaintiff claimed that the motor business was carried on by him on April 1 and, therefore, the defendants were the owner of the motor car. The defendants denied the claim of the plaintiff. The trial court held that the cause of action in the two suits was different from the cause of the two suits and that the suit was not barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Civil Procedure Code. The High Court held that the suit for partition was barred under Order 2, rule 2, of the Civil Rules. The High court held that there was no cause of action for the present suit in the two courts. The High 'Court further held that the plaintiff was entitled to recover the amount of Rs. 2,000. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit is barred under Order I, rule 2 (3), of Civil Procedure Code, and that the cause for the suit was different from that of the suit for accounts of the motor businesses. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The cause of action is different from the suit for account of the motorbusiness subsequent to March 31, 1946. The cause for the present suits was different and distinct from the cause for suit for accounts. [901 D] 2. The cause or cause of action was different from those for which the suit was filed. The cause was different from suit for accounts for the subsequent period. [902 E] 3. The cause in the two suit was different and the cause of suit was different. [903 F] 4. The cause and cause of action were different from the causes of action in both the suits. [904 F] 5. The cause is different from that in the two Suits. The cause, therefore, was different from cause of action. [905 F] 6. The cause which was the cause of actions in both the Suits was different from each other. [906 F] 7. The cause to sue in both the two suits were different from each another. [908 F] 8. The cause had been different from the one in the two separate suits. [0908 G] 9. The cause claimed in both the suit was the same as the cause of suits for accounts of motor business. [909 H] 9. In the two suits the cause of dispute was different from one in the other. [099 F] 9. It is not necessary to refer to the other two suits. The cause sought in both the appeals is different from each of the two Suits and the cause for suits for accounts is different from one. [910 G] 9 A. The cause pleaded in both the cases is different from both the suits and the cause sought in the two appeals is different. [098 H] 9 A] 10. The cause stated in both the three suits is different from cause for suits. [1010 F] 10. It is clear that the cause claimed in two suits is different and distinct. [911 G] 11. The cause shown in both the four suits is different. The cause set up in both the sets of suits is different than the cause of two suits. [1110 F] 12. The cause referred to in both the set of suits is distinct and separate. [912 F] 13. The cause mentioned in both the plaint is different from causes of action. The cause given in both the different sets of suits are different. [1012 F] 14. The cause described in both the plaints is different from those in the two sets of suits.

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of salt works in the Salt Works at Wadala, Bombay. The appellant was engaged as a salt Works at Wadalala, Bombay, for the purpose of manufacturing salt. The appellant had been working as a salt works at Wadalla, Bombay. On April 9, 1952, the appellant was engaged to manufacture salt works at a salt works in a salt works. The appellant, however, did not manufacture salt works in that salt works. On April 10, 1952, a notice was issued to the appellant to show cause why the salt works should not be classified under the head "factory " and why the salt work should not be treated as a factory " within the meaning of the Act. The appellant replied to the notice on July 12, 1949, that the salt works were not covered by the definition of the word " factory " in the Act. On July 12, 1952, an application was made to the Government of India, Department of Industries & Supply, for permission to file a written statement. The application was rejected by the Government of Bombay, on July 12. 1952. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay, challenging the order of the Government of Maharashtra, refusing permission to file the written statement. On July 13, 1952, another writ petition was filed in the High court of Bombay, praying for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the order of Government of Bombay dated July 12, 1948, rejecting the appellant 's application for permission to institute a written statement, and for a writ of mandamus to the Government to consider the question of the appellant ' s salt works in respect of the salt works in question. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant was not a factory " in terms of the definition of " factory " under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word " factory" in the definition of 'factory " in the Factories Act, 1948, is not confined to the factory of salt works. It is not confined only to the salt works, but also to the salt work. [601B] 2. The word 'factory " is not confined in the definition to the salt Works. The word is not confined merely to the saltwork. [602C] 3. The word factory " in s. 2 of the Factories Act is not confined either to the saltworks or to the salt. [603D] 4. The word Factory " in the definition is not confined, in the definition, to the salt worked. [605E] 5. The word, 'factory " has not been defined in the Act, but it has been defined in s.2 of the Act, and the word 'factory ' has not been used in the Act for the purpose for which it is used. [604F] 6. The word used in the definition in s.3 of the Factories act, 1948, has not been included in the definition. The word has not been specifically included in the Act and the word "factory " has been defined under the Act, in the sense that it has been used in s. 3 of the Factories Acts. [606F] 7. The word employed in the definition has not been expressly included in the word ' factory " in S.2 of S.2. The word must be given its ordinary meaning. [607F] 8. The word does not mean 'factory ' in the sense of the word ' in the Act but it has to be given its natural meaning. [707F] 9. The word in the definition means 'factory ' and it has to mean ' in the ordinary sense of the term ' factory ' in the definition and it has been so defined in the Factories Acts, but it does not mean any factory ' in which salt works are carried on in the open air.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Technical Education in the year 1949. He was promoted to the post of Instructor in the Technical Education Department in the year 1955. He was confirmed in that post on November 28, 1949. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Mysore challenging the order of absorption in the Department. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent filed a writ appeal in the High court. The High court held that the respondent was entitled to be absorbed in the Department in the Department and that he was entitled to the benefit of the revised pay scales applicable to the post. The High 'Court, however, held that the absorption in the department of Technical Education was not a break in his service and that he should be absorbed in that Department. The respondent, who was a permanent employee, filed a writ application in the High 'Court. The High' Court held that the order of the Government of Mysore, dated February 19, 1964, was not justified. The High. Court held that there was no justification for the respondent to be absorbed into that Department in the department. The High, Court, however, allowed the writ petition and directed that the respondent should be absorbed into the Department of technical Education from a particular date, or to be given the revised pay scale applicable to the posts. The respondent appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court was not justified on the ground that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed. [701B] 2. The respondent was not entitled to be treated as a break in service. He was not entitled for the benefit of revised pay scales. [702C] 3. The respondent had been appointed as Instructor by the Director of Technical Education, Mysore, on November 28. 1949. He had been appointed on deputation to the Polytechnics and had been appointed in the Department on November 28., 1949. He continued to work in that Department till November 28, 1950. He was, therefore, entitled to be considered for absorption in that Department in that Department, but he was not entitled, to be absorbed as Instructor in that Department for a short period in 1955. [703G] 4. The respondent 's appointment in the Department was not a permanent appointment in the department, but was a temporary appointment in the Government Department. He was a permanent appointment and was, therefore entitled to be continued in that Department until November 28, 1948. [704B] 5. The respondent could not be absorbed in any Department of Technical education, because he was not qualified or otherwise qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Instructor in that department. [705C] 6. The respondent did not acquire any right to be considered in that Department because he was a permanent appointee in that Department and he was not otherwise suitable to hold the said post. [706E] 7. The respondent's case that he was not suitable to hold that post was not a case of break in his services was not accepted by the Government. [707E] 7A] 8. The respondent cannot be absorbed in a Department of TechnicalEducation, which is a part of the Department of Engineering Education. [708E] 9. The respondent is not entitled to the benefits of the revised scales applicable to his post. [807E] 10. The respondent has no legal right, to be considered as a break In his service. [709G] 10. In the present case, the respondent was appointed in the department on November 28 1949 and he was, therefore not entitled to any relief. [710E] 11. The respondent must be deemed to have been absorbed in the department in the Department, because he had been appointed to the Department of Education in 1949. [711E] 12.

The appellant was born on 17.5.1950. He was born on 16.5.1951. He was a minor at the time of his marriage. He was married to a girl child who was born on 15.5.1953. He was living with his parents. He was given a child study report on 15.4.1951. The appellant was born in the year 1951. He was also born on 16th May, 1951. He had two children. He was studying in the school and was also a student of the school. He was admitted in the school on 15.6.1951. On 15.6, 1951, he was given a son. He was residing with his parents and was also given a child. He was not able to gather information as to who are the biological parents of the child. He had also given a son to the appellant. He was unable to gather information about the child study report and the child study reports. He was able to gather the information about the biological parents and the child. The appellant filed an application for guardianship before the court. The court directed the appellant to furnish the child study certificate and the documents. The appellant submitted an application for the guardianship before the Court. The court rejected the application. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the custody of the child and the child was not entitled for the custody of his child. The High court held that the child was entitled to the welfare of the child as he was not able and willing to take the child in adoption. The High Judge held that the custody of child was not a proper custody of the appellant. The appellant contended that the child had been taken in adoption by the foreigner and the child had not been able to gather any information about the adoption of the child in the family. The High judge held that the court was not right in rejecting the application for guardianship. The appellant has appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts were right in rejecting his application for guardianship on the ground that the child study was not a fit person for the purpose of obtaining the child. [737B] 1.2. The High courts were right in holding that the appellant had not been given the child study for the purpose for which he had taken the child in his adoption. [738B] 1.(a) The High Court was right in holding the appellant to be entitled to the benefit of the welfare of his child as he had taken his child in adoption by his parents. [739C] 1.(b) The High court was right in rejecting her application for guardianship made on behalf of the appellant on the ground of the welfare and welfare of the children. [740D] 1.(c) The High Courts have not committed any error in rejecting the appellant's application for guardianship and the appellant has not been able and willing for the child study. [741D] 1.3. The HighCourt was right in not accepting the appellant's prayer for guardianship and directing the appellant to give her child study report. [742E] 1.4. The High Curt was right in refusing to give her the child study to the appellant because the child was a minor. [744E] 1.(d) The High Cour t was right in dismissing the appellant's petition for guardianship. [745E] 1 (e) The HighCourt had not committed any mistake in rejecting the petitioner's application for the custody. [746F] 1.(f) The High Cou rt was right in allowing the appellant to take the son from the child study and to send the child to the recognised social or child welfare agency. [747G] 1.(g) The High cour t was not right.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Limited, Calcutta, is a company incorporated under the Indian Cable Company Act, 1956. The Company is a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, and it is engaged in the business of providing cable services. The Company has been carrying on the business of cable services. It has been carrying out its business in the name and style of "The Indian Cable Company" and it has been carrying business in the names and style of M/s. Indian Cable Company Ltd., Calcutta. The Company was carrying on the trade of cable services and it was carrying on its business in its name and style. The Company had been carrying on its trade of cable service and it had been carrying out the business of the Company. The Company, however, did not carry on its business of cable service. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court of Calcutta under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the Award of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The Award of the Industrial Tribunal was not correct. The Tribunal was right in holding that the amount of Rs. 65,764 was not an item of expenditure incurred by the Company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business of Cable Services. [801B] 2. The Tribunal had not accepted the evidence of the Unions on the ground that the amount was not an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. [802C] 3. The Tribunal did not accept the evidence of Unions on the basis that the amount had to be added back, but it accepted the evidence that the amount could not be added back. [803D] 4. The Tribunal has not accepted the statement of Unions on this ground. The Tribunal, therefore, was justified in rejecting the evidence of Union that the amount should have been added back. The Tribunal also did not accept that the amount which was added back was the amount which could be added back but it accepted that the amount would have to be added to the gross profits. [804E] 5. The Tribunal further held that the amount claimed by the Unions was not an amount which could not be deducted from the gross profits for purposes of computation of the available surplus. [805F] 6. The Tribunal held that the amounts claimed by the Union were not an item which could be deducted from gross profits for computation of the surplus. The Tribunal observed that the amount shown in the profit and loss account was not an asset and was not an allowable surplus. The High court, therefore, allowed the writ petition and directed the Union to pay the balance amount of Rs, 65,76 4. The Union has appealed to this court. HELD: The Tribunal was justified in holding that there was no surplus and allocable surplus. [820G] 7. The Tribunal erred in holding that it was not an allowance. [808E] 8. The Tribunal failed to consider the fact that the amount in question was an item of revenue and was not a part of the gross profits of the Company and that the amount paid by the Union was not an "deduction" for computation of available surplus. The amount of Rs 65,76,4 was not a "deduction". [808F] 9. The Tribunal committed an error in holding that a sum of Rs. 5,76,648 was not an 'deduction" in the sum of Rs 65.764. The Tribunal went wrong in holding that in the absence of any evidence of Unions, the Tribunal was not justified in holding the amount of "deduction "deduction ". [808G] 10. The Tribunal in the present case has not accepted that the sum ofRs 65,76.4 was not the "deduction", but has wrongly held that the sum was not an admissible surplus. [823G] 11.

The appellant was appointed as a Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975 and he was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax on July 7. 1975. He was promoted as a Deputy Commercial Tax Officer in 1962. He was posted as a Deputy Director of Commercial Taxes in the year 1966. He was also promoted as a Joint Commercial Tax Officer on July 7 1975. The appellant was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer by the order dated November 29, 1974. He was further promoted as a Commercial Tax Officer and posted as a Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in 1972. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Government retiring him from service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of his promotion was illegal and void as he was not promoted as a Sales Tax Officer and that the order was passed without considering the fact that the appellant was promoted to a Selection post. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the State Government retiring the appellant from service was illegal and invalid. The State Government was not competent to pass the order of retirement. [701B] 2. The order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. The appellant had been given a show cause notice and a copy of the enquiry report was served on him. The appellant submitted his explanation. The State of Tamil Nadu was not competent in law to pass the impugned order. [702C] 3. The order passed by the State Government was in violation of principles of natural Justice. [703D] 4. The order is not a speaking order. The appellant could not have been given a copy of it. The order does not show that the State Government had considered the entire history of the appellant as a Government servant. The order did not show that he was promoted to the Selection post. [704E] 5. The order cannot be sustained. The appellant is entitled to his costs.

The appellants were plying their buses on the routes in question. The Regional Transport Authority of Andhra Pradesh, which was constituted under the Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1964, was constituted under section 68C of the Act. The Regional transport Authority of Andhra State, which was formed under the Andhra State Road Transport Corporations Act, 1964 was constituted under that Act. The appellants were plying the buses on the route in question. On the basis of the recommendations of the Regional Transport Authority, the Regional Transport Authorities of Andhra Pradesh were constituted under section 69C of the Andhra Pradesh Road Transport Corporations Ordinance, 1964. The appellants challenged the validity of the schemes framed by the Regional Transport authorities of Andhra Pradesh in so far as they were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the schemes framed under section 68 C of the Act were not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C and the Rules framed thereunder. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The schemes framed by a Regional Transport Authority are not in conformity to the requirements of the Act or the Rules made under it. [701B] 2. The schemes are not in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act or in the rules made thereunder. [702C] 3. The schemes were framed by the State Transport Undertaking and the procedure laid down in section 68 C was not in conformity therewith. [703D] 4. The schemes have been framed by the Corporation under section 68D of the Act, and the rules made under it have been framed under section 69D of the Andhra State Act. [704E] 5. The schemes do not contain any provision for the grant of permits under section 68F(1) of the Act to the appellants. The schemes, therefore, do not contain a provision for the granting of permits under sections 68C and 68D of that Act. [604F] 6. The schemes contain a provision in the Act for grant of permits to the appellants and the Regional Transport Undertaking. The schemes clearly contain a provision that the Regional Transport authority of Andhra Pradesh shall be the authority which functions as the Regional Transport Officer for the purposes of the Act so long as the schemes are not inconsistent with those provisions. [705G] 7. The schemes which are framed by the appellants do not contain provisions for grant of permit under section 68B of the Act nor do they contain a provision to grant permits under section 69E of the Act in conformity with those provisions, and the Rules do not contain an express provision for grant of such permits. [706F] 8. The schemes cannot be said to be in conformity with section 68C and the Rules. [707F] 9. The schemes in question are not in consonance with the provisions in the Act and they are not in conflict with the provisions relating to grant of permits. [807F] 10. The schemes must be in conformity therewith and the rules framed thereunder must be in accordance with those provisions and the Rules and the Rules must be in consonance with those provisions in the statute or in the Rules. The schemes therefore, do contain a provision of the Act for granting permits to the appellant and the Regional transport Authority for the purposes mentioned therein. [708G] 11. The schemes under section 68E of the Andhra Act are not in consistent with the provisions made in the Act. [808H] 12. The schemes issued by the Corporation are not in accord with the provisions for grant or renewal of permits. The schemes thus contain a provision enabling the Regional Transport Office of Andhra Pradesh to grant permits to the operators of the buses on routes in question, and the Regional Regional Transport Authority is not bound to grant permits. [908H] 13. The schemes also contain a provision relating to grant or renewal or suspension of permits.

The appellant, a dealer, purchased a dealer 's certificate of registration from the Sales Tax Officer, Calcutta, under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant filed a declaration form in the prescribed form in the manner prescribed in the said sub section. The said declaration form was duly filled in and signed by the purchasing dealer 's representative. The appellant, however, did not produce the prescribed declaration form in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the said declaration form on the ground that the appellant had not furnished the prescribed declaration forms in accordance with section 5(1)(a)(i) of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the declaration form was not in accordance with law and the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the appellant was not entitled to exemption under section 5 (2)(a) (ii) of Orissa Sales Tax, 1947. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant could not be permitted to produce the prescribed form for the purpose of claiming exemption under section 10(2)(b) of the Sales Tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to section 5(3)(a)(iii) of the Bihar Sales Tax Act is not mandatory. The proviso does not say that the declaration forms are to be furnished by the dealer or by the purchasing dealers. The proviso merely says that the declaration Form is to be furnished in accordance with. the provisions of section 5(4)(a)(iv) of the said Act. [601B] 2. The proviso is not mandatory but only directory. The proviso cannot be complied with by the purchasing registered dealer. The proviso, therefore, cannot be complied by the purchasing purchasing dealer. [602C] 3. The proviso has no application to the facts of the present case. The appellant was not precluded in a case where the proviso is mandatory but only to be complied with. [603D] 4. The proviso was not mandatory but merely directory. The appellant could not produce the required declaration form in terms of section 5 (1)(a) of the aforesaid Act. [063E] 5. The proviso makes the position clear that the declaration Forms are to be produced by the dealer and r. 27A with those prescribed particulars on a prescribed form. The proviso lays down that the declaration is to be filed by the dealer. [064E] 6. The proviso provides that the declaration in writing by the purchasing manufacturer or by the dealer shall be furnished by him in the prescribed manner. The proviso further provides that the dealer shall furnish a declaration in writing in writing by him in this behalf by such dealer. [2006E] 7. The proviso clearly provides that the purchasing dealer shall furnish the declaration form in respect of the prescribed particulars on the prescribed form. [604F] 7. In the present case, the appellant had produced the prescribed declaration Form in accordance with s. 5(2) (a)(ii). The proviso does no more than make the appellant 's certificate to be furnished under section 5 of the Act, but does not say so. [605G] 8. The proviso requires the purchasing dealer to furnish the declaration in terms of the proviso. The proviso says that the purchasing dealers shall furnish the declarations in terms of s. 5 (2) (b) of Orissa Act. [2006G] 9. The proviso states that the purchasing manufacturer shall furnish the particulars on the specified form in the form prescribed by the dealer in respect of each of the sales to the registered dealers. [606E] 9. In the instant case, the purchasing dealer had furnished the declaration form and the prescribed particulars in the prescribed format.

The State of Bihar has filed a counter affidavit in response to the direction given by the High Court of Patna on 26th February, 1979. The State of Bihar filed a counteraffidavit on 26th March, 1979. In the counter affidavit filed on 26th April, 1979, it was stated that the State of Bihar had not complied with the proviso to section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct the State of BIHAR to furnish to the Magistrate a lawyer at its cost for the purpose of making an application for bail and that the State Government should provide him a lawyer at their cost for the purposes of making an order for the purpose. The High Court of Bihar by its order dated 26th February 1979 directed the State of Patna to furnish to it a lawyer at the cost of the State of Jharkhand together with the total number of pending cases in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 and 5th March, 1978. The High court of Patna by its order made on 26th May, 1979 directed the District Magistrate to furnish to him a lawyer on behalf of the State Government a lawyer at his cost for the period from 21st February, 1974 to 5th March 1979. The High Courts of Patna by their order dated 26 th February, 1979 directed that on the next remand dates when they were produced before the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be, the State Government shall provide them a lawyer at such cost for the State of the State. The High courts of Patna by the order dated 26rd February, 1979, directed that on each of the courts of magistrates and the Sessions Courts the State ofBihar should provide a lawyer at that cost for the said period. The Highcourt of Patna by his order dated 26 February, 1979 held that the State should provide a counsel at its cost and that the District Magistrate should provide him an advocate at its cost. The HighCourt of Patna by a majority of 4 Judges of the High Court held that the proviso to Section 167(2), as it was not complied with, was not complied. The Highlight of Patna by an order dated 26 March, 1979 directed: "The State of BIHAR has filed a supplementary affidavit on behalf of its officers in response to a direction given by this Court on 26th July, 1979. It is submitted that the High court of Bihar has no jurisdiction to order for the purposes mentioned in the proviso to [Section 167(2)] of the Code. The High Power Court of Patna has no jurisdiction under Section 167(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code to direct the District Magistrate, Patna to furnish the particulars to the Court of Sessions Judges and the Sessions Court, as the cases may be, together with the particulars as to the number of cases pending in each of the Courts of magistrates or the Sessions Court as the case might be, togetherwith the total number thereof pending in each court. The High power of Patna High Court has no jurisdiction in regard to the details as to the location of the courts in which the cases are pending. The High powers of Patna High court have no jurisdiction to issue any direction for the purpose mentioned in the Proviso to Section 167. The HighPower Court of Patna High Courts have no jurisdiction under section 167(1). The High Power of Patna High Curt of Patna has nothing to do with the details as regards the number of criminal cases pending in the courts of sessions in each of them. The High Curt has no jurisdiction, under section 167, to direct the Sessions Court to furnish the details to the Court. The High is, therefore, not right in the view of the High Power Court. The appeal is, therefore dismissed.

The appellant landlord filed an application under section 29(2) of the Act for obtaining possession of the land. The tenant filed an application for obtaining possession. The landlord filed an appeal against the order of the Revenue Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and held that the tenancy had not terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Act. The High court held that the landlord had not terminated the tenancy and the right to terminate the tenancy had accrued to the landlord. The High ' Court held that the tenant had not terminated his tenancy and the tenancy had terminated before the expiry of the period of notice. The High' Court held that there was no valid termination of the tenancy and that the landlord was entitled to terminate the lease. The High. Court held that since the tenancy had been terminated before the date of the notice, the landlord had no right to terminate his tenancy and that he had terminated the tenancy. The High, Court held that as the tenancy had expired before the coming in force of the Amendment Act, the landlord was not entitled to terminate his lease. The tenant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the tenancy was terminated before the commencement of the Amending act. [801 A] 2. The High was right in holding, that the tenancy having been terminated before coming into force the Amending Act, the tenancy had ceased to be valid. [802 B] 3. The High Curt was right in taking the view that the tenancy has been terminated before it came into force. [803 C] 4. The High] 5. The High Commissioner was right in not taking the view in the matter of termination of the lease. [804 D] 6. The High Power Court was right in rejecting the application of the landlord under section 29 (2) of Act. [805 E] 7. The High power of the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution is not correct and it was open to the landlord to terminate the contractual tenancy by giving notice to the tenant of the termination of the contractual tenancy. [806 E] 8. The landlord had not given notice to the landlord before the Amending Act came into force and therefore the tenancy had become effective. [807 F] 9. The landlord was entitled under section 29 to terminate the contract of tenancy and the tenant had terminated the contractual tenancy after the coming into operation of the Amending Ordinance. [808 G] 9. In the instant case, the landlord did not terminate the tenancy and therefore the notice given to the tenant had become effective before the Amending Ordinance came into force, and therefore the landlord had terminated the contract of lease. [908 G] 10. The landlord could not terminate the contractual relationship of landlord and tenant after the coming in operation of the Amendment Ordinance. [909 A] 11. The landlord has to prove that the tenancy is terminated before the Amending act came into force or that the tenancy continues before the Amending Acts came into force; and that the tenant has terminated the contractual relationship with the landlord after the coming In force of the amending Act. [910 A] 12. The landlord cannot terminate the contractual contractual relationship with a tenant after the Amending Act comes into force. The landlord can terminate the contractual contract of tenancy after the Amending act comes into force and the tenant has not terminated the contractual contractual tenancy after coming into force. In the present case, the tenant had already terminated the contractual lease after the Amending Ordinance had come into force. Therefore, the landlord could not have terminated the contractual contract by giving notice under section 34(1) of the Amending Acts. [911 A] 13. The landlord is entitled to terminate a contractual tenancy after giving notice to him under section 34 (1) of Act and the tenant cannot terminate the tenancy after giving him a notice under section 29 of the Amending ACT. [912 B] 14.

The petitioners, who were the daughters of the two brothers of Khadim Ali, were the owners of the houses in dispute. They were allotted a house in the village of Khadims Ali. The Custodian General of Evacuee Property, after holding an enquiry, held that the petitioners were entitled to the properties in question. The Custodian, after holding a preliminary enquiry, held the petitioners to be evacuees and held that the properties in dispute were evacuee properties and that the petitioners had been allotted a larger share in the houses. The Custodian held that the property in dispute was evacuee property and that the properties were evacuee properties. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of January 10, 1952, contending that the properties had already been acquired under the provisions of the Act and that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to declare the properties to be evacuee property. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners appealed to this Court. The High court held that the Custodian was not entitled to declare the property to be evacuee properties and the properties were not evacuee properties. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Custodian was not right in holding that the properties allotted to the petitioners were evacuee properties within the meaning of section 12 of the Act. [701B] 2. The Custodian had no power to declare the evacuee properties in the absence of any notification under section 7 of the Act, and that the property was not evacuee property. [702C] 3. The Custodian could not have declared the properties to the petitioners under section 7, because the properties were already acquired under the Act. The Custodian did not decide any question as to the right of Zafar Ali to the properties. [703D] 4. The Custodian has no jurisdiction to decide any question of the right of the petitioners in the properties. The Custodian is not competent to decide any such question as to his right to the properties, because the property was already acquired under section 7. [704E] 5. The Custodian cannot, therefore, have jurisdiction to decide the question of the rights of the petitioners under the will. [705G] 6. The Custodian can not, therefore, decide any question which the petitioners have to decide. [706A] 7. The Custodian does not have jurisdiction to declare any property to be the evacuee property. He can not, however, decide any such questions as to his rights under the will, if he has not already declared the properties. He can, therefore, not decide any such issue as to his title to the properties under section 7 and his rights under section 8. [707B] 7. In the present case, the Custodian had not decided any such question. He had no jurisdiction under section 7 to declare the entire properties. [807C] 8. The Custodian also did not decide the question as to whether the properties were still evacuee properties. [777E] 9. The Custodian therefore, could not have decided any such questions. [709G] 9. In the circumstances, the Custodian was right in holding the properties to have vested in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. [708E] 10. The Custodian's order dated January 10, 1953, was not a final order.

The assessee Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The assessee Company was a joint venture with a view to manufacture yarn from wool tops. The assessee company was incorporated under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The assessee was a joint undertaking for the distribution of profits and the losses which were to be deducted from the commission of the agents. The assessee had been assessed to income tax under section 10 (2)(xv). The assessee Company filed a return of income for the assessment year 1956. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee Company to income tax on the profits and gains of the business of the assessee Company. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Income tax Officer. The assessee carried the matter in further appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the assessee Company was not a joint venture and therefore the assessee Company had not been able to make any better arrangements or would have made any better arrangements and therefore the profits and losses were not taxable under section 10 of the Act and therefore the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was not a separate entity. The Tribunal further held that the business of a joint venture was not a business of the Company and therefore the Company was not entitled to claim deduction under section 10. The Tribunal also held that the profits and loss were not taxable and therefore the amounts were not deductible under section 10 and therefore the amount paid to the agents was not deductible under the Act. In appeal to this Court, the assessee contended that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the assessee had been able to sell the yarn tops. It was contended that the assessee company was not a partner of the firm and therefore the question of deduction under section 20(2)(vi) of the Income Tax Act was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee is a joint venture of the assessee company and it is not a joint enterprise. The assessee has been able to establish that the assessee is a partner of a joint enterprise and that the assessee has been unable to sell the goods tops. [601B] 2. The assessee being a joint venture, the assessee company is not entitled to any deduction under section 80P of the Act as the assessee is not a separate company. [602C] 3. The assessee having been a joint venture the assessee company cannot be said to be a joint venture. The plaintiff was the owner of the lands in question, and the defendants were in possession of the lands. The defendants were in occupation of the lands for a long time, and the plaintiff was in possession of them. The defendants claimed to have dealt with the lands in their possession, and the suit lands were Malis. The defendants filed a suit for possession of the said lands, and the trial Court decreed the suit. The defendants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the defendants were not entitled to the fair and equitable rent, and that the suit lands had been settled on the basis of the permanent settlement of the zamindari of Burdwan, and that they had been settled in 1931, and that there was no determination of tenancy, and that it was not a mere assertion of title, and that, therefore, the defendants were entitled to the benefit of the presumption of a lost grant. The High court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to a fair and equitable lease, and that since the defendants had not claimed to hold under a Lakheraj grant, the plaintiffs were not entitled for fair and equitable rents. The High Courts held that the suit properties were not Malis, and that in view of the fact that the defendants had been in possession of lands for a considerable long time, the presumption of grant could not be made in favour of the defendants. The HighCourt further held that the plaintiff was entitled to a reasonable rent, and the plaintiffs were therefore entitled to a decree for eviction. The High 'Court further held, that the defendants could not be said to have established their title to the lands, and that their possession was not adverse to the plaintiffs. The High. Court held that there was a presumption of a tenancy, and the possession of the plaintiffs was not adverse. The High, Court, however, held that the presumption of tenancy was not raised by the defendants, and that a presumption of tenancy could be made in their favour. The High Curt, however, reversed the decision of the trial Court, and held that the tenancy was not proved. The High "Court further held: "The plaintiffs were not able to establish that the defendants did not hold the lands for long time, but that the defendants, who were in possession, had been in occupation of them for a long period of time. The defendants had not established their title, and the presumption of their possession was also not rebutted by the defendants. In the result, the High Court decreed the plaintiffs suit. The plaintiffs appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The plaintiffs were not in possession of any lands for a continuous period of time, and they were not entitled, to a fair or equitable rent. [901F] 2. The plaintiffs had not established that the defendants acquired any title to the properties, and that as the defendants had failed to establish that they had acquired any title, they were not liable to be evicted. [902F] 3. The plaintiffs could not establish that the lands were Malat lands. The plaintiffs, therefore, could not be held to be entitled to a proper and equitable rent. The High [902G] 4. The plaintiffs are not entitled to a relief under article 131 of the Limitation Act. [903G] 5. The plaintiffs have not established that they had purchased any title to them. The plaintiffs cannot be held to have established that the lands had been purchased by them for a continuous long time without payment of rent for a long duration. [905G] 6. The plaintiffs having failed to establish the title of the defendants, the suit was not barred by limitation. [906G] 7. The plaintiffs failed to establish their title to them, and the High Court was in error in holding that the plaintiffs had not proved their title to it. [908G] 8. The plaintiffs' case that the lands in suit were Malat properties is not true. [909G] 9.

The assessee Company was wound up at about the end of the year ending on March 31, 1950, and the assessee Company was assessed to income tax on the sale of the chemicals and raw materials. The assessee Company was, however, assessed to tax on the sales of the chemicals, raw materials and raw materials, and the price of the chemicals was treated as its value for the purpose of assessment. The assessee company claimed that the sale of chemicals and raw material was a sale in the ordinary way of business or that the sale was of the entire assets, and that the sale did not amount to a trading activity. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the sale in the normal course of business was not a trading activity, and that, therefore, the sale was not a sale in a real sense, and that it was not a business activity. The Tribunal held that there was no sale in the course of business, and that there was a sale of the entire stock, and that no part of the sale was a trading activity and that the assessee Company had been wound up at the end of March 31, 1951, and that since the sale was in the ordinary course of business and the sale was for the purpose, the sale did amount to a sale in ordinary course of trade, and that in the circumstances, the sale could not be regarded as a sale in respect of the entire business. The Tribunal, however, held that the transaction was not a trade, and the sale did no amount to a commercial transaction, and that as the sale was only a trading activity the sale was outside the ordinary course. The Tribunal further held that the assessee company was not a dealer, and that even if the sale was to be regarded as an ordinary sale, the sale would not be a trading activity within the meaning of the expression 'sale ' in the ordinary sense of the term. The Tribunal also held that the sales were not in the ordinary manner of business, but were only a trading activities. The Tribunal observed that the sale amounted to a trading, and that if the sale amounted not to a trading or a trading activity it was not an ordinary sale. The Tribunal accordingly held that the transactions were not a trading or an ordinary sale and that the sales amounted to a sale within the ordinary sense. The Tribunal found that the sale, in the ordinary circumstances, was a trading or business in the ordinary trade, and, therefore, was a sale within section 2(g) of the Act. The Tribunal was of the view that the sale could be regarded as the sale of goods, and that section 2(h) of the Income tax Act was not applicable to the facts of the case. The Tribunal took the view that there was nothing to show that the sale had been made by the assessee Company, and that this was a trading, because the sale was made by the Company, and the sales were of the entire value of the assets, and the stock was sold as a going concern. The Tribunal did not accept the contention of the assessee that the sale by the Company was a trading transaction. The Tribunal accepted the contention of both the assessee and the Department that the sale price was not a transaction of sale, and that was a trading receipt. The Tribunal rejected the contention of either the assessee that there was an identifiable profit of Rs. 1,15,259. The Tribunal relied on the decision of the High Court of Kerala in Commissioner of Income tax vs The Commissioner of Income Tax, Kerala, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, and held that the business of the assessee Company could not be treated as a trading receipt, and that on that view the Tribunal held that it was a trading receipts. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the correctness of the decision of this Court. The High Court held that the decision of that Court was not correct.
